It addresses lessor and lessee rights and obligations, licence requirements before concluding contracts, payment schedules separating lease value from the value of the ownership right, recovery on early termination, insurance indemnity, securitisation against lessor rights with continuing disclosure duties to SAMA, and SAMA's power to set contract standards. It binds lessors — joint stock companies licensed to conduct finance leasing, including commercial banks — and is read with the Finance Companies Control Law.
lookup_terms: Implementing Regulation of the Finance Lease Law

data.summary: The Saudi Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36, 2020), the constitutive statute establishing SAMA as a financially and administratively independent legal person reporting to the King. It sets the Bank's objectives (monetary stability, financial sector stability and confidence, economic growth) and its powers, including currency issuance, supervision and regulation of financial institutions, issuing regulations and directives, monetary and FX policy, reserve management, acting as the government's bank and adviser, operating and licensing payment/settlement/clearing systems and fintech platforms, consumer protection directives, prudential policy, and crime-prevention measures. It binds SAMA itself and, through its supervisory mandate, every natural or legal person defined as a Financial Institution subject to SAMA's supervision.

This node covers Part Five (Customer Protection and Financial Inclusion) of the Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments and Payment Services, issued by SAMA to replace the earlier Rules Regulating Payment Service Providers. It sets conduct obligations owed by licensees to Customers and Consumers, including fair treatment, disclosure and financial inclusion expectations, alongside the Regulation's complaint definition (an expression of dissatisfaction submitted by a Customer or Consumer). It binds all SAMA-licensed payment service providers, and is relevant where payments conduct rules overlap with the general consumer protection regime.
lookup_terms: Implementing Regulation Law of Payments and Payment Services

data.summary: This node covers the contract and information-provision requirements chapter (Part Six, Chapter One) of SAMA's Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments and Payment Services. It governs what a licensee must agree with and disclose to the Customer before and during a payment services relationship — terms, fees, information duties and amendment/termination mechanics — and sits alongside chapters on e-money issuance and redemption and the provision of related payment services. It binds payment service providers licensed by SAMA, with a six-month corrective-action window from the Regulation's effective date.

This node covers Part Eight of SAMA's Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments and Payment Services, on the requirements for providing payment account information services and payment initiation services (open banking activities). It sets licensing scope, consent, access and conduct requirements for providers of these services and their interaction with account-servicing institutions. It binds entities licensed by SAMA to carry out these activities in the Kingdom.

This node covers Part Nine of SAMA's Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments and Payment Services, dealing with the classification of important payment systems, application of the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, SAMA's supervisory powers over systems and members, and settlement finality and insolvency. It requires periodic self-assessment against the PFMIs and adequate financial resources, including a stated minimum paid-up capital and operating-cost coverage for unclassified payment systems. It binds payment system operators and, through them, system members, who must supply information and reports on SAMA's request.
lookup_terms: كفاية الموارد المالية رأس المال المدفوع

data.summary: This node covers the treatment of unauthorised payment transactions under SAMA's Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments and Payment Services — authorisation and consent, the Customer's notification duty, refund/rectification obligations and the allocation of loss between licensee and Customer (including cases of gross negligence or fraud). It is the operative liability rule behind disputed and fraudulent payment claims. It binds SAMA-licensed payment service providers in their dealings with Customers and Consumers.

This node covers Part Eleven (Complaints and Disputes) of SAMA's Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments and Payment Services, read with the Regulation's definition of a Complaint as an expression of dissatisfaction or objection submitted to the licensee by a Customer or Consumer through available channels. It governs complaint handling, response timeframes and escalation/dispute resolution routes. It binds licensed payment service providers and is relevant to supervisory action under the Part on supervision and enforcement.

This node covers the payment-systems rulebook provisions requiring payment system operators to assess and disclose compliance with the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, including periodic self-assessment by operators of non-designated (unclassified) payment systems on terms agreed with SAMA under their licence. Adjacent articles set financial-resource and capital adequacy expectations (for unclassified systems, resources covering at least six months of highest operating cost plus SAR 10 million paid-up capital) and SAMA's powers to demand information, documents, auditor reports and operating rules from operators and their members. It binds licensed payment system operators (both systemically important and unclassified) and, indirectly, their participants/members, who must cooperate with information requests.

A SAMA circular relaying the General Real Estate Authority's designation of Al-Falah district in Riyadh as the first real estate zone under the Real Estate In-Kind Registration Law (Royal Decree M/14) and its implementing regulation. It instructs financing entities holding rights in a designated zone to treat the ownership registration deed issued by the General Real Estate Authority as the authoritative title document there, and places on them an ongoing duty to monitor subsequent Authority announcements. It is addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular easing the prior requirement (under an earlier circular) for written SAMA no-objection before credit bureaus conclude membership agreements with non-SAMA-supervised entities. Credit information companies may now sign membership agreements with fintech firms that hold or have applied for a SAMA or CMA licence/permit, subject to conditions: verifying the licence application before signing, the fintech's activity involving a credit relationship with consumers, no activation of access to consumer credit records until a copy of the licence is obtained, and, on cessation or expiry of the licence, limiting the firm to updating records of its own customers without new enquiries. Responsibility for compliance rests entirely with the credit information companies, which remain bound by the Credit Information Law and its implementing regulation.

SAMA circular issuing the mandatory standard-form consumer finance contract for individuals, based on SAMA's Law and the Banking Control Law, to reduce divergence between financiers' contracts and limit disputes. All financing entities must adopt the template from the stated compliance date and may not conclude contracts that depart from or amend it; the document includes a contract summary (APR, term cost, instalments, administrative fees, total amount payable) and articles covering scope, definitions, formation, financed asset, financial obligations, instalments, payment methods, late payment/default, termination, early repayment, fees, guarantees, undertakings, breach, death or incapacity, notices and governing law. It binds banks (local, foreign branches, digital banks) and finance companies dealing with individual beneficiaries.

The early repayment article (Article 10) of SAMA's mandatory standard consumer finance contract for individuals, flagged in the contract summary as a term the beneficiary must be pointed to. It governs the beneficiary's right to settle the financing ahead of schedule and the resulting treatment of term cost/profit and amounts due, within the uniform template that financiers may not vary. It binds banks and finance companies contracting with individual beneficiaries.

The late payment and default provisions (Article 8, with related termination steps in Article 9 and breach provisions) of SAMA's mandatory standard consumer finance contract for individuals. They set the consequences of delayed or defaulted instalments and the financier's procedure for exercising termination/enforcement, with the contract summary requiring these effects to be highlighted to the beneficiary. They bind banks and finance companies as financiers and determine the consumer's exposure on arrears.

This node covers the Rules Governing Bank Accounts provisions on opening bank accounts remotely (non-face-to-face), including for Saudi resident corporations and for foreign companies licensed under the Foreign Investment Law. It requires identity verification of the entity and its ownership/control structure from reliable, independent sources, risk standards set before approval, and a secure mechanism for activating the ATM card; for foreign companies the service is limited to the general director named in the constitutive documents. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia.

This node addresses collection accounts used by payment companies to deposit and safeguard client funds, opened under a prescribed account name identifying the payment company and its clients, on the basis of a letter from the chairperson or authorised representative stating the purpose. It sits within the juristic-person account rules of the Rules Governing Bank Accounts and binds banks opening such accounts, with practical consequences for licensed payment service providers relying on segregated client-money accounts.
lookup_terms: deposit and retention of clients' funds

data.summary: This node sets out the account-opening rules for natural persons resident in Saudi Arabia (Saudi citizens, minors, GCC nationals, expatriates and special categories) and for natural persons outside the Kingdom, including acceptable identity documents and operation by guardians or custodians. It also carries the general timing obligation to open accounts within one or two business days depending on whether internal approvals are needed, and to notify applicants in writing of missing requirements. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia.

This node covers accounts for expatriates in Saudi Arabia, including the regime for holders of a temporary 90-day work visa with no Iqama: opening on an official employer request specifying employment, purpose and source of funds, in-person meeting with the account holder, employer notification on final exit, and immediate freezing with subsequent treatment under the account-freezing rule. It classifies such accounts as high risk and connects to the dormancy rules (24 months without customer-initiated debit activity). It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia.

This node is the structural heading for account opening by juristic persons under the Rules Governing Bank Accounts, spanning resident entities (licensed businesses, companies, money changers, embassies, multilateral organisations, liquidation and restructuring accounts), non-resident entities (GCC and non-GCC companies, banks, funds, insurers, payment card companies), foreign investors outside the Foreign Investment Law, and government entities. It sets the documentary and authorisation conditions, including AML-driven restrictions on foreign investors from jurisdictions not applying FATF Recommendations or subject to Security Council measures. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia.

This node covers account opening for resident companies under the Rules Governing Bank Accounts, differentiating by legal form (joint-stock, limited liability, general and limited partnerships and similar) and the documents and authorised signatories required, alongside the broader resident/non-resident juristic person categories. It also touches the operational rules for accounts of juristic persons, such as who may transact on a dormant account. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia.

An Arabic-language SAMA circular reaffirming that lessors are responsible for the accuracy of the data they submit when applying to a licensed finance lease contract registration company for issuance of executive deed (writ of execution) extracts for a registered finance lease contract. It is issued under the Finance Lease Law and its Implementing Regulation and refers back to the earlier controls and procedures circular governing requests for and issuance of such extracts. It binds lessors (banks and finance companies) for data accuracy and any prejudice to lessee rights, while preserving registration companies' own duty to verify the lessor's entitlement and obtain the required undertakings before issuing extracts.

The SAMA Rules for Bank Accounts, the consolidated account-opening and account-operation framework for banks licensed in KSA. It covers account types and opening requirements for natural and juristic persons and specific entity categories (e.g. government bodies, courts, societies, correspondent banks, non-resident financial institutions), inoperative account lifecycle (dormant, unclaimed, abandoned), internal audit and SAMA reporting, and disclosure of and enforcement on bank balances, accounts and relationships. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom and interacts closely with AML/CTF customer due diligence obligations.

A concept node within the Rules for Bank Accounts addressing restrictions on account operation. The supplied context relates to dormant-account controls (24-month debit inactivity trigger, dual supervision for reactivation, presence/identity requirements for withdrawals and transfers, and continued acceptance of incoming credits), which restrict outgoing movement rather than effect a judicial freeze; blocking proper is dealt with under the enforcement provisions. Obligations fall on banks operating in KSA in respect of customer accounts.

The AML/CFT-facing slice of the Rules for Bank Accounts, covering customer identification and verification at account opening and ongoing due diligence expectations embedded in the account rules. The supplied context focuses on correspondent banking due diligence — obtaining an AML/CFT commitment form from each correspondent, assessing the correspondent's internal controls and shell-bank exposure, adverse-media and investigation checks, senior management approval for new correspondent relationships, and restrictions on how correspondent accounts may be used — plus limits on accounts for non-resident investment companies, mutual funds and other financial institutions. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom and should be read with the AML Law and its Implementing Regulation and SAMA's AML/CTF rules.

The inoperative-account lifecycle under the Rules for Bank Accounts: classification of accounts as dormant after 24 calendar months without a customer-initiated debit or documented correspondence, then progression to unclaimed and abandoned status, with prescribed customer notification, reactivation controls, dual supervision, separate file safeguarding, balance-of-liability treatment, deduction of outstanding obligations, transfer to suspense, and closure of small balances (SAR 1,000 or less) with notice. It also sets internal audit coverage (at least once every two years, reported to the Audit Committee) and an annual statistical report to SAMA due end of March. Obligations bind banks operating in the Kingdom.

Provisions of the Rules for Bank Accounts governing disclosure of, and enforcement on, bank balances, accounts and relationships. Enforcement is defined to include blocking, compulsory deduction, check issuance and transfers from customer accounts; requests are channelled through SAMA (save where SAMA's instructions provide otherwise), must be executed in SAMA's prescribed form, manner and timeframe, and must be treated as strictly confidential. Banks must search all relationships with the customer — active, closed, suspended and inoperative accounts, deposits, safe deposit boxes, credit cards and remittance memberships — including sole proprietorships and company participations, and verify the accuracy of what is reported. The context also touches account operation and disbursement controls for trial and enforcement court accounts.

A sub-rule within SAMA's Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts and General Operational Guidelines, addressing accounts for the Muslim World League as a specified international/charitable-type juristic person. It sets the documentary and authorisation conditions under which a bank may open and operate such an account, and how it is to be named, operated and monitored. It binds SAMA-licensed banks conducting account opening and ongoing due diligence, and interacts with AML/CTF customer due diligence and charitable-funds controls.
lookup_terms: Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts

data.summary: A sub-rule of SAMA's bank account opening rules governing accounts for the World Assembly of Muslim Youth, treated as a designated international Islamic organisation. It specifies the approvals, supporting documents, account naming and operating authorities required before a bank may open or maintain the account. It binds SAMA-licensed banks and connects to AML/CTF due diligence expectations for non-profit and charitable funds flows.
lookup_terms: World Assembly of Muslim Youth account

data.summary: Rule 300.1.7 of SAMA's bank account opening rules, covering accounts opened for liquidation, administrative liquidation and financial restructuring under the Bankruptcy Law, and liquidation under the Companies Law. It sets the court order, appointment evidence, identity and commercial registration documents, mandatory account naming convention, operating authority of the bankruptcy officeholder/liquidator/bankruptcy committee, and rules on account validity, renewal and closure. It binds SAMA-licensed banks dealing with insolvent or dissolving natural and juristic persons.

Section 300.2 of SAMA's bank account opening rules, setting the categories and conditions for accounts of non-resident juristic persons — including GCC non-banking companies, non-GCC companies with or without contracts or projects in Saudi Arabia, non-resident banks, international investment companies and funds, insurance companies, money changers and foreign payment card companies. Each sub-category carries distinct permitted account purposes and documentary requirements. It binds SAMA-licensed banks and shapes cross-border customer onboarding and correspondent-type relationships.
lookup_terms: international investment companies and mutual funds
companies with contracts or projects in Saudi Arabia

data.summary: Section 400 of SAMA's bank account opening rules, governing accounts for resident and non-resident foreign investors not covered by the Foreign Investment Law, including accounts for linking investment deposits. It conditions acceptance on source and return of funds through the investor's account in a jurisdiction applying FATF standards, and bars applicants from jurisdictions that do not adequately apply the FATF Recommendations or that are subject to UN Security Council measures. It binds SAMA-licensed banks and directly engages AML/CTF and sanctions screening obligations.

Section 500 of SAMA's bank account opening rules, setting how banks may open and operate riyal accounts for Saudi ministries and government entities, including donation-receipt accounts. It requires Ministry of Finance application and SAMA notification, prohibits accounts in a natural person's name or job title, restricts foreign-currency accounts, prohibits loans, facilities or overdrafts to government entities absent Council of Ministers approval, controls transfer and closure of accounts, and limits signatories to Saudi nationals. It binds SAMA-licensed banks and constrains their credit exposure to government counterparties.

A special-purpose account category within SAMA's Rules for Bank Accounts governing escrow accounts for off-plan real estate development projects. It sets conditions for opening and activating the account (Off-Plan Sales/Rent Committee licence, tripartite agreement among developer, bank, consulting office and certified accountant, naming convention, one account per project with defined sub-accounts), deposit restrictions (no cash; buyers and financiers only), a 5% retention or equivalent bank guarantee, and prohibitions on set-off, transfers out, card issuance and investment of project funds. The adjacent provision covers segregated collection accounts holding payment companies' client funds. It binds banks licensed in Saudi Arabia, with consequential obligations on real estate developers.
lookup_terms: Wafi / Off-Plan Sales and Rent Committee
Rules for Bank Accounts special purpose accounts
payment company client funds collection account

data.summary: Part of SAMA's Rules for Bank Accounts dealing with accounts of Hajj and Umrah organizers and related entities (including Muslim World League-type bodies), covering opening prerequisites, SAMA pre-approval via the bank's head-office compliance department, dual control, IBAN notification to the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah, service limitations, and deposit/withdrawal controls on main and sub-accounts. It also imposes timelines (same-day escalation of documents, maximum two working days to open) and a single-bank rule limiting the organizer to accounts at one bank absent Ministry and SAMA approval. It binds licensed banks and constrains Hajj/Umrah organizers.

A node grouping non-profit sector account provisions in SAMA's Rules for Bank Accounts with adjacent general account-status rules. The retrieved context covers dormant account treatment (24 months since last customer debit or documented contact, dual supervision for reactivation, permitted incoming credits without changing status, pre-five-year customer contact) and high-risk classification plus conditions for accounts of expatriates on temporary 90-day work visas, including employer undertakings, freezing and closure. It binds licensed banks operating in Saudi Arabia.

Covers accounts of private associations and private foundations under SAMA's Rules for Bank Accounts, including branch expense sub-accounts: MHRSD and supervisory authority approvals, joint-signature authorised managers who cannot be changed without MHRSD approval, bank compliance manager sign-off, one expense sub-account per branch at the same bank as the main account, funding only by periodic advances from the main account, and disbursement limited to first-beneficiary cheques and domestic transfers to support beneficiaries. The context also carries the general dormant account rules. It binds licensed banks and constrains the associations/foundations concerned.

A node on accounts for endowments (awqaf) and bequests under SAMA's Rules for Bank Accounts; the retrieved context sets out the general dormant account regime (24-month threshold, dual supervision for reactivation, permitted credits, customer contact before five years) and the high-risk classification and conditions for expatriate accounts opened on temporary 90-day work visas, including employer notification, freezing and closure. It binds licensed banks in Saudi Arabia. Open the source for the endowment-specific opening conditions, which are not fully reproduced in this extract.

Sets the account-opening conditions for international and multilateral organizations and funds of a political, developmental or service nature (e.g. UN bodies, World Bank group, IMF, GCC, Arab League, OIC), requiring a request from the Chairman or deputy, a copy of the headquarters agreement, joint signatures and identification of signatories; it also addresses cross-border transfers by OIC, personal accounts of such organizations' staff (ordinary natural-person rules, with diplomats treated under the diplomatic rule), and accounts of relief committees and campaigns requiring Royal approval and SAMA consent. The node also carries the Rules' definitions chapter (SAMA, Bank Account, Freezing of Account, Bank Verification, Special Purposes Entities, Government Entities, Foreign Schools). It binds licensed banks in Saudi Arabia.

data.summary: Node within SAMA's Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts and General Operational Guidelines, covering how banks must operate accounts after opening — in particular the account-status lifecycle (dormant after 24 months without a customer-initiated debit or documented contact, then unclaimed and abandoned), the dual-control and in-person/verified-identity conditions for reactivation and withdrawal, customer notification duties, and balance treatment (recorded as a liability, debts deducted before transfer to suspense, optional closure of balances of SAR 1,000 or less with prior notice). It binds all banks licensed in Saudi Arabia in respect of all natural- and juristic-person account holders.

Node addressing deposit handling under the SAMA Bank Account Rules, including which credits may be received into an account whose status is restricted — dormant accounts may continue to accept deposits, domestic and international transfers and dividends from third parties without the status reverting to active. It binds banks operating customer accounts and is relevant to disputes over whether incoming credits reset dormancy periods.

Node on termination and restriction of banking relationships under the SAMA Bank Account Rules, covering bank-initiated closure of low-balance accounts (SAR 1,000 or less) subject to advance and closing notification and record retention, and the obligation to search and report across all relationships — active, closed, suspended and inoperative accounts, deposits, safe boxes, credit cards and remittance memberships — when SAMA requests disclosure or enforcement (blocking, compulsory deduction, check issuance, transfer). It binds banks and stresses that such requests come only through SAMA and are strictly confidential.

Node anchoring the AML/CTF and KYC layer of the SAMA Bank Account Rules: the Rules must be read together with the Anti-Money Laundering Law and its Implementing Regulations and the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing and related guidance. It requires Compliance to have timely access to identification, due diligence and transaction records, verification of the relationship and documents for agents, custodians and authorized persons, and risk-based automated (not manual) ongoing transaction monitoring integrated with core systems; it also covers internal audit and annual SAMA reporting on unclaimed and abandoned accounts. Binds all banks.
lookup_terms: Law on Terrorism Crimes and Financing

data.summary: Node dealing with the interaction between the SAMA Bank Account Rules and the Bankruptcy Law: conditions and documents for opening liquidation / financial restructuring accounts (court order commencing liquidation or administrative liquidation, appointment of the bankruptcy officeholder or committee, prescribed account naming, identification of the entity and officeholder), and the duty to freeze an account on death, loss of legal competence, or commencement of liquidation under the Bankruptcy or Companies Law. Also covers priority of SAMA-directed compulsory deductions. Binds banks holding accounts of debtors under insolvency proceedings.

Node covering account opening for juristic persons under the Companies Law within the SAMA Bank Account Rules — documentary requirements for joint-stock companies (including companies under formation and formation-expenses accounts requiring Ministry of Commerce approval), limited liability companies, general and limited partnerships, GCC and non-resident companies, and high-risk classification where endowments, private foundations or cooperative associations hold more than 50% of capital. Binds banks opening and maintaining corporate accounts.

A SAMA circular (dated 03/09/1443H) reaffirming that a real estate financier remains bound by all statutory, contractual and supervisory obligations after transferring its rights in the secondary market (refinancing through licensed real estate refinance companies) or outsourcing collection to a third party. It stresses continuing duties for the full contract term, including prompt updating of customers' credit records within the period set in the Credit Information Law's implementing regulations, and correct handling of early repayment and debt rescheduling. Addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom, with SAMA reserving enforcement action for non-compliance.

The SAMA AML/CTF Guide sets supervisory expectations for financial institutions on anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing programs, elaborating the AML Law, the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing and their implementing regulations. The extracted parts cover governance of the AML/CTF compliance function: senior-management-level appointment of the responsible officer, independence and reporting to the board, an independent specialized AML/CTF unit staffed by Saudi nationals with adequate resources, and board/senior management duties for program design, periodic policy review, training and audit support. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

The risk assessment section of the SAMA AML/CTF Guide requires financial institutions to identify, understand and document ML/TF risks across customers and beneficial owners, products and services, geography and delivery channels, as the foundation of the risk-based approach. It mandates customer risk classification (e.g. high/medium/low), regular updating of customer risk profiles, pre-launch assessment of new products, services, practices and technologies, refresh of the risk-based approach at least every two years or on change of risk factors, and provision of risk assessment information to SAMA on request. It also discourages wholesale de-risking in favour of proportionate mitigation.

This node covers customer due diligence under the SAMA AML/CTF Guide, in particular reliance on third parties (other financial institutions or DNFBPs, including same-group entities) to perform CDD, as permitted by Articles 7/10, 7/11 and 7/13 of the AML Law implementing regulations. Conditions include ensuring the third party is regulated and supervised and applies CDD and record-keeping, immediate access to CDD information, consideration of high-risk country information from AMLPC, PCCT and SAFIU, risk assessment of the reliance arrangement, at-least-annual verification of the third party's capability, and continuous compliance monitoring. Ultimate responsibility remains with the relying financial institution.

Section 4 of the SAMA AML/CTF Guide addresses enhanced due diligence for customers and business relationships classified as high risk, requiring institutions to define the risk factors driving high-risk classification and to collect additional information to understand risk and monitor transactions more closely. The surrounding context links EDD to third-party reliance arrangements, where enhanced measures and related information must also be obtained. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions applying the risk-based approach.

This section permits financial institutions to apply simplified due diligence where ML/TF risk is assessed as low and no suspicion exists, grounded in Article 5/5 of the AML Law implementing regulations and Article 17 of the implementing regulations of the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing. Simplified measures must be documented in approved AML/CTF policies and are a streamlined, not waived, form of CDD: identity verification from independent authenticated sources, beneficial owner identification, understanding the purpose of the relationship, and understanding ownership and control of legal persons remain mandatory.

This node covers the beneficial owner identification and verification obligations within SAMA's AML/CTF guide for financial institutions, anchored in the AML Law Implementing Regulations and the counter-terrorism financing regulations. It sets out that the beneficial owner must be a natural person who directly or indirectly owns or controls a legal person, applies a 25% ownership/control threshold as a starting point, and prescribes cascading fallback measures (senior management, sub-25% controllers, EDD, record keeping) where no such person is identified or where suspicion arises. It binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA and requires that CDD intensity be calibrated to assessed risk, with reliance on the customer's own written statement expressly insufficient.

This node addresses politically exposed persons within SAMA's AML/CTF guide, treating PEP determination as a customer due diligence measure supporting the risk-based approach. It requires financial institutions to use reasonable tools and credible databases to establish whether a customer or beneficial owner is a domestic or foreign PEP, and to apply enhanced due diligence to high-risk PEP relationships, extending to family members and close associates. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions and links to the AML Law's requirement for internal procedures and tools to identify PEPs.

This node sets the record-keeping regime in SAMA's AML/CTF guide, requiring retention for at least ten years from the end of the business relationship, conclusion of the transaction, account closure, or completion of an occasional customer transaction, with extension where the competent authority instructs. It requires approved internal retention procedures, resourced and protected archiving, at least annual effectiveness testing, and retrievable auditable records available to SAMA and competent authorities. Where record keeping is outsourced or held outside Saudi Arabia, the institution remains responsible and must secure contractual access, confidentiality and inspection rights.

This node covers ongoing monitoring of transactions and activities under SAMA's AML/CTF guide, grounded in the AML Law and the counter-terrorism financing law duty to check that transactions, documents and data remain consistent with what the institution knows about the customer. It requires documented, senior-management-approved monitoring procedures calibrated by risk assessment outcomes, with enhanced scrutiny for high-risk customers and simplified treatment for low-risk ones, and treats manual monitoring alone as insufficient. It also requires periodic (at least annual) documented testing of monitoring tools and ongoing review, updating and reclassification of customer information.

This node sets out suspicious transaction reporting obligations in SAMA's AML/CTF guide, requiring board-approved documented reporting procedures covering internal escalation, investigation stages, approval/closure levels, the designated reporting officer, confidentiality and no tipping-off. Financial institutions must report immediately and directly to the SAFIU on suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect ML/TF, including attempted transactions regardless of amount, and must respond to SAFIU requests for further information. It also intersects with targeted financial sanctions, requiring notification to SAMA of accounts, relationships or transactions linked to UN Security Council and national designated-persons lists.

This node describes the AML/CTF compliance function required by SAMA's guide: an independent, specialised unit headed by a senior-management-level officer who reports administratively and technically to the board and its committees, with timely access to customer data, transaction records and any information needed. It lists the officer's mandated duties, including maintaining the AML/CTF program, policy review and monitoring, internal STR handling and SAFIU reporting, sanctions-list notifications to SAMA, branch inspections, and periodic board reporting. It also sets board and senior management responsibilities for risk identification in new products and channels, at least annual policy review, training, and adequate staffing, systems and budget; staffing of the unit is restricted to Saudi nationals.

An appendix-level concept within SAMA's bank account rules explaining the ten-digit Ministry of Interior computer number and how its leading digit signals identity type (1 for Saudi nationals, whose number is the national ID and also the identifier of a sole establishment owned by them; 2 for resident foreigners, matching the Iqama number). The surrounding appendices also list government entities and public-sector legal entities, and show where a ministry-issued computer number (e.g. from the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah) must appear in account-opening documentation. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom when identifying and verifying customers and authorised signatories at account opening, reactivation and ongoing maintenance.

A SAMA circular imposing periodic risk and financial reporting duties on licensed debt crowdfunding entities: a quarterly risk report covering the risks identified in the updated debt crowdfunding rules, mitigation measures, breaches of permitted limits, assumptions underlying risk assessment, provisions and adequacy of disclosure standards, to be reviewed by the risk and credit committee (if any) and approved by the board. It sets filing deadlines with SAMA for the risk report, quarterly and audited annual financial statements with auditor and board reports, and quarterly/annual prudential data templates certified by the chief accountant, CFO and CEO or managing director, with annual templates reviewed by the external auditor. It also requires publication of the auditor report, board report and quarterly and audited annual financial statements on the entity's website.

A SAMA circular creating a statutory reserve requirement for money exchange centres, obliging them to appropriate a minimum percentage of annual net profit (after covering accumulated losses) until the reserve reaches a set proportion of paid-up capital, at which point appropriation may stop. Use of the statutory reserve requires SAMA's prior written no-objection. The circular expressly does not affect the separate cash reserve obligation under Article 7 of the Rules Governing Money Exchange Business, and applies to money exchange centres operating in the Kingdom with effect from its date.
lookup_terms: Rules Governing Money Exchange Business Article 7

data.summary: A SAMA circular reaffirming that finance providers remain responsible for compliance with SAMA's debt collection controls and procedures for individual customers when collection tasks are outsourced to external service providers. Financiers must verify that outsourced collectors comply and that those providers have procedures in place to ensure compliance, with SAMA reserving supervisory action against violators. Addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom; note it does not displace the underlying collection rules but allocates accountability for third-party conduct.

A short SAMA circular, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its implementing regulation, directing finance companies to update their credit granting policies and procedures to keep pace with developments in the finance sector and the activities being financed, and to adopt prudential measures to limit the rise in non-performing loans. Firms must also ensure provisions and collateral are commensurate with the risks of the activity. Distribution covers finance companies operating in the Kingdom and SAMA-licensed crowdfunding entities.

A SAMA circular urging all finance providers to develop periodic financial awareness programmes tailored to small and medium enterprises, aligned with the Financial Sector Development Programme and Vision 2030 objectives on financial literacy and private-sector growth. Programmes should be calibrated to the financier's customer segment and identified awareness gaps and delivered through channels that reach SMEs, with a quarterly report on the financier's contribution submitted to SAMA's financial awareness mailbox. Addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom; framed as encouragement rather than a prescriptive rule, though the quarterly reporting expectation is explicit.

Section 10 of SAMA's AML/CTF guidance/rules for financial institutions, setting the requirement for an independent audit function to test the adequacy and effectiveness of AML/CTF internal controls, policies and procedures on a risk-based basis. It requires resourcing, competence and independence of the auditor from the AML/CTF function, permits use of the external auditor where appropriate, and places responsibility on senior management to remediate identified weaknesses. It binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA and links back to the AML Law and Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing implementing regulations.

Covers the AML/CTF training obligation and the surrounding compliance-function governance duties in SAMA's AML/CTF rules: ongoing training budgets and programs for senior management and staff, specialized annual training for AML/CTF compliance staff, and board/senior management responsibilities for policies, periodic review and resourcing. It also sets out the requirement for an independent, adequately resourced AML/CTF unit headed by a senior-level officer (Saudi nationals only) reporting to the board, with access to customer due diligence and transaction records. Binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

Section 13 of SAMA's AML/CTF rules on correspondent (correspondence) relationships, requiring pre-onboarding information gathering on the respondent institution's business, reputation, supervision and AML/CTF controls, clear allocation of responsibilities between parties, ongoing monitoring of correspondent accounts, and senior management approval with input from the AML/CTF compliance officer. It prohibits entering or continuing relationships with shell banks or with institutions that allow shell bank use of their accounts. Also touches employee screening/background verification and leave-rotation controls in the preceding section.

Section 14 of SAMA's AML/CTF rules governing cross-border and domestic wire transfers in any currency (including serial and cover payments) sent, received or processed in Saudi Arabia, including card, prepaid and mobile-initiated transfers. It sets mandatory originator and beneficiary information, a customer declaration on the legitimacy of the transfer, the domestic-transfer exemption with a three-working-day information-provision duty, and policies for handling incoming transfers with missing information (execute, reject, suspend, restrict or terminate). It also imposes currency restrictions on inbound transfers destined for beneficiaries at foreign institutions and confidentiality limits on information shared with correspondent or intermediary institutions.

Paragraphs 3.22–3.25 of SAMA's AML/CTF rules permitting a financial institution to rely on another financial institution or a DNFBP (including within the same financial group) to perform customer due diligence, subject to conditions. Conditions include that the third party is regulated and supervised, applies CDD and record-keeping consistent with the AML Law and CTF Law and their implementing regulations, provides CDD information immediately on request, and that high-risk country information from AMLPC, PCCT and SAFIU is considered. Ultimate responsibility remains with the relying institution, which must risk-assess reliance, monitor such customers, and verify the third party's capability at least annually.
lookup_terms: customer due diligence information on request

data.summary: Addresses the financial institution's suspicious transaction reporting duties to the Saudi Arabia Financial Intelligence Unit (SAFIU) under SAMA's AML/CTF rules, including the prohibition on reporting based on speculation, the grounds constituting reasonable suspicion, and the option to forgo CDD (with reasons reported) where applying it risks tipping off the customer. It requires use of SAFIU's approved reporting mechanism and form plus a detailed supplementary report and a technical report containing account statements, CDD documents and analysis. Context also includes wire transfer provisions on intermediary institutions, confidentiality of exchanged information and currency limits.

A concept node within SAMA's AML/CTF guide identifying the Financial Action Task Force as an international standard-setter whose instructions and typologies financial institutions must take into account, alongside SAMA, the PCCML and the PCCT, when developing and updating ML/TF indicators for transaction monitoring. The context also records Saudi Arabia's FATF membership (2019) and founding role in MENAFATF as background to the national AML/CTF framework. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions indirectly, through the guide's monitoring and indicator-updating obligations.

A concept node for the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing (Royal Decree M/21, 12/02/1439H) and its Implementing Regulations, cited throughout SAMA's AML/CTF guide as one of the two primary statutes underpinning institutional obligations (notably ongoing monitoring under Article 69 and suspicious reporting under Articles 70–71). It also establishes SAMA as a supervisory authority for the sector. It binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA, whose staff, directors and board members are exposed to the penalties it prescribes.
lookup_terms: Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing

data.summary: Section 1 of the governance chapter of SAMA's AML/CTF guide, setting out the board of directors' non-exhaustive responsibilities for AML/CTF compliance: ensuring an accurate institution-wide ML/TF risk assessment, adopting risk-mitigation policy, ensuring independent audit mechanisms, addressing branches or subsidiaries in jurisdictions that cannot apply the requirements, and receiving regular reports on ML/TF risks, audit findings, SAMA inspection results and targeted financial sanctions implementation. Oversight must align with international best practice and SAMA Governance Guidelines, and be documented (e.g. board or committee minutes). It binds boards of SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

Section 2 of the governance chapter of SAMA's AML/CTF guide, allocating to senior management continuous implementation and monitoring of AML/CTF compliance, complementing the board's oversight role and requiring that AML/CTF policies, procedures and controls be grounded in ML/TF risk assessment results and integrated into overall risk management. Related provisions require approval at senior management level of transaction-monitoring measures and senior management sign-off for high-risk customer relationships. It binds senior management of SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

The core methodological concept of SAMA's AML/CTF guide: a six-step risk-based approach requiring institutions to assess, understand and document ML/TF risks across customers and beneficial owners, products and services, geography and delivery channels, then apply proportionate preventive measures. It requires customer risk classification and profile updates, pre-launch risk assessment of new products, services, practices and technologies, provision of risk assessment information to SAMA on request, and review/update of the approach at least every two years or on change of risk factors. It expressly discourages de-risking by wholesale exclusion of customer classes. Binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

SAMA's Rules for Advertising Products and Services, issued under the Saudi Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36), governing the content and conduct of advertising by SAMA-licensed entities. They require due diligence in advertisement content and approach, prohibit tempting, misleading, inaccurate or exaggerated claims, mandate Arabic (with a carve-out for non-Arabic-speaker advertisements), and set minimum disclosure items including institution identity, product name, key terms, target customer/consumer, fees and commissions including VAT, and, for finance products, the APR and finance term (with fixed/variable term-cost disclosure for real estate finance). They apply to all financial institutions supervised and regulated by SAMA whenever advertising any product or service.

SAMA's Rules for Advertising Products and Services, issued under the Saudi Central Bank Law, setting minimum content, language and conduct requirements for any advertisement of a product or service by a SAMA-supervised entity. It defines Financial Institution, Customer, Consumer, Products and Services and Advertising, and imposes due-diligence duties against misleading, tempting or exaggerated messaging, mandatory Arabic, and disclosure of fees, VAT, key terms, target audience, and APR/finance term (including whether real estate finance term cost is fixed or variable). It binds all financial institutions supervised and regulated by SAMA when advertising.

A segment of SAMA's advertising rules covering conduct and control obligations in Articles 8–14: protecting sector reputation and fair competition, prohibiting use of customer personal data in advertising without written consent, banning insurance/credit advertising to under-18s, requiring opt-in consent and easy permanent opt-out for receiving ads, and making advertised offers and specifications contractually binding. It also requires use of official or licensed third-party channels with the institution retaining responsibility for third-party non-compliance, and mandates an internal advertising policy aligned with SAMA rules. Binds all SAMA-supervised financial institutions.
lookup_terms: use of customer data in advertising

data.summary: SAMA's Key Principles of Governance for financial institutions, setting minimum governance requirements across board qualifications, board formation and responsibilities, executive management, board committees, shareholder rights, and disclosure and transparency, with an appendix on money exchange sector controls. It requires separation of Chairman and CEO roles and a control framework comprising risk management, internal audit, compliance, internal controls and an external auditor. It binds entities supervised by SAMA other than insurance and reinsurance companies, and is read alongside other SAMA governance instructions without displacing them.

The board-focused provisions of SAMA's governance principles, covering member independence, conflict-of-interest disclosure on nomination, multiple-directorship and tenure limits, the prohibition on sitting on the board of a similar financial institution in the Kingdom, and the Chairman's specific duties. It requires a prior written no-objection from SAMA before nominating board/committee members or appointing leadership positions, and notification to SAMA within five working days of resignation, termination, end of membership or loss of independence. It also requires disclosure of board committees to SAMA and adoption of social responsibility programs.

Provisions on the board's relationship with executive management under SAMA's governance principles, including forming and supervising executive management, defining clear responsibility and accountability limits with full separation of duties at executive level, approving internal policies and a written delegation-of-authority policy, and selecting senior executives with a succession policy. It carries the defining terms for Executive (Senior) Management, Executive, Non-Executive and Independent Member. Binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions other than insurance and reinsurance companies.

The shareholder rights and disclosure/transparency provisions of SAMA's governance principles, requiring a written board-approved disclosure policy that enables stakeholders to access financial and non-financial information, future orientations, strategic plans and credit ratings, and that disclosure be explicit, correct and non-misleading. It sets shareholder entitlements including timely information, General Assembly participation with 21 days' notice of venue, date and agenda, cumulative voting for board members, and queries on remuneration and practices. Related board duties include risk strategy oversight, auditor independence, and notifying SAMA of regulatory or judicial penalties within ten working days.

Article 9 of SAMA's Agent Banking Rules sets the minimum eligibility gate a prospective Agent must clear before a Bank may contract with it: a commercial register permitting agent banking activity, any prior approval from its own supervisory/regulatory authority, and satisfaction of the Article 13 fit and proper criteria. The Bank must submit a CEO (or designated senior officer) declaration attesting to the assessment and the Agent's competence, and SAMA notifies the Bank of the outcome of the non-objection application. It binds licensed Banks, which retain overall responsibility for the agency relationship even where Agent employees perform the work.

Article 13 requires the Bank to run a fit and proper assessment on the prospective Agent, its proprietors and the individuals managing the agent banking business, testing competence, integrity, adequacy of management structures and sources of funding. It is the substantive standard referenced by the Article 9 eligibility gate and feeds the Bank's declaration to SAMA. The obligation sits with the contracting Bank; SAMA vets and approves Agents and connected individuals.

Article 14 sets the Bank's ongoing agent due diligence obligations: documented procedures with periodic reviews, early warning indicators and corrective actions, clear allocation of agent-management roles across internal functions, and AML/CFT, embezzlement and fraud monitoring of Agents with regular compliance checks. Minimum due diligence content covers legal status and address verification, moral/business/professional suitability, adverse credit bureau or other information, criminal records touching ML/TF, fraud or integrity, experience, and funding sources. Note this is diligence on the Agent (entity-level, KYB-style), distinct from the customer due diligence duties in Article 15.

Article 16 fixes the Bank as wholly responsible and liable for all acts and omissions of its Agents, including unauthorised acts connected to agent banking, and requires a clear, informed and documented decision to use Agents plus effective oversight. Related contractual requirements cover dispute resolution and indemnities (customer–agent, agent–bank, and agent non-compliance), termination grounds, risk mitigation measures, AML/CFT and KYC compliance with reporting to SAMA, and the Bank's ownership and confidentiality of all agent-collected customer data, surviving contract termination. Record retention of at least 10 years applies to transaction records held by the Agent and passed to the Bank.
lookup_terms: obligations and responsibilities of the Bank

data.summary: Article 19 lists the banking services a Bank may, after SAMA non-objection, delegate to an Agent — including account opening, loan application intake, account statements, account activation, domestic and international transfers, currency exchange, card and cheque issuance subject to Bank approval, cheque encashment, SME banking services, POS terminal applications, and sales and marketing. Services must be specified in the agent contract, displayed at the Agent's premises and published on the Bank's website with a full agent list; the Bank decides each Agent's permitted scope based on agent risk assessment. Related Article 18 requires pre-commencement and ongoing training of Agent employees covering KYC, AML procedures, customer information protection, complaints and fraud detection.

Article 20 bars the Bank from permitting its Agent to undertake specified activities, including offline or manual operation during communication failure, transactions without a generated receipt, non-electronic transactions off-premises, soliciting customer account details or PINs, any form of manual cash services absent written SAMA non-objection, activities outside SAMA's non-objection for that Agent, payment services outside SAMA's payment system infrastructure, accessing credit bureau reports in loan processing, disclosing information obtained through the work, and breaching the Bank's code of ethics. SAMA may add further prohibitions. The prohibition is addressed to the Bank, which must prevent the Agent from performing these acts.

Defines and regulates the status of the Independent Member on the board of a SAMA-supervised financial institution, including annual board assessment of continuing independence, the member's duty to disclose circumstances that may impair it, and notification to SAMA within five working days if independence is lost. It sits within the wider board-formation rules (board size of five to eleven, at least two independent members or one third whichever is greater, maximum two executive members, three-year renewable terms, preferred twelve-year tenure cap) and the prior written no-objection requirement for nominating board/committee members or appointing leadership positions. It binds the board, individual members and nominees of the financial institution, and imposes conflict-of-interest disclosure duties on candidates and limits on concurrent directorships.

The Regulation of Agent Banking sets the minimum standards for banks that wish to deliver banking products and services through contracted Agents, covering agent eligibility, fit-and-proper assessment, SAMA non-objection, permissible activities, the agency contract, customer due diligence and AML/CFT, information security and confidentiality, consumer protection, and supervision of agents. It defines key terms such as Agent, Exclusive Agent, Multiple Agent, Customer and Conflict of Interest. It applies to all banks contracting with an Agent; the bank's board is accountable for compliance and the bank remains fully liable for its Agents' acts and omissions.

Agent Banking is the delivery of permissible banking products and services to Customers by a contracted Agent acting on behalf of a bank, under a direct written agency contract and only after SAMA's non-objection. The Agent must hold a commercial register permitting the activity and obtain approval from its own supervisory authority before the bank seeks non-objection; agents may operate on an exclusive or multiple (non-exclusive) basis, and bank employees may perform or supervise the activity on agent premises. The concept binds banks, which retain full responsibility for the agency relationship, agent selection, and the agent's acts and omissions.

KYC in the agent banking context is a mandatory component of the bank's Customer Due Diligence programme, alongside information security and data privacy/confidentiality. Agents must establish customer identity by means the bank deems appropriate and verify the purpose and nature of the banking activity or relationship; where an agent doubts the credibility of customer information it must cease dealing with the customer and report to the bank's Money Laundering Reporting Officer. The obligation rests on the bank, which must ensure its agents comply with the CDD programme and remains liable for their conduct.

Covers the bank's due diligence on prospective and existing Agents (distinct from CDD on end customers): a fit-and-proper assessment of the Agent, its proprietors and managers, verification of legal status and address, moral/business/professional suitability, adverse credit bureau information, criminal records relating to ML/TF, fraud or integrity, experience, and sources of funds. It also requires defined internal roles for agent management, periodic reviews with early-warning indicators and corrective action, and ongoing monitoring of agents for AML/CFT, embezzlement and financial fraud. The duty binds the contracting bank, which must communicate required actions to agents and monitor their compliance.

Sets out the accountability of the bank's board of directors for agent banking: approving comprehensive policies and procedures reflecting SAMA requirements, ensuring mechanisms exist for relevant departments to implement them, and ensuring agent monitoring is proportionate to the risk posed to the bank. Banks are fully liable for their Agents' actions and compliance and must maintain adequate systems for risk management, consumer protection, AML/CFT and combating embezzlement and fraud, including independent testing of the agent's AML/CFT programme, integration of agent transactions into core banking with instant customer confirmation, clear branding, agent disclosure on the bank's website, and protection of customer information (unauthorised disclosure being punishable under the Banking Control Law). It binds the board and senior management of each bank using agents.
lookup_terms: customer information confidentiality Banking Control Law

data.summary: This node covers the corporate governance, ownership/fit-and-proper, IT and accounting systems, outsourcing and audit elements of SAMA's banking licensing criteria. It requires applicants to evidence board composition and functioning under SAMA's Principles of Corporate Governance for Banks Operating in Saudi Arabia, fit-and-proper founders, directors and significant shareholders under the Banking Control Law, adequate prudential reporting systems, BCM/DRP arrangements, and compliant outsourcing and internal/external audit arrangements. It binds applicants for a banking licence in KSA, including foreign banks applying for branch status and their significant shareholders.
lookup_terms: Principles of Corporate Governance for Banks Operating in Saudi Arabia

data.summary: This node sets the risk management and AML/CTF preconditions within SAMA's banking licensing criteria. Applicants must demonstrate adequate policies, people and systems for credit, market, liquidity, compliance, AML/CTF and operational risk, reporting arrangements consistent with SAMA prudential standards and the Banking Control Law, and compliance capability against the Rules Governing Anti-Money Laundering & Combating Terrorist Financing and SAMA's compliance manual for banks. Adequacy is assessed proportionately to the size, nature and complexity of the proposed operations; it binds banking licence applicants, including foreign bank branch applicants reporting to both SAMA and head office.
lookup_terms: Rules Governing Anti-Money Laundering and Combating Terrorist Financing

data.summary: This node addresses home-supervisor conditions for foreign bank branch licence applicants and the general application process. Applicants must hold written home-supervisor consent, be licensed and listed in their home country, and satisfy SAMA that home supervision meets the Basel Committee Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision, including consolidated supervision and willingness to cooperate with SAMA. It also frames pre-application consultation and the general licensing overview, including that foreign branches are generally subject to the same requirements as locally incorporated banks.

SAMA's Additional Licensing Guidelines and Criteria for Digital-Only Banks, issued under the SAMA Charter and the Banking Control Law, layered on top of the general Banking Licensing Guidelines and Minimum Criteria. It sets licensing conditions (locally incorporated joint-stock company, promoter experience and financial capacity), business plan content, ICAAP/ILAAP submission, physical head-office presence, governance parity with conventional banks, risk management, AML/CFT in a fully digital environment, technology/cybersecurity, independent assessment, outsourcing, exit plan, prudential/supervisory requirements and consumer protection. It binds applicants for a digital-only banking licence in Saudi Arabia.

Defines the "Digital-only Bank" as a bank conducting banking business mainly through digital channels such as web and mobile applications, and scopes the additional licensing criteria applicable to it. Core conditions include local incorporation as a joint-stock company, qualified promoters, a physical principal place of business in KSA without an expectation of branches (SAMA may require customer service centres), and the same corporate governance principles as conventional banks. It binds digital-only bank licence applicants, alongside the general banking licensing criteria.

Article 29 of SAMA's Agent Banking regulation establishes an electronic agent registry maintained by SAMA into which banks must enter prescribed details for every agent acting on their behalf, including relationship start date, agent name and business name, address and geographic coordinates, contact details, core business and years of operation, and the agent banking contract. Registration is a precondition to conducting agent banking: unregistered activity exposes the bank and agent to SAMA enforcement, and banks must refresh changed agent data within ten business days. The obligation binds licensed banks, which remain responsible for the agent's compliance with the regulation, including consumer protection requirements; the adjacent Article 30 requires an annual board-approved report to SAMA covering transaction volumes, ML/TF cases, fraud/theft incidents, monitoring visit results and customer complaints.

Covers the technology, cybersecurity and independent assessment expectations for digital-only bank applicants. Applicants must address information systems security, resilience and availability proportionate to proposed products, comply with SAMA's Cyber Security Framework and BCM Framework, and have regard to other national requirements such as National Cybersecurity Authority rules; SAMA may require a qualified third-party assessor, at the applicant's cost, to assess technology/cybersecurity and AML/CFT arrangements at design and implementation phases with remediation to SAMA's satisfaction. It binds digital-only bank licence applicants.

This node collects the AML/CFT and KYC obligations embedded in SAMA's Agent Banking regulation, covering both the mandatory contract terms between bank and agent (compliance with AML/CFT and KYC, provision of documents and periodic AML/CFT reports to SAMA, ten-year record retention, bank ownership and confidentiality of customer data) and the bank's pre-application obligations (board approval, internal agent banking policy, and a description of customer due diligence and KYC processes). It binds banks contracting agents, with the bank retaining responsibility for ensuring the agent satisfies AML/CFT, anti-fraud/embezzlement and information security requirements. Useful where an agent performs customer-facing steps but the bank remains the accountable financial institution.

SAMA's Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers sets the operating framework for bank-owned remittance centers and licensed remittance companies, covering definitions (Centers, Bank, Remittance Membership, SAFIU, FATF), working hours and days, general compliance provisions, disclosure and transparency, complaints handling, in-branch services, and customer acceptance/KYC/CDD expectations. It binds banks operating remittance centers and licensed remittance companies in the Kingdom, and cross-references the Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts, the Banking Consumer Protection Principles and SAMA's AML/CFT circulars.

Section 9 of the remittance centers guide sets customer acceptance policies and the Know Your Customer principle: verifying identity, address, business, income and source of funds, establishing the purpose of the remittance membership, and refusing fictitious, digital or anonymous names. It requires official identity documents (national ID, iqama or passport) verified against originals, membership numbers linked to name and ID, bilingual name and ID capture, branch-manager approval of membership opening, additional approvals and enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers, and termination of the relationship where identity or source of funds cannot be verified or the membership is misused. Binds banks' remittance centers and licensed remittance companies.

Section 9.6 of the remittance centers guide sets customer due diligence measures: understanding and monitoring customers' transactions, identifying and verifying beneficial owners (real beneficiaries) through reliable independent sources, applying a risk-based approach, keeping identification data current on an ongoing basis, tracking identity changes, and making identification records available to AML/CFT compliance officers. CDD applies to all permanent and temporary customers including beneficial owners, and must be continuous and proportionate to the risk of the business relationship and transactions. Binds banks' remittance centers and licensed remittance companies.

This node covers the treatment of outbound and inbound remittances by remittance centers: originator information must be complete and traceable in wire transfers and batch files; where it is missing, the center must seek it from the correspondent institution or transfer service provider, reject and return the transfer if there is no response, report suspicion to SAFIU, and document and retain decisions for ten years. It also requires specified originating/correspondent institution and country details on inbound transfers, notification to the beneficiary of changes to originator information, enhanced due diligence for politically exposed persons, rejection of remittances to prohibited countries, and refusal of remittances to or from charitable or non-profit bodies unless authorised under the bank account opening rules. Related general provisions address SAMA circular compliance, disclosure of prices, commissions and fees, and complaint-handling mechanisms.

A concept node within SAMA's Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers covering third-party money transfer services providers contracted by remittance centers. It sets pre-contract vetting (company profile, draft contract, AML/CFT compliance certificate), requires transfer to be the provider's core business, adequate AML/CFT and anti-fraud policies, and mandatory contract clauses on Saudi law and SAMA instructions, UN/FATF listings and warnings, banking confidentiality, KYC and ongoing CDD, and providing information to SAMA. It binds banks' remittance centers and licensed remittance companies, which retain supervisory responsibility over the providers operating through them, and includes escalation duties (restricting or terminating relationships, reporting suspicion) where providers repeatedly fail to supply originator information or cooperate.

A concept node identifying SARIE (Saudi Arabian Riyal Interbank Express) as a permitted modern transfer system, alongside SWIFT, for outbound and inbound domestic and international remittances under the Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers. For domestic transfers executed exclusively through SARIE, remittance centers must capture and store the transferor's name and account number for rapid retrieval by competent authorities, and verify the inbound beneficiary's identity per the Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts. It binds banks' remittance centers and licensed remittance companies.

A defined-term node for the Saudi Arabia Financial Investigation Unit (SAFIU) as used in the Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers — the authority receiving and analysing suspicious activity reports relating to money laundering and terrorist financing from financial and non-financial institutions. In this Guide, SAFIU is the reporting destination where a correspondent institution fails to supply complete originator information on a suspicious transfer and where there are reasonable grounds to suspect funds are criminal proceeds or ML/TF-related. Reporting duties fall on banks' remittance centers and licensed remittance companies.

A defined-term node for the Financial Action Task Force in the Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers, described as the inter-governmental standard-setter for AML, CTF and proliferation financing measures. Operationally the Guide uses FATF as a risk trigger: enhanced scrutiny of funds to or from countries subject to FATF warnings, treatment of FATF-listed non-compliant jurisdictions as high risk for due diligence, and contractual obligations on transfer providers to observe FATF and UN warning notices. It is relevant to banks' remittance centers, licensed remittance companies and their contracted transfer services providers.

SAMA's Licensing Guidelines and Minimum Criteria setting out the process and minimum standards for obtaining a licence to carry on banking business in KSA under the Banking Control Law, issued under SAMA's Charter and the BCL. It covers the restriction on use of the word "bank", minimum criteria on capital, ownership, corporate governance, risk management and controls, compliance and AML/CTF, IT, accounting systems and outsourcing, audit arrangements, and home-supervisor oversight for foreign bank branches, plus pre-application consultation, submission and processing steps. It binds all applicants for a banking licence, including foreign banks seeking to establish a branch.

The capital element of SAMA's minimum bank licensing criteria: SAMA assesses capital adequacy case-by-case against the scale, nature and complexity of operations proposed in the applicant's business plan. Foreign bank branches are not required to maintain capital in KSA, though SAMA may impose capital requirements on them case-by-case, for example for high-risk businesses or specialised business lines. Applies to all banking licence applicants and sits within the broader expectation of compliance with the BCL and prudential requirements from commencement of operations.

A licensing-application component of SAMA's additional requirements for Digital-only Banks, requiring an applicant to submit an exit plan setting out how customer funds, ongoing business, assets and liabilities would be handled if the targeted business objectives are not achieved (e.g. migration of accounts and continuity of service). It sits alongside the guidelines' adjacent expectations on prudential/supervisory treatment (same prudential requirements as other banks, plus electronic data accessible for supervision) and consumer protection (SAMA's Banking Consumer Protection Principles apply, with adequate customer support channels across the banking life cycle). It binds applicants for, and holders of, a Digital-only Bank licence in Saudi Arabia.
lookup_terms: migration of customer accounts and funds

data.summary: The Implementing Regulation of the Real Estate Finance Law, setting out definitions, SAMA's regulatory powers over the real estate finance sector, contract requirements between real estate finance entities and borrowers, product no-objection requirements, insurance, and the framework for the Real Estate Refinance Company and secondary-market transfers of contractual rights. It binds commercial banks and licensed real estate finance companies acting as real estate finance entities, originators, and the licensed refinance company, with supervision by SAMA.
lookup_terms: Real Estate Finance Law implementing regulation
transfer of rights / assignment of mortgage receivables
no objection letter for finance products

data.summary: Defines the Real Estate Finance Contract as a deferred payment contract extended to a borrower to own a dwelling, and anchors Chapter Two's contracting obligations: compliance with the Law, SAMA rules and any SAMA standard contracts, prior no-objection for products, and a written or electronic contract containing minimum disclosures (parties and ID details, term, finance amount, term cost and its reference rate, annual percentage rate, total amount payable). It binds real estate finance entities dealing with individual borrowers, read together with the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law.
lookup_terms: annual percentage rate (APR) real estate finance

data.summary: Defines the Secondary Market as trading of real estate finance entities' rights arising from primary-market contracts, and frames the Real Estate Refinance Company's mandate to build liquidity and stability in that market, acquire and manage finance obligations/rights, issue securities under the Capital Market Law with SAMA no-objection, and price its services under SAMA oversight. Relevant to real estate finance entities selling or assigning contractual rights — notably assignment to the refinance company without borrower or guarantor consent — and to the PIF-anchored ownership condition.
lookup_terms: securitisation / issue securities Capital Market Law
transfer of real estate finance contractual rights

data.summary: SAMA's Responsible Lending Principles for Individual Customers (Circular 46538/99 of 1439H, as amended), setting definitions and general provisions for consumer credit granted by banks and finance companies. It applies to all creditors and all finance activities directed at consumers — personal finance, vehicle finance, credit cards and real estate finance — and requires internal controls, documentation, staff awareness, and oversight of any third parties performing related work.
lookup_terms: total amount payable by the consumer

data.summary: Sets the quantitative deduction caps on consumer indebtedness under the Responsible Lending Principles, tiered by total monthly income (bands starting at SAR 15,000 and SAR 15,000–25,000), limiting salary-linked monthly credit obligations (33.33% for employees, 25% for retirees), non-real-estate obligations (45%), and total obligations (55%/65%, with a higher cap for Ministry of Housing or Real Estate Development Fund mortgage beneficiaries). It also sits with the qualitative duties to use a documented creditworthiness methodology, obtain consumer consent, check and register credit-bureau records, and disclose other obligations. Binds creditors (banks and finance companies) granting credit to individuals.
lookup_terms: Ministry of Housing / Real Estate Development Fund subsidy

data.summary: A SAMA circular (1443H) notifying the market of two regulatory amendments: the Minister of Finance's decision deleting Article 4 of the Implementing Regulation of the Real Estate Finance Law, and the Governor's decision amending Article 16 of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law. The amended Article 16 confirms that SAMA specifies in the licence which financing activity or activities a finance company may conduct and may attach special conditions limiting the geographic area, the permitted beneficiaries, or other terms. Addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: Finance Companies Control Law implementing regulation
