Real Estate Finance Law Article 4 deletion

data.summary: SAMA's Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules, setting the overarching conduct framework that financial institutions must observe in all dealings with consumers. It combines high-level principles (fair treatment, disclosure and transparency, education, conduct, data privacy, complaints handling, competition, outsourcing) with detailed general conduct rules on contracts, initial disclosure forms, fee and commission changes, notification timelines, application processing and complaint channels. Binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions across their consumer-facing products and services.
lookup_terms: Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules

data.summary: The principles section of SAMA's consumer protection framework, articulating the general obligations financial institutions owe consumers: equitable and fair treatment (with special attention to low-income, less educated, elderly and special-needs consumers), disclosure and transparency on pricing, risks and termination, and consumer education and awareness. It is the interpretive backbone for the detailed conduct rules on documentation, fee changes and application notifications. Applies to all financial institutions supervised by SAMA in their consumer dealings.

Covers Principle 7 and the associated rules requiring financial institutions to operate a clear, effective complaints mechanism and to resolve complaints fairly and without delay. Institutions must offer multiple submission channels (toll-free number, branches/website, mobile app, email), publish the handling mechanism, acknowledge complaints with a reference number and stated handling period by SMS, identify the responsible department, and retain communication records for at least five years. Also touches consumer education duties on debt, default and fraud.

Principle 6 of the consumer protection framework, requiring financial institutions to put in place mechanisms protecting the privacy of consumers' financial, credit, insurance and personal information consistent with applicable regulations and the Personal Data Protection Law, including all rights conferred by that law. It also requires high-level control systems that specify the purposes for which data is collected. Relevant where consumer protection intersects with data protection and credit information regimes.

Principle 9 of the consumer protection framework, addressing outsourcing of consumer-facing services. The financial institution must ensure outsourced service providers comply with the applicable Principles and Rules and act in consumers' interests, and it remains responsible for consumer protection even where the provider fails to comply. Relevant to third-party arrangements such as collection, servicing, distribution and call-centre functions.

This node covers the responsible-lending duty on creditors to assess a consumer's creditworthiness and repayment capacity using a documented, board-approved methodology reviewed annually, applied and evidenced in the finance file before finance is granted. It requires consumer-consented credit record enquiry, written disclosure of other credit obligations (including informal or employer loans), and use of financial models that account for a defined minimum set of basic living expenses plus existing monthly credit commitments. It binds creditors under the SAMA responsible-lending principles when granting consumer finance.

This node concerns the creditor's obligations toward licensed credit bureaus: obtaining the consumer's consent to examine the credit record, registering all credit information on the granted finance, and keeping it updated throughout the relationship, with rejection of the application mandatory if consent is withheld. It also governs how obligations (including credit card minimum payments and variable term-cost finance) must be reflected in the consumer's credit report. It binds creditors subject to the responsible-lending rules, interacting with the credit information regime.

The Rules on Outsourcing for Finance Companies set the regulatory framework for licensed finance companies that have entered or intend to enter outsourcing contracts with external service providers, read alongside the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations. They impose a board-approved annual outsourcing policy, risk review at inception and renewal, due diligence on provider licensing and capability, mandatory contract content, SAMA non-objection for material functions, monitoring, business continuity and record retention. Non-compliance is a violation of the Finance Companies Control Law, and the finance company remains responsible for the provider's conduct.

This node defines the written outsourcing policy that a finance company's board must approve and update annually, and the minimum content it must cover — board and senior management responsibilities, which functions may be outsourced, provider eligibility and due diligence, ongoing control and monitoring, conflict-of-interest criteria, information confidentiality, and verification of provider compliance including with the Finance Consumer Protection Principles. It also carries transitional duties to submit the approved policy to SAMA and to protect and retrieve or destroy consumer data on contract termination. It binds licensed finance companies and their boards.

This node defines Material Functions as any function whose default or disruption could affect the finance company's activities, reputation or financial position, or that involves sharing, transferring, processing or storing consumer data and information. Outsourcing or renewing such functions, or making material contract changes, requires SAMA's written non-objection requested at least 30 working days in advance, with a prescribed minimum content in the request; SAMA may restrict, condition, or require modification or termination. Illustrative non-exhaustive examples include external and internal audit, customer care and complaints, IT/security and cloud data storage, brokerage and agency activity, HR provision, debt collection and archiving.

This node defines the External Service Provider — any provider to whom an activity is outsourced, whether a group member, related party or unrelated third party — and sets the contractual requirements governing the relationship. The outsourcing must be documented in a legally binding written contract covering, at minimum, scope, term, performance, audit and monitoring, business continuity, liability, confidentiality, reporting, adverse-development notification, SAMA/auditor access rights, data return or destruction on expiry, a ban on subcontracting Material Functions, Saudi judicial jurisdiction (departures needing SAMA's prior non-objection), and governing language. It binds licensed finance companies in their contracting with providers.
lookup_terms: SAMA access rights to provider records

data.summary: SAMA's Rules Governing Real Estate Refinance Companies, setting out the defined terms (Real Estate Refinance Company, Real Estate Financier, primary/secondary market, borrower, contractual rights) and the general framework for licensed joint stock companies conducting real estate refinance activity. It fixes the permitted business model — buying/holding real estate finance contractual rights, issuing securities, providing liquidity to financiers — and the prohibitions, notably no direct finance to borrowers and no dealings outside the sector without a SAMA no-objection letter. It binds companies licensed by SAMA for real estate refinance, alongside the Real Estate Finance Law and Finance Companies Control Law and their implementing regulations.
lookup_terms: secondary market for real estate finance

data.summary: Chapter II of the Real Estate Refinance Rules imposes prudential requirements on the licensed refinance company: compliance with SAMA-determined capital adequacy ratio, leverage ratio and minimum liquidity ratio, and prior written SAMA approval for any capital increase or decrease. The surrounding provisions also confirm SAMA's power to control and restrict service pricing and list the activity prohibitions (e.g. no direct finance to borrowers, collateral transfer conditions, restrictions on asset acquisition and liquidation). Binds the licensed real estate refinance company and its board/senior management.

Chapter III of the Real Estate Refinance Rules governs board composition and fitness, required committees (audit, risk and credit management, executive, nomination and remuneration), an assets and liabilities committee at senior management level, and the requirement to adopt internal governance regulations and SAMA's Principles of Corporate Governance for supervised financial institutions. Policies on refinance business take effect only after a SAMA no-objection letter. It places personal liability on the board, CEO/general manager, managing director and senior executives for the company's breaches of these Rules and the underlying laws.
lookup_terms: fit and proper criteria board members
Principles of Corporate Governance for Financial Institutions

data.summary: Chapter VII of the Real Estate Refinance Rules requires a board-approved and annually updated business strategy and risk management policy covering all risk types including outsourced processes, plus procedures to identify, assess, manage, monitor and report risks within a comprehensive framework. Related provisions cover separation of executive and supervisory functions, adequacy of IT systems and data integrity/confidentiality, business continuity planning, and periodic risk reporting to SAMA covering market risk, collateral values, term cost mismatch, delinquencies, concentration and securities exposures. Binds the licensed real estate refinance company, its board, risk and credit management committee and senior management.
lookup_terms: segregation of executive and supervisory functions

data.summary: Chapter VIII of the Real Estate Refinance Rules requires the company to establish a compliance department with a head of compliance reporting to the audit committee, a written compliance policy reviewed annually, and a compliance officer appointed by the board on audit committee recommendation after a SAMA no-objection letter, acting independently with no other administrative duties. It sets a semiannual compliance report to the audit committee and board, a risk-based compliance programme, and resourcing/reporting-line requirements. Notably it also requires the company to verify that real estate financiers have internal policies and procedures to combat financial crime such as money laundering — a counterparty-level AML assurance duty rather than direct customer CDD.
lookup_terms: financial crime money laundering real estate financiers

data.summary: Chapter VI of the Real Estate Refinance Rules requires a board-issued, annually updated outsourcing policy (board/senior management responsibilities, functions that may not be outsourced, provider eligibility, risk identification and hedging) and mandates contractual audit/access rights for SAMA, the external auditor and the company. The company remains liable for the outsourcing provider's non-compliance, and a SAMA no-objection letter is required before outsourcing that could materially affect activities, reputation or financial position, or that involves transferring, processing or storing borrower data — with subcontracting likewise conditional on SAMA non-objection. Binds licensed real estate refinance companies; read with SAMA's wider outsourcing framework.
lookup_terms: SAMA and external auditor access rights

data.summary: This is the Governance domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, the first of four domains (Governance, Prevent, Detect, Respond) each expressed as a Principle plus numbered Control Requirements. It places ultimate accountability for the Counter-Fraud Programme, Strategy, Policy and culture on the Board and Executive Leadership, and mandates a Counter-Fraud Governance Structure including a dedicated Counter-Fraud Governance Committee chaired by an Executive Committee member with defined minimum membership (Head of Counter-Fraud, CRO, COO, Head of Digital). It binds Member Organisations supervised by SAMA within the Framework's stated scope.

This is the Prevent domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, covering proactive controls that stop fraud before harm occurs to the organisation or its customers. It requires a Fraud Risk Management Framework aligned to enterprise risk management (covering intelligence monitoring, Fraud Risk Assessment, Fraud Risk Appetite and KRIs) and defined, approved fraud prevention standards addressing internal and external fraud, with limits and thresholds set by reference to risk assessment outcomes, loss experience and risk appetite. It binds Member Organisations, with controls expected to be proportionate to assessed risk.

This is the Detect domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, addressing risk-based identification of actual or attempted fraud where preventive controls fail. It requires defined, approved and maintained fraud detection standards covering internal and external fraud, specifying data sources, detective controls (including Wholesale Payment Endpoint Security monitoring), systems, roles and the rationale for proportionality, with enhanced measures where inherent fraud risk is higher. It binds Member Organisations and requires periodic review and effectiveness evaluation.

This is the Respond domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, governing action after fraud is suspected or detected in order to limit losses and maximise recovery. It requires a defined, approved and maintained Fraud Response Plan—aligned where appropriate with enterprise incident management—covering alerting and reporting channels for customers, employees and third parties, roles and responsibilities, escalation and decision-making authority, prompt investigation and fair resolution, plus root cause analysis and corrective action. It binds Member Organisations, with compliance and effectiveness to be monitored and periodically evaluated.

This node sets out the Counter-Fraud Maturity Model used to measure a Member Organisation's counter-fraud maturity across six levels (0 non-existent, 1 ad-hoc, 2 repeatable but informal, through 3, 4 and 5), where higher levels require satisfaction of all preceding levels. Level 3 turns on documented policies, standards and procedures with embedded controls and KPI-monitored compliance; level 4 requires effectiveness measurement via KRIs with defined thresholds; level 5 requires continuous improvement. It provides the assessment yardstick applied to Member Organisations under the Framework.

This node covers the requirement for Member Organisations to establish and maintain a Counter-Fraud Department responsible for day-to-day operation of the Counter-Fraud Programme. Its mandated functions include monitoring compliance with counter-fraud policies, standards and procedures, designing organisation-wide controls, conducting the Fraud Risk Assessment, intelligence analysis and sharing with SAMA and the sector, tuning detection systems, investigating fraud and documenting root causes, monitoring Fraud Risk Appetite breaches, aligning with Cyber Security and Financial Crime functions, and periodic senior management reporting. The reporting line must be assessed against organisational structure and independence considerations.
lookup_terms: alignment with Cyber Security and Financial Crime

data.summary: This is the secondary-market provision (plus the concluding provisions and definitions) of SAMA's Rules Governing Real Estate Refinance Companies, addressed to the licensed Real Estate Refinance Company. It conditions any trading of real estate finance contractual rights on a prior SAMA no-objection letter and on submission of a comprehensive plan covering collection and sukuk structuring, credit enhancement methodology, and a feasibility study assessing balance-sheet, housing-sector and capital-market impact. It preserves SAMA's power to impose further requirements or to restrict or prohibit such trading, confirms the Rules are read with the Finance Companies Control Law and the Real Estate Finance Law and their implementing regulations, allows case-by-case exemptions, and sets a 180-day entry into force.

SAMA instructions (Arabic, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law) regulating the purchase/transfer of individual consumer finance debts between finance companies, i.e. debt buyout or refinancing of a customer's existing exposure by another lender. They bind both the acquiring finance company (which must hold a consumer finance licence, disclose new finance terms and costs and obtain documented customer consent, use a dedicated application form, settle the outstanding debt through the SARIE system with prescribed payment data, and withhold surplus funds until a clearance letter is received) and the selling finance company (which must issue liability statements and debt confirmation letters, effect transfer, and notify settlement within one business day). No separate SAMA approval is required for each transaction, but consumer protection instructions and limits on fees (only early settlement or administrative fees) apply.
lookup_terms: debt buyout / transfer of debt between finance companies

data.summary: A SAMA circular (Arabic) requiring compliance managers/officers at finance companies to obtain the "Compliance for the Finance Companies Sector" certificate, relying on SAMA's mandate under the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law to develop sector competence and training. The certificate must be obtained within one year of the circular's date, or at the point the finance company seeks SAMA's no-objection for an appointment to the role, and a copy must be provided to SAMA. It binds all finance companies operating in the Kingdom and is relevant to fit-and-proper/appointment approvals for the compliance function.

A SAMA circular (Arabic) to debt-based crowdfunding entities operating in the Kingdom on pooled accounts used to manage finance amounts, issued under the SAMA Law and the Finance Companies Control Law and read with the Rules for Practising Debt-Based Crowdfunding. It requires that pooled accounts be used solely for managing finance value and segregated from the entity's own funds, be named "Finance Value Management Account – [entity name]", and that SAMA be notified on opening or closing such accounts with banks in the Kingdom. It also mandates a written policy on account operation (board-approved authority matrix, multi-eyes control, reporting to senior management, no encumbrance of the account by the entity's obligations), documented reconciliation against executed financing transactions, and bank account agreements reflecting the regulatory requirements and allocating responsibilities.

A defined-term node for the "Finance Value Management Account" – the pooled account holding participants' funds at a debt-based crowdfunding entity, which SAMA requires to be named "Finance Value Management Account – [name of the debt-based crowdfunding entity]". Its purpose is restricted to managing the finance value, it must be segregated from the entity's own funds and free of any charge or claim arising from the entity's own obligations, and its opening or closing must be notified to SAMA. Operation is subject to a written policy, a board-approved authority matrix, multi-level control, senior management reporting and documented reconciliation.
lookup_terms: notification to SAMA on account opening

data.summary: SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, which sets control requirements and a six-level maturity model (0 non-existent to 5) used to assess Member Organisations' counter-fraud capability, with higher levels requiring satisfaction of all preceding criteria. It obliges Member Organisations to establish a dedicated Counter-Fraud Department responsible for the day-to-day Counter-Fraud Programme, including policy compliance monitoring, organisation-wide preventive and detective controls across people/process/technology, fraud risk assessment, intelligence analysis and sharing with SAMA and the sector, investigations and root-cause remediation, fraud risk appetite monitoring with crisis escalation, alignment with cyber security and financial crime functions, and periodic senior-management reporting. It also addresses the appropriate reporting line for the department.

Node covering the counter-fraud function's leadership and organisational placement under SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, including the requirement that Member Organisations establish and maintain a Counter-Fraud Department owning day-to-day running of the Counter-Fraud Programme. Its listed duties span policy compliance monitoring, enterprise fraud risk assessment, control design, intelligence sharing with SAMA and the sector, system tuning, investigations and root-cause analysis, risk appetite breach escalation, alignment with cyber security and financial crime functions, and periodic senior management reporting. It also frames reporting-line choice and the maturity model against which the function's effectiveness is graded, binding all Member Organisations supervised by SAMA.

Sets the requirement for Member Organisations to define, approve and implement a fraud Intelligence Monitoring process drawing on internal and external sources to identify and monitor emerging fraud threats. Covers scanning, analysis and dissemination of threat information (modus operandi, actors, jurisdiction), acting on threats, periodic effectiveness evaluation, alignment with SAMA Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles, and sharing of intelligence and confirmed-fraud log-in data (device ID, IP) via the Sectorial Anti-Fraud Committee. Binds Member Organisations supervised by SAMA under the Counter-Fraud Framework.

Defines the obligation to set a Fraud Risk Appetite stating the level of fraud risk the Member Organisation will tolerate, derived from the Fraud Risk Assessment and aligned with overall enterprise risk appetite. Requires measures, thresholds and limits addressing impact on both the institution and its customers, Board endorsement and at least annual review, updates on material business model change, and, where a customer-impacting limit is breached, escalation to Senior Management plus a CEO-involved crisis management process meeting at least weekly until resolved. Binds Member Organisations and their boards.

Covers the requirement for Member Organisations to define, approve and monitor Key Risk Indicators measuring position against the agreed Fraud Risk Appetite and giving early warning of rising fraud exposure. KRIs must rest on a documented methodology tied to the risks identified in the Fraud Risk Assessment. Binds Member Organisations as part of the Counter-Fraud Programme's governance layer.

Sets out the Detect domain requirement for defined, approved, implemented and maintained fraud detection standards covering both internal and external fraud, proportionate to the Fraud Risk Assessment outcome and risk appetite. Specifies minimum content: data sources, detective controls (including Wholesale Payment Endpoint Security measures such as counterparty white-lists and real-time payment blocking), enabling systems, roles and responsibilities for calibration, triage and escalation, and rationale for adequacy; with periodic review, compliance monitoring and effectiveness measurement. Binds Member Organisations supervised by SAMA.

Requires Member Organisations to implement and maintain a Case Management System as the database and workflow for responding to fraud, recording suspected fraud alerts, internal and external reports, and investigations from initial assessment through to resolution. Sets minimum capabilities including restricted user access, configurable workflow aligned to the operating model and Fraud Response Plan, case ownership allocation, categorisation for trend analysis and reporting, tracking, recording of investigative steps, and retention of all case evidence. Sits alongside response actions such as transaction reversal, customer contact and identity verification before reinstating frozen services; binds Member Organisations.

This node covers the whistle-blowing obligation within SAMA's counter-fraud rules for Member Organisations, which must build and maintain multi-channel reporting processes allowing employees and third parties to raise suspected fraud without retaliation, aligned to SAMA's Whistle Blowing Policy for Financial Institutions. It sits alongside internal-fraud controls (employee access audit trails, staff activity logging, monitoring of unusual behaviour, oversight of payments to staff accounts) and the Counter-Fraud Policy requirements on ownership, board intent, three-lines-of-defence responsibilities and breach escalation. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organisations, including their branches and majority-owned subsidiaries.

SAMA's Shariah Governance Framework setting the minimum governance requirements for local banks conducting Islamic banking, covering objectives, definitions, allocation of duties across the board, executive management, Shariah committee, compliance, risk management and internal audit, plus Islamic window operations and product development. It aims to contain Shariah non-compliance risk and complements, rather than displaces, other SAMA regulations. It binds local banks licensed under the Banking Control Law that conduct Shariah-compliant banking.

Defined-term node for the Shariah committee, the body responsible for supervising and issuing binding decisions on the Shariah compliance of a bank's Islamic banking transactions. It covers composition and independence criteria, appointment and performance assessment via the nomination and remuneration committee, disclosure of member CVs, meeting frequency (at least quarterly), quorum and voting, attendance thresholds and minuting requirements, as well as its supervisory duties over Shariah compliance reports and internal Shariah audit findings. It binds banks conducting Islamic banking and their committee members.

Defined-term node for the bank's board of directors under the Shariah Governance Framework: the board holds primary responsibility for the overall framework and for the Shariah compliance of Islamic banking activities, approving the framework and all Shariah policies, exercising continuous oversight proportionate to the bank's size and complexity, supervising implementation of Shariah committee decisions, and providing risk-management mechanisms protecting profit-and-loss-sharing investment account holders. It also connects to the audit committee's role over internal Shariah audit deliverables.

Defined-term node for the bank's executive management under the Shariah Governance Framework, meaning senior executives who run the business and propose and implement strategic decisions. Their duties include referring Shariah issues to the Shariah committee with timely information and disclosure, monitoring and implementing the committee's decisions, providing ongoing Shariah and finance training to the board, committee and staff, and embedding a culture of Shariah compliance across Islamic banking activities. It binds management of local banks conducting Islamic banking.

Concept node for the internal Shariah audit function: an independent, periodic assessment providing objective assurance on the degree of Shariah compliance of the bank's Islamic operations, scoped by risk and materiality and performed by internal auditors with adequate Shariah knowledge (who may use the bank's Shariah officer without compromising objectivity). Deliverables are set by the board audit committee after consulting the Shariah committee, and findings go to both. It sits within the framework's internal control chapter alongside Shariah compliance and Shariah non-compliance risk management, and extends to at least annual audit of Islamic window operations.

Defines when two or more natural or legal persons must be aggregated as a single risk for large exposure purposes under SAMA's Large Exposure (LEX) Rules for Banks, on the basis of a control relationship, economic interdependence, or any other connection the bank assesses as constituting a single risk. It sets illustrative economic-interdependence indicators (contagion of financial difficulty, linked insolvency, common funding source), allows a bank to rebut connectedness by demonstrating to SAMA that the counterparty can find alternative partners or funding, and sets a 5% of eligible capital base threshold above which economic-interdependence screening is expected. It binds banks in scope of the LEX Rules and drives both the large exposure limits and regulatory reporting.

Sets out the LEX Rules definitions — including Eligible Capital Base as the effective amount of Tier 1 capital under Basel III — which is the denominator for identifying a Large Exposure (10% or more) and for all exposure caps. It also carries the related caps applied against that base: 5% for individuals/sole proprietorships/partnerships, 25% bank-to-bank (15% where a D-SIB or G-SIB is involved), 25% for commercial undertakings majority owned by the Saudi Government, and an aggregate large exposure ceiling of 6 times eligible capital. Binds banks subject to SAMA's Large Exposure Rules.

Governs which credit risk mitigation techniques a bank may recognise when measuring exposure values for large exposure purposes: only unfunded credit protection and eligible financial collateral recognised under the standardised approach, with equities, convertible bonds and UCITS excluded, and IRB-only collateral not eligible. It also requires consistency (a CRM technique used for risk-based capital must be recognised for LEX) and sets treatment of maturity mismatches and on-balance sheet netting. Binds banks calculating exposure values under the LEX framework.

Anchors the LEX Rules to the Basel risk-based capital framework: banking book, trading book, exposure scope (on- and off-balance sheet plus counterparty credit risk instruments), eligible capital and CRM recognition all take their meaning from that framework and SAMA's Basel guidance documents. It is a definitional/cross-reference node rather than a standalone obligation, but it determines how banks measure exposures and capital for large exposure compliance.

Covers the scope, level of application and reporting hooks of the LEX Rules: they apply to locally incorporated banks, their foreign branches and subsidiaries, and foreign banks operating in KSA, on both consolidated and standalone bases at every tier of the banking group. Foreign bank branches under home-country consolidated supervision for credit concentration are largely carved out but must still document large exposure and concentration policies and report their 50 largest exposures under Section 7. Exposures to groups of connected counterparties are subject both to the limits and to the Section 7 regulatory reporting requirements.

Appendix material explaining systemically important bank classification — FSB's SIFI concept, the BCBS G-SIB methodology (cross-jurisdictional activity, interconnectedness, size, substitutability, complexity) and the D-SIB assessment framework adopted through named SAMA circulars, including annual list review and disclosure. Its operative consequence in the LEX Rules is the tighter 15% (rather than 25%) interbank exposure limit where the lending or counterparty bank is a D-SIB or G-SIB.

Node within the Respond domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework setting the requirement for Member Organisations to define, approve, implement and maintain a documented Fraud Response Plan governing how actual or suspected fraud incidents are detected, escalated, investigated and resolved, with root-cause review afterwards. It prescribes minimum content (alerting and reporting channels for customers, employees and third parties; roles and responsibilities; escalation and decision-making authority) and requires monitoring of compliance and periodic effectiveness measurement. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organisations and is expected to align with the enterprise incident management process; it is a fraud-governance obligation distinct from AML suspicious-transaction reporting.

Node requiring Member Organisations to set, approve and apply fraud-focused Due Diligence standards covering employees (including contractors), customers and third parties, so relationships outside fraud risk appetite are not established and fraud risk is managed for the life of the relationship. It includes Employee Due Diligence (identity confirmation, criminal, conflict-of-interest, qualification and prior-employment checks, at hiring, on role change and periodically on a risk basis) and Customer Due Diligence aimed at capturing and validating customer identity against external fraud. Standards must be aligned to the Fraud Risk Assessment, periodically reviewed and effectiveness-tested; note this is fraud-risk diligence and sits alongside, not in place of, AML/CTF CDD obligations.

Node requiring Member Organisations to define, approve, implement and maintain an authentication standard for customer, employee and third-party credentials and instructions, developed jointly by the Counter-Fraud Department and Cyber Security Team. The standard must reflect both the Fraud Risk Assessment and the Cyber Security Risk Assessment, cover digital and non-digital channels (online, mobile, phone, ATM, branch), and follow a risk-based approach with multi-factor authentication for higher-risk instructions or activity. It cross-refers to identity and access management and electronic banking controls in SAMA's Cyber Security Framework and binds SAMA-supervised Member Organisations.

Node imposing an immediate notification duty on Member Organisations to inform SAMA's General Department of Cyber Risk Control of new fraud typologies (whether or not a loss occurred) and significant fraud incidents, including significant external frauds and significant internal fraud or serious integrity misconduct by employees. Its purpose is sector-level containment so other customers and institutions are protected. It sits alongside the framework's Management Information and senior-management reporting expectations, and is a supervisory reporting obligation separate from AML suspicious-transaction reporting to the FIU.
lookup_terms: General Department of Cyber Risk Control

data.summary: Node concerning sector-level counter-fraud coordination as reflected in the Counter-Fraud Framework's organisational requirements: Member Organisations must maintain a Counter-Fraud Department responsible for day-to-day operation of the Counter-Fraud Programme, including sharing counter-fraud intelligence with SAMA and other sector participants. Related material covers the department's mandate (risk assessment, control design, system tuning, investigations, risk-appetite monitoring, senior-management reporting) and the Counter-Fraud Maturity Model used to assess implementation. Binds SAMA-supervised Member Organisations; open it for intelligence-sharing and counter-fraud organisational structure questions.

Node anchoring the Governance domain of the Counter-Fraud Framework and its interaction with SAMA's wider governance instruments: the Board and executive leadership are accountable for the Counter-Fraud Programme, comprising a Counter-Fraud Strategy, Counter-Fraud Policy and a Governance Structure proportionate to the organisation's size and complexity. It requires a dedicated Counter-Fraud Governance Committee chaired by an Executive Committee member, with minimum representation including the head of counter-fraud, CRO, COO and head of digital. Binds SAMA-supervised Member Organisations and should be read with SAMA's IT governance and cyber security frameworks.
lookup_terms: board and senior management accountability fraud

data.summary: This node covers the internal control and Islamic window provisions of SAMA's Shariah governance framework for banks, comprising the Shariah compliance function, Shariah non-compliance risk management and internal Shariah audit, plus the separate requirements applying where Islamic banking is conducted through a window within a conventional bank. It requires segregation of Shariah-compliant assets and funding sources, separate accounting records, separate (at least monthly) financial statements for Islamic operations, and at least annual internal audit. It binds SAMA-licensed banks, their boards and audit committees, Shariah committees, risk and internal audit functions.

This node sets the Shariah product development process within SAMA's Shariah governance framework: all Shariah issues in product design, structuring and process must be referred to the Shariah committee, which must approve every Islamic banking product and any subsequent amendment and review the related legal contracts and documents. It distinguishes pre-product approval (research, structuring, contract review before launch) from post-product approval review after offering. It binds banks conducting Islamic banking activity, their executive management and Shariah committees.

SAMA guidelines explaining how founders/shareholders apply for a licence to engage in consumer microfinance activity under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation. It sets submission instructions (unmodified forms, authorised submitters, soft-copy filing, accuracy of information) and lists the documents required, including articles of association, shareholder list, organisational structure, feasibility study and business plan, fit and proper forms, and a bank guarantee equal to 20% of minimum capital. Providing false or incomplete information is treated as a breach of the Finance Companies Control Law and can lead to refusal or cancellation of the licence.

This node isolates the fit and proper documentation element of the consumer microfinance licence application: a SAMA Fit and Proper Form must be completed and signed by each founding member and by each candidate for board membership and board sub-committees, and approved by the person authorised to submit the application. Where a founding member is a legal entity, a form is also required for every natural or legal person holding 5% or more of that entity. It binds applicants, founders, significant indirect owners and proposed board/committee members of prospective finance companies.

SAMA's Large Exposure (LEX) Rules governing concentration risk for banks: board-level responsibility and policies, stress testing, systems to identify, measure and monitor exposures, maximum exposure limits by counterparty type, exemptions, credit risk mitigation treatment, and quarterly regulatory reporting before and after CRM. Limits are measured against the eligible capital base disclosed in the latest published quarterly financial statements. The rules bind SAMA-licensed banks and their boards.

This node covers the quantitative limits and exemptions under the Large Exposure Rules: a 15% eligible capital cap on exposures to a single non-bank counterparty (excluding individuals, sole proprietorships and commercial undertakings majority owned by the Saudi government), with exemptions for Saudi sovereign, SAMA, entities connected with the Saudi Government, GCC central governments and central banks, intra-day interbank exposures and consolidated intra-group entities. Non-banking financial-sector subsidiaries remain subject to a 25% limit, and exposures hedged by credit derivatives are recognised against the protection provider even where the original exposure is exempt. Any exposure not expressly exempted is fully subject to the limits; banks must still monitor exempted exposures internally.
lookup_terms: entities connected with the Saudi Government

data.summary: This node sets out how banks must measure the exposure value of positions for large exposure purposes under SAMA's Large Exposure (LEX) Rules, covering derivatives-based positions (including sold credit protection, credit-linked notes and options) and exposures arising from clearing activity with a central counterparty. It specifies that option exposure values are default-driven rather than the risk-based capital measure, and tabulates CCP-related items (trade exposures, segregated vs non-segregated initial margin, funded/unfunded default fund contributions, equity stakes) with their applicable exposure values. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA when computing exposures against the large exposure limit.

This node identifies the measurement basis for exposures that carry counterparty credit risk under SAMA's Large Exposure Rules, requiring exposure at default computed under the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) as adopted by SAMA circulars, with separate treatment for banking book non-derivative assets and securities financing transactions. It also flags the interim SFT measurement position pending SAMA's adoption of the revised comprehensive approach, and the eligibility boundaries for credit risk mitigation in the large exposures context. It binds SAMA-licensed banks measuring counterparty exposures for the large exposure limit.

This node governs how trading book positions are valued and aggregated for large exposure purposes, requiring trading book and banking book exposures to the same counterparty to be summed. It scopes the limit to single-counterparty default risk (so debt and equity positions are captured, but commodity and currency concentrations are not) and prescribes conversion of swaps, futures, forwards, credit derivatives and options into counterparty positions, with a default-based valuation rule for options. It binds SAMA-supervised banks maintaining trading book positions.

This node defines covered bonds for SAMA large exposure purposes and sets the conditions under which a bank's holding may be assigned a reduced exposure value (not less than 20% of nominal) rather than the default 100%, with the issuing bank treated as the counterparty. Eligibility depends on cover pool composition, loan-to-value ceilings for residential and commercial real estate, and a minimum 10% over-collateralisation, tested at inception and throughout the bond's life, plus operational requirements for eligible CRE/RRE collateral. It binds banks holding covered bonds under the LEX Rules.

This node governs how banks attribute exposures held through funds, securitisation vehicles and other structures with underlying assets for large exposure purposes. It permits treating the structure itself as a distinct counterparty where each underlying exposure is below 0.25% of the eligible capital base, otherwise requiring identification of the underlying counterparties, and obliges banks to identify third parties (originator, fund manager, liquidity provider, protection seller) that constitute an additional risk factor and may form a group of connected counterparties. It binds SAMA-supervised banks investing in such structures.

This node explains the look-through approach (LTA) for exposures held indirectly through structures: when a bank must identify and assign exposures to underlying counterparties, when it may instead assign the amount to the structure, and when unidentified underlyings must be assigned to the "unknown client" and aggregated as a single counterparty subject to the large exposure limit. It also prescribes pro rata attribution for pari passu structures, a tranche-based method where investors rank differently, and an anti-arbitrage expectation where LTA is not applied. It binds SAMA-supervised banks with fund, securitisation or similar structured investments.

A concept node within SAMA's large exposures rules covering how banks treat exposures to central counterparties. Clearing-related exposures to qualifying CCPs (QCCPs, defined consistently with the risk-based capital framework) are exempt from the large exposure limits but remain subject to quarterly regulatory reporting, while exposures to non-QCCPs must be aggregated (clearing plus other exposures) and respect the general 25% eligible capital limit; the connected-counterparty grouping concept does not apply to clearing-related CCP exposures. Binds banks licensed by SAMA and their boards, which retain oversight of large exposures and concentration risk.

Reference node to the Basel Committee's April 2014 supervisory framework for measuring and controlling large exposures, which underpins SAMA's large exposure rules (including the CCP treatment in the appendix). It informs the exemptions and limits SAMA applies — intraday interbank exemption, intra-group exposures within KSA excluded from limits with non-bank financial subsidiaries capped at 25% of eligible capital, and quarterly reporting before and after credit risk mitigation. Relevant to banks calculating and reporting exposures on the basis of the latest published quarterly eligible capital base.
lookup_terms: supervisory framework for measuring and controlling large exposures

data.summary: SAMA guidance setting out how founders or their authorised representatives apply for a licence to conduct debt-based crowdfunding, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and the Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding. It specifies the unmodifiable application form, the document checklist (articles of association, organisational structure, fit and proper forms for founders and board/committee candidates, feasibility study and business plan, an irrevocable bank guarantee for 20% of minimum capital, third-party and related-party draft contracts), the submission channel and the licensing procedure. Binds applicants seeking SAMA authorisation; false or omitted material information is treated as a breach of the Finance Companies Control Law and may cause rejection or licence cancellation.

SAMA's Rules on Outsourcing (Version 2.0) set the governance, policy, due diligence, contractual, business continuity, monitoring, audit and documentation requirements for banks entering outsourcing arrangements, including annual prudential reporting and notification of regulatory breaches. They apply to banks licensed under the Banking Control Law, including local and foreign bank branches and banking subsidiaries in Saudi Arabia, and cover domestic, foreign, third-party and related-party providers. Insourcing under the bank's direct supervision and certain arrangements (market data vendors, clearing/settlement, correspondent banking, utilities) fall outside scope; SAMA retains unrestricted access to outsourcing-related records and data.

Concept node for "Material" outsourcing under SAMA's outsourcing rules — the classification that triggers heightened obligations: board-approved policy coverage, documented business case and risk-impact assessment, separate contingency plans, regular internal audit reporting to the Board or Audit Committee, possible external expert assessment at SAMA's request, enhanced register content, and immediate notification to SAMA on termination with transition arrangements. Binds banks and their boards, which must record the materiality assessment and its date for each arrangement.

Section of SAMA's outsourcing rules dealing specifically with foreign bank branches, for both Material and non-Material outsourcing. It requires KSA business to be booked in the Saudi branch absent SAMA agreement, sufficient local staffing for local control, and prohibits outsourcing of key management decision-making, compliance and AML/CFT functions; other functions may be outsourced proportionately. Outsourcing to head office or a related party does not reduce the branch's or its management's legal and regulatory obligations in Saudi Arabia, and such arrangements must be audited annually with findings — and any other regulator's control reports — shared with SAMA.

A section of SAMA's outsourcing rules for banks addressing arrangements with third-party service providers located outside the Kingdom, including the additional country, legal, confidentiality and data-access risks such arrangements create. It requires banks to obtain SAMA's written no-objection before entering cross-border outsourcing and to submit specified information (function, materiality classification, rationale for not performing it in KSA, provider details, data nature and disposal). It also sits alongside requirements on business continuity/contingency planning for material outsourcing, unrestricted SAMA and auditor access to outsourcing records and data, and ongoing monitoring of the provider relationship. It binds banks licensed in Saudi Arabia.
lookup_terms: banking secrecy Article 19 Banking Control Law

data.summary: A Governor's circular to banks operating in the Kingdom announcing the launch of the Sarie instant payments system and setting compliance expectations for participants. It requires members to sign the system participation agreement and follow the technical, operational and service-level documents, observe transaction caps (single transaction limit and quick transfer limit), apply the capped customer transfer fees, and follow the Sarie brand and customer journey guidance across channels and staff training. It binds banks participating in the national payments infrastructure.

SAMA regulation establishing the licensing and supervisory framework for banks' physical branch networks, covering opening, closing and relocating branches, service centers and remittance centers, including zone classification, use of inactive licenses, SAMA prior approval requirements and approval for branches abroad. It replaces the Annual Branch Expansion Plan with a board-approved Branch Network Policy. It applies to all locally incorporated banks and to branches of foreign banks licensed in the Kingdom that plan to expand beyond three branches.
lookup_terms: zones large medium small cities rural

data.summary: The defined-document requirement within the Branch Network Regulation obliging each bank to prepare a Branch Network Policy governing opening, closing and relocation of branches, service centers and remittance centers, and covering customer service strategy (including elderly and disabled customers), target market, delivery channels, digital modes, financial inclusion and CSR in priority areas. The policy must be approved by the Board (or a delegated board committee), or by the chief executive/authorized senior executive at head office for foreign bank branches, and submitted to SAMA within four months with specified historical data. Once approved, it replaces the Annual Branch Expansion Plan; it does not cover ATMs.

The definitional and policy-content provisions of the Branch Network Regulation dealing with financial inclusion, including the zone classification of locations by population and the designation of Zone 3 (small cities) and Zone 4 (rural areas) as Priority Areas, plus definitions of remittance centers, ATMs, digital modes and Customer. Banks' Branch Network Policies must address outreach, digital delivery channels and serving priority areas as corporate social responsibility. It binds banks subject to the Branch Network Regulation.

SAMA rules governing debt-based crowdfunding, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law framework, defining the activity, the licensed joint-stock Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company, the Platform, Institutional Beneficiaries, Participants and Eligible Participants (with net-asset, experience and certification tests). They set operational obligations including segregation of Participants' funds in a dedicated Finance Amount Management Account, prohibition of cash repayment, controls on automatic participation options, and disclosure/risk-acknowledgment duties toward Participants and Institutional Beneficiaries. They bind companies licensed to conduct debt-based crowdfunding in the Kingdom.

Concept node covering the initial margin obligation for non-centrally cleared derivatives under SAMA's adoption of the BCBS-IOSCO margin framework. It addresses how the required amount is determined (approved quantitative portfolio model versus the standardised margin schedule, including the net standardised formula using NGR), the prohibition on switching between methods to obtain more favourable terms, timing of collection at trade inception and on subsequent exposure changes, and the default bar on re-use of collected collateral. It binds SAMA-supervised banks and other covered entities transacting bilateral derivatives.

Concept node on margin calculation standards for bilateral derivatives, drawn from the same SAMA margin framework; the captured context focuses on the 99% confidence / 10-day horizon calibration including a stress period, the default expectation that banks use the standardised schedule, and the requirement for SAMA approval, validation and internal governance before any model may be used. Variation margin applies to all components of cross-currency swaps even where initial margin carve-outs apply. Binds SAMA-supervised banks and covered counterparties.

Concept node on collateral eligibility, substitution and treatment of provided initial margin under the SAMA margin framework for non-centrally cleared derivatives. It covers dispute resolution over collateral valuation, conditions for substituting alternative collateral (including sufficiency after haircuts), the requirement to exchange initial margin on a gross basis, and holding arrangements ensuring immediate availability on counterparty default and protection of the posting party in insolvency. Binds banks and covered entities collecting or posting margin.

Framework node for SAMA's implementation of the BCBS-IOSCO margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, organised by Elements (scope, calculation methods, collateral, treatment of provided margin). Scope covers all non-centrally cleared derivatives except physically settled FX forwards and swaps, with a specific carve-out for the fixed physically settled FX legs of cross-currency swap principal exchanges; repos and securities lending are outside scope. Binds SAMA-supervised banks and covered entities dealing in bilateral derivatives.
lookup_terms: physically settled FX forwards and swaps exemption

data.summary: Concept node setting the general prohibition on re-hypothecation, re-pledge or re-use of cash and non-cash collateral collected as initial margin, and the narrow conditional exception. Re-use is permitted only to hedge the collector's derivatives position arising from customer transactions, requires case-by-case SAMA approval, express written customer consent after disclosure of the right to refuse and of insolvency risks, an option to individually segregate, liquidity-risk regulation of the collector, and customer-asset segregation by both collector and third party. Binds initial margin collectors supervised by SAMA and, by contract, downstream third parties.

SAMA guidance and prudential return package for the Amended Liquidity Coverage Ratio, aligned to the January 2013 BCBS LCR standard and cross-referenced to that document's paragraph numbering, with general and specific guidance, FAQs and national discretions. It governs HQLA composition, diversification and concentration limits, the 30-calendar-day grace period for assets that become ineligible, and reporting mechanics (monthly submission due 30 days after month end, with transitional relief for the first submission). Binds Saudi banks; foreign bank branches are excluded from the monthly return requirement.

SAMA's amended Liquidity Coverage Ratio package (guidance notes, prudential return, FAQs and national discretions) implementing the Basel III LCR standard, cross-referenced paragraph-by-paragraph to the BCBS January 2013 text. It requires banks to hold unencumbered high-quality liquid assets at least equal to total net cash outflows over a 30-day stress horizon, with a 100% minimum absent financial stress, and permits temporary drawdown below 100% in stress subject to SAMA assessment. It binds Saudi banks for LCR reporting and monitoring, alongside continued NSFR reporting under SAMA's 2012 circular.

The BCBS January 2013 standard "Basel III: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio and liquidity risk monitoring tools", used as the source text that SAMA's amended LCR guidance mirrors and cites by paragraph. It sets the eligibility criteria and haircuts for Level 1, Level 2A and Level 2B assets (including corporate debt, covered bonds and qualifying common equity) and the rules for jurisdictions with insufficient HQLA. It binds Saudi banks indirectly, as adopted and modified through SAMA's circular — notably SAMA currently does not recognise Level 2B assets in LCR computation.

The alternative liquidity approaches (ALA) framework for jurisdictions whose domestic-currency supply of Level 1 (or Level 1 and Level 2) assets is insufficient to meet aggregate bank demand. It sets cumulative qualifying criteria — structural insufficiency, mitigation capacity, and commitment to supervisory monitoring, disclosure, self-assessment and peer review — assessed against a fully implemented 100% LCR. It is a jurisdiction-level eligibility regime; the context notes SAMA has not adopted any ALA option.

Sets out the three alternative treatment options for HQLA shortfalls (central bank committed liquidity facilities, foreign-currency HQLA, and expanded Level 2 use) and the supervisory cap on their usage, expressed as a percentage of required domestic-currency HQLA including any regulatory buffer above 100%. It also imposes supervisor-level obligations on monitoring, disclosure and periodic self-assessment where options are used. Relevant to Saudi banks only as background — SAMA has not utilised any alternative treatment option.

Addresses the LCR position of Shari'ah compliant banks, which cannot hold interest-bearing debt securities, by allowing national supervisors discretion to recognise Shari'ah compliant products such as Sukuk as alternative HQLA, subject to conditions and haircuts. The treatment must not result in a lower effective LCR standard than that applied to other banks. The context records that SAMA has not utilised any option under the alternative treatment.

Defines the LCR denominator — total net cash outflows as total expected outflows less total expected inflows over the 30-day stress horizon, including interest expected to be received and paid. It sets the run-off and roll-over factors for deposits, operational and cash management balances, secured funding by collateral type and counterparty, and additional requirements such as 100% treatment of net derivatives cash outflows. It binds Saudi banks in computing and reporting the LCR.

Defines the Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company as a joint-stock company licensed by SAMA to raise funds from Participants via a platform for lending to an Institutional Beneficiary, and sets out core operating duties attaching to that licensed entity. Obligations covered include segregation of Participant funds in a dedicated Finance Amount Management Account, electronic-only repayment (cash repayment prohibited), consent controls for auto-participation, and platform disclosure of business nature, risks and party relationships. It binds licensed DBC companies under the Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding, read with the Finance Companies Control Law.
lookup_terms: Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding

data.summary: Defines the Debt-Based Crowdfunding Platform as the web-based or digital channel (websites, mobile apps) operated by a licensed DBC company to conduct the crowdfunding activity, and anchors the related defined terms (Participant, Eligible Participant, Institutional Beneficiary). It is the medium through which disclosure, risk acknowledgements (pop-up consent) and pledges to Participants and Institutional Beneficiaries must be delivered before use. Relevant to determining when a digital interface falls within the licensed activity and triggers platform-level disclosure duties.

Sets the risk management obligations of a Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company: a board-approved, annually updated written risk policy covering an enumerated risk taxonomy (credit, market, operational, legal, reputational, technology, fraud, information security, cyber, ML/TF, outsourcing, platform cessation, and Participant-protection/default risk), plus procedures for identification, assessment, monitoring, escalation and reporting. Adjacent provisions cover external auditor appointment with SAMA non-objection, business continuity, 10-year record retention, staffing, and compliance with AML/CTF laws and SAMA information-security and financial-crime instructions. Binds the licensed DBC company's board and senior management.

Covers the supervisory and compliance perimeter for Debt-Based Crowdfunding Companies: duties to provide SAMA with information, documents and access to premises and digital data, the prohibition on concealment, SAMA's inspection powers and its ability to appoint a third party at the company's expense. It also requires internal controls and records evidencing compliance, confidentiality limits on third-party disclosure, and sits alongside licensing provisions (five-year term, renewal, revocation grounds, fees) and the requirement for written policies including outsourcing. Binds licensed DBC companies and their staff.

Sets the due diligence and credit-assessment duties owed in respect of the Institutional Beneficiary: AML/CTF-aligned policies verifying legal status, identity (including establishment) and address, conflict-of-interest checks, and assessment of solvency, credit history, existing financing, past performance and business plan. Results must be communicated to Participants as part of the risk assessment, and the platform must disclose credit-rating standards, fee details, eligibility criteria, default and material-change mechanisms, and contingency arrangements. Binds the licensed DBC company; note the overlap between the finance-side creditworthiness test and AML/CTF customer due diligence on a corporate borrower (KYB).

SAMA's margin framework for non-centrally cleared derivatives, setting out instrument scope (all such derivatives except physically settled FX forwards and swaps, with special treatment for the principal exchange leg of cross-currency swaps) and entity scope. Covered entities are financial firms and systemically important non-financial entities (aggregate month-end average notional for March–May exceeding SAR 30 billion group-wide, excluding inter-affiliate trades); central banks, sovereigns, MDBs, the BIS and non-systemic non-financial firms are excluded. Requirements to exchange initial and variation margin apply only to transactions between two covered entities.

Guidance node within SAMA's amended Liquidity Coverage Ratio package setting how banks classify natural-person deposits as stable or less stable and the outflow assumptions applied over the 30-day stress horizon. It records KSA-specific positions, notably that there is no effective deposit insurance scheme in the Kingdom (so insurance-linked lower run-off treatment is unavailable) and that foreign-currency deposits are not treated as less stable, with run-off rates following the Basel Committee's January 2013 standard. It binds banks licensed in Saudi Arabia when completing the LCR prudential return.

LCR guidance node defining unsecured wholesale funding (liabilities from non-natural persons not secured on designated assets, excluding derivative obligations) and the run-off factors applied by counterparty type within the 30-day horizon. It covers treatment of non-financial corporates, sovereigns, central banks, multilateral development banks and PSEs (20% or 40% depending on deposit insurance or equivalent public guarantee) and other legal-entity customers including banks, securities firms, insurers and fiduciaries at 100%. Applies to banks in the Kingdom reporting the amended LCR return; SAMA may also impose higher run-off on qualifying retail term deposits.

LCR guidance node addressing deposits held for operational purposes (clearing, custody, cash management) and the surrounding classification rules for stable and less stable deposits and deposit insurance criteria. It confirms SAMA's position that, absent deposit insurance in the Kingdom, the reduced run-off treatment conditional on an effective insurance scheme does not apply to Saudi banks, and that less stable buckets carry a minimum 10% run-off. Relevant to banks calculating LCR outflows and to supervisory review of bucket allocation.

LCR guidance node on funding treatment where obligations are collateralised by legal rights to designated assets, read against the definition of unsecured wholesale funding and the counterparty-based run-off factors in the same section. It sits within SAMA's adoption of the January 2013 Basel LCR standard and includes SAMA's discretion to apply a higher run-off to qualifying retail term deposits. Binds banks licensed in Saudi Arabia for LCR computation and prudential reporting.

The overarching SAMA circular and guidance notes implementing the Basel Committee's January 2013 Liquidity Coverage Ratio standard in Saudi Arabia, including general and specific guidance, the prudential return, FAQs and national discretions. It sets the HQLA definition and Level 1/Level 2/Level 2B composition caps, the phased minimum LCR path to 100%, and cross-references each requirement to the corresponding Basel paragraph; SAMA also continues NSFR monitoring under a separate 2012 circular. Binds Saudi banks completing the amended LCR prudential return.

SAMA rules (second edition) requiring banks to establish a Customer Care Department, replacing the earlier complaint-unit rules and setting the minimum standards for customer care, complaint handling and financial education. The department must be created by board decision, report directly to the bank's most senior executive, be independent of other departments, be adequately resourced, and contain at least three units: complaint handling, quality and performance analysis, and financial awareness and education. Applies to banks licensed to conduct banking business in the Kingdom, effective from the date stated in the circular.

A mandated sub-unit of the Customer Care Department that banks must establish under SAMA's Rules on Establishing the Customer Care Department in Banks (second edition, effective December 2022, replacing the earlier complaint-unit rules). It handles customer complaints as defined in the rules (any expression of dissatisfaction, written or oral, justified or not) and must offer multiple easily accessible intake channels published prominently on the bank's website and platforms, at minimum toll-free phone, website, mobile apps, email and branches. Binds banks licensed by SAMA to operate in the Kingdom.

One of the three minimum units banks must set up inside the Customer Care Department, focused on quality assurance and performance analysis of complaint handling, including root cause analysis of recurring complaints and measuring effectiveness of remediation policies. The surrounding rules also cover the department head's SAMA written no-objection before appointment, settlement authority for complaints below a stated riyal threshold, service-level agreements and escalation mechanisms with other departments (reviewed at least every two years), capacity analysis of staffing, and minimum professional certification and annual training for staff. Binds banks licensed by SAMA in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: no-objection for head of customer care

data.summary: The third mandatory unit of the bank's Customer Care Department, responsible for financial awareness and education of customers, aligned with the products and services the bank offers. The rules require a dedicated awareness/education policy that, at minimum, defines the staff member's duty to give the customer a full explanation of the product or service and all resulting obligations. Binds banks licensed by SAMA in the Kingdom.

A concept node for the international High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection, cited in the preamble of SAMA's Customer Care Department rules as the policy basis for accessible complaint-redress mechanisms, financial education, and clear disclosure of customer protections, rights and responsibilities. It is referenced as a standard informing SAMA's requirements rather than as a directly binding instrument; the binding obligations flow from the SAMA rules themselves on licensed banks.
lookup_terms: High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection

data.summary: A SAMA circular (re-issued by the Finance Companies Supervision Department to finance companies operating in the Kingdom) confirming that financial institutions remain bound by SAMA instructions communicated through official written correspondence or the official email of SAMA's administrative units. It clarifies that publication of circulars on SAMA's public portal does not relieve any supervised institution of its compliance obligations; compliance is required from the date of email transmission.

A concept node for SAMA's public circulars portal, announced in this circular as a transparency and financial-awareness initiative making SAMA's supervisory and regulatory instructions available to the public and practitioners. The circular stresses the portal's limited legal effect: it is an informational channel and does not substitute for, or discharge compliance with, instructions formally served on institutions by letter or official SAMA email.

A SAMA supervisory circular reaffirming that all SAMA-supervised financial institutions must fully comply with customer personal data protection requirements, following SAMA's earlier circular on the Personal Data Protection Law and issued data governance policies, controls and rules. It responds to observed practices of requiring individual customers to disclose personal data not necessary for the service or product, whether directly or via a third party. Institutions must align with SDAIA and NDMO requirements and SAMA instructions, review existing disclosure practices, put in place controls ensuring data security and purpose limitation, and report the remedial steps taken to SAMA by the stated deadline.

A SAMA circular to finance companies transmitting SOCPA-endorsed amendments and annual improvements issued by the IASB to international accounting and financial reporting standards, and directing compliance from the date the instructions were emailed. The covered changes touch IFRS 1 (first-time adoption — cumulative translation differences for subsidiaries), IFRS 9 (fees in the 10% derecognition test for modified/exchanged debt), IAS 41 (cash flows in fair value measurement), IAS 37 (cost of fulfilling an onerous contract), IAS 16 (proceeds before intended use), and IFRS 3 (business combinations). It binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom and points them to SOCPA's international standards page for the texts.

A SAMA circular mandating biometric authentication when a customer relationship is initiated or established remotely, supplementing existing requirements to identify and verify an individual customer's identity using documents, data or information from a reliable and independent source. Supervised institutions must adopt the biometric verification feature at a verification assurance level of high or above and complete integration with the approved service provider by the stated deadline, notifying SAMA and raising any challenges beforehand. It binds banks (local banks, foreign bank branches, digital banks), finance companies and payment companies operating in the Kingdom.

Nafath is the national digital identity authentication application referenced in this SAMA circular as the channel whose user verification mechanism has been upgraded to biometric authentication. SAMA requires supervised institutions to use this biometric feature, at a high or higher verification level, when establishing a customer relationship remotely, and to complete connectivity with the approved service provider by the stated deadline. Relevant to banks, finance companies and payment companies performing remote individual customer identity verification.

A SAMA circular addressed to exchange centers (money changers) in the Kingdom prohibiting an employee from holding two jobs at the same time at more than one exchange center, and reaffirming job localization (Saudization) requirements. It relies on SAMA's Law, the Rules Governing Money Changing Business (including provisions of Articles 14(b) and 21(b)), the requirements for appointment to senior positions in SAMA-supervised institutions, and the principles of conduct and work ethics. Exchange centers must verify compliance and rectify dual-employment cases within six months and notify SAMA, and must restrict all activity positions to Saudi nationals without seeking non-Saudi work permits elsewhere.

A SAMA circular reaffirming the mandatory professional certification requirement for staff of banks and their affiliated remittance centers, finance companies, and exchange centers, following earlier circulars on compulsory professional certifications and the updated target group for the Credit Advisor certification. It specifies the target populations: retail banking fundamentals certification for customer-facing bank staff (customer care, call centers, branch staff and managers), the Credit Advisor certification for bank and finance company staff directly involved in granting credit to individuals plus branch managers (excluding finance lease contract registration companies, the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company and support activity companies), and the exchange and remittance certification for front-line staff of bank remittance centers and exchange centers. Third-party contracted personnel are included; certification must be obtained within one year of joining, with a compliance rate of no less than the stated percentage.

A SAMA circular (1444) reaffirming the continuing obligation on supervised entities to meet mandatory professional certification requirements, here specifying the Credit Advisor professional certificate. It binds banks and finance companies in respect of staff directly involved in granting credit to individuals and branch managers, including persons engaged through third parties, while excluding finance lease contract registration companies, the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company and ancillary-services companies. The certificate must be obtained within one year of joining, with a compliance rate of not less than the stated threshold for covered staff.

Part of the same SAMA circular confirming continued compliance with mandatory professional certification requirements, covering the Retail Banking Fundamentals certificate. It applies to bank front-line staff dealing directly with customers — customer care, call centre, branch staff and branch managers — including individuals contracted through third parties, with the certificate to be obtained within one year of joining and a minimum compliance rate for covered employees.

The baseline user-verification and authentication controls in SAMA's cyber controls document for fintech business models, requiring multi-factor authentication at each login, OTP verification for defined transaction and account-status events, verification of phone-number ownership through a licensed trusted party, and session-timeout and single-device restrictions. These are security/authentication obligations on member organizations and are distinct from, and do not substitute for, AML/CTF customer due diligence and identification requirements.

Section 3 of SAMA's cyber controls document for member organizations providing e-wallets, lending products, crowdfunding or other fintech models, setting registration and onboarding requirements. It mandates one registration per phone number or National ID/Iqama per application, a secure user validation process, strong authentication via an independent licensed trusted party (e.g. National Single Sign-On for e-wallets), OTP verification to a verified number, SMS notifications on status changes, and secure deactivation/reactivation and device re-registration processes.

The one-time-password mechanism required under SAMA's fintech cyber controls, used both as a registration verification step and as transaction authentication. OTP is required for wallet-to-wallet transfers below a defined value, marketplace transactions, first-time bill and government service payments, password resets, wallet reactivations and risk-flagged transactions; for higher-value, IBAN, international and high-risk transfers, the OTP must be delivered through a different channel. Session-timeout controls apply to all issued OTPs and the defined value threshold is communicated and revised separately by SAMA memo.

The requirement in SAMA's fintech cyber controls that member organizations implement multi-factor authentication to authenticate each login to their applications. It sits alongside single-device assignment, disabling concurrent logins and OTP-based transaction verification, and binds any SAMA-supervised member organization offering e-wallet, lending, crowdfunding or other fintech services.

Defines the Red Team role within SAMA's Financial Sector ethical red teaming framework — the offensive testing party (staffed by the procured Red Teaming Provider) that simulates realistic adversary attacks against a Member Organization's critical information assets. It sits alongside the Green Team (SAMA IT Risk of Financial Sector Supervision, which approves the provider and appoints a Test Manager), the White Team (a maximum of five internal SPOCs, led by a White Team Leader, who control and can halt the exercise) and the Blue Team (the organization's monitoring/SOC function, kept unaware). Binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA that are in scope of the framework, and shapes their contracting, scoping and escalation duties.

Sets out who may act as the external Red Teaming Provider and the selection, procurement and contracting expectations — proven experience and references, independent quality feedback, certified staff, and a documented red teaming methodology, governance, QA and risk management process. Provider selection requires Green Team (SAMA) approval before the Member Organization procures, with NDA, liability and Letter of Authorization terms agreed. Binds Member Organizations in their supplier selection and, contractually, the provider itself.

Explains the Cyber Kill Chain as the conceptual attack model underpinning the framework, with seven stages from reconnaissance through weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, to actions on objective, and expects defensive measures at each stage. It also distinguishes red teaming (resilience against realistic attacks, TTP-based, detection and response focus) from penetration testing (vulnerability oversight, predefined scope, preventive controls). Used by Member Organizations and Red Teaming Providers to structure attack scenarios and the evaluation report.
