Covers the scenario phase (up to five weeks) in which the Green Team supplies sector-wide and national threat intelligence, the White Team supplies internal/incident intelligence, and the Red Teaming Provider combines these with its own external sources to build high-level then detailed attack scenarios mapped to critical information assets. Scenarios, strategy and TTPs require Green Team agreement, and the final red teaming plan must also set escalation procedures and communication protocols. Binds Member Organizations and their providers during test preparation.

Defines the Remediation Plan the White Team must draft after the exercise, based on the Red Team Evaluation Report and the Blue Team Report, setting out agreed improvements, risk-based priorities and a roadmap for prevention, detection, response and recovery capabilities. Progress must be monitored and reported periodically to the Member Organization's Cyber Security Committee and to the Green Team (SAMA). Also covers the replay sessions for IT staff and Senior Management that feed awareness and remediation.

Specifies the Red Team Evaluation Report produced by the Red Teaming Provider at the end of the exercise: scope and out-of-scope items, control framework references, execution methodology and kill chain/TTPs used, timeline, tools, risk rating method, recommendations, conclusions and evidence appendices, classified Confidential and shared only via secure channels to the White, Blue and Green Teams. It follows the reporting step after test execution and the White Team Leader's decisions on detection, continuation or stopping the test. It is the primary input to the Remediation Plan.

A discrete set of additional cyber/fraud controls that SAMA imposes on lending platforms on top of the general registration, onboarding and transaction controls in the same circular, covering verification that the disbursement IBAN belongs to the loan applicant, use of an authorised digital signature provider, and creation and custody of promissory notes through a national trusted party. It binds Member Organizations under SAMA supervision that offer lending products via digital applications (including fintech/finance company models). Relevant to loan origination integrity and fraud prevention rather than credit underwriting or consumer-disclosure duties.

The onboarding and general security control set applied to e-wallet and similar fintech applications under SAMA supervision, covering one-application-per-phone-number/National ID registration, strong authentication via an independent trusted party, multi-factor authentication at login, OTP triggers for wallet-to-wallet, bill, marketplace, IBAN and international transfers, and out-of-band OTP for higher-value or high-risk transactions. It also addresses terms and conditions/data privacy consent, inactive account policy, fraud handling, SMS notification content, and board-approved internal policies. Binds Member Organizations providing e-wallets, lending, crowdfunding or other fintech models.

SAMA's Financial Entities Ethical Red Teaming (F.E.E.R.) Framework, setting out a four-phase intelligence-led cyber attack simulation process (preparation, threat intelligence/scenario development, execution, lessons learned) with defined roles for the Green, White, Red and Blue Teams. It also specifies selection and procurement requirements for external Red Teaming Providers, including experience, references, certified staff, methodology, governance and risk management. Applies to SAMA-supervised Member Organizations directed to undertake red teaming exercises.

Defines the Green Team as the SAMA-side body (IT Risk of Financial Sector Supervision) that oversees red teaming exercises, appoints the Test Manager and Backup Test Manager, approves selection of the Red Teaming Provider, and supplies sector-specific threat intelligence. It sits outside the Member Organization and provides guidance and oversight rather than accountability for test outcomes. Relevant to understanding the supervisory role and approval gates in the F.E.E.R. process.
lookup_terms: SAMA IT Risk Financial Sector Supervision

data.summary: Defines the White Team within the Member Organization — a limited group (maximum five) of security and business experts led by a White Team Leader, being the only staff aware of the red teaming test and the single points of contact. The White Team contracts and manages the Red Teaming Provider, defines scope and critical information assets, monitors execution, and decides whether to stop, adjust or continue a test when detected by the Blue Team; it also organises debriefing and the replay exercise. Binds the Member Organization as the accountable internal owner of the exercise.

Defines the Blue Team as the Member Organization's cyber security monitoring function (e.g. SOC) that monitors and analyses security alerts, is expected to detect the Red Team's simulated attacks and invoke incident response procedures, and is generally unaware that a test is underway. In the lessons learned phase the Blue Team produces its own report of alerts detected, actions taken and recommendations, and participates with the Red Team in the chronological replay exercise. Its performance is the primary measure of detection and response capability assessed by the exercise.

A defined deliverable within SAMA's ethical red teaming (F.E.E.R.) framework: the Blue Team's own report on a completed red teaming test, covering alerts and events detected, actions taken and their outcomes, plus improvement recommendations. It is produced alongside the Red Teaming Provider's report and feeds the joint replay exercise, 360-degree feedback and lessons-learned phase. It binds the Member Organization's monitoring function (e.g. SOC) as part of the test lifecycle coordinated by the White Team.

A defined term in the glossary of SAMA's ethical red teaming framework, describing security testing that mimics real-world attacks against live systems and data to circumvent security features, typically chaining multiple vulnerabilities. It is distinguished from Red Teaming, which is a broader scenario-based simulation of adversarial compromise of missions and business processes. Relevant to Member Organizations scoping cyber resilience testing obligations.
lookup_terms: Green Team / White Team / Blue Team / Red Team

data.summary: SAMA's Banks Remuneration Rules set minimum requirements and supervisory guidance for bank remuneration policies, procedures and practices, aimed at managing risks (including misconduct risk) rather than fixing absolute pay levels. They supersede the 2010 Rules on Compensation Practices and require compliance with any regulatory caps set by SAMA or other authorities. They bind all locally incorporated licensed banks, with group-level application to majority-owned financial-sector subsidiaries in and outside KSA (subject to host-country law).

The core governance obligation under the Banks Remuneration Rules: a written Remuneration Policy for Senior Management approved by the General Assembly and a separate policy for all other employees approved by the Board, designed to ensure prudent management of remuneration-related risk. Prescribes minimum policy content including objectives, scope (regular, contractual and outsourced staff), pay structure and mix, perquisites, an approval authority matrix, and the role of control and HR functions in misconduct identification and reporting. Binds banks' Boards, General Assemblies and Nomination and Remuneration Committees, with independent annual review and reporting to SAMA.

Defines and mandates ex post remuneration adjustment tools: malus (reducing unvested deferred remuneration before vesting) and clawback (recovery of variable remuneration already paid or vested). Banks must document such mechanisms in policies and procedures and apply them where risks, misconduct, material error, performance downturn or risk-management failure subsequently emerge, including clawback of unvested amounts on negative contributions during the vesting period. Binds banks' Boards and remuneration governance, with justifications for reductions submitted to SAMA with the compliance report.

Addresses how bank remuneration systems must capture misconduct risk alongside other hard-to-measure risks (liquidity, cost of capital, reputational, regulatory), using ex ante non-financial performance criteria such as compliance quality and fair treatment of customers, supported by training. Sets factors for determining individual accountability (proximity to misconduct, rank, motivation, negligence, history, supervisory failures, root cause) and severity indicators (fines, regulatory actions, losses, reputational and customer impact), including freezing awards during investigations. Binds banks' Boards, senior management, control functions and HR under the Banks Remuneration Rules.

Section of SAMA's remuneration rules for banks setting out the requirement to operate an objective, documented performance measurement system feeding into performance-based pay, and the related remuneration structure requirements (fixed/variable mix, bonus pools, control-function independence, risk adjustment). It requires appraisal processes free of undue influence and conflicts of interest, weighting of conduct and regulatory-compliance risks, and prohibits guaranteed minimum bonuses. Binds banks licensed by SAMA, their boards and remuneration committees.

Reporting and supervisory-review provisions of SAMA's bank remuneration rules, requiring banks to file a semiannual Compliance Report assessing alignment with the rules, with gap analysis and action plans, plus remuneration breakdowns and data on the top 12 highest-paid employees. It sets filing deadlines (before 31 March and 31 August), submission of the annual independent remuneration review results, and SAMA's powers to require rectification, additional capital/liquidity, penalties or limits on total remuneration. Binds banks, their boards and Nomination and Remuneration Committees.

SAMA rules governing Profit Sharing Investment Accounts (PSIA) offered by banks and Islamic windows, defining PSIA, restricted vs unrestricted accounts, Investment Account Holders (IAH), and reserves (PER, IRR). They cover how PSIA funding may be raised via Mudarabah and Wakalah contracts, loss-bearing by IAH absent bank negligence/misconduct/fraud/breach, product awareness disclosures, and product governance including contract terms and conditions. Binds banks in KSA operating Shari'ah-compliant investment accounts and their Shari'ah Committees.

Defined-term node within the PSIA Rules describing Mudarabah as a partnership contract where the capital provider (Rabb-ul-Mal / IAH) supplies capital managed by the Mudarib (the bank), with profits shared on a pre-agreed ratio and losses borne by the capital provider unless caused by the bank's negligence, misconduct, fraud or breach. It underpins how banks may raise PSIA funding and how loss allocation and reserves (PER) operate. Relevant to banks and Islamic windows offering Shari'ah-compliant investment accounts.

Defined-term node within the PSIA Rules identifying Wakalah as an agency-based contract under which the bank acts as Wakeel for Investment Account Holders, as an alternative to Mudarabah for raising PSIA funding. It is relevant to determining the bank's role, fee/profit entitlement and liability posture in Shari'ah-compliant investment accounts. Applies to banks and Islamic windows offering PSIAs.

Defined-term node within the PSIA Rules describing Musharakah as a partnership where partners contribute capital to an enterprise, sharing profits as agreed and losses in proportion to capital contributed. It sits alongside the PSIA product governance requirements on disclosure, terms and conditions, and contract form that state parties' rights and loss-bearing circumstances. Relevant to banks and Islamic windows structuring Shari'ah-compliant products.
lookup_terms: loss sharing in proportion to capital

data.summary: A referenced external standard-setting body (Islamic Financial Services Board) whose standards SAMA cites as the basis for the 2022 update of the Related Parties Rules for Banks; the covering circular states the updated rules were aligned to IFSB standards and supersede the earlier version. IFSB standards are not directly binding in themselves here — the binding instrument is SAMA's Related Parties Rules, which apply to all local banks. Relevant when tracing the international-standards provenance of related-party definitions, control tests and exposure limits.

Cross-reference to SAMA's Rules on Large Exposures of Banks, which supply the measurement methodology and group-of-connected-counterparties concept used to size related-party exposures under the Related Parties Rules. In this context it drives hard caps (5% of eligible capital base for a non-bank related party, 10% for Saudi-listed non-bank related parties, up to 25% for non-banking financial-sector subsidiaries, 50% cumulative), immediate breach notification to SAMA with a remediation plan, security requirements under Article 9 of the Banking Control Law, and quarterly reporting of exposures above 5%. Binds all local banks; effective from 1 September 2022.

Reference to SAMA's Shariah Governance Framework (circular no. 41042498 dated 18/06/1441H, as amended), used in the Related Parties Rules to identify who counts as a Shariah Committee Member. That status pulls the member, their relatives, and entities/companies they own, direct or hold 5%+ in, into the "Related Party" definition and the associated exposure limits and reporting duties. Binds banks applying the related-party regime, particularly those with Shariah governance structures.

The foundational tier of SAMA's Financial Sector Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles, covering the planning, production, processing and dissemination of threat intelligence that underpins the strategic, operational and technical/tactical tiers. It includes duties such as classifying shared information under the Traffic Light Protocol per SAMA's Cybersecurity Communication Protocols, delivering actionable intelligence with defined actions/owners/timeframes, internal sharing with SOC and IT, and continuous improvement. Applies to Member Organizations, including where the CTI capability is outsourced; phasing of implementation is at the organization's discretion.

The strategic tier of SAMA's Financial Sector Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles, addressing the specialized practice of identifying the objectives, motivations and intent of threat actors. It sits on top of the Core CTI Principles and feeds board- and risk-level decision-making on sector resilience. Applies to Member Organizations, including those outsourcing CTI, with discretion over phased implementation.

The operational tier of SAMA's Financial Sector Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles, covering identification of threat actors' modus operandi, behaviours and techniques. It complements the Core, Strategic and Technical/Tactical tiers within a holistic CTI practice. Applies to Member Organizations, including where CTI is outsourced, with phased implementation left to their discretion.

A domain within SAMA's Financial Sector Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles covering the specialised CTI practice of identifying technical components and indicators of cyber attacks (as distinct from the Core, Strategic and Operational domains). It sits alongside expectations that intelligence be actionable, shared internally (e.g. with the SOC and IT) and classified under the Traffic Light Protocol. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA, including those that outsource their CTI capability, with phasing of implementation left to the organisation.

Concept node for the intelligence lifecycle that structures Domain 1 (Core CTI Principles): planning, collection, processing, analysis and dissemination of threat intelligence, plus continuous improvement. It underpins principles on defining CTI roles and responsibilities, collecting from diverse intelligence sources (OSINT, TECHINT, SOCMINT, HUMINT, deep/dark web), maintaining standard operating procedures, and processing/classifying and securely storing intelligence. Applies to Member Organizations, including where the CTI function is outsourced.

Concept node for the Traffic Light Protocol classification scheme as applied under the CTI Principles: all threat information produced by Member Organizations is to be classified using TLP, consistent with the SAMA Cybersecurity Communication Protocols. It governs how collected and produced intelligence is labelled, stored and how far it may be distributed when shared internally or with external parties. Relevant to any question about permissible onward sharing of threat information in the KSA financial sector.

Node referencing the SAMA FEER framework as a related instrument cited within the Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles context; the supplied material itself concerns the obligation to deliver actionable intelligence, share it with internal functions such as the SOC and IT, and continuously improve CTI methods. Use this node to trace links between CTI outputs and SAMA's threat-led testing/resilience expectations for Member Organizations. Confirm the FEER content in the underlying document, as the excerpt here does not set out its terms.

SAMA's updated Guidelines on the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Plan (ILAAP), superseding the 1438AH circular and effective from the 2021 ILAAP submission. They define the ILAAP as the bank's processes for identifying, measuring, managing and monitoring liquidity under SAMA liquidity risk regulations, and set governance expectations placing ultimate responsibility on the Board, with approval of the governance framework, risk appetite alignment and annual Board assessment of liquidity adequacy. They bind banks, which remain responsible for ensuring their ILAAP is sound, effective and proportionate to their nature, scale and complexity.

The liquidity stress-testing component of the ILAAP guidelines, including Annexure (1) on stress-testing and the Contingency Funding Plan. It requires banks to run regular stress tests identifying sources of liquidity strain, to test institution-specific, market-wide and combined scenarios, to check exposures against the board-set liquidity risk tolerance, and to analyse governance of scenario design, assumptions and how results feed risk frameworks, strategic planning and liquidity recovery. It also covers restrictions on intra-group liquidity transferability and aggregation of results into an overall liquidity adequacy view.

Defines and situates two Shari'ah-banking reserve mechanisms under SAMA's Profit Sharing Investment Accounts Rules: the Profit Equalization Reserve (appropriated from mudarabah profit to smooth returns to the mudarib and unrestricted IAHs) and the Investment Risk Reserve (appropriated from IAH profit after the mudarib's share, to absorb future investment losses). It ties these reserves to board oversight of reserve levels and fairness between existing and new IAHs, and to senior management policies on reserve management and reversion on write-off or recovery. Binds local SAMA-licensed banks conducting Shari'ah compliant banking that operate PSIAs.

Definitional node from SAMA's Profit Sharing Investment Accounts Rules setting out the Shari'ah Committee as the body supervising compliance with Shari'ah principles in the bank, with "Shari'ah Compliant" defined by reference to that committee's decisions. It sits alongside the Rules' other defined terms (Islamic Window, IAH, PSIA, Mudarabah, Musharakah, Wakalah) and the Rules' legal basis, objectives and scope. Applies to local Saudi banks licensed under the Banking Control Law that conduct Shari'ah compliant banking.
lookup_terms: Profit Sharing Investment Accounts Rules scope

data.summary: Covers the defined term Investment Account Holder (bank clients holding Shari'ah compliant investment accounts) and the allocation of risk between IAHs and the bank under PSIA arrangements. It distinguishes unrestricted from restricted PSIAs, explains the bank's role as Mudarib or Wakeel, and states that IAHs bear investment and counterparty losses except where the bank's fraud, negligence, misconduct or breach of contract is proven. Relevant to banks offering PSIA products and to the protection of IAH interests.

Sets the prudential treatment of PSIAs: banks must apply SAMA's regulatory capital requirements to risk-weight assets funded by PSIAs and correctly reflect PSIA funds in the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio. PSIA funds and PER/IRR reserves cannot count toward regulatory capital, concentration risk must be managed under the Large Exposures Rules, and outsourced management of IAH funds must comply with SAMA outsourcing rules. SAMA retains discretion to direct whether a given mudarabah, musharakah or wakalah arrangement is treated as a PSIA.
lookup_terms: risk weights assets funded by PSIA

data.summary: SAMA's Related Parties Rules for Banks (June 2022 update, aligned to IFSB standards) define related parties and impose governance, exposure-limit, security and reporting requirements on bank dealings with them, reinforcing Article 9 of the Banking Control Law. Key limits are 5% of eligible capital per non-bank related party (10% if Tadawul-listed, up to 25% for a non-banking financial-sector subsidiary) with a 50% cumulative cap, plus immediate breach notification to SAMA with a remediation plan. Binds all local banks; supersedes the earlier related parties rules circular.

Identifies the Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36, 11/04/1442AH) as one of the statutory bases, together with the Banking Control Law and its enforcing rules, on which SAMA issued the Related Parties Rules for Banks. Useful for tracing SAMA's rule-making authority and the instrument's hierarchy, effective date and supersession of the prior 1441AH circular. Relevant to anyone assessing the enforceability and legal footing of the Rules on licensed banks.

A component of SAMA's ILAAP Guidelines (Version 2.0, October 2020) addressing how banks must set, disclose and evidence liquidity risk limits and funding strategy by reference to the regulatory liquidity metrics — Liquidity Coverage Ratio, Net Stable Funding Ratio, Loan to Deposit Ratio and the SAMA Liquidity Ratio. It requires banks to distinguish regulatory minimum requirements from internally set treasury limits, to show limit positions under normal and stressed conditions, to reconcile limits to SAMA returns, and to present a board-approved three-year funding strategy. It also sets out how liquidity risk quantification must be performed (pricing, collateral, intraday/overnight, cross-entity and cross-currency, funding diversification) and compared against LCR/NSFR outcomes. It binds banks supervised by SAMA that are required to prepare an ILAAP.

The stress-testing element of SAMA's ILAAP Guidelines, including the annexure on stress-testing and the Contingency Funding Plan. It requires banks to run regular institution-specific, market-wide and combined scenarios to identify sources of liquidity strain, confirm exposures remain within the board-set liquidity risk tolerance, and assess impacts on cash flows, liquidity position, profitability and solvency; it also calls for a defined stress-testing programme across normative and economic perspectives, reverse stress-testing on a proportionate basis, at least annual review, and internal review/independent validation of the ILAAP. Binding on SAMA-supervised banks.

A June 2020 circular from SAMA's Finance Companies Supervision Department reinstating the compliance deadline for the standard (model) form of the individual vehicle finance lease contract, originally mandated by circular 41038534 and suspended in April 2020 as a COVID-19 relief measure. Lessors must adopt the model form and complete internal procedures by 30/11/1441H (21 July 2020), and may not conclude contracts that depart from or amend that form. Binds finance companies acting as lessors to natural persons.
lookup_terms: الصيغة النموذجية لعقد الإيجار التمويلي للمركبات

data.summary: A June 2020 SAMA circular permitting finance companies to offer all financing products and credit cards to individuals and SMEs through electronic channels using nationally approved digital certification (e-signature) services, subject to the Electronic Transactions Law (Royal Decree M/18) and its implementing regulations. It sets minimum conditions: level 3 maturity compliance with the Cyber/Information Security Framework verified by an independent party, prior SAMA no-objection for electronic services, use of a provider accredited by the National Digital Certification Center, no dilution of KYC and identity/capacity/authority verification, call-centre confirmation of the customer's consent, cooling periods of 24 hours for individuals and three business days for entities, security and data-privacy controls, record retention, contract updates, a financing cap aligned to risk policy, and periodic control review. It does not apply to products in SAMA's regulatory sandbox.

A July 2020 SAMA circular clarifying who bears the increase in VAT from 5% to 15% (effective 1 July 2020) on cooperative insurance contracts linked to finance lease agreements. SAMA confirms the lessor must absorb the increase and may not pass it on to the lessee, relying on Article 9(3) of the Finance Lease Law, under which the lessor bears cooperative insurance on the leased asset and cannot stipulate it on the lessee. Binding on finance companies acting as lessors.

An August 2020 SAMA circular directing finance companies to keep their websites continuously updated, to verify (or otherwise delete) their social media accounts, and to add and maintain branch geolocations and business hours on mapping platforms such as Google Maps. Compliance was required within one month, with the steps taken to be reported to SAMA's communications officer within two weeks. Issued under SAMA's supervisory mandate over finance companies and framed as a customer-protection measure.

A SAMA circular activating the GCC-NET point-of-sale payment service for acceptance of transactions in Qatar as of a stated go-live date, building on earlier circulars on GCC-NET POS and its tariff. It requires banks to make the technical and operational changes needed to accept and process GCC-NET card transactions on their systems and POS terminals, to arrange commercial terms with GCC cardholders and acquiring merchants so transactions are processed at approved pricing, to inform and educate cardholders that purchases in Qatar route via the Qatari national network linked to GCC-NET, and to accept GCC-NET branded cards. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom.

Controls setting the minimum requirements for exchange centres and bank-affiliated remittance centres when receiving customer funds through electronic payment means for currency exchange or transfer purposes; they replace the earlier circular permitting such receipts. Key obligations include a dedicated bank account, restricting receipts to members with a unified reference number tied to the customer ID and to SAR amounts, a ban on receiving customers' transfers from banks or transfer companies outside the Kingdom for currency exchange, verification and record-keeping, restrictions and refund routing/timelines for cancelled transactions, pre-agreed and documented fees and exchange rates, customer awareness, CDD under the AML and counter-terrorism financing laws and their regulations, and continuous updating of internal procedures. Binds exchange centres and bank remittance centres supervised by SAMA (distributed also to banks).
lookup_terms: money transfer centre dedicated bank account
electronic payment means for currency exchange

data.summary: A circular reaffirming the disclosure duties in Articles 72 and 73 of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law regarding audited annual and quarterly financial statements, the auditor's report and the board report. It requires finance companies to publish those reports and statements on their own websites within ten business days after the end of the prescribed submission period. Binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom and the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company.
lookup_terms: finance company annual audited financial statements
Articles 72 and 73 Finance Companies Control Law Implementing Regulation

data.summary: A circular notifying a Governor's decision amending specific articles of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Lease Law (issued under the Law's Article 27 powers, agreed with the Minister of Justice). The amendments cover the lessor's duty to obtain a SAMA no-objection letter for finance lease products aimed at individuals or microfinance beneficiaries before launch to ensure fairness of terms, the requirement that contract signing take place at the lessor's premises with the lessor bearing the related costs, and a change to a paragraph of Article 25 referencing the Enforcement Law. Binds banks, finance companies and finance lease contract registration companies in the Kingdom.

A circular extending SAMA's earlier acceptance of the Absher/Tawakkalna digital identity to the electronic Family Record (سجل الأسرة) document for citizens, viewable via QR code. It obliges financial institutions to accept the digital Family Record in processes that do not require taking a copy of the document, with the same rules and provisions applying as to printed copies. Binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA.

A circular reaffirming SAMA's rules on the time limits for issuing clearance (release) letters and transferring accounts and indebtedness, as applied to real estate finance, and confirming that mortgage contracts between real estate financiers and individual customers fall under SAMA's finance laws and instructions. Real estate financiers must execute customer requests to transfer Murabaha-based real estate finance debt within the prescribed timelines, comply with the rules on purchase and transfer of real estate finance debt between financiers, exclude from the timelines business days linked to mortgage release procedures where the delay is caused by an external party, and update internal policies accordingly. Binds banks and real estate finance companies operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: real estate finance debt transfer timelines
real estate financier obligations individual customers

data.summary: A SAMA circular instructing supervised financial institutions to apply the emergency evacuation guide for persons with disabilities issued by the Authority for the Care of Persons with Disabilities, as a follow-on to SAMA's earlier instructions on serving persons with disabilities in financial institutions. It sets expectations for security and safety arrangements — evacuation planning, escape routes and assembly areas, alerting and communication systems, and accessible exits — so that persons with disabilities can be safely evacuated. It binds all financial institutions under SAMA supervision, with the attached guide providing definitions of disability types and procedural steps.
lookup_terms: Authority for Care of Persons with Disabilities

data.summary: SAMA reporting guidelines governing how banks prepare and submit the quarterly return on interest/commission rates for assets and liabilities, superseding the earlier guidance note on quarterly prudential returns for loans and deposits commissions. It fixes scope (domestic-level data only), submission timing (within 30 calendar days of quarter end), CFO sign-off, format, and the methodology for weighted average rates, balances and maturity buckets, with templates by product, by sector (ISIC4) and by Sharia-compliant vs conventional. It binds all banks operating in Saudi Arabia, including branches of foreign banks.
lookup_terms: interest rates on assets and liabilities return
quarterly prudential return loans and deposits commissions

data.summary: A concept node for the International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC4) as used in SAMA's interest rates on assets and liabilities reporting. ISIC4 is the mandated basis for the sector-level template, requiring banks to categorise asset and liability balances and weighted average rates by economic activity rather than by product. It is relevant to all banks in Saudi Arabia, including foreign bank branches, completing the quarterly return.

SAMA's revised Loans to Deposits Ratio (LDR) guidelines, issued under the Central Bank Law and the Banking Control Law and superseding the prior LDR circulars, effective June 2023. They define the ratio as net loans over weighted deposits, specify the components of the numerator (loans net of provisions, unearned commission income and commission in suspense) and denominator (deposits, repos and long-term debt including sukuk/bonds, syndicated and subordinated debt), exclude interbank and SAMA transactions, set maturity-based weights, and state SAMA's expectation that total LDR stay below 90%. They bind all banks, which must report the ratio monthly on a consolidated basis covering local and foreign currency, resident and non-resident.

A SAMA circular requiring financial institutions to accept the electronic/digital national identity available through Absher (Afrad) and Tawakkalna — including the QR-coded digital ID, which carries the same legal effect as the physical ID card under the Civil Affairs Law and its implementing regulations — for existing customers in transactions that do not require taking a copy of the ID. Institutions must continue to assess and review risks arising from reliance on electronic identity and must establish a suitable means of obtaining an electronic copy where a copy is required. It binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA, effective from its date, and interacts directly with identification/verification duties under the AML/CTF regime.

SAMA's Banks Investment Rules, setting the regulatory framework for banks' investment activity, including defined terms distinguishing Local Investment from International Investment (based on where the investment takes place, regardless of currency or issuer residency). The rules impose prudential expectations on concentration, liquidity, documented investment rationale, alignment with the bank's investment strategy, diversification, annual portfolio stress testing, and adequate resources and expertise. They also set approval controls, requiring SAMA non-objection for investments needing regulatory approval under the Banking Control Law and the relevant Ministerial Decree, and conditions on channels such as money market funds licensed by the CMA. They bind banks licensed and operating in the Kingdom.

SAMA's guidance document implementing the Basel III Net Stable Funding Ratio in Saudi Arabia, setting the standard, its calibration, scope and implementation timeline. It covers frequency of calculation and reporting (at least quarterly, within Basel capital-standard reporting lags), consolidated application to internationally active banks with discretion to extend to other banks and entity subsets, and detailed treatment of items such as derivative assets, netting and cash variation margin. It binds banks supervised by SAMA and operates alongside the Sound Principles for liquidity risk management at legal entity, branch, subsidiary and group level.

Defines Available Stable Funding — the portion of a bank's capital and liabilities treated as reliable over the NSFR's one-year horizon — and the ASF factors applied to each liability and capital category. Calibration turns on funding tenor and on funding type/counterparty, with retail and small business deposits assumed more stable than comparable wholesale funding; factors range from 100% for regulatory capital and long-dated liabilities down to 0% for residual liabilities and equity. Relevant to banks calculating the NSFR numerator and to SAMA's supervisory assessment of funding risk.

Defines Required Stable Funding — the amount of stable funding a bank must hold against its assets and off-balance-sheet exposures, measured by assigning carrying values to categories and applying RSF factors, with definitions mirroring the LCR unless stated otherwise. Allocation depends on residual maturity or liquidity value, assuming investors exercise maturity-extension options and allowing SAMA to weigh reputational constraints on bank-held options. It governs the NSFR denominator for banks supervised by SAMA.

The Net Stable Funding Ratio itself: available stable funding divided by required stable funding, which must be at least 100% on an ongoing basis. It limits overreliance on short-term wholesale funding and requires banks to fund assets and off-balance-sheet activities with a stable funding profile; SAMA may impose more stringent standards on an individual bank reflecting its funding risk profile and compliance with the Sound Principles. Applies to banks in Saudi Arabia, based on the BCBS October 2014 standard.
lookup_terms: Basel III: The Net Stable Funding Ratio

data.summary: SAMA's August 2014 circular and enclosed framework for identifying and designating Domestic Systemically Important Banks in Saudi Arabia, aligned with the BCBS D-SIB approach. It introduces an indicator-based measurement methodology and requires designated banks to meet additional Higher Loss Absorbency capital requirements, effective 1 January 2016. Addressed to all banks, at managing director / CEO / general manager level.

The assessment methodology component of the D-SIB framework: an indicator-based measurement approach using size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity, calibrated to the externalities a bank's failure would impose on the Saudi domestic economy and any cross-border effects. Outputs a systemic-importance score used by SAMA to designate D-SIBs and set their Higher Loss Absorbency requirement. Applies to banks assessed by SAMA's Banking Supervision Department.

Governance and general-requirement provisions of SAMA's Banks Investment Rules (April 2022), covering prudent investment management, documented investment rationale, and the definitions of Local and International Investment. It allocates ultimate oversight of investments to the bank's Board (or, for Foreign Bank Branches, the Head/Regional Office authority), requires a management-level investment committee, and sets the minimum content of the internal Investment Policy including eligibility criteria and prudential exposure limits. Binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA, including foreign bank branches.
lookup_terms: Board of Directors oversight of investments

data.summary: Risk management and monitoring provisions of the Banks Investment Rules, requiring banks to assess current and prospective investments against credit, market (including IRRBB), operational, liquidity and concentration risks and to report results to the responsible investment committee. It also requires the Investment Strategy to be proportionate to the bank's size and footprint, supported by operational guidelines integrated into the risk management framework, and mandates AML/CTF compliance before entering any investment. Binds SAMA-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: IRRBB banking book interest rate risk

data.summary: Approval, control and portfolio-monitoring provisions of the Banks Investment Rules, including continuous portfolio performance monitoring, diversification, annual portfolio-level stress testing available to SAMA on request, and adequate staffing. It requires SAMA non-objection for investments needing regulatory approval under the Banking Control Law and Ministerial Decree No. 3/2149 (approved at portfolio level, with prior non-objection for changes to structure or limits) and sets conditions for investing in Money Market Funds through CMA-licensed entities. Binds SAMA-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: Money Market Funds MMF bank investment

data.summary: Core definitions, purpose and scope of SAMA's Rules Regulating Money Changing Business, establishing the licensing and supervisory framework for Money Changers and defining key terms (Money Changing Business, Money Changer, Customer, Invested Capital, Third Party). It prohibits unlicensed practice of, or holding out as conducting, money changing business, with a narrow carve-out allowing licensed hotels, hotel apartments and travel agencies to exchange currency for their own customers subject to AML Law compliance and onward sale to a licensed bank or Money Changer. Binds Money Changers licensed by SAMA and, through the prohibition, any person operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: hotels travel agencies currency exchange exemption

data.summary: Licensing-maintenance, supervisory reporting and license-termination provisions for Money Changers, listing grounds on which SAMA may terminate a license (failure to meet license or business requirements, false information, obstruction of inspection, insolvency, accumulated losses of 50% or more of capital, dissolution or death of a sole proprietor). It also requires appointment of a licensed external auditor (maximum five continuous years), permits SAMA to appoint an auditor at the Money Changer's expense, and mandates periodical data submissions and updates to SAMA. Binds licensed Money Changers and their employees.

AML/CTF and enforcement provisions of the Rules Regulating Money Changing Business, requiring Money Changers to comply with the Anti-Money Laundering Law and its Implementing Regulations, the Law of Terrorism Crimes and Financing and its Implementing Regulations, related SAMA circulars and controls, and the Guideline on implementing UN Security Council resolutions on proliferation financing of weapons of mass destruction. It also sets SAMA's supervisory sanctions ladder (notification, warning, corrective action, branch closure, service suspension, license suspension or revocation, fines under Article 12 of SAMA's Charter) with publication of penalties. Binds licensed Money Changers.
lookup_terms: Law of Terrorism Crimes and Financing

data.summary: This node covers SAMA's Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) framework circular of August 2014 and, specifically, the Higher Loss Absorbency (HLA) capital add-on. It sets out the indicator-based scoring (size, interconnectedness, substitutability, complexity), a cut-off score with five buckets, and the requirement that designated D-SIBs hold HLA capital fully in CET1 on top of the SAMA-set target capital adequacy ratio, with scope for supervisory judgment and further measures such as recovery and resolution plans. It binds all banks licensed in Saudi Arabia, addressed to managing directors, CEOs and general managers, effective from 1 January 2016.

This node is SAMA's adoption/guidance material for the Basel capital framework, covering scope of application, minimum capital requirements for credit risk, and the associated Pillar 3 disclosure templates (including the capital distribution constraints template and composition-of-capital rows for Tier 2 deductions and TLAC holdings). It explains how regulatory capital components, buffers, thresholds and Pillar 2 add-ons interact and what must be disclosed and how often. It binds banks subject to SAMA's capital adequacy rules on a consolidated and solo basis as specified.

This node concerns the standardised approach (SA) for credit risk as applied in SAMA's Basel-aligned capital rules and its reporting/disclosure treatment. It defines what falls within SA risk-weighted assets, how credit risk mitigation is recognised (simple vs comprehensive approach with supervisory haircuts), the carve-outs for counterparty credit risk, equity, settlement risk and securitisation, and the phase-in of the prohibition on IRB for equity exposures. It binds banks calculating Pillar 1 credit risk capital and completing the related RWA templates.

This node covers the internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches to credit risk — foundation IRB, advanced IRB and the supervisory slotting approach — as reflected in SAMA's capital framework and RWA disclosure instructions. It addresses which exposures may be modelled with SAMA approval, the boundary with the standardised approach, the equity-exposure IRB prohibition phase-in, and IRB interactions with the securitisation framework (SEC-IRBA, KIRB) and equity investments in funds. It binds banks that have, or seek, SAMA permission to use internal models for credit risk capital.

This node addresses eligible External Credit Assessment Institutions (ECAIs) and the use of external credit ratings to determine risk weights, including the stricter operational conditions applied in the securitisation context (public, non-selective, free-of-charge availability of ratings and methodologies; demonstrated securitisation expertise; treatment where multiple ECAIs disagree). It also covers how credit risk mitigation reflected in an external rating is treated to avoid double counting. It binds banks relying on external ratings for regulatory capital purposes under SAMA's capital rules.

This node sets out the securitisation capital framework: definitions of securitisation and resecuritisation exposures, when a bank is an originator, the range of exposures captured (ABS, MBS, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities, swaps, reserve accounts), and the hierarchy of capital approaches including SEC-SA, SEC-ERBA, SEC-IAA and SEC-IRBA with the 15% risk-weight floor and resecuritisation adjustments. It binds banks holding, originating or sponsoring securitisation positions when calculating risk-weighted assets.

Guidance note setting out SAMA's policy on the scope of application of its Basel Framework in Saudi Arabia, confirming that local banks apply the risk-based capital, leverage, liquidity, large exposure, Pillar 2 and Pillar 3 requirements on both a standalone and consolidated basis, including at holding-company level and every tier of a banking group. It also covers prudential reporting alignment and disclosure templates (e.g. reconciliation of accounting versus regulatory scopes of consolidation). Binds locally incorporated banks and their parent/holding entities supervised by SAMA.

Concept node for the Basel III standards as adopted by SAMA, covering the leverage ratio framework, LCR and NSFR liquidity standards and the associated available/required stable funding factors, netting and collateral treatment for derivative exposures. It operates through SAMA circulars that transpose BCBS documents with Saudi-specific adjustments (e.g. residential mortgage risk weights). Binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA.

Sets the eligibility criteria SAMA applies when recognising External Credit Assessment Institutions (resources, credibility, conflict-of-interest disclosure, cooperation with SAMA) and the rules banks must follow when using ECAI ratings for standardised-approach risk weighting. Key obligations: consistent use of chosen ECAIs and global rating scales, no cherry-picking, and prescribed treatment where two or more ratings map to different risk weights (higher of two, or higher of the two lowest). Binds banks using the standardised approach for credit risk.

Explains how banks determine whether an exposure is rated, distinguishing issue-specific ratings from issuer ratings: issuer ratings apply to senior unsecured claims only, low-quality ratings contaminate pari passu and subordinated exposures, and restricted-class ratings (e.g. deposit or counterparty ratings) apply only within that class. Also requires the rating to reflect the full amount owed (principal and interest) and bars double-counting where credit enhancement is already embedded in the issue rating. Binds banks applying the standardised approach; the related material also addresses classification of equity exposures.

Governs use of short-term external ratings in standardised-approach risk weighting: short-term ratings are issue-specific, limited to short-term bank and corporate exposures, and can never support a risk weight for an unrated long-term exposure. It sets the short-term risk weight table, contagion rules where a rated facility attracts 50% or 150%, the interaction with the general preferential treatment for interbank exposures up to three months, the bar on using one group entity's rating for another, and the prohibition on unsolicited ratings. Binds banks calculating credit risk RWA.

Covers credit risk mitigation within the standardised approach, requiring banks to use either the simple approach or the comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts when recognising mitigation, and situates CRM within the wider RWA/minimum capital reporting architecture (standardised versus IRB and slotting approaches, counterparty credit risk, CVA, equity, settlement and securitisation exposures). Includes the phase-in arrangement restricting IRB treatment of equity exposures. Binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating and disclosing credit risk capital requirements.

A capital-adequacy node dealing with how maturity differences between an exposure and its hedge or credit protection are treated, both in the default risk charge (DRC) under the standardised market risk approach and in credit risk mitigation. It sets recognition conditions (original maturity of at least one year, residual maturity of at least three months for credit protection), the pro-rata adjustment formula for partially recognised protection, the conservative definition of effective maturity for exposure and hedge, and the three-month floor on maturity weighting for short-dated positions. It binds SAMA-licensed banks computing regulatory capital.

Covers the capital treatment of collateralised and repo-style transactions — OTC derivatives, margin lending, repos/reverse repos and securities lending/borrowing — including exemptions from the one-year maturity floor for short-term, daily-remargined and self-liquidating trade exposures, and the trading-book rules on eligible collateral and counterparty credit risk charges. It also introduces minimum haircut floors for non-centrally cleared securities financing transactions. Applies to banks under SAMA's credit risk and counterparty credit risk frameworks.

Describes the simple approach to recognising financial collateral in credit risk mitigation, under which the counterparty's risk weight is substituted by the risk weight of the collateral instrument. Recognition conditions include pledging for at least the life of the exposure and revaluation at least every six months; maturity mismatches are not permitted. Binds banks calculating credit risk RWA under the standardised approach.

Covers the comprehensive approach to financial collateral, under which exposure and collateral values are adjusted by supervisory or own-estimate haircuts rather than substituting risk weights, and relates to disclosure of collateral composition for counterparty credit risk exposures. Relevant to banks using the standardised approach for credit risk mitigation and to Pillar 3 collateral reporting.

Concerns the standard supervisory haircut parameters applied to collateral and exposures in credit risk mitigation, and their interaction with related prudential calculations and disclosures (including liquidity metrics computed after haircuts and internal rating assignment requirements). Relevant to banks applying the comprehensive approach or reporting haircut-adjusted figures to SAMA.

Addresses the recognition of master netting agreements for securities financing transactions and derivatives, including calculation of the net exposure (E*) used as EAD, treatment of margin agreements spanning multiple netting sets, collateral taken outside netting sets, and the alternative VaR models approach (retaining 99% VaR) subject to SAMA recognition. It binds banks seeking netting benefits in counterparty credit risk capital calculations, conditional on the agreement meeting the legal enforceability criteria of the standardised approach.

A definitional node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk (v2.1, December 2022) setting out what constitutes a corporate exposure for the internal ratings-based (IRB) asset-class categorisation, and linked in the surrounding material to Pillar 3 disclosure of how corporate versus retail loans are categorised (including non-performing and forborne treatment under SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Assets, No. 41033343). It matters because asset-class assignment drives which risk-weight function and risk components apply. It binds banks subject to SAMA's credit risk capital framework, including for their regulatory scope of consolidation.
lookup_terms: Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk

data.summary: Defines specialized lending (SL) as a sub-set of corporate exposures where repayment depends primarily on the income generated by the financed asset(s) rather than the borrower's broader commercial capacity, and identifies its sub-classes — project finance, object finance, commodities finance and, under IRB, also income-producing real estate and high-volatility commercial real estate. Under the standardized approach, SL exposures use issue-specific external ratings only (issuer ratings are excluded); under IRB, supervisory slotting criteria and slotting risk weights may apply. Binds banks calculating credit risk RWA under SAMA's framework.
lookup_terms: project finance object finance commodities finance

data.summary: Defines project finance (PF) as funding where the lender looks primarily to a single project's revenues as both source of repayment and security, typically via an SPV, and sets the unrated standardized-approach risk weights: 130% pre-operational, 100% operational, and 80% for high-quality operational-phase exposures meeting the stated conditions. It also defines "operational phase" (positive net cash flow sufficient to cover remaining contractual obligations plus declining long-term debt) and the high-quality criteria. Binds banks risk-weighting PF exposures under SAMA's credit risk capital rules.

Defines object finance (OF) as funding the acquisition of equipment (e.g. ships, aircraft, satellites, railcars, fleets) where repayment depends on cash flows from the specific financed assets pledged or assigned to the lender. Where no issue-specific external rating is available, OF exposures are risk-weighted at 100% under the standardized approach. Binds banks classifying and risk-weighting specialized lending exposures under SAMA's credit risk framework.

Defines commodities finance (CF) as short-term lending against reserves, inventories or receivables of exchange-traded commodities (e.g. crude oil, metals, crops), repaid from sale proceeds where the borrower has no independent repayment capacity. Unrated CF exposures attract a 100% risk weight under the standardized approach; issue-specific ratings, not issuer ratings, apply where available. Binds banks calculating credit risk capital on specialized lending under SAMA's framework.

Covers income-producing real estate — under IRB an SL sub-class, and under the standardized approach the real estate exposures classified as "materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property" (IPRRE for residential, IPCRE for commercial). It sits within the real estate exposure class, which also distinguishes regulatory versus other real estate and land acquisition, development and construction (ADC) exposures, and feeds Pillar 3 disclosure row definitions. Binds banks assigning risk weights to real-estate-secured exposures under SAMA's credit risk framework.
lookup_terms: materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property
ADC land acquisition development and construction

data.summary: A concept node on on-balance sheet netting as recognised for regulatory capital purposes, and how it differs from accounting netting and from the incremental netting applied under the Basel/SAMA counterparty credit risk rules. It also covers how netting sets and margin agreements interact when a single margin agreement spans several netting sets, and how such differences must be reflected in Pillar 3 reconciliation templates (LI1/LI2). It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating exposure values, RWA and regulatory disclosures.

A concept node on guarantees and credit derivatives as eligible credit risk mitigation, including allocation of secured exposures across collateral, financial guarantees and credit derivatives for disclosure (Template CR3), and the treatment of written credit derivatives and offsetting of purchased protection. It sets the conditions (identical reference name, comparable or more conservative terms, pool-level equivalence) under which protection sold may be offset. It applies to banks computing credit risk mitigation and related capital and disclosure.

A concept node on preferential risk weighting of exposures guaranteed by a sovereign or central bank, including the extension of the 0% risk weight for Saudi sovereign/SAMA exposures denominated and funded in Saudi Riyal to guaranteed portions. It sets the three conditions under which an indirect sovereign counter-guarantee may be treated as a direct sovereign guarantee, subject to SAMA's satisfaction as to robustness. It binds banks applying the standardised credit risk framework.

A concept node covering SAMA's minimum capital requirements framework for counterparty credit risk (CCR) and credit valuation adjustment (CVA), including the definition of CCR as bilateral risk of loss before final settlement and related risks such as rollover risk and general/specific wrong-way risk. It also fixes the effective date (1 January 2023) and the quarterly Q17 reporting obligation to SAMA within 30 days of quarter-end. It binds banks with derivative, SFT and long-settlement exposures.

A concept node on the standardised approaches used for credit and counterparty credit risk capital calculation, including the standardised approach for credit risk (simple or comprehensive CRM with supervisory haircuts) and the SA-CCR exposure measure feeding CCR RWA. It clarifies the boundary between modelled (IRB/IMM) and standardised RWA for Pillar 3 reporting rows. It binds banks computing and disclosing RWA under the SAMA capital framework.

A concept node introducing the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, its asset classes, and the distinction between foundation and advanced approaches and supervisory slotting. It sets SAMA's conditions for phased rollout across asset classes and business units, the requirement for a SAMA-agreed implementation plan, the all-exposures rule within an asset class and business unit, and the bar on capital relief from intra-group transactions during rollout. It binds banks seeking or operating IRB permission.
lookup_terms: own estimates of LGD and EAD

data.summary: Defines High-Volatility Commercial Real Estate (HVCRE) as a sub-category of specialised lending within the IRB credit risk framework, distinguished from Income-Producing Real Estate (IPRE) by higher loss-rate volatility and asset correlation. It captures commercial real estate exposures in property types SAMA designates as volatile, plus land acquisition, development and construction (ADC) financing where repayment depends on uncertain future sale or cash flows. Binds SAMA-licensed banks for capital calculation and, via the related disclosure definitions (General/Income-producing RRE and CRE, ADC), for Pillar 3 reporting.
lookup_terms: real estate exposure class risk weights

data.summary: The IRB asset-class definition of sovereign exposures within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk, used to categorise exposures for internal ratings-based capital calculation and for the related standardised-approach treatment of sovereigns. It sits alongside the parallel definitions of corporate, bank and retail exposures that drive asset-class segmentation. Binds banks subject to SAMA's credit risk capital framework.

The IRB asset-class definition of bank exposures in SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk, delimiting which counterparties fall into the bank class versus corporate, sovereign or retail classes for capital purposes. It complements the standardised-approach chapter on exposures to banks, securities firms and other financial institutions. Binds banks calculating credit risk RWA under SAMA rules.
lookup_terms: securities firms and other financial institutions

data.summary: Sets out how exposures qualify as retail for credit risk capital, including the regulatory retail criteria (low individual value with an aggregate SAR 4.46 million cap per counterparty and a 0.2% granularity limit), the "transactor" concept for credit/charge cards and overdrafts, and "other retail". Drives the applicable risk weights (45% for transactor regulatory retail, 75% for other regulatory retail, 100% for other retail) and the IRB retail asset class. Binds banks subject to SAMA's credit risk capital framework.
lookup_terms: small business exposure treated as retail

data.summary: Defines Qualifying Revolving Retail Exposures (QRRE) as one of the three IRB retail sub-classes (alongside residential mortgages and other retail), requiring the sub-portfolio to be revolving, unsecured and uncommitted, with criteria applied at sub-portfolio level consistent with the bank's retail segmentation. Relevant to IRB adoption scope, since QRRE is a standalone asset class for the roll-out expectation. Binds banks using the IRB approach under SAMA's credit risk rules.

Defines eligible purchased receivables and splits them into retail and corporate receivables, setting when the "top-down" IRB approach may be used instead of obligor-by-obligor default risk assessment. Corporate purchased receivables may use top-down only where eligibility and minimum operational requirements are met (chiefly for securitisation-bound receivables, and for on-balance sheet exposures only with SAMA approval); retail purchased receivables use the A-IRB approach. Binds banks applying the IRB approach, including for asset-class roll-out scope.

Concept node for the Foundation Internal Ratings-Based (F-IRB) approach to credit risk as it appears in SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosure instructions, where own-estimated PD is combined with supervisory values for other risk parameters. It matters here mainly for scoping and populating disclosure templates: F-IRB exposures are reported as modelled (non-standardised) RWA and, for counterparty credit risk, require a separate portfolio breakdown from A-IRB exposures in template CCR4. Binds SAMA-licensed banks that have supervisory approval to use IRB models for credit and counterparty credit risk.

Concept node for the Advanced Internal Ratings-Based (A-IRB) approach, under which a bank uses its own estimates of PD and additional risk parameters, subject to SAMA approval. In the Pillar 3 instructions it drives template scope: A-IRB exposures are disclosed as modelled RWA, require separate portfolio breakdowns where a bank also uses F-IRB, and are subject to PD backtesting disclosure. Applies to SAMA-licensed banks approved to use advanced internal models for credit and counterparty credit risk.

Concept node for the supervisory slotting criteria approach, used for specialised lending exposures where a bank maps exposures to supervisory categories with prescribed risk weights instead of full own estimates. In SAMA's Pillar 3 instructions it is reported as a distinct 'of which' line within credit risk RWA, separate from the standardised, F-IRB and A-IRB lines, and is grouped with the IRB approaches for template scoping. Relevant to banks using IRB-family treatments for specialised lending.

Concept node for the IRB risk weight functions — the prescribed formulas converting risk components into risk weights and RWA for exposures treated under the IRB approaches. In the Pillar 3 context it underlies the modelled-RWA figures disclosed in the overview and credit risk templates, including the equity-exposure phase-in floor where the IRB-derived risk weight is compared against the standardised phase-in weight. Relevant to SAMA-licensed banks computing IRB credit risk capital.

Concept node for the IRB risk components — the inputs (probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default and effective maturity) that feed the IRB risk weight functions, with the split between own estimates and supervisory values determining F-IRB versus A-IRB treatment. In SAMA's Pillar 3 instructions these components are the disclosed parameters in IRB templates, including EAD post-CRM, average PD and average maturity by PD band. Applies to banks with SAMA approval to use IRB approaches.

Concept node for Probability of Default (PD), the estimated likelihood that an obligor defaults over a one-year horizon and a core IRB risk component, as used in SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosure templates. It governs the PD-band breakdowns in IRB templates and the annual backtesting disclosure comparing modelled PD against realised default rates, using at least a five-year average annual default rate; it also links to the defaulted-exposure definitions (e.g. past due more than 90 days under the standardised approach). Binds banks using A-IRB or F-IRB, with PD models requiring SAMA approval.

Concept node for Loss Given Default (LGD) as used in SAMA's credit risk capital framework, covering the requirements for banks permitted to use own LGD estimates under the advanced IRB approach. It sets the substantive standards: LGD must reflect economic downturn conditions, cannot fall below the long-run default-weighted average loss rate for the facility type, and must conservatively address dependence between borrower and collateral/collateral provider as well as currency mismatches. It binds banks approved by SAMA to use internal ratings-based approaches; related material also appears in Pillar 3 disclosure templates.

Concept node for Exposure at Default (EAD), the exposure amount risk component used in credit risk capital calculation and in related Pillar 3 disclosure templates (including credit risk mitigation and problem-asset disclosures). It anchors how carrying amounts, secured and unsecured exposures, and non-performing/forborne classifications feed the exposure measure. It binds banks subject to SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk and disclosure requirements.

Concept node for Effective Maturity (M), the IRB risk component measuring the maturity of a facility for credit risk capital purposes. It fixes 2.5 years under the foundation approach (6 months for repo-style transactions), requires banks using advanced approaches to calculate M per facility subject to a one-year floor and five-year cap, and specifies treatment for cash-flow-scheduled instruments, netted derivatives and revolving exposures. It binds banks applying IRB approaches; related maturity-scaling concepts also arise in the market risk default risk charge.

Concept node for the firm-size adjustment applied to the corporate IRB risk-weight formula for micro, small and medium-sized enterprise borrowers. It defines MSME borrowers by consolidated group revenue thresholds in SAR, sets the adjustment formula and the revenue floor used in it, and allows SAMA to permit substitution of total assets where revenue is not a meaningful size indicator. It binds banks using the IRB approach for corporate credit.

Concept node for the IRB treatment of expected losses (EL) and provisions, covering calculation of EL amounts, calculation of eligible provisions, and the comparison of the two for capital purposes (shortfall deduction or surplus inclusion). It sits within SAMA's credit risk capital framework alongside the IRB risk components and supervisory slotting rules. It binds banks approved to use IRB approaches.

Concept node for the IRB calculation of risk-weighted assets on purchased receivables, covering default risk and dilution risk components, treatment of purchase price discounts, and recognition of credit risk mitigants. It forms part of SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk and feeds the related Pillar 3 RWA disclosure rows. It binds banks using IRB approaches for eligible purchased receivables.

A capital-framework concept node covering dilution risk on purchased receivables and how credit risk mitigants (collateral, guarantees, first-loss protection) are recognised against default risk, dilution risk, or both under the IRB and securitisation chapters. It sets out substitution of the guarantor's risk weight where a guarantee covers one or both risk components, and proportional/tranched treatment of uncovered portions. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating risk-weighted assets under the IRB approach.

Concept node on the minimum requirements and adoption conditions for the Internal Ratings-Based approach to credit risk, including the distinction between standardised, F-IRB, A-IRB and supervisory slotting treatments and what RWA is reported under each. It covers SAMA-agreed phased rollout across asset classes and business units, the required implementation plan, the bar on capital-minimisation motives, and the prohibition on IRB for equity exposures subject to phase-in. Binds banks seeking or using SAMA approval for internal models.

Concept node defining what constitutes a "rating system" (methods, processes, controls, data and IT supporting credit risk assessment and default/loss estimation) and the design standards it must meet. It requires two distinct rating dimensions for corporate, sovereign and bank exposures (borrower default risk and transaction-specific factors), prohibits cherry-picking between multiple rating systems, and imposes documentation duties covering rating criteria, exceptions, governance, default and loss definitions, and statistical model methodology. Binds banks using IRB approaches under SAMA supervision.

Concept node on the market risk capital framework, focusing on internal risk transfers between the banking book, trading book, the SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk and the CVA portfolio, and the conditions for regulatory capital recognition (including exact matching of external hedges and documentation of hedged CVA risk). It also states that all banks, D-SIB and non-D-SIB, must calculate market risk capital using the Standardised Approach, with RWA derived by a 12.5 multiplier. Binds SAMA-licensed banks with trading book or FX/commodities banking book exposures.

Concept node on the use of external credit assessments (ECAIs) for standardised-approach risk weighting: consistent use of SAMA-recognised ECAIs, prohibition on cherry-picking or arbitrarily switching ECAIs, use of global rating scales, and the multiple-ratings hierarchy (higher risk weight where two ratings differ; second-lowest rule where three or more). It also governs when issue-specific versus issuer ratings may be relied on and bars double-counting of credit enhancement already reflected in a rating. Binds banks determining risk weights for rated and unrated exposures.

Concept node addressing constraints on overriding or selectively applying ratings when assigning risk weights: banks must apply recognised ECAI ratings consistently and may not cherry-pick among agencies, and the rules dictate which rating governs where multiple, issuer-level or issue-level ratings exist. Low-quality issuer or issue ratings are pushed onto pari passu or subordinated unassessed exposures, and limited-class ratings (e.g. deposit or counterparty risk ratings) may only be used within that class. Binds banks applying the standardised approach to credit risk.

A prudential node combining market-risk framework material on internal risk transfers (the conditions under which banking-book/trading-book and inter-desk hedges receive regulatory capital recognition, including the SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk) with the market risk glossary of quantification concepts such as risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class, sensitivity and delta risk. It governs how banks identify and measure the drivers of value change used in market risk capital requirements. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating minimum capital requirements for market risk.

Sets out the minimum requirements for banks' own estimates of probability of default under the IRB approaches, including the requirement that PD be a long-run average of one-year default rates per borrower grade or retail pool, and the related expectations for LGD and EAD estimation, data sources and empirical grounding. It also covers where supervisory parameters must be used instead (F-IRB, specialised lending, HVCRE). Binds banks permitted by SAMA to use foundation or advanced IRB approaches for credit risk capital.

Specifies the standards for own estimates of exposure at default under the advanced IRB approach: EAD as expected gross exposure at default, floors at current drawn amount for on-balance sheet items, focus on off-balance sheet conversion factors, long-run default-weighted averages with a margin of conservatism, and data-quality expectations (no capping of reference data, handling of the ULF instability region). Binds banks using A-IRB for credit risk capital, subject to SAMA approval.

Covers the regulatory reference definition of default and its use in credit risk disclosure, including the standardised-approach anchor of exposures past due more than 90 days and the flows into and out of defaulted status (new defaults, cures, write-offs). It also frames PD backtesting against observed default rates for IRB models. Relevant to all SAMA-supervised banks for credit risk measurement and Pillar 3 disclosure; the backtesting element binds F-IRB/A-IRB banks.

Defines loss for operational risk capital purposes: gross loss, net loss and recoveries, what must be included in gross loss (direct P&L charges, consequential external costs, provisions, pending losses), and the loss event thresholds and data used in the internal loss multiplier and related disclosure. It requires documented policies for building and maintaining the loss data set, with evidence available to SAMA on request. Binds banks applying the standardised approach to operational risk capital.

Requires banks to maintain documented re-ageing policies governing the counting of days past due and the granting of extensions, deferrals, renewals and rewrites, with mandatory minimum content (approval authorities, minimum facility age, eligible delinquency levels, maximum re-ageings, reassessment of repayment capacity) applied consistently and consistent with the use test. Adjacent material covers overdraft limits and days-past-due triggers, and work-out/monitoring systems for purchased receivables. Binds banks using the IRB approaches for credit risk.

A node covering non-financial/"other" collateral within SAMA's credit risk mitigation and Pillar 3 disclosure material, including the CCR5 template breakdown of collateral posted and received for derivative and securities financing transaction exposures, and the CR3 illustrations allocating secured exposures between collateral, financial guarantees and credit derivatives. It sets what collateral categories must be reported at fair value or carrying value and how multi-secured exposures are split. It binds all banks subject to SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk and the Pillar 3 disclosure framework.

A node on how leasing activity features in SAMA's credit risk capital rules, principally in the supervisory slotting criteria for specialised lending (income-producing real estate), where pre-leasing, leasing performance against projections and stabilisation drive the strong/good/satisfactory/weak grading. It also sits alongside the collateral and netting provisions used to compute exposure at default. Relevant to banks using the IRB/supervisory slotting approaches for real estate and project-type exposures.

A node on the Pillar 3 disclosure obligations applicable to banks using foundation or advanced IRB approaches, including template CR7 showing the RWA effect of credit derivatives used as CRM, and the overarching disclosure principles (meaningfulness, consistency over time, comparability, proportionality) and assurance requirements. Templates are mandatory for banks applying A-IRB and/or F-IRB to any exposures, with semiannual frequency and accompanying narrative commentary. Requires a formal board-approved disclosure policy.

A node on transitional and phase-in arrangements in SAMA's capital framework, covering capital instruments subject to phase-out (caps on CET1, AT1 and Tier 2 legacy instruments and amounts excluded), caps on provisions included in Tier 2, and the linear phase-in for the removal of the IRB approach for equity exposures. It also explains how banks must disclose exposures during transitional periods. Applies to banks completing the composition-of-capital and credit risk disclosure templates.

Defines traditional securitization as a structure where cash flows from an underlying exposure pool service at least two stratified/tranched risk positions, with investor payments depending on pool performance rather than the originator's obligation, and distinguishes it from ordinary senior/subordinated debt. It sits within the securitization framework's scope provisions, which require capital treatment based on economic substance rather than legal form, and define securitization exposures, resecuritization and originator status. Binds banks determining regulatory capital for securitization exposures.

Defines synthetic securitization as a tranched structure where credit risk of an underlying pool is transferred through credit derivatives or guarantees rather than by transferring the assets themselves, and places it alongside traditional securitization within the securitization capital framework. Related provisions define securitization exposures (including credit enhancements, liquidity facilities, swaps, tranched cover and reserve accounts), resecuritization and when a bank is an originator. Binds banks calculating regulatory capital for securitization exposures, with SAMA consultation encouraged where classification is uncertain.

A node on data quality and record-keeping obligations underpinning model-based and loss-based capital calculations: alignment, documentation, justification and notification to SAMA of adjustments to risk-theoretical P&L input data used in the market risk internal models approach and the profit-and-loss attribution test, together with the minimum standards for internal operational loss data under the standardised approach (observation period, linkage to current business, consequences of non-compliance including a floor at the business indicator component and possible supervisory multiplier, with Pillar 3 disclosure of exclusions). It binds banks subject to SAMA's capital adequacy framework, particularly those using internal models for market risk and those above the business indicator threshold for loss-data use.

Despite the label, the retrieved content is Pillar 3 disclosure material on capital: the capital distribution constraints template (the CET1 ratio levels at which distributions become restricted, taking account of minimum ratios, buffers, Pillar 2 and TLAC needs) and the composition-of-capital line explanations for Tier 2 deductions and holdings of capital and other TLAC liabilities. It governs disclosure content, scope, frequency and accompanying narrative, and binds banks reporting under SAMA's capital framework.
