Despite the label, the retrieved content concerns the standardised approach to credit risk: the mandatory due diligence banks must perform on external ratings (with the requirement to notch up a risk-weight bucket where due diligence shows higher risk, and the prohibition on notching down), and the definition and risk weighting of exposure classes including covered bonds, securities firms and other financial institutions, and corporates (general, specialised lending, MSMEs, unrated exposures). It binds banks calculating minimum credit risk capital requirements, including their overseas operations.

Sets the qualitative model-governance conditions for using internal models to measure counterparty credit risk exposure (IMM) and market risk (IMA): an independent risk control unit reporting to senior management, initial and ongoing independent validation separate from model development, regular backtesting and profit-and-loss attribution at trading desk level, active board and senior management involvement, integration of model output into day-to-day risk management and trading/exposure limits, and documented policies and procedures. It binds banks seeking or maintaining SAMA permission to use internal models for capital purposes.

Despite the label, the retrieved content addresses internal risk transfers between the banking book and the trading book and their recognition for regulatory capital: the conditions for a banking book exposure to be treated as hedged, the exact-match requirement with an external hedge, the SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk for general interest rate risk, treatment of short credit and short equity positions created by internal risk transfers, and recognition of transfers between trading desks. It binds banks applying the market risk framework and the trading book/banking book boundary rules.

Groups the internal-model use and control requirements with the internal risk transfer rules: the independent risk control unit and separate model validation unit (annual validation of all internal models used for the internal models approach), desk-level backtesting and profit-and-loss attribution, board and senior management engagement, alignment between capital models and day-to-day risk management models, and the conditions under which internal risk transfers between the banking book and trading book receive capital recognition. It binds banks using internal models for market risk capital requirements under SAMA's framework.

A node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk dealing with how overdraft facilities are treated for capital purposes (exposure recognition and risk weighting). The material retrieved around it sits in the standardised-approach chapters, covering use of external ratings for bank exposures (short-term rating interaction with the preferential treatment for exposures of up to three months, the bar on unsolicited ratings and on using a group entity's rating for affiliates) and offsetting of matched positions. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating regulatory credit risk capital; open the source to confirm the specific overdraft provisions.

Defines eligible purchased receivables for the IRB approach, split into retail and corporate receivables, and sets when the "top-down" treatment may be used instead of assessing individual obligor default risk. Corporate purchased receivables may use top-down only where the programme meets the eligibility criteria and minimum operational requirements and where applying full corporate IRB minimums would be an undue burden (primarily receivables bought for asset-backed securitisation structures; on-balance sheet use requires SAMA approval); retail purchased receivables are A-IRB only, and corporate purchased receivables are a separate asset class for the IRB roll-out requirement. Binds banks using internal ratings-based approaches under SAMA supervision.

Covers the risk-quantification and validation standards for banks' own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD under the IRB approaches, including the requirement that PD be a long-run average of one-year default rates per grade or pool and that estimates be grounded in historical experience and empirical evidence rather than judgement alone. Estimates must incorporate all relevant, material and available data (internal, external or pooled) and be demonstrably representative of long-run experience. Binds SAMA-supervised banks on the IRB approach; related market risk material on internal risk transfer desks appears alongside it.

Addresses when banks must fall back on supervisory LGD and EAD values instead of own estimates: for corporate, sovereign and bank exposures, banks that do not meet the minimum requirements for own-estimates of LGD or EAD must use the supervisory parameters, with the standards for their use set out in the foundation-approach requirements. The surrounding material sets the own-estimate benchmark, including EAD defined as expected gross exposure at obligor default, floored at the current drawn amount for on-balance sheet items, and long-run default-weighted average EAD with conservatism for off-balance sheet items. Binds SAMA-supervised banks applying the IRB approaches.

Sets the definition and operational requirements for recognising commercial and residential real estate as eligible collateral for corporate claims under IRB, including legal enforceability and perfected lien, valuation at or below current fair value, and revaluation at least annually (more often in volatile markets); income-producing real estate falling within the specialised lending asset class is excluded from recognition as collateral. Related disclosure definitions distinguish general versus income-producing residential and commercial real estate and land acquisition, development and construction exposures. Binds SAMA-supervised banks applying credit risk mitigation and the related Pillar 3 disclosures.

Concerns the recognition of receivables as eligible collateral for credit risk mitigation purposes and how secured exposures are reported. The supplied material focuses on the disclosure side: how to allocate exposures across unsecured amounts, amounts secured by collateral, financial guarantees and credit derivatives (including over- and under-collateralised cases and which mitigant is expected to be extinguished first), and the breakdown of collateral types posted or received for counterparty credit risk in derivatives and SFTs. Binds SAMA-supervised banks applying CRM and completing the mandatory Pillar 3 templates.

Defines a resecuritization exposure as a securitization exposure whose underlying tranched pool contains at least one securitization exposure, including exposures to one or more resecuritization exposures, with a carve-out for retranchings whose cash flows can be replicated by exposure to a non-securitization pool. The classification drives the more punitive capital treatment and disclosure of such positions under the securitization framework. It binds banks in Saudi Arabia calculating minimum regulatory capital for credit risk and completing related Pillar 3 disclosures.

Concept node for the special purpose entity/vehicle used to hold securitized assets and issue securitization or commercial paper positions, and referenced in capital instrument disclosure as the issuer legal entity of regulatory capital instruments. Its relevance is to identifying who the originator, sponsor or issuer is and whether exposures to the vehicle are securitization exposures attracting capital. It binds banks applying the credit risk and market risk capital frameworks and the associated capital disclosure templates.

Covers the asset-backed commercial paper conduit and programme, including the defined roles of conduit, programme, assets/asset pool, investor, obligor, seller, sponsor and transaction, and the requirement that short-term STC criteria be satisfied at conduit level and transaction level as applicable. It determines eligibility for the simple, transparent and comparable short-term securitization capital treatment and the treatment of programme-wide credit enhancement and liquidity support. It binds banks acting as sponsor, investor or liquidity provider to ABCP structures for capital purposes.

Concerns when a transfer of risk is recognised for regulatory capital purposes: in the securitization context whether the originator may treat exposures as transferred, and in the market risk context the conditions for recognising internal risk transfers between the banking book, trading desks, the approved internal risk transfer desk and the CVA portfolio, including exact-match external hedge and documentation conditions. Non-recognition means the bank must hold capital as if no transfer or protection occurred. It binds banks calculating credit risk and market risk minimum capital requirements.

Sets the conditions under which a clean-up call is acceptable, notably that it must be at the originator's discretion, must not be structured to avoid loss allocation or to provide credit enhancement, and must be exercisable only when 10% or less of the original portfolio or reference portfolio remains. Failing those conditions triggers capital consequences: traditional securitizations are treated as unsecuritized with no gain-on-sale recognition, and synthetic protection purchasers must capitalise the full exposures; an exercised call serving as credit enhancement is treated as implicit support and deducted from capital. It binds originating and protection-purchasing banks.

Sets the ongoing due diligence condition for using the securitization risk weight approaches and, more broadly, for assigning counterparty risk weights: banks must understand the risk profile and performance of underlying exposures and counterparties at origination and at least annually, with sophistication proportionate to activity. Failure to obtain the required information results in a 1250% risk weight on the securitization exposure; banks must also maintain policies, processes and controls and demonstrate adequacy to SAMA. It binds all banks calculating credit risk capital.

Concept node for the ordering rule that determines which securitisation capital approach a bank must apply to a given securitisation exposure, sitting within SAMA's credit risk/securitisation framework. It draws on the framework's definitional scaffolding (securitisation and resecuritisation exposures, underlying pools, originator/investor roles) and on the treatment of full, pro rata and tranched credit protection, where protection buyer and protection provider each calculate capital by reference to the hierarchy. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating risk-based capital requirements for banking book securitisation positions.

Concept node for the Securitisation Internal Ratings-Based Approach, the model-based method at the top of the securitisation hierarchy, built on KIRB, attachment and detachment points and the supervisory parameter p, with an alternative treatment for qualifying STC securitisations. Related Pillar 3 disclosure rules require banking book securitisation exposures treated under the securitisation framework, including those risk-weighted under SEC-IRBA, to be reported in the dedicated securitisation templates. It binds banks with SAMA permission to use IRB approaches for the underlying pool.

Concept node for the Securitisation External Ratings-Based Approach, which risk-weights securitisation exposures by reference to external credit assessments, subject to operational requirements for using ratings and for inferred ratings, with an alternative treatment for term and short-term STC securitisations. It ranks below SEC-IRBA in the hierarchy and its outputs feed the Pillar 3 securitisation disclosure templates. It binds banks holding rated (or inferably rated) banking book securitisation positions.

Concept node for the Internal Assessment Approach, which permits a bank to use its own internal assessments of exposures to ABCP-type programmes as a proxy for external ratings when determining securitisation capital charges, subject to supervisory qualifying conditions. It sits within the securitisation hierarchy alongside SEC-IRBA, SEC-ERBA and SEC-SA and is referenced in RWA reporting as a modelled approach requiring SAMA approval. It binds banks seeking to apply internal assessments to unrated securitisation exposures.

Concept node for the Securitisation Standardised Approach, the formula-based fallback in the securitisation hierarchy using the capital charge on the underlying pool, delinquency inputs and tranche attachment/detachment points. It applies where a bank cannot use SEC-IRBA or SEC-ERBA, and its outputs are reported as standardised-approach RWA in Pillar 3 templates for banking book securitisation exposures. It binds all SAMA-licensed banks with securitisation positions not eligible for the higher approaches.

Concept node for the caps that limit capital requirements on securitisation exposures, including the maximum look-through style cap by reference to the capital that would apply to the underlying pool and the cap available to originators and sponsors. It operates as an overlay on whichever approach in the hierarchy a bank applies, and interacts with definitions of securitisation/resecuritisation exposure and originator status. It binds banks calculating risk-based capital for securitisation positions, with originator-specific conditions.

This node covers the concept of inferred ratings within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk, specifically the securitization external-ratings-based approach (SEC-ERBA). It sets when a securitization exposure lacking its own external rating may nonetheless be risk-weighted off a rating inferred from another position, and it links to the operational requirements that must be satisfied before such a rating can be used. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating credit risk RWAs for securitization exposures.

This node concerns the alternative SEC-ERBA capital treatment for term and short-term securitizations that meet the STC (simple, transparent and comparable) criteria for capital purposes, sitting within the securitization chapters of SAMA's credit risk capital framework and connected to the Pillar 3 securitization disclosure templates (SEC1–SEC4, Table SECA). It determines preferential risk weights where STC eligibility conditions are met and how such exposures are reported. It binds banks acting as originators, sponsors or investors in securitizations.

This node defines the attachment point (A) and detachment point (D) used to locate a tranche in the loss waterfall and thereby determine its risk weight under the securitization internal-ratings-based approach (SEC-IRBA), with worked tranche examples including dilution-risk scenarios. It governs how tranche thickness and seniority feed into RWA calculation. It applies to banks using SEC-IRBA for securitization exposures under SAMA's credit risk capital rules.

This node concerns the supervisory parameter p used in the securitization internal-ratings-based approach, which drives the capital surcharge applied to securitization tranches above the underlying pool's capital requirement; the surrounding material also covers other supervisory-set parameters (supervisory delta, supervisory factor, maturity factor) in the market and counterparty credit risk calculations. It governs how regulator-prescribed inputs enter RWA formulas. It binds banks computing capital under SAMA's credit and market risk frameworks.

This node covers the capital treatment of securitizations of non-performing loans within SAMA's credit risk framework, and connects to the prudential definition of non-performing and forborne exposures (SAMA Rules on Management of Problem Loans No. 41033343, January 2020) and the related Pillar 3 disclosure table CRB-A. It governs how NPL securitization exposures are risk-weighted and how problem assets are defined and disclosed. It binds SAMA-supervised banks.
lookup_terms: Rules on Management of Problem Loans 41033343

data.summary: This node covers the capital treatment of equity investments in funds, setting out the look-through approach (LTA), mandate-based approach (MBA) and fall-back approach, treatment of funds-of-funds, partial use, and leverage adjustment; the related material also defines what counts as an equity holding and the 250%/400% risk weights for equity exposures. It governs how banks risk-weight fund holdings depending on the transparency of the fund's underlying exposures. It binds SAMA-supervised banks under both the standardised and IRB approaches.

A concept node on how credit risk mitigation is recognised for securitization exposures under SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk, sitting alongside the definitional provisions that identify what counts as a securitization exposure (including ABS, MBS, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities, swaps, credit derivatives, tranched cover and originator-recorded reserve/cash collateral accounts) and a resecuritization exposure. It also touches the related Pillar 3 disclosure context for problem assets and regulatory scope of consolidation. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA when calculating risk-weighted assets for, and disclosing, securitization positions.
lookup_terms: Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk

data.summary: Defines the scope of, and gateway conditions for, the simple, transparent and comparable (STC) securitization framework: only traditional securitizations, including ABCP conduits and transactions financed by them, fall within scope, and STC-compliant exposures may attract alternative (preferential) capital treatment under SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA and SEC-IRBA. It allocates duties: the originator/sponsor must disclose transaction-level information sufficient for investors to assess STC status, the investor must make its own assessment before applying the alternative treatment, and for retained positions with significant risk transfer the determination rests with the retaining originator. Criteria must be met on an ongoing basis, with some checks required only at origination. Binds SAMA-supervised banks acting as originators, sponsors or investors.

Covers the STC criteria applicable to non-ABCP (term) traditional securitizations, compliance with which makes exposures eligible for the alternative capital treatment available under the external-ratings-based and internal-ratings-based securitization approaches. It sits within the broader STC scope provisions, including the originator/sponsor disclosure duty and the investor's independent assessment obligation, and requires the criteria to be satisfied on a continuing basis. Relevant to SAMA-supervised banks holding or issuing term securitization positions, and to related Pillar 3 disclosure.

Covers the STC criteria for short-term securitizations, i.e. exposures to ABCP conduits and to transactions financed by such conduits, which must be met at conduit and/or transaction level for the alternative capital treatment to apply. Related context addresses use of short-term external ratings, their issue-specific nature, ECAI eligibility, and the interaction with preferential treatment for short-term bank exposures. Binds SAMA-supervised banks investing in, sponsoring or providing facilities to ABCP programmes.

A concept node for the KSA parameter — the capital charge of the underlying pool of exposures computed under the standardised approach to credit risk — used as the key input when applying the standardised securitization approach to determine risk weights for securitization positions. Supporting context links it to the wider regulatory capital and Pillar 3 disclosure material, including capital ratio and distribution-constraint templates. Relevant to SAMA-supervised banks calculating securitization RWAs; note the abbreviation is unrelated to "Kingdom of Saudi Arabia".

A concept node for KIRB — the IRB capital requirement on the underlying pool of a securitization, the core input to the securitization internal-ratings-based approach (SEC-IRBA), including its decomposition into default-risk and dilution-risk components and its use with pool and tranche parameters (N, LGD, attachment/detachment points, maturity). Illustrated by worked examples on recognising dilution risk in SEC-IRBA. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks permitted to use IRB approaches for securitized underlying exposures.

The Mandate-Based Approach is one of three hierarchical methods (alongside the look-through approach and the fall-back approach) for risk-weighting a bank's equity investments in funds under the SAMA credit risk framework. It allows a bank that cannot look through to a fund's actual holdings to assign risk weights on the basis of the fund's mandate or prospectus limits, and interacts with leverage adjustment rules, partial use, funds investing in other funds, and application by IRB banks. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating credit RWA and is also referenced in Pillar 3 disclosure templates.

The Fall-Back Approach is the most conservative tier in the hierarchy for risk-weighting equity investments in funds, applied where neither the look-through nor the mandate-based approach can be used. It results in a punitive risk weight for the fund exposure and sits alongside rules on partial use of approaches, leverage adjustment and funds investing in other funds. It applies to banks computing credit RWA under SAMA's credit risk framework and feeds the related Pillar 3 RWA reporting rows.

Leverage adjustment covers two related concepts in the SAMA framework: the leverage adjustment applied when risk-weighting equity investments in funds, and the reconciling adjustments between published accounting assets and the leverage ratio exposure measure disclosed in Pillar 3 template LR1 (regulatory consolidation, securitised exposures, temporary central bank reserve exclusions, fiduciary assets, regular-way purchases/sales, cash pooling). It binds banks calculating the leverage ratio and preparing quarterly leverage disclosures.

Credit Valuation Adjustment risk is the risk of loss from changes in the value of derivatives and securities financing transactions due to potential counterparty default; regulatory CVA is defined at counterparty level and may differ from accounting CVA. The node covers the CVA capital framework (RWA derived by multiplying the CVA capital requirement by 12.5) and its separate reporting in Pillar 3 RWA templates. It binds SAMA-licensed banks with derivative and SFT exposures.

This node covers the capital treatment of unsettled securities, commodities and foreign exchange transactions and failed trades, requiring recognition of exposure from trade date irrespective of booking or accounting treatment, with escalating capital requirements after five business days. It excludes instruments in the counterparty credit risk/CVA framework and permits SAMA to waive requirements during system-wide settlement failures. It binds banks calculating credit RWA and their related Pillar 3 settlement risk disclosures.

Delivery-versus-payment transactions are settlements providing simultaneous exchange of securities for cash, exposing the bank to loss on the difference between the agreed settlement price and current market price (positive current exposure). Banks must hold capital against such exposures where payment has not occurred five business days after the settlement date; failure of a counterparty to settle is not itself a default for credit risk purposes. Applies to SAMA-licensed banks trading securities, FX and commodities.

Delta risk is one of the three components of the sensitivities-based method within SAMA's standardised approach to market risk capital, capturing linear sensitivity of instruments to prescribed risk factors (GIRR, credit spread, equity, FX, commodity) before aggregation with vega and curvature charges. The node sits in the market risk capital framework that SAMA mandates for all banks, D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs alike, and its risk weights also feed the curvature calculation. It binds licensed banks computing Pillar 1 market risk RWA.

Vega risk is the optionality-related component of the sensitivities-based method, capturing sensitivity to implied volatility; only instruments whose cash flows cannot be written as a linear function of notional (i.e. instruments with optionality) attract vega and curvature charges. It is aggregated with delta and curvature to form the sensitivities-based capital requirement under SAMA's standardised market risk rules. Applies to all banks calculating market risk capital.

Curvature risk captures non-linear (second-order) price sensitivity not covered by delta, computed by applying prescribed upward and downward shocks—for GIRR, CSR and commodities, a parallel shift based on the highest delta risk weight—and aggregated using squared delta correlations, with special treatment for CSR non-securitisations and securitisations (CTP). Banks may extend curvature to non-optional instruments only under stated consistency conditions. Binds banks applying SAMA's standardised approach to market risk.

The Default Risk Capital (DRC) requirement is the standardised market risk component covering jump-to-default losses on trading book exposures, sitting alongside the sensitivities-based method and the residual risk add-on and reported in Pillar 3 RWA and capital disclosure templates. This node is anchored in SAMA's disclosure/capital-requirement instruments, where DRC amounts feed minimum capital and RWA reporting. It binds banks computing and disclosing Pillar 1 market risk capital.

The Residual Risk Add-On is a supplementary standardised market risk charge for exotic underlyings and other residual risks (e.g. behavioural prepayment features, securitisation tranches with embedded options) not captured by delta, vega, curvature or DRC. It is also relevant to whether internal CVA risk transfers subject to RRAO can receive capital recognition, which requires an exactly matching external hedge. Applies to banks under SAMA's standardised market risk framework.

The Correlation Trading Portfolio is a defined subset of securitisation and related hedging positions treated separately within market risk capital, notably in credit spread risk (CSR securitisations (CTP)) bucketing, correlation parameters and curvature aggregation. Its distinct correlation treatment (name-based rather than basis/tenor) changes how capital is computed for those positions. Relevant to banks holding securitisation and correlation trading exposures in the trading book.

Node covering the Trading Book Policy Statement requirement within SAMA's minimum capital requirements for market risk: the bank-level documented policy that sets out how instruments are assigned to the trading book, how trading desks are defined and approved, and how internal risk transfers between the banking and trading books are documented and treated for capital purposes. It binds SAMA-supervised banks applying the market risk capital framework, and its adequacy is subject to SAMA review/approval. Relevant when assessing whether a hedge or desk structure will be recognised for regulatory capital.
lookup_terms: SAMA minimum capital requirements for market risk

data.summary: Defines the regulatory concept of a trading desk for market risk capital purposes: an unambiguously identified group of traders or trading accounts with a designated head trader, a defined risk scope, a documented business strategy with annual budget and management information reporting, and a clear risk management and limits structure. Desk definitions require SAMA validation against these attributes, while purely internal operational sub-desks may be created without approval but carry no capital-framework effect. Binds banks calculating market risk capital requirements.

Node on the regulatory boundary between the banking book and the trading book: scope of the trading book, standards and supervisory expectations for assigning instruments to each book, documentation of instrument designation, restrictions on reclassifying instruments between books, and the capital consequences of internal risk transfers across the boundary. It determines which capital regime (credit/banking book versus market risk) applies to a position and binds SAMA-supervised banks.

Sets the capital treatment of internal risk transfers — internal written records of risk moved within the banking book, between the banking and trading books, or between trading desks. Transfers from the trading book to the banking book get no capital recognition; transfers from the banking book to the trading book are recognised only where strict conditions are met, including an exactly matching external hedge with an eligible third-party protection provider for credit and equity risk, and use of a SAMA-approved dedicated internal risk transfer desk for general interest rate risk. Binds banks determining market risk and banking book capital requirements.
lookup_terms: banking book to trading book hedge

data.summary: Node on the standardised approach in the market risk capital framework and its interaction with standardised risk-weighted asset reporting across risk types. It covers the general provisions and structure of the standardised approach — the sensitivities-based method, default risk charge and residual risk add-on — and how standardised RWA and minimum capital requirements are identified relative to modelled/internal ratings-based approaches. Binds SAMA-supervised banks computing Pillar 1 capital requirements.

Describes the sensitivities-based method component of the standardised approach for market risk, built on delta, vega and curvature risk measures applied to regulatory risk factors, with risk-weighted sensitivities aggregated using prescribed correlation parameters. Banks must compute the capital requirement under three correlation scenarios to reflect stressed conditions, and the method sits alongside the default risk charge and residual risk add-on. Binds SAMA-supervised banks using the standardised market risk approach.

Concept node for the Internal Models Approach (IMA), the SAMA-approved alternative to standardised methods for computing market risk capital, built on expected shortfall (ES), default risk capital (DRC) and stressed ES for non-modellable risk factors, applied at trading desk level. It also connects to the modelled-approach columns of the capital/RWA overview templates, which distinguish RWA from approaches a bank has SAMA approval to use from standardised-approach RWA. It binds SAMA-licensed banks that have obtained supervisory approval to use internal models, including group-wide disclosure duties (Table MRB qualitative disclosures).

Concept node for General Interest Rate Risk (GIRR), one of the defined market risk classes used to calculate market risk capital requirements and a key reference point in the internal risk transfer rules between banking book and trading book. It governs how interest-rate-driven risk positions are identified, allocated to a dedicated SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk, and recognised for regulatory capital. Binds banks calculating minimum market risk capital under the SAMA framework.

Concept node for Credit Spread Risk (CSR), a defined market risk class (split into non-securitisation, securitisation non-correlation trading portfolio and correlation trading portfolio) and also a delta/vega risk class within the standardised CVA (SA-CVA) capital calculation, where it separates counterparty credit spread from reference credit spread. It governs classification of spread-sensitive positions and eligible hedges for capital purposes, including the rule that a hedge must sit wholly in one spread risk class. Binds banks computing market risk and CVA capital requirements.

Concept node for equity risk as a defined market risk class and as a separately reported exposure category in the capital/RWA overview templates, where equity positions are excluded from general credit risk rows and reported under the simple risk weight approach or internal models method. It governs how equity positions attract sensitivity-based (delta/vega) market risk capital and how they are disclosed alongside credit and counterparty credit risk RWA. Binds banks subject to SAMA minimum capital and Pillar 3 disclosure requirements.

Concept node for Foreign Exchange (FX) risk, a defined market risk class capturing losses from exchange rate movements on trading book and certain banking book positions. It appears in the internal risk transfer recognition rules (FX and commodity risk in the banking book fall within the market risk capital scope) and as a standalone capital component in the simplified standardised approach, including non-delta option risk add-ons. Binds banks calculating market risk capital requirements under the SAMA framework.

Concept node for commodity risk, one of the defined market risk classes used to calculate market risk capital requirements and expressly included, together with FX risk, within the market risk capital scope even when arising in the banking book for internal risk transfer purposes. It governs identification of commodity risk positions and their capital treatment under the sensitivities-based and simplified standardised approaches. Binds banks holding commodity exposures subject to SAMA minimum capital requirements.
lookup_terms: commodities risk in the banking book

data.summary: A component of SAMA's minimum capital requirements for market risk dealing with the equity risk class under the sensitivities-based standardised approach: how equity risk factors are grouped into buckets (by issuer characteristics such as market capitalisation, economy and sector) and the associated risk weights and intra/inter-bucket correlations used to aggregate delta, vega and curvature sensitivities. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA that hold trading book or otherwise in-scope equity positions and must compute market risk RWA.

Part of SAMA's market risk capital framework covering the commodity risk class under the sensitivities-based standardised approach: allocation of commodity risk factors into buckets by commodity type and grade/location, with prescribed risk weights and correlation parameters for aggregation. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks with commodity positions in the trading book, and to commodities risk in the banking book where it falls within the market risk capital scope.

A segment of SAMA's market risk capital rules addressing the FX risk class under the sensitivities-based standardised approach: identification of FX risk factors (currency pairs against the reporting currency), bucket structure, risk weights and correlations, alongside the simplified standardised approach treatment of FX risk. Binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating market risk capital requirements, including FX risk arising in the banking book.

Defines jump-to-default (JTD) risk as the core concept behind the default risk capital (DRC) requirement in SAMA's market risk framework, covering gross JTD computation, offsetting of long and short exposures to the same obligor, allocation of net JTD to buckets, and the limited hedge benefit recognition. It applies to SAMA-supervised banks holding instruments subject to default risk across non-securitisation, securitisation (non-CTP) and correlation trading portfolios.

Sets out the default risk capital requirement for non-securitisation exposures under SAMA's standardised approach to market risk: gross and net JTD determination including LGD ratios, bucketing by obligor type, credit-quality-based risk weights, the hedge benefit ratio, and the rule that bucket-level requirements are simply summed with no cross-bucket hedging or diversification benefit. Binds SAMA-licensed banks with trading book credit and equity exposures, including the treatment of sovereign, PSE, MDB and fund exposures.

Covers the default risk capital requirement for securitisation exposures in the correlation trading portfolio (CTP), and its relationship to the non-CTP securitisation treatment: gross JTD based on market value of the tranche, restricted offsetting rules, tranche-based risk weights derived from the banking book securitisation framework with the maturity component set to zero, and inclusion of non-securitisation hedges in the CTP calculation. Binds SAMA-supervised banks running correlation trading and securitisation positions in the trading book.

Node covering the Profit and Loss Attribution (PLA) test within SAMA's minimum capital requirements for market risk, which compares a trading desk's risk-theoretical P&L against its hypothetical P&L to verify that the desk's risk management model adequately captures the risks driving actual valuation changes. It sets the gateway that determines whether a desk may use the internal models approach (IMA) or must fall back to the standardised approach, using green/amber/red zone outcomes from two statistical metrics. It binds SAMA-supervised banks operating trading desks seeking or maintaining IMA approval for market risk capital.

Defines risk-theoretical P&L (RTPL), the daily P&L predicted by a trading desk's risk management model using only the risk factors contained in that model, and used as one of the two inputs to the PLA test. The node also addresses the limited circumstances in which RTPL input data may be aligned with hypothetical P&L data (differing market data providers, snapshot times or data transformations), with documentation, validation, notification and impact-assessment duties owed to SAMA. Applies to banks using or seeking IMA approval for market risk.

Defines hypothetical P&L (HPL), the revaluation of a desk's unchanged end-of-day positions using the same market data as the front-office P&L, excluding intraday trading, new or modified deals, fees and commissions, and certain valuation adjustments already capitalised or deducted from CET1. HPL serves as the benchmark series for both backtesting and the PLA test, with specific rules on which valuation adjustments must be included at desk versus bank-wide level. Binds banks applying the internal models approach to market risk under SAMA rules.

Defines actual P&L (APL), the P&L produced by the bank's daily P&L process including intraday trading, time effects and new or modified deals, but excluding fees, commissions and valuation adjustments subject to separate capital treatment. APL is used alongside HPL in backtesting internal market risk models against VaR measures at desk and bank-wide level. Relevant to SAMA-supervised banks with IMA-approved or candidate trading desks.

Sets out the Spearman rank correlation metric, one of the two PLA test statistics, which ranks the most recent 250 trading days of HPL and RTPL observations and measures the correlation between the two rank series. The resulting coefficient feeds the green/amber/red zone classification that determines a trading desk's continued eligibility for the internal models approach. Applies to banks calculating market risk capital under IMA supervision by SAMA.

Sets out the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distributional test metric, the second PLA test statistic, measured as the largest absolute difference between the empirical cumulative distribution functions of RTPL and HPL. Together with the Spearman metric it drives allocation of a trading desk to the PLA green, amber or red zone, with red-zone desks losing IMA eligibility and reverting to the standardised approach until they return to the green zone and clear backtesting exception requirements for twelve months. Binds SAMA-supervised banks using internal models for market risk.

Concept node labelled Hedge Benefit Ratio sitting within SAMA's Basel-aligned capital and Pillar 3 disclosure material; the retrieved context is drawn from the fixed-format CDC template on capital ratios that trigger capital distribution constraints (buffers, Pillar 2, leverage) and the flexible REMA table on remuneration policy and material risk-takers. It binds banks subject to SAMA's minimum capital and disclosure framework, at the level of regulatory consolidation, on an annual disclosure cycle. Open the source if you need the exact ratio definitions, template rows or the narrative expected where distribution constraints have actually been imposed.

Node covering general internal-models provisions in SAMA's minimum capital requirements, spanning IRB risk quantification standards (own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD, long-run averages, data representativeness, conservatism) and the general framing of internal model use for capital purposes. It binds banks authorised to use internal ratings-based or internal model approaches; banks not meeting own-estimate conditions must fall back to supervisory parameters. Useful when checking estimation standards and the boundary between foundation and advanced approaches.

Node on the specific model requirements for banks using the internal models approach to market risk, including the trading desk structure, expected shortfall models, default risk capital, stressed expected shortfall for non-modellable risk factors, and the mandatory MRB qualitative disclosure table. It binds banks permitted by SAMA to use the IMA for market risk capital, at group-wide regulatory consolidation level, with annual flexible-format disclosure. Consult for what must be described about model scope, coverage percentages and soundness criteria.

Defines the Risk Factor Eligibility Test, the quarterly quantitative gate (real price observation counts and gap conditions) determining whether a market risk factor may be modelled in the expected shortfall model or must be treated as non-modellable. It also sets bucketing, parametric-curve and systematic-versus-idiosyncratic allocation rules, plus qualitative modellability principles that SAMA may apply to reject data. Binds banks using the IMA for market risk capital.

Concept node for non-modellable risk factors: risk factors that fail the RFET or whose data SAMA deems unsuitable, which are excluded from the expected shortfall model and instead attract a stressed expected shortfall capital requirement. Includes the criteria for what counts as a real price, third-party vendor price conditions, and SAMA's narrow discretion during systemic market stress. Binds banks using the IMA for market risk.

Sets out backtesting obligations for market risk internal models, including bank-wide green/amber/red zone interpretation, the resulting multiplier add-ons or withdrawal of model permission, documentation and explanation of every exception, and daily trading-desk-level backtesting. Also covers the narrow allowance to disregard a desk-level exception driven by an NMRF with sufficient SES capital, subject to notification and no SAMA objection, and quarterly updating of the backtested portfolio. Binds banks using internal models for market risk capital.

A definitional/reporting node explaining what counts as the "standardised approach" for each risk type (credit, counterparty credit, CVA, securitisation, market and operational risk) when banks populate SAMA's capital comparison template (modelled RWA vs RWA under full standardised approach, plus residual RWA). It fixes how banks split RWA between SAMA-approved internal models (IRB, IMA) and standardised calculations, and addresses the phase-in for equity exposures where IRB use is withdrawn. It binds SAMA-licensed banks subject to Pillar 1 capital and Pillar 3 disclosure requirements.

Part of SAMA's market risk framework covering general interest rate risk under the simplified standardised approach, together with the defined vocabulary used across the market risk rules (risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class, sensitivity, delta, look-through, embedded derivative). It also carries the rules on internal risk transfers of interest rate risk between the banking book and a SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk, and when such transfers get capital recognition. Binds banks calculating minimum market risk capital.

Covers the equity risk component of the simplified standardised approach for market risk, sitting alongside the RWA/minimum capital reporting explanations (Pillar 1 capital as RWA × 8%, and where equity positions, simple risk weight approach and internal models method amounts are reported). It also includes the internal risk transfer rules that determine regulatory capital recognition between trading desks. Binds SAMA-licensed banks computing and disclosing market and credit risk capital.

Sets out the foreign exchange risk element of the simplified standardised approach for market risk, within the structure where total capital is the arithmetic sum of interest rate, equity, FX and commodity risk charges plus non-delta option risks, converted to RWA by multiplying by 12.5. It also covers internal risk transfers involving FX and commodities risk in the banking book and their capital recognition. Applies to banks using the simplified standardised approach for market risk capital.

Covers commodities position risk under the simplified standardised approach, identifying the risks captured (directional/spot, basis, interest rate cost-of-carry, forward gap) and the two permitted measurement alternatives, including the maturity ladder approach. It cross-refers funding-related interest rate and FX exposures to the corresponding risk classes and counterparty credit risk on OTC derivatives to the CCR/CVA rules. Binds banks holding commodity positions and calculating market risk capital.

Concept node for the maturity ladder method used to measure commodities position risk under the simplified standardised approach (time-band based capture of forward gap and interest rate risk), read together with maturity-related rules in the standardised default risk charge, including the three-month maturity floor and the use of derivative rather than underlying maturity for offsetting. It also links to the RWA reporting definitions distinguishing standardised from modelled approaches. Binds banks computing market risk capital under SAMA's framework.

Concept node for Expected Shortfall (ES), the internal models approach risk measure used to set market risk capital requirements, disclosed in both unconstrained form and in the constrained form that applies supervisory limits on cross-risk-factor correlations (summed as partial ES across interest rate, equity, FX, commodity and credit spread classes). The node sits within SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosure material, where ES appears alongside non-modellable risk factor charges, default risk capital and the amber-desk surcharge in the aggregation of IMA capital requirements. It binds banks authorised to use the IMA for market risk and drives what they must report publicly.

Concept node for IMCC, the internally modelled capital charge covering modellable risk factors under the market risk internal models approach, built from the constrained and unconstrained expected shortfall figures and feeding the aggregate IMA capital requirement. The surrounding context is SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosure framework, which sets out RWA and minimum capital requirement templates (including the standard RWA*8% Pillar 1 relationship) and capital distribution constraint disclosures. Relevant to banks using the IMA and to their public disclosure obligations.

Concept node for the Stressed Expected Shortfall (SES) capital add-on for non-modellable risk factors (NMRFs) — risk factors in model-eligible trading desks that fail modellability criteria and therefore attract a separate aggregate capital measure rather than inclusion in the ES model. It is one of the three IMA regulatory model components (ES, DRC and SES for NMRFs) that banks must describe qualitatively and quantify in Pillar 3 disclosures. Binds banks using the internal models approach for market risk.

Concept node for the liquidity horizon — the supervisory-set holding period assigned to each risk factor category (10 to 120 days) used to scale expected shortfall from a 10-day base horizon when computing market risk capital under the internal models approach. The source sets out the scaling formula, the nested risk factor subsets and the full table of horizons by risk factor class (interest rate, credit spread, equity, FX, commodity and their volatilities), with specific rules for repo, dividend, basis and inflation risk factors. Binds banks calculating market risk capital under the IMA.

Concept node for the Default Risk Capital (DRC) requirement under the market risk internal models approach — the modelled measure of jump-to-default risk on trading book positions (including sovereign, equity and defaulted debt exposures) other than those on desks subject to standardised capital requirements. It is one of the IMA components banks must describe and quantify in SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosures, entering the aggregate capital requirement alongside ES-based charges. Binds banks with IMA-approved trading desks.

Concept node for how the components of the market risk internal models approach are aggregated into a total capital requirement — combining the modelled ES-based charge, the non-modellable risk factor add-on, default risk capital, any amber-zone trading desk surcharge, and the standardised approach charge for desks ineligible for the IMA. The surrounding source is SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosure framework, including the fixed-format templates and capital distribution constraint disclosures. Relevant to banks calculating and disclosing market risk capital.

A market risk capital methodology node within SAMA's Basel-aligned capital framework, setting out how banks that write options may include delta-weighted option positions in the simplified standardised approach, with the delta-equivalent amount carrying the applicable general market risk charge. Because delta alone does not capture option risk, banks must additionally measure and hold capital against gamma and vega sensitivities, computed via an approved exchange model or the bank's own options pricing model under SAMA oversight. Binds SAMA-licensed banks with options exposures using the simplified standardised market risk treatment.

Describes the scenario (grid simulation) alternative for measuring market risk capital on options portfolios, where the general market risk charge is set by the scenario combination of underlying price and volatility changes producing the largest loss. Specific risk is calculated separately by applying specific risk weights to each option's delta-equivalent, as under the delta-plus method. Applies to banks using the simplified/standardised options treatment, subject to SAMA supervisory acceptance.

Sets the carve-out treatment under which option positions and their associated cash or forward hedges are excluded from the standardised methodology and given separately calculated capital requirements covering both general and specific market risk, with the resulting figures added back to the relevant risk category (interest rate, equity, FX, commodity). Prescribes position-by-position treatments such as long cash with long put and standalone long call/long put. Relevant to banks with limited options activity; banks with significant trading activity are expected to use the standardised or internal models approaches instead.
lookup_terms: specific and general market risk charge

data.summary: Concept node for the backtesting traffic-light classification (green, amber/yellow, red zones) used to assess internal model performance against realised outcomes and to drive multiplier add-ons or model use restrictions. The retrieved context is dominated by credit risk mitigation disclosure material (Template CR3), so the backtesting zone provisions themselves must be confirmed in the underlying market risk/internal models sections. Applies to banks with SAMA-approved internal models.

Governs when a risk factor may be modelled inside a bank's expected shortfall model versus being capitalised as a non-modellable risk factor (NMRF), building on the risk factor eligibility test (RFET) and supporting data-quality principles. SAMA may deem data unsuitable and force NMRF treatment, and may in extraordinary systemic circumstances treat a failed risk factor as modellable without reducing capital; banks must evidence modellability (e.g. regression diagnostics, price recovery from risk factors) rather than relying on real price counts alone. Binds banks using the internal models approach for market risk.

Node for the minimum regulatory capital requirement for operational risk within SAMA's Basel-aligned capital framework, covering the standardised measurement of operational risk capital and its interaction with overall capital ratios, buffers and disclosure templates. The retrieved context shows adjacent capital-adequacy and Pillar 3 disclosure material (capital distribution constraints, Tier 2 deductions), so the operational risk calculation detail should be verified in the underlying document. Binds SAMA-licensed banks on a consolidated and solo basis.

Node covering the standardised approach as a prescribed regulatory capital calculation method, including its use for operational risk and, in the disclosure material drawn on here, the standardised approach to credit risk and how standardised versus modelled (IRB/slotting) portfolios are split across Pillar 3 template rows and columns. It fixes which exposures and RWA belong in the standardised bucket, the treatment of credit risk mitigation (simple versus comprehensive approach with supervisory haircuts), and the phase-in for equity exposures leaving IRB. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating and disclosing minimum Pillar 1 capital requirements.

The Business Indicator (BI) is the financial-statement-based volume proxy that drives the standardised operational risk capital charge, built from the interest, lease and dividend component, the services component and the financial component, each averaged over three years. Its subcomponents and any exclusion of divested activities (which requires SAMA approval) must be disclosed annually in the fixed Pillar 3 template with supporting narrative. It binds banks supervised by SAMA that compute operational risk capital.
lookup_terms: ILDC interest lease and dividend component

data.summary: The Business Indicator Component (BIC) is the Business Indicator transformed by the regulatory marginal coefficients and is the base figure for the standardised operational risk capital requirement. It is also the benchmark against which the Loss Component is compared to derive the Internal Loss Multiplier, and banks lacking sufficient high-quality loss data must calculate capital on the BIC alone. It applies to SAMA-supervised banks for both capital calculation and annual Pillar 3 disclosure.

The Internal Loss Multiplier (ILM) scales the Business Indicator Component up or down according to a bank's own operational loss experience, equalling one where the Loss Component and BIC are equal. It requires ten years of high-quality annual loss data, with a transitional minimum of five years subject to SAMA approval; banks below five years must either use the BIC alone or obtain SAMA's direction on using shorter data or an ILM above one. Banks must also disclose whether losses are used in the ILM and why not, where applicable.

The Loss Component (LC) equals fifteen times average annual operational risk losses over the preceding ten years and is the loss-sensitive input to the Internal Loss Multiplier. Its calculation rests on loss data quality standards, net-of-recovery loss amounts, loss event thresholds (SAR 44,600 and SAR 446,000) and any SAMA-approved exclusions such as divestitures, all of which feed prescribed annual disclosure rows. It binds SAMA-supervised banks computing standardised operational risk capital.
lookup_terms: operational risk losses net of recoveries

data.summary: Operational Risk Capital (ORC) is the Pillar 1 minimum capital requirement for operational risk under the standardised approach, derived from the Business Indicator Component multiplied by the Internal Loss Multiplier and converted into RWA for the overall capital ratio. It sits alongside credit, counterparty credit, market and other Pillar 1 charges in the RWA overview and feeds ratio-based consequences such as capital distribution constraints. It binds SAMA-supervised banks for calculation, reporting and Pillar 3 disclosure.

Concept node for the potential future exposure (PFE) add-on component of counterparty credit risk exposure on derivatives, as used in SAMA's adopted Basel-based capital and leverage ratio framework. It governs how banks quantify and report the forward-looking element of derivative exposures (alongside replacement cost, with the prescribed alpha factor) in the leverage ratio exposure measure and related Pillar 3 templates. Binds banks subject to SAMA's minimum capital and disclosure rules on a regulatory consolidation basis.

Concept node for the net independent collateral amount (NICA) used in measuring counterparty credit risk exposure on derivatives and in related capital deductions and credit risk mitigation disclosures under SAMA's Basel-aligned framework. It matters for how collateral other than variation margin is recognised in exposure and for how secured/collateralised exposures are presented in Pillar 3 templates. Applies to banks calculating regulatory capital and making mandated disclosures.

Concept node for the effective notional of a derivative trade — the adjusted notional scaled by the maturity factor and supervisory delta — which feeds the add-on calculation under the standardised approach to counterparty credit risk. It governs trade-, entity-, maturity-bucket- and hedging-set-level aggregation for both margined and unmargined netting sets. Relevant to banks computing counterparty credit risk capital under SAMA's minimum capital requirements.

Concept node for the supervisory delta adjustment applied at trade level to adjusted notional amounts to reflect direction (long/short in the primary risk factor) and non-linearity of options and CDO tranches. It is a prescribed parameter set (including option formulas using supervisory volatility) within the standardised counterparty credit risk calculation. Binds banks determining derivative exposure amounts for capital and leverage ratio purposes under SAMA rules.

Concept node for the maturity factor used to scale adjusted notionals in the counterparty credit risk add-on calculation, with distinct treatments for margined and unmargined netting sets (and related maturity-bucket concepts appearing in market risk risk-factor modellability rules). It determines the time-horizon scaling of derivative exposure. Applies to banks computing regulatory capital under SAMA's adopted Basel minimum capital requirements.

Concept node covering SAMA's minimum standards for identifying, collecting and treating internal operational loss data used as a direct input to the operational risk capital calculation under the standardised approach. It sets the general criteria (e.g. observation period, documented identification procedures, linkage to current business activities) and the consequence of non-compliance, namely capital of at least 100% of the Business Indicator Component, a possible supervisory Internal Loss Multiplier above 1, and mandatory Pillar 3 disclosure of the exclusion. It binds banks above the specified Business Indicator threshold, with disclosure of loss data and thresholds in the prescribed reporting templates.

Concept node on the specific criteria for building the standardised approach operational loss data set, including definitions of gross loss, net loss and recoveries, the reference date and grouped losses. It specifies which items must enter the gross loss computation (direct P&L charges and write-downs, consequential external costs, provisions/reserves, and material pending losses) and restricts netting of recoveries to amounts actually received, with evidence available to SAMA on request. It binds banks calculating operational risk capital under the standardised approach.

Concept node for the counterparty credit risk regime: the risk that a counterparty defaults before final settlement where there is bilateral risk of loss, together with related risks (rollover risk, general and specific wrong-way risk) and the linkage to CVA capital. It sets the framework's effective date and requires quarterly reporting of CCR and CVA risk-weighted assets and capital charges on SAMA's designated template within 30 days of quarter end, with corresponding Pillar 3 template disclosure. It binds banks subject to SAMA's minimum capital requirements.

Concept node on the Internal Models Method for measuring exposure/EAD for counterparty credit risk, and on internal models governance more generally. Use of IMM requires prior SAMA approval, satisfaction of the stated qualitative and quantitative requirements, and application across all CCR exposures (or all exposures within an approved category such as OTC derivatives or SFTs), with a transition plan for any portion still on the standardised approach. Related model-governance duties (independent risk control unit, backtesting/P&L attribution, independent model validation, board and senior management involvement) bind banks using internal models.

Concept node for the Credit Valuation Adjustment capital framework: CVA is the counterparty-level adjustment to default risk-free prices of derivatives and securities financing transactions for potential counterparty default. It distinguishes regulatory CVA from accounting CVA, sets the conversion of CVA capital requirements into risk-weighted assets, and frames the SA-CVA/BA-CVA approaches and any alternative treatment. It binds banks with in-scope derivative and SFT exposures under SAMA's minimum capital requirements.

Concept node on replacement cost, a core component of exposure at default under SA-CCR, including the formula for margined netting sets based on trade value less collateral, threshold, minimum transfer amount and net independent collateral amount, floored at zero. The framework illustrates its operation through worked examples covering standard margin agreements, variation margin and independent amounts. It applies to banks computing counterparty credit risk exposures under SA-CCR.

data.label: Netting Set
data.summary: Defined unit of aggregation in SAMA's counterparty credit risk capital framework: the group of transactions with a single counterparty that may be netted for exposure measurement. The material sets out how replacement cost and PFE add-ons are computed at netting set level, how several netting sets under one margin agreement are aggregated (with unmargined PFE treatment where collateral is exchanged on a net basis across netting sets), and how collateral taken outside a netting set is attributed. Binds banks calculating regulatory exposure at default for derivatives and other CCR exposures.

data.label: Effective Expected Positive Exposure (EPE)
data.summary: Concept node for Effective EPE, the exposure metric used under the Internal Models Method to derive exposure at default for counterparty credit risk (typically scaled by alpha). The cited source documents also carry the related Pillar 3 credit risk mitigation and problem-asset disclosure material, so the node spans both the capital measurement concept and its disclosure context. Relevant to banks with SAMA approval to use internal models for CCR, and to those preparing regulatory disclosures.

data.label: Margin Period of Risk (MPOR)
data.summary: Sets the supervisory floors on the margin period of risk used when measuring exposure on margined netting sets, and the exceptions that lengthen them — large netting sets not facing a central counterparty, illiquid collateral or OTC derivatives that cannot be easily replaced, and a doubling of the floor following repeated prolonged margin call disputes. Binds banks calculating counterparty credit risk exposure for margined transactions.

data.label: Wrong-Way Risk
data.summary: Covers the identification and management of general and specific wrong-way risk — where counterparty exposure is positively correlated with deterioration in the counterparty's creditworthiness. Requires stress testing and scenario analysis designed to surface such correlations, monitoring by product, region and industry, and regular reporting to senior management and the board or its delegated committee. Binds banks running counterparty credit risk exposures.

data.label: IMM Stress Testing Program
data.summary: Sets the minimum content and frequency of a bank's counterparty credit risk stress testing programme: complete trade capture and counterparty-level aggregation, at least monthly single-factor exposure stress tests, at least quarterly multifactor and non-directional stress tests, joint stressing of exposure and counterparty credit quality, reverse stress testing, and senior management ownership with results measured against risk appetite. Binds banks measuring counterparty credit risk, particularly those using internal models.

data.label: IMM Model Validation
data.summary: Sets the ongoing validation expectations for EPE models and related risk measures used under the Internal Models Method, including backtesting against realised exposures, independent benchmarking of pricing models, assessment of parameter update frequency, validation out to horizons matching trade maturity, and coverage of all relevant counterparties. Also addresses SAMA's power to require correction or additional capital where model performance is deficient, and prior SAMA approval for using a more conservative measure in place of alpha times Effective EPE. Binds banks with IMM approval.

Concept node for the alpha multiplier used in the internal models method (IMM) for counterparty credit risk, where exposure at default equals alpha times Effective EPE. It fixes alpha at 1.4, permits SAMA to impose a higher value based on a bank's CCR exposure profile (e.g. low counterparty granularity, general wrong-way risk, high correlation of market values), and allows bank-specific internal estimates subject to prior SAMA approval and a 1.2 floor. Binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating regulatory capital for counterparty credit risk.

Concept node relating to counterparty credit risk scope within SAMA's CCR framework, covering the bilateral nature of CCR and the transaction categories that attract a CCR charge (OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives, long settlement transactions and securities financing transactions). The qualifying central counterparty notion sits within this scope as the basis for preferential treatment of cleared exposures. Applies to banks supervised by SAMA when calculating credit RWA.

Node covering the disclosure/reporting template mechanics in the Pillar 3 part of the framework, including CCR and securitisation templates (e.g. CCR5, CCR7, SEC1, OV1) and interpretive Q&A on what to report where. It sets out the distinction between fixed-format templates (prescribed rows/columns, deletion allowed for irrelevant items but no renumbering) and flexible-format templates, plus signposting of disclosures made in other documents. Binds banks subject to SAMA disclosure requirements.

Concept node on wrong-way risk in the counterparty credit risk framework, distinguishing general wrong-way risk (exposure positively correlated with deterioration in counterparty credit quality across a portfolio) from specific wrong-way risk (future exposure to a particular counterparty highly correlated with that counterparty's own credit quality). It requires identification, stress testing and scenario analysis, monitoring by product/region/industry, and regular reporting to senior management and the board or its delegated committee. Binds banks measuring and managing CCR under SAMA supervision.

Concept node for the Effective EPE (expected positive exposure) model used under the internal models method to determine counterparty credit exposure at netting-set level. It sets out model validation, backtesting, benchmarking of pricing models, parameter-update frequency and ongoing performance assessment expectations, including SAMA's power to require correction of model or data deficiencies and to impose additional capital, and the option to use a more conservative measure than alpha times Effective EPE with prior SAMA approval. Binds IMM-approved banks.

Concept node on the stressed calibration requirement for Effective EPE under the internal models method: banks must compute credit RWA as the higher of current-parameter and stressed-parameter results, calibrating Effective EPE with at least three years of data including a period of stress to counterparties' credit spreads, or with market-implied data from a suitable stress period. It sets quarterly demonstration and data-update obligations, mapping rules where counterparty credit spread data is unavailable, and constraints on reverting from IMM to the standardised approach. Binds banks using IMM for counterparty credit risk.
lookup_terms: higher of current and stressed parameters

data.summary: Sets out the conditions under which a bank using the internal models method (IMM) for counterparty credit risk may recognise netting across securities financing transactions, or across SFTs and OTC derivatives, for regulatory capital purposes. It imposes legal criteria: a written bilateral cross-product netting arrangement producing a single net obligation on default or insolvency, plus reasoned legal opinions confirming enforceability under the laws of all relevant jurisdictions (counterparty's charter/branch jurisdiction, transaction governing law, and law governing the netting contract). Binds SAMA-supervised banks seeking IMM/netting recognition, subject to SAMA approval and internal verification procedures before a trade enters a netting set.

Concept node covering the capital treatment and Pillar 3 disclosure of bank exposures to central counterparties, distinguishing qualifying CCPs (QCCPs) from non-qualifying CCPs. It links the capital requirement rules for trade exposures, initial margin and default fund contributions with the mandatory CCR8 disclosure template and the wider capital adequacy/disclosure architecture (including capital distribution constraint disclosures). Applies to SAMA-supervised banks acting as clearing members or clients of CCPs.

Concerns trade exposures arising from transactions cleared through a CCP — current and potential future exposure and variation margin — excluding initial margin and default fund contributions, and their EAD/RWA treatment and disclosure. The CCR8 disclosure template requires banks to break these down by QCCP versus non-QCCP and by product type (OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives, SFTs, and cross-product netting sets). Mandatory for all SAMA-supervised banks, reported semi-annually with narrative explanation of material changes.

Covers exposures arising from a bank's pre-funded and unfunded contributions to a CCP's default fund, and their capitalisation and disclosure separately from trade exposures and initial margin. The CCR8 template requires segregated reporting of these contributions split between qualifying and non-qualifying CCPs. Binds SAMA-supervised banks that are clearing members contributing to CCP mutualised loss-sharing arrangements.

Defines KCCP, the hypothetical capital requirement of a central counterparty computed from its counterparty credit risk exposures to all clearing members and their clients. It is a purely notional figure calculated on a consistent basis solely as the first step in determining a clearing member bank's capital charge for its default fund contribution, and does not represent the CCP's own regulatory capital requirement. Relevant to SAMA-supervised banks that are clearing members of QCCPs.
lookup_terms: hypothetical capital requirement of the CCP

data.summary: Sets the risk-sensitive capital requirement (KCMi) that a clearing member bank must hold against its default fund contribution to a qualifying CCP, calculated in two steps: first the CCP's hypothetical capital requirement (KCCP), then the allocation to the individual clearing member. The risk weight reflects the size and quality of the CCP's financial resources, its counterparty credit risk exposures, and the operation of its loss-bearing waterfall on member default. Binds SAMA-supervised banks acting as clearing members of QCCPs.

Node covering how counterparty credit risk arising on trading book positions is capitalised under SAMA's Basel-aligned minimum capital framework, including the treatment of repo-style and collateralised OTC derivative transactions (which follow the banking book CCR rules), eligible trading book collateral and applicable haircuts, and related RWA/capital reporting lines that separate CCR from general credit risk, CVA, settlement and securitisation exposures. It also touches the boundary rules for internal risk transfers between banking book and trading book and when the trading book leg may be recognised for market risk purposes. Binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating Pillar 1 capital requirements.

Sets the minimum haircut floors regime for non-centrally cleared securities financing transactions with in-scope counterparties, defining which SFTs are captured, the exemptions (central bank SFTs, certain cash-collateralised securities lending, non-re-usable collateral upgrade trades) and the floor percentages by collateral type and residual maturity. Also frames the consequence of breaching a floor for capital treatment. Applies to banks conducting SFTs under SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit/counterparty risk.

Covers the basic approach (BA-CVA) as the default method for calculating the CVA risk capital requirement, applicable to derivatives and fair-valued SFTs in both banking and trading book, excluding trades with qualified CCPs and other carved-out transactions. Explains that BA-CVA is mandatory unless SAMA grants approval to use SA-CVA, and that it has full and reduced variants. Binds banks with covered derivative/SFT exposures.

Covers the standardised approach for CVA risk capital (SA-CVA), the more risk-sensitive alternative to BA-CVA that a bank may use only with prior SAMA approval. Defines regulatory CVA (excluding own default), the scope of covered transactions including fair-valued SFTs where CVA loss exposure is material, and the standalone CVA portfolio basis of calculation. Binds banks seeking or holding SAMA permission for SA-CVA.

Defines the reduced version of BA-CVA, in which CVA hedges are not recognised, calculated by aggregating stand-alone CVA capital across in-scope counterparties with a supervisory correlation parameter and a discount scalar. Intended for banks that do not hedge CVA risk, and also forms a component of the full BA-CVA calculation as a constraint on hedge recognition. Applies to banks using BA-CVA under SAMA's capital framework.

Defines the full version of BA-CVA, which recognises eligible counterparty credit spread hedges and is intended for banks that actively hedge CVA risk; it incorporates the reduced BA-CVA result to limit hedge recognition. Related rules distinguish eligible from ineligible external and internal CVA hedges and their allocation between the CVA portfolio and the trading book for market risk capital, and permit capping the IRB maturity adjustment factor at 1 for netting sets in the CVA charge. Binds banks using BA-CVA under SAMA's capital framework.

A component concept within SAMA's Basel-aligned capital/disclosure framework covering how derivative positions enter the leverage ratio exposure measure and the related prudential disclosure templates (e.g. key metrics and capital distribution constraint templates). It governs measurement of replacement cost and potential future exposure for derivatives and their reflection in publicly disclosed leverage metrics. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA on a consolidated group basis.

Addresses securities financing transaction (SFT) exposures as a component of the leverage ratio exposure measure and the associated prudential disclosure obligations under SAMA's Basel-aligned framework. It concerns how repos, reverse repos, securities lending/borrowing and margin lending are measured and disclosed in leverage and key-metrics templates. Applies to SAMA-licensed banks at consolidated group level.

Covers the treatment and disclosure of off-balance sheet items — guarantees, irrevocable loan commitments and similar contingent exposures — as credit risk exposures under the Basel-aligned disclosure framework, including their gross carrying value measurement before credit conversion factors or credit risk mitigation. Relevant to credit quality templates (e.g. CR1) and to the leverage ratio exposure measure. Mandatory for all SAMA-supervised banks.
lookup_terms: Template CR1 credit quality of assets

data.summary: Defines written credit derivatives broadly as any instrument through which a bank effectively sells credit protection, and sets the conditions for offsetting effective notional amounts against purchased credit protection (identical reference name, pari passu or junior reference obligation, same or more conservative material terms, strike price test). Determines the amount added to the leverage ratio exposure measure for sold credit protection. Binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating leverage and counterparty credit exposures.
lookup_terms: credit default swap total return swap

data.summary: Sets the cumulative conditions under which cash variation margin exchanged on derivatives may be treated as a settlement payment rather than collateral — including non-segregation, at-least-daily exchange based on mark-to-market, eligible currency, full mark-to-market amount, and coverage by a single legally enforceable master netting agreement. Where met, cash variation margin received reduces replacement cost and margin provided may be deducted from the leverage ratio exposure measure. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks with derivative portfolios.

Sets the prudential treatment of exposures arising where a bank acts as clearing member providing client clearing services, or as a client clearing through a member or CCP, including capitalisation of client exposures as bilateral trades, the reduced five-day margin period of risk, recognition of client collateral passed to the CCP, and conditions for applying CCP treatment to client-leg exposures. Also covers multi-level client structures and defines initial margin, variation margin and trade exposures. Binds SAMA-licensed banks acting as clearing members or clearing clients.
lookup_terms: margin period of risk five days

data.summary: A concept node for the stand-alone CVA capital requirement (SCVAc) component within SAMA's Basel-aligned capital framework, sitting alongside Pillar 3 disclosure templates on regulatory capital composition and capital distribution constraints. It relates to how credit valuation adjustment risk is capitalised separately from counterparty credit risk and how the resulting figures feed disclosed capital ratios and buffer-trigger levels. It binds banks subject to SAMA's risk-based capital and disclosure requirements at the consolidated group level.
