Node for the minimum requirements a bank must satisfy to use the internal ratings-based approach under SAMA's credit risk capital rules, including rating system design, corporate governance and oversight, use test, risk quantification, validation and data maintenance, plus the rules on adopting IRB by asset class. It also covers phased rollout: SAMA may allow staged adoption across asset classes and business units against an agreed, realistic implementation plan, but once IRB is applied to an asset class in a business unit all exposures in that class and unit must be treated on IRB, and no capital relief is permitted for intra-group transactions designed to reduce the group charge during rollout. Binds banks seeking or holding SAMA approval for foundation or advanced IRB.

Node on the operation of rating systems for credit risk capital purposes; the supplied context concentrates on external rating usage under the standardised approach — consistent use of SAMA-recognised ECAIs for both risk weighting and risk management, prohibition on cherry-picking between ECAIs, use of global rating scales, and the multiple-rating and issue-specific versus issuer rating rules (including short-term rating treatment). Binds SAMA-licensed banks applying external ratings to determine risk weights.

Node covering loss-given-default determination under the IRB approach in SAMA's credit risk capital rules, including the effective LGD for collateralised transactions (LGD* as an exposure-weighted blend of unsecured and secured LGD with haircuts for collateral type and currency mismatch), the unavailability of the standardised simple collateral approach to IRB banks, and supervisory LGD parameter floors by collateral type for corporate exposures (with pro-rata treatment for partially secured exposures). Binds banks using foundation or advanced IRB for credit risk capital.

Node on the use of statistical models and mechanical rating inputs in credit risk assessment; the supplied context addresses the related rules on consistent and non-selective use of external credit assessments (ECAI ratings) for risk weighting and risk management, multiple-rating resolution, and the scope of short-term versus long-term ratings. Relevant to banks determining risk weights and to the broader IRB expectation that model outputs be used consistently and not chosen to minimise capital.

Node covering the requirement that an IRB bank maintain sound stress testing processes for assessing capital adequacy, identifying events or changes in economic conditions that could adversely affect credit exposures and testing the bank's ability to withstand them (examples include economic or industry downturns, market-risk events and liquidity conditions). The surrounding context also covers IRB data maintenance for corporate and retail exposures and, separately, the securitisation internal assessment approach requiring prior SAMA notification and approval. Binds SAMA-licensed banks on the IRB approach.

A node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk framework dealing with the internal credit risk control function that banks must maintain as a condition of using internal ratings-based approaches, sitting alongside rules on recognition of credit risk mitigants, guarantees and off-balance-sheet conversion factors. It concerns independence of rating system oversight from business origination and the supervisory expectations attached to IRB eligibility. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating regulatory capital for credit risk, particularly those seeking or maintaining IRB permission.

Sets out when commercial and residential real estate qualifies as recognised collateral for capital purposes, including the operational conditions of legal enforceability and perfected lien, objective market valuation, and at least annual revaluation, and excludes income-producing real estate falling in the specialised lending asset class from recognition against corporate exposures. It also frames the real estate exposure class (regulatory residential/commercial, other real estate, ADC) used in the standardised approach. Binds banks under SAMA supervision when computing risk-weighted assets and applying credit risk mitigation.
lookup_terms: materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property

data.summary: Defines eligible financial receivables as collateral — claims with original maturity of one year or less repaid from commercial or financial flows of the borrower's underlying assets — and excludes receivables tied to securitisations, sub-participations or credit derivatives. It imposes legal certainty conditions: robust security mechanism, perfected first-priority claim, registration where required, binding and enforceable documentation supported by legal review. Relevant to banks using the foundation IRB approach (and the wider CRM framework) to reduce LGD or exposure values.

Covers the conditions under which leasing exposures are recognised and treated within the credit risk capital framework, including the supervisory slotting criteria for income-producing real estate where leasing activity, pre-leasing and stabilisation are grading factors. Related material addresses collateral haircuts, master netting agreements and VaR-based treatment of securities financing transactions. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks holding lease exposures or specialised lending.

Addresses residual value risk — the exposure to the future value of leased or collateralised property at contract end — and the associated conservative valuation expectations, including independent appraisal excluding expected price increases and recognition of guarantees, financial collateral and mortgage insurance as mitigants. Also intersects with default and dilution risk treatment of purchased receivables. Binds banks calculating credit risk RWA and applying credit risk mitigation under SAMA rules.

Conditions IRB eligibility on compliance with the Pillar 3 Disclosure Requirements Framework: failure to meet those disclosures makes a bank ineligible to use the relevant IRB approach. Related securitisation criteria impose documentation disclosure, legal review and investor transparency conditions for STC treatment. Binds SAMA-licensed banks using internal models for credit risk and originators/sponsors seeking preferential securitisation treatment.

Transition node within SAMA's Basel III-aligned capital adequacy/risk-weighted assets framework, covering phase-in arrangements (notably for the standardised treatment of equity exposures and the removal of the IRB approach for equity exposures). Surrounding material in the source addresses credit conversion factors for off-balance sheet commitments and eligibility conditions for external credit assessment institutions (ECAIs). It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia in computing regulatory capital during the phase-in periods.

General provisions of the securitisation chapter of SAMA's capital framework: it defines securitisation and resecuritisation exposures, the underlying pool, and roles such as originator, and sets scope, risk-transference recognition, due diligence, RWA calculation, caps and credit risk mitigation treatment. It binds banks calculating risk-based capital for exposures to traditional and synthetic securitisations.

Node on the Internal Assessment Approach (SEC-IAA), one of the hierarchy of methods for risk-weighting securitisation exposures, used for unrated exposures (e.g. liquidity facilities, credit enhancements) to pools within an ABCP programme. Use requires SAMA approval of the bank's IRB approach for non-securitisation exposures and consultation with SAMA on its application. Binds IRB-approved banks in Saudi Arabia calculating capital on ABCP-related securitisation exposures.

Node on the Securitisation Standardised Approach (SEC-SA), the fall-back method for risk-weighting securitisation exposures where SEC-IRBA, SEC-ERBA or SEC-IAA cannot be used. It covers the KA/W inputs, the 15% risk-weight floor, inference of risk weights for market-risk hedges, and adjustments for resecuritisation exposures (including the p parameter of 1.5). Binds banks computing securitisation RWAs.

Sets the scope and conditions for the simple, transparent and comparable (STC) framework, which allows alternative (lower) capital treatment for qualifying traditional term securitisations and for ABCP conduits and conduit-financed transactions. It lists the lettered STC criteria (asset nature, performance history, underwriting consistency, disclosure, alignment of interest, etc.), requires originator/sponsor disclosure and an independent investor assessment, and requires continuous compliance. Binds originators, sponsors and investing banks claiming STC capital treatment.

Addresses asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) conduits within the securitisation/STC framework: it defines conduit-level roles (sponsor, transaction, beneficial interest) and distinguishes conduit-level from transaction-level compliance with the short-term STC criteria. Exposures at conduit level qualify only if criteria are met at both conduit and transaction levels; transaction-level exposures need only transaction-level compliance. Binds banks sponsoring, supporting or investing in ABCP programmes for capital purposes.

This node is SAMA's Basel III guidance issued under Circular 341000015689, covering minimum capital requirements for credit risk, including IRB rating system governance and securitization rules. The extracted material sets documentation obligations for internal rating systems (design, rating criteria, exception approval, review frequency, model methodology, default/loss definitions, change history) and securitization STC criteria on investor voting/enforcement rights and disclosure/legal review of transaction documentation. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating regulatory capital, particularly those using internal ratings-based approaches.
lookup_terms: minimum capital requirements for credit risk

data.summary: This node addresses the simple, transparent and comparable (STC) framework as applied to asset-backed commercial paper conduits and the transactions they finance, alongside rules on use of short-term external ratings. It sets who determines STC compliance (originator/sponsor must disclose; investor must self-assess; originators retaining positions with significant risk transfer determine it), requires STC criteria to be met at all times, and restricts banks to solicited ratings from eligible ECAIs. It binds banks holding or originating securitization and ABCP exposures for capital purposes.

This node collects the treatment of the "sponsor" concept across the credit risk framework: as a rated strength factor in specialised lending/project and real estate exposure slotting criteria, and as the party required to provide full liquidity and credit protection support at conduit or transaction level under the ABCP STC criteria. It establishes that where multiple sponsors support an ABCP programme, the majority of support must come from a single "main sponsor", with limited exception on credit deterioration. Relevant to banks acting as sponsors or investors in ABCP programmes and to banks slotting specialised lending exposures.

This node concerns KIRB, the IRB capital requirement that would apply to the underlying pool had it not been securitized, and its use as a maximum capital charge (cap) for securitization exposures under SEC-IRBA, SEC-ERBA and SEC-SA, including mixed-pool aggregation and worked examples incorporating dilution and default components. It also notes interaction with the 15% risk weight floor. It binds originator, sponsor and investor banks calculating securitization capital.

This node defines a non-performing loan (NPL) securitization by reference to the delinquency variable W being at or above 90% at origination cut-off and on any subsequent asset addition/removal, limits eligible underlying exposures to loans and loan-equivalent instruments, and bars resecuritization. It reserves SAMA's discretion to impose a stricter definition, precludes SEC-IRBA where the foundation approach is used to compute KIRB, and applies a risk weight floor to NPL securitization exposures. It binds banks holding exposures to NPL securitizations.

This node covers the capital treatment of unsettled transactions and failed trades, distinguishing delivery-versus-payment (DvP) settlement — where exposure is limited to the positive current exposure and capital is required once payment is five business days past settlement date — from non-DvP free deliveries, where the full amount paid or delivered is at risk. It also touches maturity-floor exemptions for short-term collateralized and self-liquidating trade transactions. It binds banks with unsettled securities, commodities and FX transactions, requiring monitoring of failed trades from the first day of failure.

SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans, issued under the SAMA Charter and Banking Control Law, set enforceable requirements for how banks identify, monitor, restructure and resolve loans showing stress or already non-performing. It sets out objectives (rehabilitation of viable borrowers, fair customer treatment especially for MSMEs, adequate controls over NPL and restructuring processes), scope, and the defined terms used throughout (problem loans, non-performing loans, watch-list, early warning signals, cooperating/viable borrower, viability assessment, covenant, KPIs). It binds all banks licensed under the Banking Control Law and is read together with SAMA's Rules on Credit Risk Classification and Provisioning and the accompanying Guidelines on Management of Problem Loans.
lookup_terms: Rules on Management of Problem Loans

data.summary: Defines Early Warning Signals (EWS) as quantitative or qualitative indicators based on liquidity, profitability, market, collateral and macroeconomic metrics, and sets the obligation for banks to build policies, procedures, tools and governance around EWS fully integrated into the risk management system. Banks must run EWS in three stages — identification (portfolio-specific indicators pointing to payment difficulty, factoring the economic environment), action/escalation with cause, severity and timelines, and ongoing monitoring calibrated to borrower risk. Applies to banks licensed under the Banking Control Law as part of problem loan prevention and identification.

Requires banks to develop and implement a Board-approved NPL strategy setting the bank's approach, objectives and annual quantitative targets across short, medium and long-term horizons, acting as a roadmap for resource allocation and controls. The strategy must consider all resolution options (hold/restructure, portfolio sales, write-offs of unrecoverable provisioned NPLs, taking collateral onto balance sheet, legal and out-of-court routes) applying proportionality and materiality, and be subject to regular review and integration into the risk management framework, with unit and team incentives aligned to its targets.

Requires banks to establish a dedicated Workout Department/Section/Unit, independent of business and loan-originating units to avoid conflicts of interest, and staffed with analytical, legal and financial-analysis skills to manage NPL resolution. Sets performance-management requirements: appraisal and compensation structures aligned with the NPL strategy and code of conduct, not based solely on NPL volume reduction, and including qualitative measures such as negotiation competency and quality of proposals. Related provisions cover mandatory time-bound transfer of loans from originating units to the Workout Unit, borrower appeal forms, and workout fee policy including impact analysis on borrower cash flows.

Sets the viability conditions banks must meet before granting long-term or short-term restructuring measures, including documented financial evidence that the borrower can afford the solution, treatment of outstanding arrears, and, for short-term measures, evidence of capacity to resume full principal and interest payments afterwards without leading to repeated consecutive restructurings. Where prior restructurings exist on the same loan, additional internal controls, early warning signals and approval by a designated Senior Management Committee are required. Viability assessment must be grounded in the borrower's financial characteristics and the workout plan must be approved under the bank's delegation of authority.

Sets collateral management requirements applying throughout the credit process regardless of loan performance: Board-approved (or delegated) collateral policies and procedures reviewed at least every three years and aligned with the risk appetite statement, governance over internal and external valuers, and regular internal audit review of policy quality, valuer independence and valuation appropriateness. Banks must document accepted collateral types (financial collateral, lease exposures, other funded credit protection, guarantees) and ensure documentation, legal enforceability across all areas of operation including foreign branches and subsidiaries, and mitigation of valuation, termination and concentration risks.

A provision within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk dealing with purchased receivables under the IRB approach, specifically how collateral, partial guarantees and other first-loss mitigants covering default risk, dilution risk or both are recognised, including the exposure-weighted LGD calculation where a bank uses the Securitisation Internal Ratings-Based Approach. It sets out substitution treatment for guarantees from the seller or a third party, distinguishing full cover of default and dilution risk, cover of only one component, and partial or tranched cover of the uncovered portion. It binds banks in the Kingdom that have been permitted to use IRB approaches for credit risk capital.

The root node for SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk (version 2.1, December 2022), the Kingdom's Basel-aligned credit risk capital rulebook. It covers scope and implementation timing, SAMA reporting, due diligence, the standardised approach (individual exposure classes, external ratings, credit risk mitigation), the full IRB framework (asset classes, risk-weight functions, risk components, supervisory slotting, purchased receivables, expected loss and provisions, minimum qualifying requirements), transition arrangements and the securitisation framework. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia for regulatory capital purposes.
lookup_terms: Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk

data.summary: A SAMA circular (Arabic text) confirming earlier circulars that the ownership document issued by the Economic Cities Authority must be accepted for any property or land owner inside the economic cities as an official, recognised title document standing in place of the title deed used outside those cities. It removes doubt about collateral and property documentation within economic cities. It is addressed to banks and real estate finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular (Arabic text) directing all licensed banks and finance companies to begin registering finance lease contracts with the Saudi Finance Lease Contract Registration Company (Sijil) as of the stated commencement date. It rests on the Finance Lease Law and its Implementing Regulation, under which the lessor must register the contract and any amendments within ten business days of conclusion or amendment, and record all dispositions affecting the contractual rights of lessor and lessee. It binds banks and finance companies acting as lessors.

A SAMA circular (Arabic text) making use of the Ministry of Commerce and Investment "Qawaem" programme mandatory as the source of financial statements for commercial entities required to file there, before any credit facility is extended. It is grounded in SAMA's supervisory powers over the finance sector under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation, and is aimed at the reliability and transparency of accounting information used in credit decisions. It binds all finance companies licensed in the Kingdom, with credit information companies also in the distribution scope.
lookup_terms: Ministry of Commerce and Investment filing

data.summary: A SAMA circular (Arabic text) permitting the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company (SRC) to purchase residential real estate finance portfolios from real estate financiers once at least three months have elapsed from the date the related financing was granted, or from receipt of the first instalment from the beneficiary. It is issued as an exception under the rules on disposal of finance assets and the rights arising from them, which allow SAMA to exempt certain disposals given their nature or size. It is addressed to banks and finance companies in the Kingdom and takes effect from its date.
lookup_terms: residential real estate finance portfolio sale

data.summary: SAMA's framework setting the minimum regulatory capital requirements for market risk, implementing the Basel FRTB standards in KSA. It covers the trading book/banking book boundary, treatment of internal risk transfers (including CVA risk transfers and hedges with eligible third-party protection providers), the standardised approach, the internal models approach subject to SAMA approval, and the simplified alternative. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA, with distinctions drawn between D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs.

The default methodology all SAMA-supervised banks must use to calculate market risk capital, with risk-weighted assets derived by multiplying the capital requirement by 12.5. Use of any alternative (internal models approach or the simplified alternative) requires prior SAMA approval, and IMA-approved banks must still compute and report standardised approach figures across all trading desks. SAMA may also demand a standardised approach calculation at any time.

The trading book concept as used for market risk capital purposes, and in particular the rules on internal risk transfers between the banking book and trading book. Internal transfers from trading book to banking book get no capital recognition; banking-book credit, equity and general interest rate risk hedged via the trading book are recognised only where an exactly matching external hedge with an eligible third-party protection provider (or a SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk arrangement for GIRR) is in place. Applies to banks calculating market risk capital under this framework.
lookup_terms: external hedge eligible third-party protection provider

data.summary: Defines which portfolios, trading desks and risks fall within the market risk capital requirement, including the three-prong test for eligibility to use internal models (qualitative criteria, desk-by-desk nomination, and SAMA model approval). Desks not nominated or not approved must be capitalised under the standardised approach, and banks cannot exclude desks simply because the standardised outcome is lower. Binds banks seeking or holding IMA permission from SAMA.

An optional, less granular calculation regime that SAMA may permit for banks with smaller or simpler trading books, subject to SAMA approval and ongoing oversight. Indicative eligibility criteria exclude G-SIBs/D-SIBs, IMA users and holders of correlation trading positions, and SAMA may still mandate the full standardised approach for banks with complex or sizeable risks. It includes maturity ladder and simplified commodity approaches and delta-plus/scenario options treatments.
lookup_terms: simplified alternative to the standardised approach

data.summary: Defines the trading desk as the unambiguously defined group of traders or trading accounts that forms the basic unit for market risk capital and model approval. Sets out required attributes: a head trader with direct oversight, single-desk assignment of trading accounts, a defined risk scope, a documented business strategy with budget and management information, and a clear risk management and trading limits structure. Desk structures require SAMA approval; internal operational subdesks do not, but are not used in the capital framework.

A required component of SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans: each bank must adopt a written Code of Conduct setting out its problem-loan resolution process, so that viable borrowers are offered a workout before enforcement. It prescribes documented procedures for borrower communication after missed instalments, information gathering, financial/repayment-capacity assessment, and proposing solutions to cooperating borrowers. Binds all banks licensed under the Banking Control Law, with particular emphasis on fair treatment of MSME borrowers.
lookup_terms: Rules on Management of Problem Loans

data.summary: Refers to SAMA's Rules on Credit Risk Classification and Provisioning, which the Problem Loans Rules must be read alongside; the extracted material here covers eligibility and management of credit risk mitigants (leased assets, third-party cash deposits and assimilated instruments, and guarantees) and general collateral requirements. It sets conditions for legal enforceability, documentation, notification of pledges/assignments, valuation and concentration risk for collateral used to mitigate credit exposures. Binds banks licensed under the Banking Control Law.
lookup_terms: pledge or assignment of cash deposit

data.summary: The Implementing Regulation of the Credit Information Law (Royal Decree M/37, 1429H), issued in Arabic, covering definitions, licensing of credit information companies, scope of credit information services, governance, the credit record, supervisory requirements, confidentiality, member obligations, objections/complaints, and the disputes committee. It prohibits any person from conducting credit information activity without a SAMA licence and sets capital, corporate form, fee, approval and licence-duration conditions. Binds licensed credit bureaus and their Members (public and private entities exchanging credit information), and protects Consumers (natural or legal persons with credit dealings).

Defined term in the Implementing Regulation of the Credit Information Law: the credit record (السجل الائتماني) is the report issued by a licensed credit information company containing a consumer's credit information. The Regulation devotes a dedicated chapter to the credit record, and links it to adverse decisions and negative information reported by Members against the consumer's interest. Relevant to credit bureaus, Members relying on records for credit decisions, and consumers exercising objection rights.

Defined term and licensing subject of the Implementing Regulation of the Credit Information Law: a credit information company licensed by SAMA to collect, maintain and supply consumer credit information to Members on request. Licensing conditions include being a joint stock company headquartered in the Kingdom, minimum paid-up capital of SAR 50 million, SAMA approval of constitutive documents and the credit information system, fees, a five-year renewable licence, and prior written SAMA approval for branches, mergers/acquisitions and constitutional amendments. Binds founders and licensed credit bureaus operating in KSA.
lookup_terms: prior SAMA written approval branches mergers

data.summary: The Committee for Considering Violations and Adjudicating Credit Information Disputes established under the Implementing Regulation of the Credit Information Law, with its own chapter in the Regulation. It handles violations of the Law/Regulation and resolves disputes over credit information, sitting alongside the objections and complaints mechanism available to consumers. Relevant to licensed credit information companies, Members and consumers contesting record accuracy or alleging breaches.
lookup_terms: لجنة النظر في المخالفات والفصل في نزاعات المعلومات الائتمانية

data.summary: A concept node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk covering the banking book as the counterpart to the trading book, specifically how banking book credit, equity and interest rate exposures are treated when hedged via internal risk transfers with the trading book. It sets the conditions under which a banking book exposure is deemed hedged for capital purposes, and how unrecognised short credit/equity positions fall into the market risk rules instead. Binds banks subject to SAMA's capital framework.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: Concept node on the regulatory boundary between the banking book and the trading book under SAMA's market risk capital standard, as applied through the internal risk transfer rules. It determines which leg of a hedge is capitalised under banking book rules versus market risk rules, including the asymmetric treatment that transfers from trading book to banking book get no capital recognition. Relevant to banks calculating regulatory capital and to desk-level allocation of exposures.
lookup_terms: boundary between banking book and trading book

data.summary: Defines internal risk transfer as an internal written record of a risk transfer within the banking book, between banking and trading book, or between trading desks, and sets the conditions for capital recognition. Key requirements include exact matching between the internal transfer and an external hedge, use of a SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk for general interest rate risk, and the exclusion of trading-to-banking-book transfers from capital recognition. Binds banks applying SAMA's market risk capital requirements.
lookup_terms: SAMA approval internal risk transfer desk

data.summary: Concept node for foreign exchange (FX) risk as one of the market risk classes under SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk, including its treatment in the simplified standardised approach and in internal risk transfers (FX and commodities risk in the banking book fall within the market risk capital scope). Capital requirements for FX risk are summed with interest rate, equity and commodity risk, plus non-delta option risk add-ons. Applies to banks computing market risk RWAs.

Covers the profit and loss attribution (PLA) test used alongside backtesting to validate trading desks' eligibility for the internal models approach under SAMA's market risk standard. Banks must begin the PLA programme when the internal models capital requirement takes effect, provide a one-year report for model approval, and reassess desk eligibility quarterly; SAMA may impose capital add-ons or withdraw model permission. Binds banks using or seeking internal model approval.

Sets out backtesting requirements at bank-wide and trading desk level under SAMA's market risk standard, comparing one-day VaR against actual and hypothetical P&L over the prior 12 months. It defines the green/amber/red zone response framework, including capital add-ons for amber zone outcomes, an automatic multiplier increase or model disallowance in the red zone, documentation of all exceptions, and limited grounds for disregarding exceptions driven by non-modellable risk factors. Binds banks using internal models for market risk capital.

A set of qualitative principles within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk that banks must apply, in addition to the risk factor eligibility test (RFET), to decide whether a risk factor can actually be modelled in the expected shortfall model. It stresses that passing the real-price observation count alone is not sufficient — data accuracy, sourcing, update frequency and stress-period representativeness also matter — and SAMA may reject data as unsuitable, forcing the factor into non-modellable (NMRF) capital treatment. Binds banks using the internal models approach for market risk; SAMA retains discretion, including an exceptional systemic-stress override that must not reduce capital.

A concept node covering value-at-risk and the associated defined vocabulary of SAMA's market risk capital framework — risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class, sensitivity/delta, look-through approach, embedded derivative. VaR appears chiefly as a benchmark in backtesting and exception analysis rather than as the primary capital measure (which is expected shortfall). Relevant to banks calculating market risk capital and to supervisory review of internal models.

Defines the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distributional metric used in the profit and loss attribution (PLA) test: the largest absolute gap between the empirical cumulative distributions of hypothetical P&L and risk-theoretical P&L. Together with the correlation metric it allocates each trading desk to a PLA green, amber or red zone, with red-zone desks barred from the internal models approach and pushed to the standardised approach until they return to green and clear backtesting requirements. Binds banks seeking IMA permission at trading desk level.

Sets out SAMA's traffic-light interpretation of backtesting exceptions for bank-wide and trading desk-level internal models: green generally attracts no add-on, amber triggers a higher capital requirement scaled to the number of exceptions, and red leads automatically to an increased multiplication factor or possible withdrawal of model permission. It also covers documenting and explaining exceptions, quarterly rescoping of the backtested portfolio, and the narrow conditions for disregarding an exception driven by a non-modellable risk factor. Binds banks using internal models for market risk capital.

Covers the stressed expected shortfall measure and the data principles governing it — in particular that inputs must reflect prices observed or quoted during the identified stress period and be sourced directly from that historical window where possible, with documented handling where current instruments differ from stress-period instruments. It sits alongside data update-frequency and calibration expectations and feeds the internal models approach capital calculation. Binds banks approved to use the IMA for market risk.

This node covers the stress testing and backtesting expectations attached to banks using the internal models approach (IMA) for market risk capital under SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk. It requires a rigorous stress testing programme at both trading desk and bank-wide level, combining SAMA-prescribed and bank-specific scenarios, with quantitative and qualitative elements and reporting to senior management and the board; the linked backtesting material sets out the green/amber/red zone consequences, including capital add-ons, an increased multiplication factor, or withdrawal of model permission. It binds SAMA-licensed banks permitted to use internal models for market risk.

This node gathers the credit-related elements within SAMA's market risk capital framework: specific risk capital treatment for first-to-default and nth-to-default credit derivatives (including hedging offsets), internal CVA risk transfers between the CVA portfolio and the trading book, and the general provisions of the standardised approach. Notably, it records that all banks (D-SIB and non-D-SIB) must compute the market risk capital charge using the standardised approach, with RWA derived by a 12.5 multiplier. It binds SAMA-licensed banks with trading book and derivative exposures.

This node reflects the Basel-derived calibration embedded in SAMA's market risk standard, including the simplified standardised approach for foreign exchange and commodities risk (8% of the overall net open position, gold treated as FX) and the sensitivities-based delta GIRR bucket structure, tenor risk weights and correlation parameters. It also records the de minimis FX exemption available at SAMA's discretion, referenced to eligible capital as defined in SAMA's Basel III regulatory capital guidance. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating market risk capital.

This node sets out the default risk charge (DRC) treatment of securitisation exposures under SAMA's market risk standard, covering gross and net jump-to-default (JTD) calculation for non-correlation trading portfolio securitisations. It specifies that LGD is not separately applied (the market value of the tranche is the JTD), that offsetting is confined to tranches of the same underlying asset pool, and that maturity-based and decomposition-based netting is permitted only on strict conditions, with no hedging recognised across buckets. It binds SAMA-licensed banks holding securitisation positions in the trading book.

This node governs when banks must look through index instruments, multi-underlying options and equity investments in funds to their constituent risk factors for delta and curvature risk, and when a single index-level sensitivity may instead be used. It lists the eligibility criteria for opting out (known constituents, at least 20 constituents, concentration limits, and a minimum aggregate market capitalisation), requires consistent application over time, and excludes index CTP instruments from decomposition. It binds SAMA-licensed banks applying the sensitivities-based standardised approach to market risk.

This node addresses the expected shortfall (ES) internal model under SAMA's market risk standard, focusing on risk factor modellability: the risk factor eligibility test (RFET), the principles for data quality and real price observations, and the consequence that risk factors failing these standards are excluded from the ES model and capitalised as non-modellable risk factors (NMRF). It also records SAMA's narrow discretion to treat a failing risk factor as modellable only in extraordinary systemic stress, without reducing capital, and includes the statistical backtesting error-probability material underpinning exception thresholds. It binds SAMA-licensed banks with internal model permission for market risk.

A concept node within SAMA's Guidelines on Management of Problem Loans describing the watch list generated from the Early Warning Signals (EWS) process for borrowers showing potential payment difficulty. It sets out the minimum data content of the list (loan details, group/related-party status, materiality, date added, reviews and outcomes, mitigation measures, reasons for inclusion), the approval gate for removal, time-limited retention before transfer to the Workout Unit or return to the originating unit, and monthly escalation to a designated management committee and the Board for material cases. It binds banks' credit risk management, relationship management and governance functions.

A concept node explaining NPL portfolio segmentation under SAMA's Guidelines on Management of Problem Loans: dividing non-performing loans into homogeneous groups to drive differentiated resolution strategies (hold/restructure, dispose, legal enforcement). It sets timing (immediately on transfer to the Workout Unit, before assignment to an officer), the principles of proportionality and materiality for resource allocation, and stage-one criteria such as nature of business (MSME vs corporate), legal status, arrears buckets/days past due and loan balance. Applies to banks' Workout Units handling NPL stock.

A concept node covering the stage-two initial viability assessment applied to NPLs not yet in legal proceedings, screening borrowers as viable, marginally viable or non-viable using financial (or cash-flow) ratios and loan-to-value. It lists indicative, non-prescriptive benchmarks including Debt/EBITDA leverage, loan service coverage against sector averages, EBITDA trend comparison with industry, and an LLCR of 1.4 for project finance and multi-year loans, with thresholds to be set from general market indicators. Directed at banks' Workout Units designing restructuring strategies.

A concept node on the loan-to-value ratio as one of the two screening criteria (alongside financial/cash-flow ratios) in the initial viability assessment of non-performing loans. LTV indicates the quantitative level of collateral coverage against the outstanding loan and is drawn from information already in the loan file, supporting early selection among workout strategies. Relevant to banks' Workout Units and credit risk functions under the problem loans guidelines.

A concept node (Appendix 2 of the problem loans guidelines) defining and computing the Loan Life Coverage Ratio: the present value of cash flows available for debt service over the loan life plus debt reserve, divided by outstanding loan at assessment date, discounted at the weighted average cost of capital. It is positioned as a multi-period alternative to DSCR and is to be used by Workout teams for project finance and other multi-year loans, with 1.4 cited as the indicative benchmark. Addressed to banks assessing long-term borrower viability.

A concept node on the Debt/EBITDA leverage ratio used as a proxy indicator in the initial viability assessment of distressed borrowers, sitting within the broader set of illustrative financial ratio categories (liquidity, solvency/leverage, profitability) that Workout Units apply. The guidance is indicative rather than prescriptive, and directs banks to cash-flow based analysis for MSME borrowers where audited financials are unavailable. The analysis must be performed by Workout Unit staff not previously involved in the original loan approval.

A market-risk capital node within SAMA's minimum capital requirements for market risk, covering the stress-scenario dimension of capital calculation: the mandatory stress testing programme for banks using the internal models approach (desk-level and bank-wide, quantitative and qualitative, with senior management and board reporting), and the three prescribed correlation scenarios (medium, high, low) under the sensitivities-based method, where the capital requirement is the largest of the three. It binds banks supervised by SAMA, with IMA obligations applying only to banks using internal models and the correlation-scenario mechanics applying to all banks calculating under the standardised approach.

A concept node on interest rate risk within SAMA's market risk capital framework, covering general interest rate risk (GIRR) as a defined risk class and the supporting definitions (risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class, sensitivity, delta), plus the conditions for internal risk transfers of banking book interest rate risk into the trading book through a SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk. It binds banks calculating regulatory capital for market risk and determines when a banking book hedge and its trading book leg receive capital recognition.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: A concept node on the delta-plus method for option positions under the simplified standardised approach to market risk. It explains that delta-equivalent positions feed into the general market risk charges for interest rate, equity, FX/gold and commodity categories, with separate capital requirements applied to gamma and vega risk, and specific risk determined by applying specific risk weights to delta-equivalents; it sits alongside the simplified and scenario approaches. It binds banks eligible to use the simplified standardised approach rather than the full standardised or internal models approaches.

A concept node on specific risk (issuer-specific, as distinct from general market risk) within SAMA's market risk capital framework, including its interaction with internal risk transfers between banking book and trading book and the conditions under which hedges and their trading book legs receive regulatory capital recognition. It also underpins the treatment of short credit and short equity positions created by internal risk transfers. It binds banks calculating market risk capital requirements.

A concept node on general market risk within SAMA's market risk capital framework, covering the general provisions and structure of the standardised approach — including the requirement that all banks (D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs) calculate the market risk capital charge using the standardised approach, the 12.5 multiplier to convert capital requirements into risk-weighted assets, and SAMA's power to demand standardised-approach figures. It also frames internal risk transfers (including CVA risk transfers) that fall within the scope of the market risk capital requirement. It binds all SAMA-supervised banks.
lookup_terms: scope of market risk capital requirement

data.summary: A concept node on offsetting and hedge recognition for credit derivatives in the specific risk capital calculation, covering full allowance (an 80% specific risk offset on the higher-requirement leg where long and short positions fully offset, with zero on the other side), partial allowance where asset, currency or maturity mismatches exist, and the capital treatment of first-to-default and nth-to-default basket credit derivatives, including when offset against underlying reference credit instruments is permitted. It binds banks calculating specific risk capital for credit derivative and hedged cash positions.

Node covering the workout function under SAMA's non-performing loan management guidance: the requirement for banks to maintain a dedicated, permanent Workout Unit segregated from loan origination and reporting into Risk Management, and the principles for selecting and tailoring restructuring options for defaulted borrowers. It sets the pre-conditions a borrower must meet for a restructuring plan (sustainable projected cash flows and cooperative behaviour) and favours out-of-court settlement where documented recovery exceeds foreclosure or bankruptcy outcomes. Binds licensed banks; relevant to their risk governance, staffing/training of workout officers, and to syndicated/multi-creditor situations where dissenting lenders may fall back on the Bankruptcy Law.
lookup_terms: conflict of interest segregation of duties

data.summary: Node on the design, implementation and embedding of a bank's NPL strategy and its supporting operational plan, including monitoring of results, at least annual review, documented roles and reporting lines, and staff goals/incentives aligned to NPL reduction targets. It also covers strategic inputs such as NPL investor demand, the NPL servicing market, and the capital implications of the strategy, which must be modelled against the risk appetite framework and ICAAP and reflected in capital planning. Binds bank boards and senior management responsible for NPL strategy, budgeting and capital adequacy.

Node describing the financial viability assessment a bank's Workout Unit must perform on a distressed borrower before choosing between restructuring, debt swap or legal proceedings, and which must be carried out by staff not involved in the original loan approval. It covers indicative ratio categories (liquidity, solvency/leverage, profitability), balance sheet review of total debt burden and priority claims such as wages and taxes, and cash flow analysis as the defining test of viability, with a cash-flow-based approach for MSMEs lacking reliable audited financials. Binds banks conducting NPL workouts.

Node on the qualitative counterpart to financial analysis: assessing the borrower's business model, business plan and medium-to-long-term projections, distinguishing sustainable from unsustainable debt, and checking alignment with existing credit terms. It also addresses validation of assumptions and sensitivity analysis, review of documentation features such as cross-default and notification obligations, the option to appoint a financial advisor for an independent business review, and verification that collateral remains formalised, valid and enforceable. Guides bank Workout Units in identifying commercially sustainable restructuring options.

Node focused on cash flow analysis and the short-term cash budget as the core tools for judging a distressed borrower's capacity to service debt, sitting alongside balance sheet review of total obligations and priority claims. It stresses forecasted cash generation over accrual measures, monthly breakdown of sources and uses to reveal financing needs and timing of funds available for loan service, and ongoing monthly monitoring with immediate corrective action. Applies to bank workout teams assessing viability and restructuring terms.
lookup_terms: micro and small enterprise financial information

data.summary: Node setting out the requirement that banks compare the economic value of a proposed restructuring against the alternatives (note sale, enforcement, insolvency) using net present value analysis before settling on a resolution approach. It explains the NPV mechanics, the use of the bank's standard risk-adjusted discount rate or alternatively the original effective interest rate used for IFRS 9 provisioning, and the parameters to model under each option (new tenor and pricing, collateral haircuts and litigation costs, insolvency costs and timelines). It also requires banks to revisit the chosen approach when new or contradictory borrower information emerges.

This node sets out how a bank identifies and selects workout options for defaulted or distressed borrowers, including the two pre-conditions for approving a restructuring plan (sufficient projected cash flow to clear past-due obligations within a reasonable period, and cooperative borrower behaviour) and the preference for out-of-court settlement where documented recovery value exceeds foreclosure or bankruptcy. It also carries the generic restructuring principles (good faith, transparency, prompt response, sustainable rather than repeated short-term fixes, confidentiality) and points dissenting minority lenders in syndicated deals to the Bankruptcy Law. It is directed at banks' Workout Units and credit/legal functions handling viable and marginally viable borrowers.

Covers short-term (temporary) restructuring measures — relief granted for an identified, evidenced short-term cash-flow disruption or to give creditors time to assess the situation — and the expectation that the borrower resumes the existing payment schedule at the end of the period, with a tenor cap (24 months, shorter in certain cases). It also addresses the restructuring agreement as the governing workout document, including the choice between a replacement agreement and an amendment to the original facility. Applies to banks restructuring borrower exposures, with simplified documentation contemplated for MSMEs.

Identifies the long-term/permanent restructuring toolkit (arrears and interest capitalisation, interest rate reduction, maturity extension, debt consolidation, rescheduled payments, covenant alterations, sale by owner and similar) as distinct from short-term temporary relief, and situates them within the restructuring options taxonomy. It is paired with guidance on documenting the outcome in a restructuring agreement, whether as a new agreement or an amendment. Binds banks selecting a permanent workout solution matched to the borrower's sustainable repayment capacity.

Describes conditional loan forgiveness as a restructuring tool used where the net present value of the borrower (including collateral and potential cash flow) is below the total loan, conditioned on owners making an additional financial contribution so their interests align with the bank's. It appears alongside related measures such as loan-to-asset swaps, interest rate reduction, maturity extension, partial repayment and balloon/bullet payments. Relevant to banks' Workout Units deciding write-off/concession terms for marginal borrowers.

Explains loan splitting as a workout technique addressing collateral and cash-flow shortfalls: the sustainable portion is amortised in equal principal-and-interest instalments to a set maturity, while the residual 'excess loan' may be subordinated, tranched, made non-interest bearing, or repaid from asset sales or at maturity. It sits within the additional-measures and marginal-borrower workout guidance, together with restrictions on fresh money and roll-overs (permitted only in limited situations). Addressed to banks structuring restructurings for marginally viable borrowers.

Covers debt/loan-to-equity conversion and related owner-contribution measures — conversion of owner loans into equity or another subordinated form, capital increases, personal guarantees, additional collateral, sale of excess assets and financial-indicator covenants — treated as additional measures that strengthen the bank's position rather than stand-alone restructuring solutions. It is presented with the borrower-type/workout-measure mapping for viable and marginal borrowers. Relevant to banks assessing equity participation and owner support as part of a workout package.

Concept node describing the loan-to-asset (and loan-to-equity) swap as an additional, non-standalone restructuring measure in which all or part of a distressed loan is transferred into "other assets owned", with recovery dependent on subsequent sale of that asset. It is presented as something to be combined with other options (e.g. conditional forgiveness, partial repayment with maturity extension), requiring specialist asset/real-estate management expertise and a supporting business plan. It binds banks operating workout units, which must monitor swapped exposures by asset type and stay within any holding limits set by applicable national rules.

Concept node on the restructuring agreement as the principal document governing a workout, setting out how the borrower will restructure debt and operations and how and when creditors will be repaid. It notes there is no standard form (a letter may suffice for simple rescheduling, while changes to maturity, principal or profit/interest may require a new or amending agreement) and lists the minimum content a typical agreement should cover. Directed at banks and their legal functions handling distressed borrowers, with simplified documentation expectations for MSMEs.

Concept node on the term sheet as the negotiation instrument used to record agreed restructuring terms before formal legal documents are drafted, revised at each stage of the workout and especially useful where multiple creditors or stakeholders are involved. It sets out indicative term-sheet content (parties, repayment schedule, pricing, revised events of default, security, governing law) and a sequencing checklist from draft term sheet through signed workout documents. Aimed at banks' workout units and legal counsel structuring restructurings of medium to large exposures.

Concept node describing the standstill agreement as typically the first step in a multi-creditor workout: creditors agree not to enforce rights against a defaulting borrower for a limited period so the borrower can gather information and prepare a survival strategy while creditors form a joint approach. It may also carry further obligations such as new working-capital funding or deferral of principal and profit/interest payments, may be simplified for MSMEs, and may be dispensed with where a single cooperative creditor relationship exists. Guidance for banks as creditors in distressed-borrower workouts.

Concept node covering the viability and negotiation analysis a bank's workout unit should perform before agreeing a rehabilitation plan, including key financial ratios (liquidity, solvency/leverage, profitability), balance sheet composition and total debt burden, and cash flow analysis as the test of financial viability. It also frames SWOT analysis as a tool to identify account strengths and weaknesses and build a negotiating strategy, including educating borrowers who do not understand the restructuring. The analysis must be conducted by workout staff not involved in the original loan approval.

Concept node on ongoing monitoring of borrowers showing increased credit risk and of restructured loans, covering early warning signals, watch-list classification at a lower rating, corrective action plans (additional collateral, site visits, credit committee updates, revised forecasts) and defined timelines proportionate to loan size and risk. It extends the early warning system to restructured as well as never-defaulted performing loans, and addresses bank oversight of borrower cash-flow management and expenditure controls during a workout within the rights conferred by the restructuring agreement. Binds banks' business, risk and credit committee functions.

Node covering the BCM strategy requirement in SAMA's Business Continuity Management Framework, sitting alongside the BCM governance provisions (board accountability, BCM committee and charter, BCM function and manager). It requires each Member Organization to define, approve, implement and maintain a business continuity strategy setting long-term objectives, a dated roadmap and periodic validation of alignment with business objectives. Binds all SAMA member organizations, with ultimate responsibility on the board or a delegated executive.

Node for the business continuity plan/policy layer of SAMA's BCM Framework, linking the required business continuity policy (objectives, scope, responsibilities, monitored compliance, documented and approved scope exclusions) to the governance structure above it. It establishes documented commitment to continuity and communication to relevant stakeholders. Applies to all SAMA member organizations; policy exclusions need BCM committee and senior management approval.

Node covering the IT Disaster Recovery Plan requirements under the SAMA BCM Framework: an approved IT DRP aligned to the BIA, an alternative data centre (site chosen on risk assessment and subject to SAMA approval), mirrored configurations and security controls, backup/recovery processes, offsite backup storage, and continuity clauses in third-party contracts. Accountability sits with the IT manager for currency of the plans and with the BCM manager for integration into the BCM programme. Binds all member organizations.

Node for the Business Impact Analysis and Risk Assessment requirements in the SAMA BCM Framework. It requires an approved BIA/RA methodology, periodic continuity risk assessment (threats, single points of failure, prioritisation, control selection and treatment plans) and prioritisation of activities with defined RTOs, RPOs and Maximum Acceptable Outage, interdependencies and recovery resources. Results and the prioritised list must be endorsed by the BCM committee; applies to all member organizations.

Node covering the Crisis Management Plan requirement of the SAMA BCM Framework: an approved, monitored plan for responding to major incidents, including criteria for declaring a crisis, a command centre for centralised management, and rapid internal and external stakeholder communication. It connects to the testing requirements, which expect crisis management team activation to be exercised in BCP and DR tests. Binds all SAMA member organizations.

Node addressing the cyber/technology resilience dimension of the SAMA BCM Framework, drawing on the framework's definitions (BCM, IT Disaster Recovery, MAO) and its IT DR controls requiring the alternative data centre to carry the same logical, physical, environmental and cyber security controls as the primary site. The framework cross-refers to the SAMA Cyber Security Framework for threat and vulnerability management, and expects cyber scenarios in continuity testing. Binds all member organizations.
lookup_terms: cyber security scenarios in BCP testing

data.summary: Defines "Platform" under SAMA's Instructions for Practicing Aggregation Activity as any electronic means (websites, applications) through which a licensed aggregation entity carries out the activity, and carries the associated operational duties attached to it. These include confidentiality of consumer data obtained via the platform, no disclosure to external parties without prior SAMA approval, security/integrity/availability of information, record retention for at least 10 years after the relationship ends, conflict-of-interest policy, and on-platform disclosure of terms, security instructions and payment methods. It binds entities licensed by SAMA to practice aggregation activity (a finance support activity).

Covers the mandatory contract between a SAMA-licensed aggregation entity and the Consumer, together with the entity's pre-contractual conduct duties (clear, non-misleading product information, reasons for declined finance applications, notification of approval via documented channels, complaint channels). The contract must be documented with a copy to each party and state, at minimum, parties, scope, term, desired finance type and requirements, rights and obligations, pricing and fees, withdrawal, dispute resolution, and termination/expiry. Binds the licensed aggregation entity in its dealings with consumers.

Sets the minimum content of the paper or electronic contract between the aggregation entity and each Financier (banks, finance companies and other licensed finance providers). Required clauses include the financier's licence number and date, contract term aligned with both parties' licence validity, data-exchange and offer-update mechanisms, service levels and escalation, notification when the finance contract is issued, confidentiality and security, an express prohibition on subcontracting, and confirmation that the financier remains responsible for its own regulatory obligations. Binds the licensed aggregation entity and shapes its outsourcing-style arrangements with financiers.

Cross-reference node for the Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities, which supply the defined terms used in the Instructions for Practicing Aggregation Activity and the licensing gateway for the activity. Aggregation may not be carried out without a SAMA licence granted under those Rules, and the Instructions operate without prejudice to the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations. Relevant to any entity seeking or holding a finance support activity licence.
lookup_terms: Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities

data.summary: The SAMA Business Continuity Management Framework sets mandatory continuity and operational resilience requirements for Member Organizations, drawing on SAMA expectations and standards such as ISO 22301. It covers BCM strategy and policy, business impact analysis and risk assessment, resilient architecture and availability requirements, crisis management planning and IT disaster recovery. All Member Organizations must comply and formally integrate the requirements into their BCM programs.

Sets the governance layer of the SAMA BCM Framework: the board or a delegated executive holds ultimate responsibility for the BCM program, must allocate sufficient budget, and must mandate a BCM committee with a charter and at least quarterly meetings. It also requires a staffed BCM function, an appointed and suitably qualified BCM manager/head with adequate authority, and cross-functional strategic, tactical and operational teams. Binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA.

A node within SAMA's guidance on loan restructuring/workouts for banks, sitting alongside the restructuring principles appendix and the guidance on documenting a restructuring agreement. It addresses how banks should frame, measure and monitor restructuring activity (including expected conduct during the life of a restructuring agreement and the terms captured in it), rather than imposing licensing conditions. It is directed at banks managing distressed and MSME borrowers; the appendix material is framed as encouraged practice rather than hard obligation, so the binding weight of each item should be checked in the source.

Appendix of generic restructuring principles that SAMA encourages banks to adopt as part of their credit culture, covering good faith, transparency and disclosure between bank and borrower, prompt response to borrower proposals, reasonable borrower response time, sustainable rather than repeated short-term solutions, and confidentiality. It also explains the role and drafting of the restructuring agreement, including whether the workout replaces or amends the original loan documentation (especially relevant for MSMEs with simplified documentation). Addressed to banks dealing with distressed borrowers; the principles are hortatory ('encouraged', 'should'), not a closed list.

Part of the restructuring toolkit guidance describing loan restructuring options and additional measures available to banks, including loan splitting, loan-to-asset swaps, interest rate reduction, maturity extension and rescheduled payments (partial, balloon/bullet, step-up), together with cautions on new money and roll-overs and the use of independent sector experts to validate business plans and cash-flow projections. Additional measures are presented as supplements that do not on their own reduce the exposure. Relevant to banks structuring workout terms and the conditions/covenants attached to them.

Guidance on handling borrowers with exposures to more than one bank: the coordinator role should be taken by the bank with the largest exposure, with duties covering setting goals, deadline compliance, transparent communication with all creditors, minuting creditor meetings, assessing the need for external financial or legal advisers, drafting the proposed restructuring solution, and possibly acting as agent post-restructuring (including the right to withdraw). It also covers use of external advisers, borrower counselling/mediation, and keeping guarantors informed and re-confirming guarantees when loan terms change. Directed at banks; negotiated out-of-court restructuring is stated as preferable to court proceedings.

SAMA's Instructions for Practicing Aggregation Activity (May 2023), issued under the Finance Companies Control Law, setting minimum standards and procedures for entities licensed by SAMA to operate finance-comparison/aggregation platforms. It defines key terms (Activity, Entity, Financier, Consumer, Platform, Documented Channels), requires a licence under the Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities, and covers technological capability, standard interfaces with financiers, verification of consumer identity from reliable and independent sources, accuracy of finance offers, and electronic consumer records under the Electronic Transactions Law. It binds licensed aggregation entities and operates without prejudice to other SAMA instruments, including the Business Continuity Management Framework and the Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules.

Defines the licensed aggregation Entity and sets out its ongoing obligations under SAMA's aggregation instructions: platform cybersecurity and immediate breach notification to SAMA, restricting the electronic link with financiers to aggregation purposes only absent SAMA approval, an in-platform complaints/feedback channel with recordkeeping, pop-up consumer consents and acknowledgements, informing consumers through documented channels of rejection reasons or additional document requests, clear and non-misleading disclosure, consumer risk-awareness materials, a list of participating financiers, a prohibition on handling funds for financiers without SAMA approval, and restrictions on marketing for individual financiers. Binds SAMA-licensed aggregation entities; note the overlap with consumer-protection and outsourcing/technology requirements elsewhere.

A component concept within SAMA's Business Continuity Management (BCM) Framework, which sets mandatory business continuity requirements (governance, strategy, plans and their exercising/testing) for Member Organizations. The surrounding framework defines BCM, IT Disaster Recovery and Maximum Acceptable Outage, and fixes board-level accountability, a mandated BCM committee, a BCM function and qualified BCM manager. It binds all SAMA-supervised Member Organizations, including banks operating in Saudi Arabia, their banking subsidiaries and subsidiaries of foreign banks in KSA.

A reference concept identifying the international standards on which SAMA's BCM Framework requirements are based, notably ISO 22301 and ISO 27001 alongside BCI and DRII good-practice guidelines. It signals that the SAMA requirements are aligned to, but not substituted by, these standards; SAMA remains owner and sole interpreter of the framework. Compliance obligations fall on Member Organizations, which must adopt and embed the requirements in their BCM programs.

SAMA's Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements: a baseline cyber security and resilience control set aimed at newly established entities in the early stages of operation, notably firms in or graduating from SAMA's Regulatory Sandbox. It is structured around domains covering cyber security leadership and governance, operations and technology, and resilience, applying a risk-based approach with uniquely numbered control requirements. SAMA owns and interprets the document and may refuse sandbox graduation or licensing where an entity cannot demonstrate compliance.

A cross-reference concept linking the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements to SAMA's broader Cyber Security Framework, and the source of the defined terms used (cyber security governance, cyber security incident, incident management, cyber security policy, cyber security risk), several drawn from NIST glossary definitions. It matters for scope questions about which instrument governs a given entity: the lighter Fundamental Requirements for early-stage/sandbox entities versus the fuller Cyber Security Framework for established supervised entities.

The SAMA Regulatory Sandbox framework, established in November 2019, permitting local and international firms to test new digital financial solutions in a live KSA environment ahead of full deployment. In the cyber context it is the gateway population for the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements: sandbox entities must demonstrate compliance, and SAMA may block graduation or licensing if they cannot. Relevant to firms seeking authorisation and to supervisors assessing readiness for a full licence.

The cyber security leadership and governance domain of SAMA's cyber requirements, setting board- and management-level obligations: a resourced governance structure, approved and communicated cyber security policies, procedures and supporting standards, periodic review against the evolving threat landscape, embedding cyber and fraud risk considerations in the business operating model, password controls, and documented, periodically reviewed IT and cyber risk assessments held in a central register. It binds the entities in scope of the relevant SAMA cyber instrument and is directed at senior/executive management, information asset owners and heads of cyber security.

This node covers the operational and technical control domain of SAMA's cyber security requirements, sitting alongside leadership/governance and resilience domains, and drawing on defined terms such as cyber security governance, cyber security incident, cyber security policy and cyber security risk. It sets expectations for governance structures, approved and periodically reviewed policies, standards and procedures, embedding cyber and fraud risk considerations in business operating models, password/access controls, and documented IT and cyber risk assessments held in a central register. It binds entities subject to the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements (notably newly established/early-stage and sandbox-type firms) and, via the parallel framework, Member Organizations supervised by SAMA.

This node is the Resilience domain of SAMA's Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements, one of the framework's structural domains alongside Cyber Security Leadership and Governance and Cyber Security Operations and Technology. It frames the risk-based control architecture and numbering scheme, with the stated aim of safeguarding sensitive data, transactions and continuity of financial services in the Saudi financial sector. It is directed at entities recently established or at an early operational stage, including firms testing solutions under SAMA's Regulatory Sandbox.

This node describes SAMA's cyber security maturity model, a six-level scale (0 non-existent through 5) used to measure a Member Organization's attainment against the framework's control domains, with higher levels conditional on meeting all preceding level criteria. It is the measurement lens SAMA applies when assessing compliance, and it links to the required contents of the board-endorsed cyber security policy and to defined cyber security roles and responsibilities. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA and engages Board-level accountability.

This node sets out the cyber security risk management and compliance domain: a defined, approved and implemented risk management process covering identification, analysis, response, and monitoring/review, aligned with the organisation's enterprise risk management process and aimed at confidentiality, integrity and availability of information assets. It also requires periodic review and audit of compliance with cyber security controls. It binds Member Organizations, with maturity assessed against the framework's maturity model.
lookup_terms: cyber security compliance review and audit

data.summary: This node addresses third party cyber security within SAMA's cyber security framework, i.e. expectations that cyber risks arising from external parties and contractual relationships are governed through approved policy, defined responsibilities and compliance with regulatory and contractual obligations. The supplied context anchors it to the framework's policy content requirements, board accountability and the six-level maturity model used for assessment. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA; note the interaction with outsourcing and vendor governance expectations.

This node covers the Chief Information Security Officer and the information security function: a function independent from information technology, headed by the CISO and reporting directly to the CEO/managing director or the general manager of a control function. Its mandate includes supporting security policies, defining roles and responsibilities, providing security and information risk management frameworks, identifying emerging issues and shifts in risk appetite, and assisting management in designing controls. It binds Member Organizations and is relevant to segregation-of-duties and reporting-line questions, with related definitions for cyber security awareness programmes, controls and examinations.

Concept node for the cyber security committee referenced in the SAMA Cyber Security Framework, sitting within the framework's governance layer alongside board-level accountability, the cyber security policy and defined roles and responsibilities. It is the body to which matters such as accepted cyber security risk (risk within appetite and not conflicting with SAMA rules) are reported, and it anchors oversight of policy approval, resourcing and control ownership. It binds Member Organizations (entities affiliated with SAMA) and their boards and senior management, not customers or third parties directly.

Concept node for the security operations centre function as referenced across SAMA cyber security requirements, covering monitoring and detection capability that feeds the maturity assessment and incident handling expectations. It is a capability/control concept rather than a standalone rulebook, assessed through the framework's maturity levels (0–5) and the associated control considerations. Applies to Member Organizations subject to the SAMA cyber security regime.

Concept node for cyber security incident management under the SAMA cyber security regime, covering identification, reporting and handling of cyber security breaches and suspected weaknesses, including the expectation that reporting channels are embedded in the cyber security policy and linked to business continuity. Maturity of this process is measured under the framework's maturity model and is subject to periodic review. Binds Member Organizations; relevant where incidents also trigger notification duties to SAMA.

Concept node for the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard as adopted within the SAMA Cyber Security Framework's compliance requirements, where Member Organizations are expected to comply with mandatory international industry standards including PCI-DSS and EMV. It links the cyber security regime to card payment and payment-systems controls (including mada and SARIE references elsewhere in the framework). Binds Member Organizations handling card data and payment systems.
lookup_terms: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

data.summary: Concept node for the SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework as incorporated by reference into the SAMA Cyber Security Framework's mandatory industry-standards compliance requirement. It is relevant to Member Organizations using SWIFT messaging for cross-border and interbank payments, and compliance status feeds the framework's regulatory compliance and review processes.

Concept node for NIST (US National Institute of Standards and Technology) as a terminology source used in the SAMA Cyber Security Framework, whose glossary definitions (e.g. confidentiality, malware, multi-factor authentication, compensating control, control effectiveness) underpin the framework's defined terms. It is a definitional reference rather than an obligation in itself, useful when interpreting framework vocabulary applied to Member Organizations.
lookup_terms: glossary of key information security terms

data.summary: A cluster of provisions from SAMA's IT Governance Framework covering IT operations and, in the adjacent sections, the IT risk management lifecycle (identification, analysis and classification, treatment, reporting, monitoring and profiling). It sets principle-plus-control-requirement expectations that IT risk processes be defined, approved, implemented, aligned to enterprise risk management, and reported to business owners, senior management, the risk committee and the IT Steering Committee, covering information assets, people and third-party relationships. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA.

Section of the SAMA IT Governance Framework establishing system change management as a governed process for defining, designing, testing and deploying changes to information assets (applications, software, devices, data). It requires an approved change management policy and procedure, classification, risk and impact assessment, asset-owner and Change Advisory Board approval, cyber security function review, and controlled handling and post-implementation review of emergency changes. Applies to Member Organizations.

Provision of the SAMA IT Governance Framework requiring an IT incident management process to identify, respond to and handle incidents affecting information assets, and to report relevant incidents to SAMA under a defined communication protocol. It specifies a designated incident team, communication and notification plans, trained staff, prioritisation and classification, evidence and log protection, root-cause analysis, lessons learned, logging of user requests and incidents, and periodic effectiveness evaluation. Binds Member Organizations.

Sub-section of the SAMA IT Governance Framework requiring a documented, approved and communicated system development methodology so that development is performed under strict control.
