It covers asset ownership and custodianship, classification, labelling and handling, discovery of new assets, and links to dependent processes such as finance, procurement and IT. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA and sits alongside the framework's physical security and cyber security architecture controls.

A control domain of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework (section 3.3.4) requiring Member Organizations to define, follow and periodically review a cyber security architecture that sets out the cyber security requirements for the organisation. Associated expectations include formal approval of the architecture, qualified cyber security architects, and security-by-design principles for developing controls. Maturity of compliance is assessed against the framework's six-level cyber security maturity model.

A control domain of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework (section 3.3.5) requiring Member Organizations to restrict access to information assets on need-to-have and need-to-know bases through a defined, approved and implemented identity and access management policy. It addresses joiner/mover/leaver handling for internal staff (driven by HR) and for third parties (driven by an accountable party), formal approval of access requests, and monitoring and periodic evaluation of control effectiveness. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organizations and interacts with the framework's cyber security risk management expectations.

A control domain within the technology-security part (section 3.3) of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework addressing cyber security requirements for applications used by Member Organizations. It sits within the framework's policy, roles-and-responsibilities and maturity-model structure, under which controls must be defined, approved, implemented, monitored and periodically evaluated. Open the source for the specific application security control considerations, which are not reproduced in this extract.

A control domain of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework requiring Member Organizations to define, approve and implement a change management process covering changes to information assets, with monitored compliance and periodically measured control effectiveness. It sets expectations on impact assessment and classification of changes, security testing (penetration testing and internal/external code review or equivalent assurance), business-owner, cyber security function and Change Advisory Board approvals, segregation of development/test/production, emergency change procedures and fall-back/roll-back. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organizations and feeds into infrastructure security controls.

A control domain of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework (section 3.3.8) requiring Member Organizations to define, approve and implement cyber security standards for infrastructure components, monitor compliance with those standards and periodically measure their effectiveness. The aim is that all infrastructure-level cyber security controls are formally documented and supervised. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organizations and is assessed against the framework's maturity model.

Glossary and control-domain node within the SAMA Cyber Security Framework covering cryptography and cryptographic solutions, alongside related defined terms (confidentiality, compensating control, control effectiveness, containerization, custodianship). It anchors the Framework's section on cryptography as one of the mandated cyber security operations and technology domains. Binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA (banks, insurers and financing companies within the Framework's scope).

Framework sub-domain requiring a defined, approved and implemented cyber security standard where a Member Organization permits personal devices (smartphones, tablets, laptops) to be used for business purposes, supported by staff agreements and awareness training. It sets expectations on user responsibilities, consequences of control enforcement on personal devices, separation of business from personal data, application controls and mobile device management, with monitoring and periodic effectiveness evaluation. Binds Member Organizations and, through internal policy, their staff and contractors.

Framework sub-domain requiring information assets to be securely disposed of once no longer required, under a defined standard and procedure. It extends the obligation to third party service providers used for disposal, transport and storage, whose compliance and control effectiveness must be periodically measured and evaluated. Binds Member Organizations, including for their outsourced arrangements.

Framework sub-domain requiring Member Organizations to define, approve, implement and monitor a cyber security standard for payment systems, with periodic effectiveness measurement, aimed at protecting the confidentiality and integrity of shared banking systems. Rather than setting detailed controls, it cross-refers to the SARIE Information Security Policy and the mada Rules and Standards Technical Book (security framework, HSM requirements, SAMA CA IPK certificate procedures). Binds Member Organizations participating in these shared payment infrastructures.

Framework sub-domain requiring a defined, approved, implemented and monitored cyber security standard for electronic banking services, to protect the confidentiality and integrity of customer information and transactions. Control expectations include multi-factor authentication at registration, sign-on, beneficiary and payee changes, high-risk transactions and password reset; channel separation for beneficiary and MFA activation; access revocation after failed attempts; restriction of mobile number changes to branch or ATM; service availability; notification of scheduled downtime to SAMA and customers; contractual allocation of roles and liabilities with customers; and SAMA approval in specified cases. Binds Member Organizations offering online and mobile banking to customers.

Node covering the Framework's cyber security event management area together with its governance underpinnings: the six-level cyber security maturity model (0 to 5, cumulative) used to measure compliance, the required content of the cyber security policy, and the allocation of cyber security roles and responsibilities with ultimate accountability at the Board of Directors. It frames how controls must be defined, approved, implemented, demonstrable and reported, including reporting of breaches and suspected weaknesses. Binds Member Organizations, their boards and senior management.

A concept node for the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard as referenced in SAMA's Cyber Security Framework (v1.0, May 2017), where it appears both as a glossary term for the card-scheme data security standard and as a mandatory external industry standard. Under the Framework's compliance section, member organizations are required to comply with PCI-DSS alongside the EMV technical standard and the SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework, and to maintain a process for identifying and meeting regulatory and industry-standard obligations. It binds SAMA-regulated banks, insurance and financing companies subject to the Framework.
lookup_terms: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

data.summary: A node identifying the Saudi Central Bank (formerly Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority) as issuer and supervisor of the Cyber Security Framework (v1.0, May 2017), including its IT Risk Supervision function under the Deputyship of Supervision. It covers SAMA's role in receiving framework update and waiver requests from member organizations (submitted to the Deputy Governor, with CISO and cyber security committee approval) and in expecting board and senior management oversight of implementation. Relevant to banks, insurance and financing companies regulated by SAMA.

Orientation node for SAMA's Guidelines on Repurchase Agreements, issued under SAMA's Charter and the Banking Control Law, setting binding policy requirements for the Saudi repo market. They cover scope (SAR-denominated repo/reverse repo in eligible securities), definitions, mandatory use of the SAMA-approved Master Repurchase Agreement, eligible counterparties, eligible collateral and risk management expectations, and are to be read with CMA rules and the Bankruptcy Law. They bind all repo market participants defined as eligible counterparties.

Defined-term node for a repurchase agreement (repo) under SAMA's repo guidelines, covering the sale of eligible securities with an agreement to repurchase equivalent securities at an agreed future date or on demand; the term is used to cover repo and reverse repo equivalently unless stated otherwise. Related defined roles include Repo Buyer (cash provider) and Repo Seller (securities provider), plus Custodian, Held-in-Custody and Eligible Security. Relevant to any SAMA-supervised institution or eligible counterparty transacting SAR-denominated repo in Saudi Arabia.

Defined-term node for a reverse repurchase agreement (reverse repo) in SAMA's repo guidelines: the buyer purchases securities from a seller with a simultaneous arrangement to resell or repurchase the same or equivalent securities at an agreed price on a future date or on demand. The guidelines treat repo and reverse repo interchangeably unless otherwise specified, so the same policy requirements (MRA, eligible securities, eligible counterparties) apply. Relevant to repo market participants in the Saudi market.

Node for the standard Master Repurchase Agreement for the Sale and Purchase of Securities (2020 version) approved by SAMA and annexed to the repo guidelines. The guidelines require all repo transactions in Saudi Arabia to be governed by this MRA, with any variations recorded in annexures and mutually agreed, and made clear in trade confirmations or equivalent documentation; foreign-currency legs governed by the GMRA are not prohibited subject to applicable KSA rules. Binding on all repo market participants/eligible counterparties.

Section of SAMA's Guidelines on Repurchase Agreements dealing with how repo collateral is priced and valued, requiring counterparties to agree price sources in advance, to value securities on a dirty-price basis including accrued interest/profit, and to use a waterfall of fallback sources if a primary source fails. It sits alongside the eligible-collateral and custody provisions and connects to the default-valuation mechanics of the SAMA-approved Master Repurchase Agreement. It binds all repo market participants in Saudi Arabia, with additional custody obligations falling on licensed banks.

Default-related provisions of the SAMA-approved Master Repurchase Agreement annexed to the Repo Guidelines, covering service of a Default Notice, the effectiveness of notices by various delivery channels, the Early Termination Date, and close-out netting into a single Cash Settlement Amount. It governs how the non-Defaulting Party establishes Default Market Values and takes an account of amounts due between the parties. It binds counterparties to repo transactions documented under the mandated MRA, which is governed by Saudi law.

Margin provisions of the SAMA-approved Master Repurchase Agreement, setting out when a party may call for a Margin Transfer based on Net Exposure, how Net Exposure and Net Margin are computed across Transaction Exposures, the currency and composition of margin, and the related defined terms (Margin Securities, Margin Percentage, Market Value). It establishes the contractual collateralisation mechanics for repo exposures. It binds the two counterparties to each repo transaction under the mandated MRA.

Defines SARIE (Saudi Arabian Riyal Interbank Express, or any future instant payments system) within the Repo Guidelines and anchors the settlement rules requiring cash legs of SAR repo transactions between licensed agents to settle through SARIE, with securities legs through Tadawul or SAMA depending on the issuer. Where a counterparty is not a licensed agent or the currency is not SAR, other mutually agreed systems may be used. Relevant to banks and other repo market participants settling repos in Saudi Arabia.

Defines Tadawul as the Saudi Exchange for purposes of the Repo Guidelines and underpins the delivery rules requiring non-SAMA issued eligible securities to be delivered through Tadawul (with cash through SARIE) where both counterparties are licensed agents and the transaction is in SAR. It also frames eligibility of bonds/sukuk listed on the Saudi Exchange as repo collateral. Applies to repo market participants transacting in the Saudi repo market.

Defines SOCPA (Saudi Authority of Auditors and Accountants) in the Repo Guidelines and links it to the requirement that repo market participants apply the accounting standards for repo transactions endorsed by SOCPA. It appears within the risk management requirements, which also mandate documented policies covering governance, authorisation, credit, counterparty, market, legal and operational risks. It binds banks and other repo market participants.
lookup_terms: Saudi Authority of Auditors and Accountants

data.summary: A control area of the SAMA Cyber Security Framework requiring Member Organizations to define, approve and implement a threat intelligence management process, and to measure and periodically evaluate its effectiveness. It prescribes the sources (internal logs, SIEM, support functions; external feeds including SAMA and government agencies), an analysis methodology, the threat attributes to capture, actionability for follow-up, and sharing of relevant intelligence with stakeholders such as SAMA and BCIS members. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA and sits within the wider cyber security risk management and compliance regime.

A control area of the SAMA Cyber Security Framework requiring Member Organizations to define, approve and implement a vulnerability management process covering identification and mitigation of application and infrastructure vulnerabilities, with effectiveness measured and periodically evaluated. It is positioned alongside threat intelligence within the cyber security risk management and compliance requirements, which are themselves subject to periodic review and audit. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organizations.

A third-party cyber security control requiring Member Organizations to define, approve, implement and monitor cyber security requirements inside their contract and vendor management processes, so that requirements are settled before contract signature and compliance is monitored across the contract life-cycle. It covers when the cyber security function must be involved (e.g. due diligence), baseline security requirements applicable in all cases, and rights to periodic cyber security review. It binds Member Organizations dealing with third parties, defined broadly to include service providers, outsourcing and cloud providers, vendors, suppliers and government agencies.

A third-party cyber security control governing Member Organizations' use of hybrid and public cloud services (expressly not private/internal cloud), requiring a cloud computing policy and process with monitored, periodically evaluated controls. Substantive conditions include prior SAMA approval before using cloud services or signing with a provider, a contract containing cyber security requirements, in-principle data location within Saudi Arabia (with explicit SAMA approval for offshore), no secondary use of the Member Organization's data, provider security controls per risk assessment, logical data segregation, business continuity alignment, rights of review, audit and examination, and exit arrangements. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organizations and is read with the outsourcing control and SAMA's outsourcing circular.

Covers cyber security event management and the SIEM/monitoring concepts in the SAMA Cyber Security Framework: Member Organizations must define, approve and implement a security event management process to analyse operational and security logs and respond to events, supported by an approved security event monitoring standard keyed to asset classification or risk profile. Requirements include a designated Security Operations Center, trained staff, a restricted SOC workspace, 24x7 monitoring resources, and detection/handling of malicious code and suspicious anomalies; related customer-facing provisions require SMS notification for retail and personal financial transactions and for beneficiary additions, modifications and activations. It binds Member Organizations and interacts with fraud and consumer-notification expectations.

Sets the SAMA Cyber Security Framework expectations for multi-factor authentication in electronic banking, requiring MFA at customer registration and across all electronic banking services, password protection of hard and soft tokens, revocation after three successive incorrect passwords or PINs, mobile number changes only via branch or ATM, and use of different delivery channels for requesting/activating MFA and for adding/activating beneficiaries. MFA is mandated for sign-on, adding or modifying beneficiaries, adding utility and government payment services, high-risk transactions above predefined limits, and password reset. Related identity and access management controls apply need-to-have/need-to-know access governance internally; the provisions bind Member Organizations offering online and mobile banking to customers.

SAMA-issued standard Master Agreement for the Sale and Purchase of Securities — a Shari'ah-compatible repo-style framework under which a Seller sells securities to a Buyer with unilateral undertakings to re-sell/re-purchase at a Second Purchase Price. This node carries the core definitional and close-out valuation machinery (Default Market Value, Net Value, Deliverable/Receivable Securities, Transaction Costs) used by the non-Defaulting Party after an Early Termination Date. It binds the two contracting counterparties (typically banks and other market participants transacting under SAMA-standardised documentation) rather than imposing supervisory obligations directly.
lookup_terms: Master Agreement for the Sale and Purchase of Securities

data.summary: The representations and warranties clause of the SAMA securities sale and purchase master agreement, given by each party on execution and deemed repeated on each transaction and transfer date. It covers capacity and authorisation, acting as principal, regulatory approvals, unencumbered title to transferred securities, and — notably — a party's own responsibility for satisfying itself as to Shari'ah Compliance, with a waiver of Shari'ah-based challenge and non-reliance on the counterparty's fatwa or opinions. Breach of these representations is itself an Event of Default, so the clause drives close-out risk allocation between the counterparties.
lookup_terms: ordinary course of business not speculative

data.summary: The Events of Default and close-out provisions of the SAMA securities sale and purchase master agreement. It lists default triggers (failure to transfer or margin, Act of Insolvency, untrue representations, anticipatory repudiation, suspension or expulsion by a securities exchange or Competent Authority on financial-resource or credit-rating grounds, and a 30-day cure period for other breaches), and sets the mechanics for designating an Early Termination Date on up to 20 days' notice, including Automatic Early Termination if elected in Annex I. It binds Buyer and Seller and determines how outstanding Transactions are accelerated and valued on close-out.

Annex I supplementary terms and the related Confirmation/undertaking mechanics of the SAMA securities sale and purchase master agreement. Annex I is where the parties elect transaction-specific and counterparty-specific variables (including whether Automatic Early Termination applies and the notice/contact details used for Exercise Notices), while the linked provisions describe Confirmation content (Second Purchase Date, Pricing Rate, settlement accounts) and the unilateral Seller and Buyer undertakings. It binds the two contracting counterparties and is the place to check elections before applying the general terms.

Annex II sets out the standard form of Confirmation documenting an individual Transaction under the SAMA master agreement, restating the reciprocal Seller and Buyer unilateral undertakings and recording economic terms such as Second Purchase Date, Second Purchase Price, Pricing Rate and settlement accounts. A Confirmation supplements and forms part of the master agreement, is prima facie evidence of agreed terms absent prompt objection, and prevails over the master agreement in case of conflict for that Transaction only. It binds the Buyer and Seller to the specific trade.

Annex III provides the form of Exercise Notice and the surrounding exercise mechanics under the SAMA securities sale and purchase master agreement. It operates with the Seller Exercise Condition and Buyer Exercise Condition (tested by comparing Market Value, or Default Market Value after an Early Termination Date, against the Second Purchase Price) to determine which party is the Exercising Party; delivery of the notice is an offer that the Undertaking Party accepts orally or in writing, with deemed acceptance after five hours. It binds the two counterparties and governs settlement of the Second Purchased Securities and Second Purchase Price.

This node covers the legal documentation layer of SAMA's repo guidelines: the scope of application (SAR-denominated outright sale/repurchase of eligible securities among eligible counterparties), the key defined terms (Custodian, Eligible Security, Held-in-Custody, Repo Buyer/Seller, Saudi Repo Market, SARIE, Tadawul), and the requirement that Saudi repo transactions be documented under SAMA's approved standard Master Repurchase Agreement (2020 version), governed by Saudi law, with variations confined to annexures and mutually agreed. It clarifies that existing foreign-currency repos documented under the GMRA are not prohibited, subject to applicable KSA rules. It binds all repo market participants, with a bank licensed by SAMA required as a principal.

This node defines who may transact repos in Saudi Arabia: SAMA-licensed financial institutions (banks, insurers, finance companies), CMA-approved capital market institutions, KSA-incorporated corporates assessed for sophistication, and non-domiciled corporates subject to maturity restrictions (no securities with under one year to maturity; foreign financial corporates' collateral must mature at least three months beyond the repo). At least one principal to every repo must be a SAMA-licensed bank. It also carries confidentiality of counterparty identity (except regulatory reporting to SAMA) and legal-risk requirements on full transfer of title and adequate documentation.

This node concerns what may serve as repo collateral and how it is valued, including listed bond/sukuk issuances and any other securities SAMA specifies, the rule that a security's legal maturity must be at least as long as the repo, and the prohibition on securities issued or guaranteed by the repo seller. The associated context also covers default-related valuation concepts from the master agreement (Net Value, Default Market Value, Deliverable/Receivable Securities, Transaction Costs) used by a non-defaulting party on early termination. Relevant to all repo market participants and their collateral and close-out practices.

This node sets the binding risk-management expectations for repo activity: documented policies and procedures covering governance, authorisation, risk management, internal controls and reporting; coverage of credit, counterparty, market, legal and operational risk; coordination across treasury, back office, risk, compliance and IT; SOCPA-endorsed accounting treatment; and exposure limits for counterparties and collateral issuers reviewed periodically. It also carries the guidelines' legal basis (SAMA Charter and Banking Control Law) and confirms all policy requirements are binding on Saudi repo market participants, to be read with SAMA, CMA and Bankruptcy Law requirements.
lookup_terms: legal basis SAMA Charter Banking Control Law

data.summary: This node addresses custodial arrangements in repo: participants must understand the terms, rights and obligations of any custody agreement before entering repos with custodial arrangements, and licensed banks must maintain custody arrangements and processes for held-in-custody eligible securities, including monitoring and segregation to prevent duplicative use of the same securities. Surrounding context covers collateral price sources and valuation (agreed sources, dirty prices, waterfall approach, dispute handling) and leads into reporting and settlement. Binds repo market participants, with the heavier obligation on SAMA-licensed banks acting as custodians.

This node concerns reporting and settlement of repo transactions (including bank participants' reporting of repo trades to SAMA), with the attached context drawn from the master agreement's event-of-default, insolvency and margin/representation provisions, including express reference to proceedings under the Saudi Bankruptcy Law and to margin securities substitution mechanics. Useful for questions on when a repo counterparty is in default, close-out triggers, and the contractual representations each party gives. Applies to repo market participants, with reporting duties falling on bank participants.
lookup_terms: Applicable Rate Appropriate Market Base Currency

data.summary: A SAMA circular to all banks operating in the Kingdom directing adherence to the Basel Committee's guidelines on the prudential treatment of problem assets, covering non-performing loans and forbearance. It addresses harmonised definitions and criteria for asset quality across supervisory reporting, internal ratings-based credit risk management, Pillar 3 disclosure and published asset-quality indicators. It binds banks as a supervisory expectation rather than setting out its own detailed criteria.

A Governor-level SAMA circular requiring supervised entities to promptly receive, accept and execute judicial judgments and decisions issued against them, without delay or procrastination, and to raise any objection through the competent channels within the prescribed statutory periods. It is addressed to banks, insurance and reinsurance companies and related free professions, finance companies, money exchangers and credit information companies, which must inform their relevant internal departments to act on it.

SAMA circular issued under the Banking Control Law, Finance Companies Control Law and Finance Lease Law (and Article 10(2) of its Implementing Regulation) mandating a standard-form vehicle finance lease (Ijara) contract for individuals. Lessors must use the annexed template, complete internal procedures by the stated deadline, and may not conclude contracts that deviate from or amend the standard form. It binds banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom acting as lessors to individual lessees.

The clauses of SAMA's mandatory individual vehicle Ijara template dealing with early partial repayment and early ownership (early acquisition of the leased asset by the lessee), including the associated procedures set out in the contract summary. They determine the lessee's exit and prepayment rights and the lessor's permitted charges and steps for transferring title. Binding on banks and finance companies acting as lessors, which cannot vary these terms.
lookup_terms: transfer of title of leased asset

data.summary: The provisions of the mandatory individual vehicle Ijara template governing late payment of rental instalments, breach and termination of the contract, lessee withdrawal, and expiry without the lessee acquiring the asset. They fix the consequences of arrears and the lessor's remedies, together with treatment of guarantees where their value declines. Binding on lessors (banks and finance companies) in dealings with individual lessees.

The clause of the mandatory individual vehicle Ijara template addressing total and partial destruction (loss) of the leased asset, and the related insurance and procedural steps for handling such cases. It allocates risk of loss between lessor and lessee and determines settlement of outstanding amounts from insurance proceeds. Binding on lessors under the standard form, which may not be amended.

A SAMA circular imposing mandatory pre-contractual conduct requirements on banks and real estate finance companies before extending residential (individual) real estate finance. It sets out affordability/suitability assessment against approved credit-granting policies, a documented plain-language explanation of terms and risks by a competent officer, a written financing offer valid for a minimum period with a full document pack the customer may take away, a mandatory briefing by an independent credit advisor (not the officer who dealt with or made the offer), and a minimum reflection period before signing. Concluding an individual real estate finance contract is prohibited unless all steps are completed and evidenced in the financing file, with SAMA verification and enforcement action for breach.

The annexed acknowledgment form by which a customer confirms acceptance of the credit risks of variable-cost (variable profit/term-cost) real estate finance, in the standard wording attached to the circular. It must be included in the documents given to the customer as part of the financing offer for variable-rate products, with the lender documenting receipt, and it captures income, total credit obligations to income ratios before and after the finance, and other fees or costs. It binds banks and real estate finance companies offering variable-rate individual real estate finance.
lookup_terms: variable term cost real estate finance
debt burden ratio / نسبة الالتزامات إلى الدخل

data.summary: A SAMA circular requiring financial institutions under its supervision, their subsidiaries and branches of foreign financial institutions operating in KSA to hold a valid and up-to-date Legal Entity Identifier issued by a GLEIF-accredited operating unit, building on an earlier SAMA circular on LEI adoption. It also permits those institutions to enter an agreement with SIMAH, as the accredited local operating unit (LOU), to issue, update and renew LEIs on behalf of existing and prospective corporate customers. Rationale is risk management, financial stability, market transparency and KSA's G20-related international commitments.

The template agreement annexed to the LEI circular, concluded between SIMAH (as the GLEIF-accredited local operating unit) and a SAMA-supervised financial institution, enabling the institution to issue, update and renew LEIs for its legal-entity (business) customers. Its recitals frame SIMAH's authority under the ROC charter, the GLEIF–LOU master agreement and SAMA instructions, and the institution's role as holder of corporate customer data subject to SAMA supervision. It is operative only once signed by the institution; it does not itself create the LEI obligation, which arises from the circular.
lookup_terms: اتفاقية إصدار وتحديث وتجديد معرف الكيانات القانونية
business customer LEI on behalf of

data.summary: The Shariah oversight component of SAMA's Shariah Governance Instructions for finance companies, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its implementing regulation. It addresses monitoring and verification that the company's finance business complies with Shariah rulings and principles, alongside board and senior management responsibilities, the Shariah committee's composition and operating controls, independence criteria and confidentiality. It binds finance companies licensed for real estate finance, productive assets finance, SME finance, finance lease, credit card finance and consumer finance, and is indicative (guidance) for other licensed finance activities unless other rules make provisions mandatory.

A SAMA decision (transmitted by circular to the Saudi Company for Finance Lease Contracts Registration, "Sijil") defining the powers, appointment conditions and duties of the Head of the Contract Registry and the registry clerks, issued under the Finance Lease Law and its implementing regulation. It covers SAMA non-objection for appointment, reporting lines, SAMA's power to remove for breach of legal or professional duties, grievance routes where registration or attestation is refused, responsibility for accuracy of registered finance lease contracts and data, minimum ten-year record retention, verification of contracting parties' identity and capacity, Arabic-language documentation with certified translation, sealing of ownership documents (including by accepted electronic means), and safekeeping of registry entries.

An Arabic-language SAMA circular (issued by the Deputy Governor for Supervision) addressed to all banks operating in the Kingdom, prohibiting them from dealing or negotiating with non-Saudi representatives of private civil security-guarding and cash-transport companies. Banks must instead report the employing company to the competent regional police authority for legal action, and must fully comply with SAMA's prior instructions on the Private Civil Security Guards Law and the Law on Transport of Cash, Precious Metals and Valuable Documents and their implementing regulations. It is a conduct/counterparty restriction on banks in procuring guarding and cash-in-transit services, not a customer-facing rule.
lookup_terms: ban on dealing with security company agents
Transport of Cash and Precious Metals Law

data.summary: Arabic SAMA circular from the General Department for Supervision of Finance Companies transmitting the Terms of Reference for Finance Company Committees, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law (Royal Decree M/51) and Article 98 of its Implementing Regulation, which empowers the Governor to form committees that propose measures to develop the finance sector. It sets the definitions (standing vs temporary committee), the committee structure (General Committee of General Managers, Executive Committee, subcommittees), and rules on formation, nomination and removal, meetings and quorum, agendas, minutes, reporting, responsibilities, and SAMA's role and representatives. It is addressed to finance companies and governs sector-level industry committee governance rather than firm-level prudential obligations.
lookup_terms: Terms of Reference for Finance Company Committees

data.summary: Sub-node covering the General Committee of General Managers of finance companies, established by Governor's decision and governed by the Terms of Reference for Finance Company Committees issued under Article 98 of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law. The Terms of Reference address its formation, nomination and removal of members, meetings and quorum, agenda/minutes/reporting, and responsibilities. It binds participating finance companies and their general managers as a sector-representative body channelling proposals to SAMA.
lookup_terms: nomination and removal of committee members

data.summary: Sub-node covering the Executive Committee established under the Terms of Reference for Finance Company Committees, issued pursuant to the Finance Companies Control Law and Article 98 of its Implementing Regulation. The Terms of Reference set out its composition, nomination and exemption of members, meetings and quorum, agenda, minutes and reporting lines, and its responsibilities within the finance-sector committee structure. Relevant to finance companies whose representatives sit on or report to this committee.

Sub-node covering the subcommittees (standing or temporary) formed under the Terms of Reference for Finance Company Committees, issued under Article 98 of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law. It concerns their formation, member nomination and removal, meetings and quorum, agendas, minutes and reporting, and responsibilities, including the limited lifespan of temporary committees formed for a specific task. Applies to finance companies participating in the sector committee structure overseen by SAMA.
lookup_terms: finance companies committee terms of reference

data.summary: Extract from the Rules Governing BNPL Companies setting the definitions chapter and the licensing regime: BNPL activity is defined as financing enabling a Consumer to purchase goods or services without bearing a term cost, carried on by a joint stock company licensed by SAMA. It prohibits conducting BNPL activity without a SAMA licence, restricts licensees to the licensed activity absent SAMA's prior written non-objection, and covers verification steps, a five-year licence term with renewal three months before expiry, revocation on request subject to creditor/consumer rights and financial stability, and licence fees. It binds companies licensed (or applying to be licensed) by SAMA for BNPL activity, alongside the Finance Companies Control Law and senior-appointment requirements.

A clause-level node within SAMA's mandatory standard-form vehicle finance lease (Ijarah) contract for individuals, issued by circular to banks and finance companies in the Kingdom. It concerns the treatment of total and partial loss/damage of the leased asset, including how the parties' payment and insurance positions are settled when the vehicle is partially destroyed. It binds lessors (banks and licensed finance companies) writing consumer auto Ijarah, who may not conclude contracts departing from the approved form.

A clause-level node in SAMA's approved standard vehicle finance lease (Ijarah) contract for individuals setting out the insurance arrangements for the leased vehicle, including how insurance cost is reflected in the financing disclosure summary. It sits alongside the maintenance and loss/destruction clauses and is binding on lessors that must use the model form without amendment.

A clause-level node covering breach, late payment consequences and termination of the standard individual vehicle finance lease (Ijarah) contract mandated by SAMA. It links to the contract's late-payment provisions and the summary disclosure of consequences of missed rental payments, and governs when the lessor may terminate and what the lessee owes. Binding on banks and finance companies acting as lessors.

Appendix 3 to SAMA's mandatory standard vehicle Ijarah contract for individuals: the ownership transfer certificate evidencing passage of title in the leased vehicle to the lessee on completion of the contract or early purchase. It supports the contract's ownership-transfer procedures and early-ownership clauses and binds lessors using the prescribed form.

Appendix 2 to SAMA's mandatory standard vehicle Ijarah contract for individuals: the certificate by which the lessee acknowledges receipt and acceptance of the leased vehicle. It evidences delivery/receipt of the asset and is the trigger point for the lessee's obligations under the delivery clauses; binding on lessors required to use the approved form unamended.
lookup_terms: delivery and receipt of leased asset

data.summary: The Law on Practising the Transport of Money, Precious Metals and Valuable Documents, issued by Royal Decree and approved by Council of Ministers resolution. It defines money, precious metals, valuable documents and the licensed activity, sets the licensing regime administered by the Ministry of Interior/General Security (three-year renewable licences, fees, security-department requirement), mandates insurance cover for transported items, and requires advance notification and route coordination for consignments above a stated value. It binds financial institutions (banks, exchange houses, investment and insurance firms), precious-metals factories and outlets, and licensed private security companies carrying out such transport.
lookup_terms: transport of money and precious metals

data.summary: A SAMA circular instructing local banks and licensed money exchangers to exercise caution when disposing of obsolete or damaged bank-owned equipment and media — ATMs, POS terminals, computers, imaging devices, related documents, tapes and recording/imaging discs. It requires firms to adopt policies and procedures for disposal that preserve the confidentiality of information stored on such assets and prohibits simply discarding them as waste, where they could be tampered with or misused. It binds local banks and exchange houses, reaffirming their legal responsibility for damaged devices and the data they contain.
lookup_terms: disposal of old or damaged devices

data.summary: SAMA's Rules Governing Bancassurance Activities regulate the marketing and distribution of insurance products by banks to their Clients under a written Agreement with a licensed insurance Company. They set definitions (Bancassurance Activities, Agreement, Authorised Employee, Client), scope, objective, minimum Agreement contents, conduct standards and the respective obligations of bank and insurer. They bind banks licensed under the Banking Control Law and insurance companies licensed under the Cooperative Insurance Companies Control Law; the Rules are supplemented by those laws and other SAMA instructions on matters not expressly addressed.
lookup_terms: marketing and distribution of insurance products

data.summary: A referenced instrument rather than a standalone node: the Cooperative Insurance Companies Control Law is the licensing statute under which the insurance "Company" in the Bancassurance Rules is authorised to conduct insurance business in the Kingdom. Within the Bancassurance Rules it fixes who qualifies as a Company and, together with its Implementing Regulation, the Banking Control Law and other SAMA and competent-authority rules, governs any matter the Bancassurance Rules do not expressly address. It binds licensed insurers; banks encounter it indirectly through the counterparty eligibility requirement.

The bank-facing duties under the Bancassurance Rules: the bank is fully responsible for Authorised Employees' conduct of Bancassurance Activities and must ensure they are carried out consistently with SAMA instructions and transparency principles. A linked professional-conduct article requires honesty, fairness and competence, ongoing staff training and market awareness, adequate managerial, financial, operational and human resources, timely and clear disclosure of coverage, conditions, exclusions and restrictions so Clients can make an informed decision, and confidentiality of Company and Client data. It binds banks licensed under the Banking Control Law that market insurance products to their Clients.

The insurer-facing duties under the Bancassurance Rules: the Company must obtain SAMA approval before any material amendment to the Agreement with the bank, file an annual training plan for Authorised Employees covering marketing and distribution techniques, product workshops and AML/CTF training, keep bank and Client data confidential, periodically review the bank's conduct of Bancassurance Activities across electronic and non-electronic channels, and pay the agreed commission within the Agreement period and within SAMA's limits. A related prohibition bars tying insurance to banking products (or vice versa) unless coverage is mandated by a competent authority. It binds licensed insurance companies distributing through banks.

The Agreement is the defined contract by which an insurance Company and a bank agree that the bank will carry out Bancassurance Activities, and it is the legal basis on which the bank markets and distributes the insurer's products to its Clients. The Rules prescribe minimum contents: term and termination procedures, the electronic and non-electronic marketing and distribution channels used, the Authorised Employee training plan, KYC and compliance procedures, insurance classes and products covered, marketing/distribution and premium-collection procedures, commission and its calculation, due date and collection, client care and complaints resolution, and claims receipt and transfer to the Company. It binds both contracting parties; material amendments require SAMA approval.

This node covers the definitional, scope and licensing architecture of SAMA's Rules Governing BNPL Companies, including the defined terms (BNPL Activity, BNPL Company, Consumer, Stores), the prohibition on carrying on BNPL activity without a SAMA licence, and the licensing lifecycle (initial approval and commercial register timelines, verification visits, five-year licence term and renewal, revocation on request, and issuance/renewal fees). It binds joint stock companies licensed or seeking licence by SAMA to conduct BNPL activity, and is expressly subordinate to the Finance Companies Control Law and the senior-appointments requirements.
lookup_terms: buy now pay later scope of application

data.summary: This node sets out the conduct and consumer-facing obligations of licensed BNPL companies, principally the Article 19 duties: compliance with SAMA's Responsible Lending Principles for Retail Consumers, consent-based verification and documentation of the consumer's credit record, registration and updating of credit information with licensed credit bureaus, documented creditworthiness and repayment-capacity methodology, clear pop-up disclosures and acknowledgements, identification and independent verification of the consumer's identity, and a prohibition on contracted stores passing additional fees to the consumer. It binds SAMA-licensed BNPL companies and reaches their merchant arrangements through monitoring duties. Note the cross-regime interaction: the identification/verification duty sits alongside AML/CTF customer due diligence, and the BNPL "Consumer" is not coextensive with the AML "Customer"; Saudization and non-Saudi appointment controls for control functions also appear here.
lookup_terms: Responsible Lending Principles for Retail Consumers

data.summary: An Arabic-language SAMA guidance manual (issued with a disclaimer of liability) explaining how the mandatory uniform method for calculating the early repayment amount works for monthly-instalment finance contracts such as personal finance, vehicle lease-to-own and real estate finance. It restates the beneficiary's right to early settlement without bearing term cost for the remaining period, the permitted lender compensation (reinvestment cost capped at three months' term cost on a declining-balance basis, plus non-recoverable third-party payments), and the amortization table disclosure, with worked examples and FAQs. It is explanatory of obligations resting on banks and finance companies under the Finance Companies Control Law and Finance Lease implementing regulations and the Consumer Finance Rules, rather than a free-standing rule.

A short SAMA Banking Supervision circular (in Arabic) reaffirming a series of earlier circulars on the mechanism for disclosing banking data and information. It prohibits supervised entities from providing any financial or banking information about customers or their transactions to any party — individuals, institutions, government bodies, or any other local or foreign entity — without first referring to SAMA and obtaining its no-objection. Addressed to banks and money exchange institutions operating in the Kingdom and to the Saudi Credit Bureau (SIMAH), with a requirement to cascade it to all departments and branches and confirm compliance.
lookup_terms: information requests from government or foreign authorities

data.summary: A SAMA circular (Arabic) from the General Department for Supervision of Finance Companies transmitting a Ministry of Finance letter and a Crown Prince/National Committee for Drug Control cable on the launch of the National Drug Prevention Project (Nebras). It asks supervised entities to coordinate with the General Secretariat of the National Committee for Drug Control and to place any similar preventive programmes under the Nebras banner to unify and integrate efforts. Addressed to banks, insurance companies, finance companies and SIMAH; it is a coordination/branding instruction rather than a prudential or AML obligation.

A SAMA Currency Department circular (Arabic) implementing Ministry of Interior recommendations requiring large companies and commercial outlets to contract only licensed cash transport companies for moving cash, and to use security bags/containers approved by SAMA — including containers permitting automatic tracking and self-destruction of notes if the planned route is changed. It binds banks, exchange companies, licensed cash transport companies and operators of licensed consolidated cash centres, and notes that SAMA will conduct field inspections and impose penalties on violators.
lookup_terms: consolidated cash centres مراكز النقد الموحدة

data.summary: Describes the first stage of SAMA's Regulatory Sandbox process: the innovator submits the application form and SAMA assesses its completeness against the Sandbox framework's eligibility criteria, returning a final decision within 60 business days. Success at this stage yields an initial approval letter permitting progression to operational readiness, not authorisation to operate. It binds FinTech applicants seeking temporary permission to test in the KSA market, and sets SAMA's own processing timeframe.

Sets out Stage 2 of the Regulatory Sandbox, in which an applicant holding a Sandbox initial approval letter must demonstrate compliance with the Operational Readiness Assessment Criteria (AC) within roughly 120 days, covering matters such as fit and proper approvals for management, shareholder approvals and a three-year financial model. The initial approval letter allows company formation/update with the Ministry of Commerce as a FinTech but expressly does not permit commencement of operations or customer onboarding. Completion of the AC, monitored by the Sandbox Risk Management Unit, results in the temporary permission (Letter of Authorisation).

Covers Stage 3 of the Regulatory Sandbox: permitted innovators test their products live under the temporary permission for a minimum of six months and up to twelve months. Successful testing is expected to inform SAMA's issuance or amendment of regulations, enabling the innovator to apply for a full regulatory licence. Relevant to FinTechs operating under a Sandbox LoA and to teams assessing the status of live-tested propositions.

Describes the final Sandbox stage, exit or 'graduation', following successful completion of live testing. It is the transition point from temporary Sandbox permission towards application for a full SAMA licence under the applicable regulatory framework. Relevant to FinTechs concluding testing and to assessing whether an entity's permissions are transitional or permanent.

A 2017 SAMA circular to all banks, insurance companies and finance companies clarifying the accounting treatment and financial statement presentation of Zakat and income tax. It discontinues the SAMA Accounting Standards for Commercial Banks from 1 January 2017 and requires financial statements to be prepared under IFRS as adopted by SAMA (i.e. IFRS except IAS 12 and IFRIC 21 insofar as they relate to Zakat), with standalone guidance annexed and applied consistently across the three sectors. Addressed to managing directors, CEOs and general managers of supervised entities.
lookup_terms: SAMA Accounting Standards for Commercial Banks

data.summary: Part of SAMA's Rules Governing Credit Risk Exposure Classification and Provisioning, setting out IFRS 9-based definitions and staging used for credit risk classification: probability of default, exposure at default, loss given default, financial asset, expected credit loss (12-month and lifetime), and Stage 1/2/3 exposures. It adds regulatory-only sub-categories (Stage 2A special monitoring and 2B substandard; Stage 3A doubtful and 3B loss) for reporting purposes, maps them to earlier SAMA provisioning categories, and defines past due and default (including the 90 days past due trigger). Binds SAMA-supervised credit-granting institutions for classification, provisioning and regulatory reporting.

This node sets out the professional conduct duties banks must observe when carrying on bancassurance activities under SAMA's bancassurance rules, covering honesty, transparency and fairness, competence and training of Authorised Employees, adequate resources, full and timely disclosure of policy coverage, conditions, exceptions and restrictions to Clients, accuracy of information, and confidentiality of Company and Client data. Surrounding provisions address the bancassurance unit's management (director appointment subject to SAMA non-objection), permitted electronic and non-electronic marketing and distribution channels, the Insurance Foundations Certificate Exam requirement for Authorised Employees, insurer approval plus SAMA notification before expanding channels, and the prohibition on conducting bancassurance with anyone other than the bank's own Clients. It binds banks (and their authorised staff) distributing insurance products in partnership with insurance companies.

This node covers the AML Law's core preventive obligations on financial institutions and DNFBPs: risk-based customer due diligence (with enhanced measures for higher risk), PEP identification and additional measures for domestic, foreign and international-organisation PEPs, cross-border correspondent banking safeguards and the shell-bank prohibition, and wire transfer originator/beneficiary information and recordkeeping requirements (including refusing transfers where information cannot be obtained). It also touches supervisory authority powers to inspect, compel information, assess sector risk and issue instructions. It binds all FIs and DNFBPs subject to the Anti-Money Laundering Law and its Implementing Regulation.

This node describes the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence under the AML Law: its status as the national central agency for receiving, analysing and disseminating suspicious transaction reports, its operational independence under the President of State Security, confidentiality duties of its personnel, and its powers to exchange information with domestic competent authorities and foreign counterparts (subject to use-limitation undertakings). Adjacent provisions cover the reporting entity's duty to file detailed STRs and respond promptly to Directorate requests, the tipping-off prohibition, and good-faith reporting immunity, plus cross-border currency/BNI customs declarations. It binds FIs, DNFBPs and NPOs and their boards, management and employees, as well as the Directorate itself.

This node sets out the powers and duties of supervisory authorities under the AML Law — collecting data, on-site and off-site supervision, compelling production of documents, conducting sectoral ML risk assessments, issuing guidance and instructions, cooperating with foreign counterparts, verifying group-wide application to foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries, and fit-and-proper screening of managers and controllers. It also includes key statutory definitions (Supervisory Authority, Competent Authority, Beneficial Owner, Customer, Business Relationship, Shell Bank, Bearer Negotiable Instruments, Provisional Seizure, Confiscation). Relevant to SAMA as AML supervisor and to all supervised FIs, DNFBPs and NPOs.

This node covers the AML Law's confiscation regime: mandatory court-ordered confiscation on conviction of laundered funds, proceeds (including intermingled proceeds up to value) and instrumentalities; confiscation regardless of whether funds are held by the defendant or a third party, subject to a bona fide purchaser defence; non-conviction-based confiscation where the perpetrator dies, absconds or cannot be identified; and value-based confiscation of substitute assets. Related articles address international cooperation — information exchange, mutual legal assistance in tracing, seizure and recovery, enforcement of foreign confiscation judgments, and extradition. It binds courts, prosecutors and competent authorities, and affects third parties holding potentially tainted funds.

Guidance notes explaining how to complete the SAMA Regulatory Sandbox application form and describing the four-stage sandbox operating model: application assessment against eligibility criteria (60 business days), operational readiness against the Assessment Criteria (120 days, leading to a temporary permission or Letter of Authorisation), live testing (six to twelve months), and graduation/exit toward a full regulatory licence. It clarifies that the initial approval letter permits company formation as a FinTech with the Ministry of Commerce but does not authorise commencing operations or onboarding customers. It is directed at FinTech innovators applying to test products under SAMA supervision.

Definitional and governance core of SAMA's Rules Governing Credit Risk Exposure Classification and Provisioning for finance companies, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation. It fixes IFRS 9-aligned terms (PD, EAD, LGD, financial asset, 12-month and lifetime expected credit loss, stage definitions) and imposes board-level duties to adopt, document, approve and at least annually review ECL methodologies, report quarterly on adequacy of provisions, and subject credit risk measurement to annual internal audit. Binds SAMA-licensed finance companies; effective 1 July 2021, superseding the earlier Provisioning Guidelines circular.

Sets the regulatory staging framework for credit risk exposures of finance companies, including the bifurcation of Stage 2 into sub-tiers for quarterly prudential reporting only (not for accounting). It prescribes minimum documented eligibility conditions for re-staging Stage 2 exposures back to Stage 1, including no arrears beyond 30 days past due, a 90-day cure period for non-retail borrowers (60 days for retail), and evidence that the drivers of significant increase in credit risk have disappeared. Binds SAMA-licensed finance companies.

Defines restructuring for finance companies and splits it into forbearance (concession granted because of borrower financial difficulty) versus renegotiation/refinancing/rescheduling (borrower convenience, no deterioration). Forborne exposures may only be reported in Stage 2B, 3A or 3B, and exit from Stage 3 requires cure periods (12 months non-retail, 6 months retail, with shorter steps between sub-stages), restarting if the exposure re-defaults, plus specified repayment conditions for first- and second-time restructurings. Binds SAMA-licensed finance companies.

Prescribes when finance companies must de-recognise uncollectible credit exposures, requiring write-off after collection and recovery options are exhausted and internal audit review, with maximum time limits from Stage 3 classification: 360 days unsecured, 720 days secured, and 1,080 days for mortgages and corporate exposures (more conservative internal policies permitted). It confirms write-off does not extinguish recovery rights and that multiple exposures to one counterparty are treated at counterparty level. Also clarifies that partial write-off or collateral repossession does not by itself restore a forborne exposure to performing.

Annexure to the provisioning Rules listing indicative eligible collateral for LGD and provision calculation (cash, gold, deposits, government and investment-grade securities, listed shares, receivables, financial and Kafalah guarantees, immovable and other physical collateral, leased assets) and setting collateral policy, monitoring, haircut and stress-testing expectations. Immovable collateral securing Stage 3/defaulted exposures must be revalued at least annually by licensed appraisers, with the valuation showing market and forced-sale values and the lower of two valuations used where judgement is material. Binds SAMA-licensed finance companies.

Sets the liquidity risk governance expectations for finance companies: the Board holds ultimate responsibility for liquidity risk, must set liquidity risk tolerance, approve the liquidity strategy, policies, contingency funding plan and stress-testing framework at least annually, and be kept informed of the liquidity position and any material change. Senior management must implement these into documented procedures and controls, understand interaction with credit, market and operational risk, and report cash-flow mismatches, maturity gaps, funding concentration and early warning indicators to the Board and SAMA, typically quarterly; establishing an ALCO is recommended.

A section of SAMA's Rules on Liquidity Risk Management for finance companies requiring a comprehensive liquidity stress testing programme covering multiple scenarios, severities and time horizons, combining scenario and sensitivity analysis, and testing behavioural cash-flow assumptions for assets, liabilities and off-balance-sheet items. It sits alongside related requirements on unencumbered/pledged assets, collateral management and SAMA's power to impose specific liquidity exposure limits. The node also carries the Rules' defined terms (liquidity risk tolerance, net cash outflows, HQLA, unencumbered assets, contractual maturity mismatch, stress test, CFP) and binds finance companies licensed and supervised by SAMA.

This node covers the Contingency Funding Plan requirement in SAMA's Rules on Liquidity Risk Management for finance companies, together with the surrounding funding-strategy and liquid-asset-cushion expectations. It requires a CFP setting out crisis strategy, available funding sources and volumes, activation authority, roles, escalation, early warning indicators and periodic testing. It binds SAMA-licensed finance companies, including those using originate-to-distribute/securitisation funding models.
lookup_terms: liquidity buffer / cushion of unencumbered HQLA

data.summary: Concluding sections of SAMA's Rules on Liquidity Risk Management dealing with CFP testing and updating (at least annually, integrated with stress testing), internal controls over the liquidity risk management process, and the internal audit review role. It also records the implementation date of the Rules (in force 1 January 2023) and the obligation to align liquidity risk management and regulatory reporting systems. Binds finance companies supervised by SAMA.

Chapter 3 of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations 2020, setting SAMA's internal governance and risk management requirements for DTFCs: proportionality to nature, scale and complexity; clear organisational structure; job descriptions for senior managers tied to fit-and-proper pre-approval; a Management Responsibilities Description Document; and segregation of functions. The excerpt also carries AML/KYC-related duties placed on DTFCs, including the compliance officer's access rights, scrutiny of nominees/trustees/authorised representatives, ongoing transaction monitoring, risk classification of accounts and STR reporting to the FIU with notification to SAMA.

Chapter 4 of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations 2020 on minimum capital: DTFCs must maintain records enabling computation of a 20% capital adequacy ratio and the prescribed minimum capital, with SAMA determining compliance and empowered to impose higher ratios (e.g. capital deficiency, significant risk exposure, poor asset quality, rapid growth, holding-company contagion). It also sets risk-weighting of on-balance-sheet exposures into categories and includes completion instructions defining core capital, supplementary capital components (term subordinated debt, statutory loan loss reserve capped at 1.25% of RWA) and total capital.

Chapter 5 of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations 2020 imposing liquidity obligations on DTFCs: a Board-approved liquidity risk management plan (management structures and MIS, net funding requirements, contingency funding planning, internal controls); a statutory minimum liquid asset holding of 20% of deposit and short-term liabilities; statutory deposits with SAMA of at least 4% of deposit liabilities; and a cap of 15 times total capital on deposit liabilities with a one-month remediation route. It also sets monthly liquidity reporting to SAMA by the 15th business day, with Appendix B completion instructions for the liquidity statement.

Rules within the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations governing the General Account, a purpose-limited account whose sole function is to support the operation of Term Deposit Accounts. It sets permitted credit sources (only the accountholder's own bank accounts or their linked Term Deposit Account), name-matching and return-of-funds duties, mandatory record fields for credit postings, and withdrawal rules requiring funds to be remitted back to a source account of the same accountholder; transfers between General Accounts are allowed only in the same name. Binds DTFCs licensed in KSA in relation to their non-individual depositors.

Provisions on opening and operating Term Deposit Accounts at Deposit Taking Finance Companies, including the precondition of an active General Account in the same customer's name, acceptance of a Term Deposit Deal, and permanent linkage of each Term Deposit Account to one General Account. It fixes a minimum six-month tenor, one-deal-per-account and no-recycling rules, naming conventions, and the minimum deal data (currency, dates, day-count, principal, profit rate, status) plus Sharia-compliant commodity details where applicable. Binds DTFCs taking savings and time deposits from non-individual customers.

Chapter of the DTFC Regulations requiring that customer relationships operate only under valid identification, with mandatory freezing of General Accounts of juristic persons 90 days after expiry of their licence or commercial registration, or where opening documents carry no validity date. It also requires monitoring of directors' and authorised signatories' IDs (suspending operating powers rather than the account), contractual disclosure of the freezing right, customer notification before freezing, and related disclosure/blocking of accounts where SAMA so instructs. Binds all DTFCs.

DTFC rules classifying a General Account as Inactive after one year without customer-initiated movement and Dormant after two years, with dual control (and higher-authority dual control) for reactivation, and a bar on withdrawals from Dormant accounts absent the duly authorised person. Periods during which the General Account is linked to a live Term Deposit Account do not count as inactivity. Requires board-approved policies for supervision, customer contact, file isolation and annual internal audit; applies to all customers including those holding other active accounts.

The parent instrument: SAMA's 2020 Regulations for Deposit Taking Finance Companies, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law (Royal Decree M/51) and its Implementing Regulation. It sets the conditions for exercising deposit-taking activity by finance companies authorised to mobilise savings and time deposits from non-individual customers and to lend from them, covering corporate governance, depositor record-keeping (five-year retention), liquidity and prudential returns, and account operation rules. Applies to all DTFCs in KSA, in addition to the Finance Companies Control Law and general SAMA finance company regulations.

The Saudi Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and their Financing, setting out definitions (Terrorist Crime, Terrorism Financing Crime, Terrorist), offences and penalties, and the institutional architecture for enforcement. It covers mutual legal assistance and extradition, the Permanent Committee's role in implementing UN Security Council resolutions on terrorism and its financing, and the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence's mandate to receive, analyse and disseminate suspicious transaction reports. Binds persons in the Kingdom generally and imposes reporting and information-provision duties on financial institutions, with requests routed through the supervisory authority.
lookup_terms: Combating Terrorism Crimes and their Financing Law

data.summary: Node within the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations 2020 keyed to SAMA's authorization of DTFCs, with the retrieved material drawn from the account-opening and Know Your Customer chapters. It covers KYC programme design (customer acceptance policy, identification, ongoing monitoring of high-risk accounts), prohibitions on anonymous, numbered, fictitious or inaccurate-name accounts, refusal to open or transact where KYC doubts exist with referral to SAMA's Financial Investigation Unit, account-holder acknowledgements on source of funds and data updating, and the bar on fully remote opening of a first General Account. It binds licensed deposit-taking finance companies and, indirectly, their customers through the account agreement.

Chapter 6 (Asset Quality) requirement that each DTFC operate a loan review function assuring that lending conforms to a board-approved written lending policy, that management and the board are properly informed of credit risk and control effectiveness, that problem accounts are identified and classified on time, and that adequate provisions are maintained. It links directly to the quarterly review/classification duty and the Appendix C classification criteria. Binds every deposit-taking finance company and its board.

Sets the DTFC loan classification and provisioning regime: at least quarterly review and classification of the loan portfolio per Appendix C, contagion treatment where one loan to a borrower is non-performing, rules for renegotiated/restructured and twice-restructured facilities, suspension and reversal of profit on non-performing exposures, return to accrual only on full settlement, and minimum provisioning percentages for Normal, Watch, Substandard, Doubtful and Loss grades, including where IFRS impairment falls short. Binds every deposit-taking finance company.

Appendix C of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations 2020, the reference schedule for asset quality risk classification used with the Chapter 6 review, classification and provisioning duties. The surrounding return guidance explains reporting lines for loans and advances net of provisions, other investments, fixed and other assets, group exposures, total on-balance-sheet assets and credit risk equivalents for off-balance-sheet items feeding the capital ratio calculation. Binds DTFCs when classifying exposures and completing prudential returns to SAMA.
lookup_terms: loans and advances net of provisions

data.summary: Appendix A is the Capital to Risk Weighted Assets return for DTFCs, defining core and supplementary capital components (including term subordinated debt and the statutory loan loss reserve capped at 1.25% of risk weighted assets), on- and off-balance-sheet asset reporting, and the capital ratio calculations against minimum requirements. It operates with Chapter 4, which sets a 20% capital adequacy requirement, allows SAMA to impose higher minimum ratios on individual firms, and prescribes the risk-weight categories. Binds every deposit-taking finance company reporting to SAMA.
lookup_terms: capital to risk weighted assets return

data.summary: Appendix B is the monthly Liquidity Statement return for DTFCs, listing the liquid asset and liability lines (cash, balances and time deposits with banks, finance and mortgage finance companies, treasury bills and bonds) used to evidence compliance with Chapter 5. Chapter 5 requires a board-approved liquidity risk management plan, a minimum 20% holding of liquid assets against deposit and short-term liabilities, statutory deposits with SAMA of at least 4% of deposit liabilities, a deposit liabilities cap of 15 times total capital with a one-month cure, and submission by the 15th business day of the following month. Binds every deposit-taking finance company.

This node covers the preventive-measures chapter of the KSA counter-terrorism and terrorism-financing law, setting TF risk assessment, customer due diligence (including enhanced due diligence for high risk and for new products/technologies), and record-keeping duties of at least ten years, extendable by the Public Prosecution for investigations. It also reaches information exchange by the Directorate (FIU) with domestic competent authorities and foreign counterparts subject to use-limitation undertakings, and the supervisory powers chapter. It binds financial institutions, DNFBPs and, for risk assessment and supervision purposes, NPOs, with detail left to the Implementing Regulation.

This node defines the Supervisory Authority under the counter-terrorism financing law as the body responsible for verifying compliance by FIs, DNFBPs and NPOs with the Law, its Implementing Regulation and related decisions, and sets out the ladder of administrative measures available on non-compliance. Measures range from written warnings and compliance orders to fines up to SAR 5,000,000 per violation, employment bans, restriction or removal of directors and senior management, business suspension and licence withdrawal. It binds supervised entities and their directors, board members and executive or supervisory management personally.
lookup_terms: Permanent Committee for Counter Terrorism and its Financing

data.summary: A SAMA Banking Supervision circular addressed to all banks (CFOs and CROs) revisiting SAMA Circular BCS 311 of 5 December 2008 on Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision. It requires banks to conduct an internal audit assessing their implementation of those principles and to submit the findings report to the Director of Banking Supervision by 31 March 2015. It binds all SAMA-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision

data.summary: This node refers to the Basel Committee's September 2008 Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision as adopted into KSA through SAMA's 2008 circular. Banks were required to embed the principles in internal systems and processes and to audit compliance against them, with a follow-up self-assessment reported to SAMA. Relevant to all banks operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA Banking Supervision instruction specifying additional risk information banks must include in their ICAAP submissions, covering connected-party lending concentrations, liquidity metrics (LCR, NSFR, top-ten depositor and wholesale funding concentrations), off-balance-sheet derivative activity by currency, and leverage ratios including the legal leverage ratio under the Banking Control Law. Data is generally required on a year-end basis with three-year history. It binds all banks supervised by SAMA.

A SAMA circular to all banks implementing the Basel III countercyclical capital buffer in Saudi Arabia, effective for calculations from 1 January 2016. It sets the 0%–2.5% range, reciprocity based on published jurisdictional buffer rates, a default 2.5% where no rate is published, the exposure scope (private sector credit exposures on an ultimate-risk basis, excluding interbank and public sector but including non-bank financial sector), and the weighted-average calculation. SAMA pre-announces the KSA rate at least one year ahead, with increases effective after one year and decreases effective immediately. Binds all banks in the Kingdom.

SAMA circular to all banks applying the Basel III countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) in Saudi Arabia, addressed to senior bank management. It sets out how the bank-specific buffer is calculated as a weighted average of jurisdictional buffer rates based on the ultimate-risk geographic location of private-sector credit exposures (excluding interbank and public-sector exposures, including non-bank financial sector), with a 2.5% default where no rate is published and SAMA's discretion to impose more prudent rates. It also fixes the 1 January 2016 start date and SAMA's pre-announcement practice (increases effective after one year; decreases immediate).

Short SAMA circular (Payment Systems and Companies Control) forwarding the CST/Communications, Space and Technology Commission's Local Technology Products Guide, an indicative list of locally developed technology products serving sectors including banking, insurance and finance. It is informational rather than a new obligation, but expressly reiterates that supervised entities must continue to comply with SAMA's existing rules, particularly those on outsourcing to third parties.

SAMA circular requiring the upgrade of point-of-sale (POS) terminals operating in the Kingdom to at least 4G connectivity, following CITC's decision to sunset 2G/3G networks (3G end-2022; 2G during Q4 2024). It obliges POS suppliers to supply 4G-capable devices and obtain technical certification from Saudi Payments, requires all new and replacement installations to be 4G-capable from January 2023, and sets a minimum monthly replacement rate for existing terminals with progress reporting to SAMA and Saudi Payments. It binds banks, payment service providers/sponsoring entities and Saudi Payments.

SAMA circular to payment service providers reaffirming that effective customer verification and Know Your Customer procedures must be completed before selling or activating POS terminals, and that any third party marketing or promoting such devices must itself be SAMA-licensed (marketing/promotion of payment services being a licensable activity under the PSP Rules). It also requires PSPs to ensure internal policies and procedures cover all customer (merchant) categories, identify and monitor risks with reporting, and to verify that the POS terminal is linked only to the merchant customer's own bank account and not diverted to another account.

SAMA circular amending the pricing applied to e-wallet top-up transactions made with mada cards through the e-commerce route, replacing percentage-based pricing with fixed caps: a Merchant Service Charge capped at a fixed riyal amount and a fixed Interchange Fee. It restricts these rates to e-wallet charging transactions only and requires banks and PSPs to disclose all fees in new Merchant Service Agreements, update existing agreements, and obtain merchant acceptance before signing; effective from the stated date.

SAMA circular directing all institutions under its supervision to deal and contract only with real estate brokers licensed by the Real Estate General Authority (REGA), relying on the Real Estate Brokerage Law which prohibits practising brokerage or providing real estate services without REGA licensing. It points supervised entities to REGA's online register for verification, making licence status a counterparty due-diligence condition rather than creating new brokerage rules.

A SAMA circular implementing the national mandate (with the Anti-Commercial Concealment Programme, Ministry of Municipal and Rural Affairs and Ministry of Commerce) that all groceries and supply stores in the Kingdom must offer electronic payment means from 17 Ramadan 1441 / 10 May 2020. It directs banks and payment service providers to be ready to open bank accounts and e-wallets for merchants in that sector, to receive and process requests for SAMA-authorised payment instruments (POS terminals, QR) through all channels, and to apply the correct merchant category code 5411.
