It binds all banks and PSPs operating in KSA, including an internal-communication duty to staff.

A SAMA circular (No. 45040399, dated 25/06/1445H) permitting charities and non-profit associations to be provided with all SAMA-authorised electronic payment solutions, including GPRS mobile POS terminals, conditional on the entity obtaining approval from the National Center for Non-Profit Sector Development. It relaxes an earlier SAMA instruction that limited such entities to fixed-line POS terminals, and should be read with the circular on upgrading POS devices to 4G. It binds banks and payment service companies operating in the Kingdom, effective from its date.
lookup_terms: National Center for Non-Profit Sector Development

data.summary: SAMA's January 2017 circular adopting the Basel Committee's revised standards on Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book, covering identification, measurement, monitoring, control and disclosure of IRRBB, including interest rate shock scenarios, behavioural/modelling assumptions, an updated standardised framework and a tighter outlier test (15% of Tier 1 capital, down from 20% of total capital). It is addressed to domestic banks only and expressly does not apply to foreign bank branches, and is accompanied by annexures on regulatory returns and FAQs including national discretions.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: Concept node for the Basel Committee's 2004 Principles for the management and supervision of interest rate risk, the predecessor framework that the SAMA-adopted IRRBB standard revises. It set supervisory expectations for banks' identification, measurement, monitoring and control of interest rate risk and guidance for supervisors. Relevant as baseline context when reading the enhanced IRRBB obligations applicable to domestic banks.
lookup_terms: principles for management and supervision of interest rate risk

data.summary: Concept node for the updated standardised framework within the IRRBB standard adopted by SAMA, providing a prescribed methodology for measuring interest rate risk in the banking book. It sits alongside the enhanced disclosure requirements based on common interest rate shock scenarios and the outlier threshold set at 15% of Tier 1 capital. Applies in the context of domestic banks subject to the IRRBB circular.
lookup_terms: standardised measurement approach interest rate risk

data.summary: Concept node for the Basle (Basel) Committee on Banking Supervision as the issuer of the "Sound Practices for Banks' Interactions with Highly Leveraged Institutions" paper transmitted by SAMA to all banks in March 1999 following the near-collapse of LTCM. The paper promotes prudent assessment, measurement and credit risk management of exposures to HLIs and hedge funds, complementing general credit risk principles. SAMA expects banks with such exposures to manage them consistently with SAMA's Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks and their own internal credit policies.
lookup_terms: Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks

data.summary: This node covers the counterparty credit risk management expectations applied to banks dealing with highly leveraged institutions (HLIs), including hedge funds: a board-approved credit risk strategy defining risk appetite, written policies governing HLI relationships, and an end-to-end credit process (documentation, financial information, due diligence, risk mitigants, exposure measurement, limits, ongoing monitoring). It stresses that commercial pressure must not override these policies and that collateral is not a substitute for day-to-day monitoring of a counterparty's strategies, leverage and concentrations. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia that have or contemplate HLI exposures, with responsibility allocated to the board and senior management.

This node reflects SAMA's 1999 circular transmitting the Basel Committee paper on banks' interactions with HLIs, in which SAMA states that any such exposures are to be managed in line with its Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks and the bank's own prudent internal credit policies. It also sets SAMA's expectations that credit and risk management staff be familiar with the practices described. It binds all banks in the Kingdom, addressed to general managers and managing directors.
lookup_terms: Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks

data.summary: The parent instrument: the Basel Committee's "Sound Practices for Banks' Interactions with Highly Leveraged Institutions", circulated by SAMA to Saudi banks as its supervisory expectation. It sets out prudent approaches to assessing, measuring and managing credit exposures to HLIs — opacity, leverage and rapidly shifting trading positions — covering credit strategy, information gathering and due diligence, exposure measurement, limit setting and collateral/documentation practices. It applies to banks with HLI or hedge fund counterparty relationships and complements general credit risk management principles.
lookup_terms: Sound Practices for Banks' Interactions with Highly Leveraged Institutions

data.summary: This node addresses how banks taking OTC derivatives positions against HLIs should measure credit exposure and feed those measures into management decision-making. It identifies three focus areas: more useful potential future exposure (PFE) measures, better assessment of unsecured risk embedded in collateralised derivatives positions (thresholds, margin gaps, liquidation delays), and stress testing of counterparty exposures under volatile markets, including collateral value and liquidity effects. It applies to banks with derivatives and trading exposures to HLI counterparties.

This node concerns potential future exposure as the loan-equivalent measure used to aggregate derivatives exposures to a counterparty across products and instruments. It expects peak exposure measures that reflect netting of long and short positions, portfolio effects across products, risk factors and maturities, multiple time horizons, and industry convergence on confidence intervals and volatility assumptions; PFE should also inform judgments about whether a counterparty can meet implied margin calls. It binds banks measuring and limiting counterparty credit risk on derivatives, particularly with HLIs.

This node sets expectations for counterparty credit limits: banks should establish overall limits at individual counterparty level that aggregate different exposure types on a comparable basis, anchored in meaningful PFE measures and covering on- and off-balance-sheet activity. Actual and mark-to-market exposures must be monitored against initial limits, with clear procedures to reduce exposure as limits are approached; limits should be binding and not driven by customer demand. It applies to banks with HLI and other derivatives counterparty relationships.

SAMA's New Banking Products and Services Regulation, updating the 2017 guidelines, sets minimum requirements for how banks develop, approve, launch and monitor new or materially modified products and services, and when they must notify SAMA or obtain its non-objection before launch. It defines "product or service", "new product or service" and "existing product or service" by reference to banking business under the Banking Control Law. It binds all banks licensed in Saudi Arabia under the Banking Control Law.

This part allocates accountability for the new-products regime between the Board and senior management: the Board oversees that policies and procedures exist, that product risks are managed and consumer needs and rights are addressed, and reviews consistency with (and any revision of) the approved risk appetite. Senior management owns design, implementation and compliance, periodic review of the internal policies, reputational risk mitigation, and full operational readiness plus any other authorities' approvals before launch. It binds banks' boards and senior management.

Sets the minimum content of a bank's internal policies and procedures for offering new products and services — integration into the governance, risk and internal control framework, defined stakeholder roles, approval and delegation parameters, pilot/testing phases — together with internal audit, product development function, ongoing monitoring, complaint handling, corrective action, documentation, retention and the annual product report to SAMA. It also frames the notification/non-objection gateway. It binds licensed banks and their control and business functions.

Requires banks to assign responsibility for product risk, perform a full life-cycle risk assessment as the basis for deciding whether to launch, apply risk management standards (due diligence, approvals, identification/measurement/monitoring/reporting/mitigation, change management), and assign an overall risk classification to each product. It also requires third-party risk controls where products are offered with Fintech companies, agents or similar entities, and gives the risk management function documentation, review and approval duties over product risk profiles. Binds banks and their risk management function.

Sets the regulatory gateway before launch: banks meeting the required maturity levels under the Cyber Security, Counter-Fraud, Business Continuity and IT Governance Frameworks (independently validated annually) may proceed by notifying SAMA, while home loans, financial lease, financial derivatives and products not covered by existing SAMA rules require prior non-objection. Both routes carry a 12-month launch window, re-submission on lapse, re-notification/new non-objection for products discontinued over 12 months, SAMA's right to request further information and its power to prohibit a product on safety-and-soundness grounds. It also covers the annual CEO-signed product report to SAMA and documentation/retention duties. Binds licensed banks, with submissions channelled through the compliance function.
lookup_terms: home loans financial lease derivatives non-objection

data.summary: Conduct and gatekeeping conditions specific to financial derivatives and complex/structured products: banks must demonstrate profit and loss scenarios, ensure customers understand the risks and sign off on terms, assess suitability against the customer's business or investment objectives, risk appetite and prior experience, and show the instrument has a bona fide economic purpose rather than mere speculation, leverage or regulatory arbitrage. Banks must also evidence internal organizational and operational capacity to manage the resulting risks; these products additionally require SAMA's prior non-objection. Binds licensed banks offering derivatives to customers.

A section of SAMA-adopted Basel Committee sound practices on banks' interactions with highly leveraged institutions (HLIs), addressing collateral, early termination and other contractual provisions as credit risk mitigants. It expects banks to align margining terms, haircuts, initial margin, minimum transfer amounts, loss thresholds, two-way margining and rehypothecation rights with counterparty credit quality, and to recognise residual liquidity, legal, custody and operational risks and wrong-way correlation between counterparty default and collateral impairment. It binds banks dealing with HLI counterparties in secured lending, repo and OTC derivatives.

This section of the HLI sound practices guidance covers stress testing of counterparty credit exposures and its link to limit setting, requiring banks to model large market moves, liquidation effects and liquidity impacts on positions and pledged collateral rather than relying on higher confidence intervals or longer horizons for potential future exposure (PFE). It also sets expectations that overall credit limits be established per counterparty on an aggregated, comparable basis, be binding, and be monitored with clear procedures for reducing exposure. It applies to banks with material exposures to highly leveraged institutions and, by extension, to counterparty credit management generally.

This section addresses ongoing monitoring of exposures to highly leveraged institutions, expecting at least quarterly credit quality reviews of material HLI exposures (more often on exposure or volatility triggers), use of quantitative risk information such as VaR and internal stress results rather than net asset value alone, and understanding of risk concentrations. It also sets expectations for collateral management systems to capture all positions, mark to market at least daily, and revise haircuts regularly. It binds banks that deal with HLI counterparties, alongside board-approved credit risk strategy and policy requirements.

SAMA guidance document explaining how to apply for a licence to conduct Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) activity under the Finance Companies Control Law and the Rules Regulating BNPL Companies. It covers application instructions, defined use of "Applicant" (founders/shareholders), required attachments and the licensing process, and warns that false or omitted material information breaches the Finance Companies Control Law and may cause rejection or cancellation. It binds prospective BNPL companies and their founders/authorised representatives.

The procedural part of SAMA's BNPL licensing guidelines, setting out how the Applicant submits the completed application with checklist attachments and how SAMA notifies completeness and processes the request. It reinforces submission rules (no modification of the form, submission by founders or an authorised representative, soft copies with originals retained for SAMA on demand) and the consequences of inaccurate or incomplete disclosure. It binds founders/shareholders seeking SAMA approval to incorporate and licence a BNPL company.

Lists the documentation that must accompany a BNPL licence application, including the application letter and SAMA form, draft or existing articles of association and commercial register, organisational structure with departmental mandates, Fit and Proper forms for each founder and each board/sub-committee candidate, a feasibility study and business plan, and an irrevocable, auto-renewing bank guarantee equal to 20% of the minimum required capital issued to SAMA by a local bank. Documents are filed in soft copy per the checklist with originals produced on request. It binds BNPL licence Applicants and their proposed governance appointees.

A concept node within SAMA's operational risk management guidance for banks, treating political and regulatory instability in foreign markets as a component of operational (pure) risk. It expects Saudi banks with cross-border operations or significant international trade exposure to maintain monitoring systems, early-warning indicators and mitigation/contingency plans for political and regulatory risk. Directed at boards and senior management of banks operating in the Kingdom, as supervisory guidance rather than a prescriptive rule.

A concept node describing self-insurance as an internal risk financing option for bank operational risk, covering unfunded and funded retention, single-parent captives and contractual risk transfer, and treating risk retention groups, group captives and pooling arrangements as economically equivalent to self-insurance. It frames retention decisions as governed by loss retention guidelines set within the bank's Operational Risk Management Plan. Relevant to bank boards and senior management deciding how much operational loss to retain versus transfer.

A concept node on conventional (regular) insurance as an external risk financing mechanism for bank operational risk, contrasted with self-insurance and alternative vehicles such as retention groups, captives and pools. It addresses insurer/reinsurer selection, broker relationships and remuneration, coverage enhancement and multi-year placements as matters of prudent management judgement. Addressed to Saudi banks' senior management in framing an integrated operational risk financing programme.

A concept node identifying the Bankers Blanket Bond / Financial Institution Bond as a core insurance coverage for bank operational risk, typically bundling insuring agreements on employee dishonesty, loss of property on premises and in transit, and forgery. It is presented as the final layer of fraud control after training, prevention/detection programmes, operational management and internal audit. Guidance-level material for bank management structuring insurance coverage.

A concept node describing finite risk insurance as an external risk financing option that blends conventional risk transfer with self-insurance and carries an upper limit on the insurer's exposure. It sits alongside captives, retention groups and pools in the guidance's catalogue of alternatives to pure conventional cover. Relevant to bank senior management choosing operational risk financing structures.

A concept node referring to the operational risk management evaluation questionnaire associated with SAMA's operational risk guidance, used as a self-assessment tool against the expected elements of a bank's Operational Risk Management Plan and Programme. It links to the governance architecture described in the guidance, including the Operational Risk Manager reporting to the Managing Director/General Manager and the Operational Risk Management Committee. Intended for bank directors, senior management and supervisory review.

A sub-node of SAMA's New Banking Products and Services Regulation (v2.0, Nov 2023) setting out the second- and third-line duties around new products: compliance function review of every new product/service from a compliance, regulatory and financial-crime angle, annual non-compliance risk assessment and Board reporting; internal audit of new products within about a year of launch with annual Audit Committee reporting; risk management duties on identifying, assessing and capital-impact-testing new product risks; product development (business unit) competence duties; and ongoing post-launch monitoring, target-market suitability and corrective action. It binds locally licensed banks and allocates accountability across compliance, internal audit, risk management and business units.
lookup_terms: new banking products and services regulation
compliance function review of new products

data.summary: Covers the consumer-fairness design considerations and the submission checklist (Annexure 1) under SAMA's New Banking Products and Services Regulation. It requires customer appropriateness and fairness assessments before approval, avoidance of mis-selling, unfair terms and conflicts of interest, proportionate product-risk control across the value chain, phased launch, and cross-compliance with instruments such as the Responsible Lending Principles, Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules and the advertising rules; the checklist mandates a CCO letter, application form, statement of compliance, a signed consumer protection checklist for retail products, contracts/SLAs/NDAs for third parties, a multi-risk assessment report (including AML/CFT, fraud, cyber, data privacy) and Shari'ah Committee approvals where relevant. Binds banks notifying SAMA or seeking no-objection for new retail and other products.
lookup_terms: Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules

data.summary: A sub-node of the New Banking Products and Services Regulation dealing with the technology, fraud and cyber information a bank must supply in the product application form, including whether the product is onboarded to fraud monitoring with scenario configurability, third-party adherence to SAMA's cloud computing cybersecurity controls, integration method, the internal function monitoring the product, and customer cancellation terms and fees. It supports the product notification/no-objection package rather than setting standalone cyber rules, and binds banks submitting new products to SAMA.
lookup_terms: cyber risk in product risk assessment

data.summary: Sets the additional conditions in the New Banking Products and Services Regulation for launching new financial derivatives and structured products: demonstrating suitability and prior investment experience of the intended customer, disclosing profit and loss scenarios, showing a bona fide economic purpose (not speculation, leverage or regulatory arbitrage), holding the organisational capacity to manage the risks, avoiding adverse effects on SAIBOR/SAR, observing the separate circular on SAR-foreign currency derivatives, and complying with SAMA's 2019 Rules on Trade Repository Reporting and Risk Mitigation for OTC Derivatives. It also states the documentation gate (complete Annexure 1 checklist or the application is not processed) and the 1 March 2024 effective date superseding the 2017 guidelines.
lookup_terms: OTC derivatives trade repository reporting rules 2019

data.summary: SAMA's Operational Risk Management Guide for banks in the Kingdom, aimed at directors and senior management, explaining operational risk as pure risk (loss or no loss) distinct from financial risk and the techniques to control and finance it. It defines the governance architecture — Operational Risk Manager reporting to the Managing Director/General Manager, an Operational Risk Management Committee, a Board-approved and annually reviewed Operational Risk Management Plan, risk assessment and control matrices, risk financing and loss retention policies, and penalty/reward incentives — and is intended to be read with SAMA's internal control, disaster recovery and physical security guidelines.
lookup_terms: internal control guidelines for commercial banks

data.summary: A concept node within SAMA's Operational Risk Management Guide covering crime as a category of operational risk — losses from fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and similar criminal activity — alongside system outage, professional liability, regulatory non-compliance and reputational losses. The Guide treats crime as one of the risk categories that the Board-approved Operational Risk Management Plan must expressly address, through internal controls, retention or risk transfer; it is guidance for bank directors and senior management, not an AML/CTF obligation in itself.
lookup_terms: physical security guidelines for Saudi banks

data.summary: A short SAMA circular reaffirming, in light of rising cyber threats to the Saudi financial sector, that supervised entities must comply with SAMA's cybersecurity policies, frameworks and standards as well as the national cybersecurity authority's requirements. It specifically stresses implementation of the Essential Cybersecurity Controls and the Critical Systems Cybersecurity Controls and prioritising cybersecurity in approved budgets. Issued through the Payment Systems and Companies Control Department, so it is directed at banks and payment service providers under SAMA supervision.

A SAMA circular relaying a communication from the Communications and Information Technology authority on governance of bulk SMS sender IDs (Tag Names) through a unified electronic portal for SMS service providers, aimed at preventing misuse of text messages. It directs supervised entities to cooperate promptly with their contracted SMS providers and complete registration within the transitional period set by the authority. Addressed to payment sector entities supervised by SAMA's Payment Systems and Companies Control Department.

A follow-up circular to SAMA's earlier instruction on standardising the elements of SMS notifications sent to financial institutions' customers, intended to raise customer awareness of transactions on their accounts, memberships and e-wallets. It attaches the mandatory core notification elements for newly introduced mada transaction types and sets a compliance deadline of the end of Q1 2022, with an implementation plan due to SAMA by 4 November 2021. Binds financial institutions/payment service providers supervised by SAMA.

An informational circular conveying the Ministry of Commerce's approach to approving company incorporation contracts (articles of association) and their amendments, under which partners and the submitting party bear responsibility for the contents in line with the Companies Law. SAMA notes this arrangement does not relieve financial institutions of their obligations under SAMA-issued regulations (relevant to onboarding/KYB verification of corporate customers). Circulated to payment sector entities for information only.

A SAMA follow-up circular on the unified pricing model for POS and e-commerce services for mada card transactions, extending to transactions at money transfer and exchange centres and international transfers via e-wallets. It requests banks and payment service providers to report their level of compliance and application of the unified pricing model by 15 June 2022 to the designated SAMA mailbox. Binds banks and licensed payment service providers.

A circular responding to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development's concerns about integration failures and technical outages between the Mudad platform's payroll management system and partner financial institutions, which delay wage payments and employers' compliance with the Wage Protection programme. SAMA stresses adherence to the service level agreement with Mudad and due care in resolving technical issues. Directed at payment companies and financial institutions integrated with Mudad.

A sub-element of the criminal-risk category in SAMA's operational risk guidance for banks, describing fraud as historically the largest single source of operational loss in the Saudi banking system. It characterises internal (employee) versus external fraud across cash handling, ATMs, credit card issuance (application, account set-up, embossing, statement distribution) and point-of-sale/merchant channels, and supports the expectation that banks identify, control and finance this exposure. It orients bank boards, senior management and the operational risk function rather than imposing product-specific rules.

Sub-element of criminal risk in SAMA's operational risk framework covering forgery, including cheque forgery and forgery of negotiable instruments such as letters of credit, historically the second largest reported operational loss category for Saudi banks. It links losses to failures by staff to verify document authenticity and warns that technology raises the sophistication and value of forgeries, so bank risk policies and procedures should address prevention of forgery by electronic means, including in electronic signature verification and payment systems. Directed at banks' boards, management and control functions.

Concept node covering electronic and computer crime as an operational risk element and its treatment in insurance-based risk transfer under SAMA's operational risk guidance. It describes Electronic and Computer Crime (ECC) cover — responding to third-party fraud or unexplained loss involving computer and telecommunications systems, and available only alongside a Bankers Blanket Bond / Financial Institution Bond — and situates it among D&O and professional indemnity covers. Relevant to banks' operational risk managers and boards deciding on retention versus transfer of e-crime exposure.

The second main category of operational risk in SAMA's guidance, covering professional errors and omissions, professional liability, and contingent client-related liability, as distinct from criminal risk. It sits within the framework requiring banks to identify and analyse operational risks and to select integrated control and financing techniques, including training, product risk analysis, contractual indemnities and professional indemnity insurance. It binds banks' senior management, the Operational Risk Manager and the board through the operational risk management plan.

Sub-element of professional risk addressing liability losses arising from shareholder suits, customer claims, regulatory non-compliance fines and negligent or imprudent acts of directors, officers and employees. The guidance treats such litigation risk as controllable through product risk analysis, staff training, careful contractual indemnities with customers, and professional indemnity insurance, and distinguishes liability attaching to the bank from that attaching to directors and officers. Aimed at bank management and boards setting the operational risk management plan.

Concept node distinguishing directors' and officers' (D&O) liability from the bank's own professional liability within SAMA's operational risk guidance. It explains that personal assets of executive and non-executive directors and senior officers may be exposed to claims of negligent or imprudent acts and omissions, that D&O cover is purchased by the bank to indemnify those individuals (including where the bank cannot legally indemnify them), and that its scope of wrongful acts is broader than professional indemnity while covering fewer persons. Sources of exposure include shareholder actions, client services, employment practices and environmental claims.

This node points to SAMA's Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks Operating in the Kingdom (1989), referenced within a SAMA Banking Inspection guide on operational risk management and insurance. It is cited as one of the foundational internal-control instruments to be read together with the Disaster Recovery Planning Guideline (1993) and the Guidelines on Physical Security for Saudi Banks (1995) to build an integrated operational risk control programme. It is directed at directors and senior management of SAMA-licensed commercial banks.
lookup_terms: Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks

data.summary: This node captures the Saudi Company Law (Royal Decree M/6 of 1985), cited in SAMA's operational risk guidance for Articles 66–82 on the joint liability of board members to compensate the company, shareholders or third parties for damages. It appears in the context of lender liability and directors' and officers' exposure, both inside and outside the Kingdom. It binds board members of Saudi joint stock companies, including banks, as a source of civil liability rather than a SAMA-issued rule.

A SAMA instrument setting out general rules for savings products offered by banks operating in the Kingdom. The provided context contains only the title page (Arabic/English) and issuance details, so scope and substantive obligations must be read from the full document. On its face it binds SAMA-licensed banks offering savings products to retail customers.

SAMA rules issued under the SAMA Charter (M/36) and the Banking Control Law imposing additional capital adequacy requirements for Shari'ah compliant banking, to be read alongside SAMA's Basel framework (circular 44047144). They set out how Shari'ah compliant contracts (e.g. Murabahah with binding and non-binding purchase orders) are mapped to credit risk and market risk treatment across the stages of the contract. They bind all domestic banks licensed by SAMA that conduct Shari'ah compliant banking, including their foreign subsidiaries and branches conducting such business.
lookup_terms: credit risk and market risk weights

data.summary: The Credit Information Law establishes the principles and controls for collecting, exchanging, protecting and correcting consumer credit information, and defines key terms including Credit Information, Consumer, Member, Companies, Credit Record and Public Records. It requires licensing of credit information companies by SAMA, consumer consent for a member to obtain a credit record, confidentiality duties on members, companies and their staff, and lists the acts deemed violations (unlicensed activity, unlawful disclosure or use, delayed updating, false data). It binds credit information companies, members (government and private entities party to exchange contracts) and other entities maintaining credit information.

A SAMA circular on QR Code payments issued under the SAMA Charter (M/36) and Council of Ministers Resolution No. 226, confirming SAMA as the competent authority for operating and supervising payment and financial settlement systems in the Kingdom. It requires entities that have already launched QR-based payment services to comply with the technical and commercial requirements and standards of the associated payment environment and to complete technical certification/testing with Saudi Payments by end-2021. It binds banks and licensed fintech/payment participants offering QR code payment services.

A SAMA supervisory reporting template issued by the Exchange Centers Supervision Division (version 2.0) for licensed money exchange centers to submit comparative quarterly and annual financial statements. It fixes the line items to be reported across the balance sheet (e.g. foreign currency inventory, amounts due from/to related parties for cash withdrawals, credit sales and cash support, zakat and end-of-service provisions, owner's equity and retained earnings) and the income statement (revenues, salaries, general and administrative expenses, zakat), with income-statement data covering three months for quarterly filings and a full year for annual filings. It binds SAMA-licensed exchange houses as a periodic prudential/supervisory submission format rather than a substantive conduct rule.

SAMA circular directing supervised financial institutions (issued via the payment systems and companies supervision channel) to adopt the National Cybersecurity Authority's Data Cybersecurity Controls (DCC-1:2022), which extend and complement the Essential Cybersecurity Controls. It relies on the SAMA Cyber Security Framework provisions on regulatory compliance and compliance with (inter)national industry standards, and requires continuous compliance, a self-assessment using the attached assessment/compliance-measurement tool, and full implementation by end-September 2023. Binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA; queries routed to SAMA's cyber risk supervision function.

SAMA circular reminding payment companies of their know-your-customer duties, requiring them to verify the legal/regulatory status of customers served, including validity of official identification documents, and to reflect this in service policies and agreements (e.g. obliging the contracting party to notify changes in its legal status). It invokes the PSP Regulatory Rules provision allowing a payment service provider to refuse payment orders where execution would breach its legal or regulatory obligations, and transmits lists of entities with cancelled/deregistered commercial registers for re-assessment and appropriate action. Binds licensed payment service providers.

A SAMA circular from the Payment Systems and Companies Control Department addressed to payment companies concerning the execution of judicial orders, effective from its date of issue. The available extract contains only the closing/issuing block, so the substantive obligations are not captured in this node and the source document must be opened to establish scope and requirements.
lookup_terms: Payment Systems and Companies Control Department

data.summary: SAMA circular on payment services provided to entities licensed under the Integrated Logistics Zone regime (established by Royal Order No. 17/1 dated 01/02/1440H). It requires payment sector companies to take account of the special nature of these entities, update their policies and service agreements accordingly, and verify their identity using the commercial register issued by the General Authority of Civil Aviation, the articles of association and annexes, and identification of persons authorised to open and manage accounts. Binds companies operating in the payments sector when onboarding ILZ-licensed entities.
lookup_terms: General Authority of Civil Aviation commercial register

data.summary: SAMA circular urging financial institutions to use the Ministry of Commerce "electronic authorisation" service to appoint a delegate to receive judicial notifications filed against them, and to monitor judicial orders for and against them through the Najiz portal. It builds on the Royal Order approving electronic means of judicial notification (verified mobile SMS, email, notification via registered government system accounts) and on the Enforcement Law and its Implementing Regulation provisions on notification timing, so institutions can settle claims within the notification period and avoid compulsory enforcement measures. Addressed to SAMA-supervised financial institutions, including payment companies.

SAMA (then the Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency) circular to money exchange centres reaffirming compliance with the rules and instructions governing the movement of cash and with the Security Safety Guide. It consolidates earlier circulars on contracting with cash-in-transit companies, use of specification-compliant security bags, organisation of cash movement for local banks and exchange houses, and the Law on Dealing in Money and Precious Metals, including requirements for armoured vehicles when transporting cash and valuables above the stated threshold. Binds all exchange centres operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: money and precious metals dealing law

data.summary: A SAMA user guidance manual explaining how supervised entities access and use the Returns Management System (RMS) portal to complete, validate, submit and, where SAMA raises observations, resubmit supervisory and prudential returns on quarterly and annual cycles. It describes the two portal interfaces (SAMA supervisors and supervised companies), account provisioning by SAMA, notification of open reporting periods, and the finality of submitted returns pending supervisory approval. It is procedural in nature and binds entities subject to SAMA supervision that are required to file regulatory returns.

A SAMA reporting template (Version 2.0) issued by the Exchange Centres Supervision Division requiring money exchange centres to report quarterly data on foreign currency sales and purchases by counterparty type (local banks, exchange houses, individuals, cross-border), inbound and outbound transfers, largest customers, counterfeit currency detected, and staff data. It is a periodic supervisory return rather than a rule text, but the data points support AML/CTF and market-conduct supervision of exchange centres. It binds licensed exchange centres subject to SAMA supervision.

A SAMA annual regulatory data template for money exchange centres, collecting ownership and partner shareholding details, licence issue/renewal/expiry dates, cash insurance policy validity, branch list and addresses, senior and control-function appointments (CEO/manager, internal audit, executive vs non-executive roles) and contracted external third-party firms. It is a supervisory data collection instrument supporting fit-and-proper, licensing and outsourcing oversight rather than a substantive rulebook. It binds licensed exchange centres reporting to SAMA.

Royal Decree M/148 together with the accompanying Council of Ministers resolution enacting amendments to the Personal Data Protection Law (originally issued by Royal Decree M/19), revising defined terms such as destruction, disclosure, sensitive data and data subject, and amending provisions including data subject rights and cross-border transfer/adequacy assessment and fee arrangements. It also repeals a clause of the earlier decree and sets the effective date of the amendments. It binds controllers and processors handling personal data in the Kingdom, with SDAIA as the competent authority, and is relevant to financial institutions' data handling obligations.

A guide issued by the Authority of Persons with Disabilities on emergency evacuation planning for persons with disabilities, covering definitions (evacuation, emergency, safe areas, escape routes), disability categories, building hazards, self-preparedness, evacuation planning steps, and accessible alerting, communication and assistive listening, visual alarm, tactile warning surface and access-control arrangements. It is a safety/accessibility guidance document, not a SAMA financial regulation, but is relevant to premises and branch accessibility obligations of regulated entities. It is addressed to entities operating buildings serving employees and visitors.

A Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development decision restricting remote customer-service occupations and jobs to Saudi nationals, whether engaged through direct employment or indirect arrangements, including outsourcing contracts covering remote work forming the establishment's core activity. It applies to establishments serving customers remotely via telephone, email, chat, social media or other direct-interaction channels, read with the earlier ministerial decisions it references, and penalties follow the violations and penalties schedule. It binds employers in the Kingdom, including financial institutions and their outsourced customer-service providers.

The Currency Law, issued by Royal Decree No. 6 of 1379H, is the foundational monetary statute establishing the Saudi Riyal as the national monetary unit, its subdivisions and parity value, and SAMA's exclusive privilege to mint, print and issue Saudi currency. It sets the rules on full gold and foreign-currency cover for issued notes and coins, legal tender status and discharge power, replacement and withdrawal of unfit or damaged currency, seizure of counterfeit money, record-keeping and periodic publication of the issuance position. It binds SAMA (with roles reserved to the Council of Ministers and the Minister of Finance) and, as to legal tender and acceptance limits, the public generally.

A SAMA circular from the Finance Companies Supervision Department (1442H) transmitting earlier e-mailed instructions on how financial institutions must treat expired National ID and Iqama documents. Relying on the AML Law and its Implementing Regulations, the CTF Implementing Regulations and the CDD section of SAMA's AML/CTF Guide, it confirms that IDs covered by the Ministry of Interior and Passports Directorate validity-extension announcements (COVID-era) may be treated as valid for customer due diligence purposes. It binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular reaffirming how government housing support is treated under the Responsible Lending Principles for Individuals when assessing affordability. It confirms that government subsidies are excluded from a customer's monthly income except periodic cash support paid by the Ministry of Municipal, Rural Affairs and Housing or the Real Estate Development Fund (non-cash or non-recurring support remains excluded), and that the applicable debt-burden ratio for such beneficiaries is computed on total monthly income where the support is paid monthly. It binds banks, finance companies and credit information companies.
lookup_terms: Ministry of Municipal Rural Affairs and Housing support

data.summary: Council of Ministers Resolution No. 637 (17/10/1441H) approves amending Article 12 of the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism so that persons accused under that Law may be released provisionally only temporarily, by order of the Public Prosecution, where there is no prejudice to the investigation and no flight or disappearance risk. It also approves repealing Article 9 of the Law's Implementing Regulations. It is directed at the criminal-procedure aspects of the CTF regime and is implemented through an accompanying Royal Decree.
lookup_terms: Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism amendment

data.summary: Royal Decree No. M/142 (19/10/1441H) enacts the amendment approved by Council of Ministers Resolution No. 637, replacing Article 12 of the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism with a provision limiting provisional release of accused persons to temporary release ordered by the Public Prosecution where the investigation is not prejudiced and there is no flight or disappearance risk. It is addressed to ministers and heads of independent entities for implementation within their competences.
lookup_terms: نظام مكافحة جرائم الإرهاب وتمويله تعديل

data.summary: A template bilateral agreement between the Saudi Credit Bureau (SIMAH), acting as the GLEIF-accredited Local Operating Unit, and a SAMA-supervised financial institution, allowing that institution to arrange issuance, updating and renewal of Legal Entity Identifiers (LEI) for legal entities it deals with. It covers the LEI governance framework (ROC charter, GLEIF master agreement, SAMA instructions), fees per issuance and renewal request with monthly invoicing and VAT exclusion, data protection obligations under the Credit Information Law and its Implementing Regulations plus SAMA and national cybersecurity requirements, amendment and severability terms, notices, and amicable settlement followed by Saudi courts for disputes. It binds the contracting financial institution and SIMAH.

data.theme: Channel-specific SAMA directives narrowing which external entities financial institutions may interface with for non-core services: charitable collections and digital document verification.
how_members_connect: Both are supervisory circulars restricting or designating a single authorized counterparty/channel for a service offered through bank platforms.
Shared consequence: institutions must discontinue unapproved arrangements and route the activity through the named entity only.
Charity-collection channelling carries CTF/terrorist-financing-abuse relevance; document linkage supports identity and documentary verification in CDD.

data.theme: Restriction on the channels used to exchange customer or institutional data, prohibiting social media and comparable public platforms for such exchanges.
how_members_connect: Standalone directive; reads as a data confidentiality and banking-secrecy control on communication channels rather than a data-processing regime in itself.
Interacts with consumer protection and customer data confidentiality obligations elsewhere in the framework.
start_here: Prohibition on Social Media for Data Exchange

data.theme: Governance requirements for appointing senior leadership in supervised entities, including SAMA no-objection and fitness criteria.
how_members_connect: Standalone update amending prior appointment-notification and approval requirements.
Operationally linked to fit-and-proper assessment obligations applied across licensed sectors.
start_here: Update to Senior Leadership Appointment Requirements

data.theme: The finance-company prudential and conduct regime: licensing, ownership and control, internal governance (compliance and internal audit), outsourcing, and permitted portfolio and debt-transfer transactions.
how_members_connect: The Finance Companies Control Law is the parent statute; nearly every other member is issued under or expressly cites it, forming a law-to-rules-to-circular hierarchy.

Governance chain: compliance principles and internal audit principles cross-reference each other, with the mandatory compliance-certificate circular imposing a personal qualification condition on compliance officers.
Licensing chain: microfinance licensing guidance depends on the fit-and-proper form for founders, board and senior management.

Activity-specific instructions (digital brokerage, consumer-debt purchase between finance companies, SRC mortgage-portfolio purchases) sit on top of the outsourcing rules and the Law's activity-authorisation scope.
start_here: Compliance Principles for Finance & Real Estate Refinance Companies

data.theme: Observance of the national Founding Day holiday and its effect on financial-sector working days, service availability and the computation of regulatory and contractual time limits.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a SAMA holiday notification addressed to supervised entities.
Links outward to operating-hours and business-continuity instructions, since a declared non-working day shifts settlement, reporting and customer-service obligations.
Relevant to any deadline counted in business days under other SAMA rules (e.g. complaint handling, reporting).

data.theme: Legal enforceability of close-out netting and collateral (financial security) arrangements in KSA, including their treatment on counterparty default or insolvency.
how_members_connect: Standalone regulation establishing the recognition and enforceability of netting and collateral arrangements as a distinct legal regime.
Interacts with prudential/risk governance rules (exposure measurement on a net basis) and with insolvency law carve-outs.
Scope turns on the defined terms for qualifying parties, eligible agreements and collateral — these should be read before applying the netting outcome.

data.theme: SAMA's seasonal operational instructions setting working hours, service readiness and cash-logistics arrangements for Ramadan, Eid and Hajj across banks, exchange centres, ATMs and the SARIE settlement system.
how_members_connect: All members are circular-level operational directives issued for the same Hijri season and applied to overlapping supervised populations (banks, exchange houses, payment infrastructure).
Obligation chain: general working-hours/Eid holiday instruction sets the calendar; the SARIE and ATM/cash-transport notices tailor it to settlement windows and cash availability.
Shared compliance consequence — service continuity and customer access duties under consumer protection rules must still be met on reduced-hour days.
Exchange-centre readiness for Hajj extends the same continuity logic to pilgrim-serving FX and remittance demand.

SARIE Working Hours Ramadan & Eid Holidays 1447H

data.theme: The requirement that supervised entities notify SAMA in advance of publishing or issuing periodic financial statements, supporting supervisory oversight of disclosure timing.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a notification/pre-clearance obligation running from the entity to SAMA.
Sits upstream of accounting, audit and public-disclosure requirements — the notice duty is procedural and additional to the substantive reporting rules.
Relevant to listed entities where SAMA and capital-market disclosure timetables must be reconciled.
start_here: SAMA Notification Before Periodic Financial Statements

data.theme: Verification of a customer's income as part of due diligence — relevant both to affordability/creditworthiness assessment in consumer finance and to source-of-funds/wealth understanding under CDD.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: the obligation to obtain and verify income evidence rather than rely on customer self-declaration.

Sits at the intersection of two regimes — responsible-lending affordability testing and AML/CTF customer due diligence — so the same evidence can serve different legal purposes with different retention and refresh triggers.
Consequence for a decision: an unverified income figure undermines both the credit decision's defensibility and the CDD risk rating.

data.theme: Consumer-facing conduct duties for financial service delivery: handling and escalating customer complaints, and the conduct/distribution conditions attached to selling investment fund units through electronic channels.
how_members_connect: Linked by a shared consumer-protection premise: any electronic distribution channel must be backed by an accessible complaint-handling route with defined turnaround and escalation.
Complaint-management requirements operate as a cross-cutting obligation layered onto product-specific distribution rules, not as a standalone regime.
Phased implementation of complaint systems sets the compliance timeline against which channel-specific offerings must be assessed.

data.theme: Periodic prudential and financial reporting to the supervisor — the content, form and timing of financial statements and prudential returns submitted by supervised entities.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster covering the reporting obligation chain: preparation, internal approval, and submission to SAMA within prescribed deadlines.
Underpins off-site supervision; accuracy and timeliness of returns are enforceable in their own right, separate from the prudential ratios they report.
Cross-reads to governance clusters, since responsibility for the integrity of submitted data typically rests with board and senior management.
start_here: Financial Statements and Prudential Data Reporting

data.theme: The credit card regime: issuance, operation, disclosure, fee and profit-rate treatment, dispute handling and cardholder protections for issuers and operators.
how_members_connect: Clear hierarchy — the Rules are the binding instrument; the FAQ is interpretive guidance that references and explains them and does not create new obligations.
Both share the defined terms for cardholder, issuer and card product, so scope questions resolve against the Rules' definitions.
The FAQ is the practical route to SAMA's reading of ambiguous provisions (billing, grace periods, fee caps, consent to limit changes), useful where the Rules are terse.
start_here: Rules for Issuing and Operating Credit Cards

data.theme: Retail credit conduct: how consumer finance (including credit cards) must be priced, disclosed, serviced and collected from individual customers, with fraud-control duties attached to card issuance.
how_members_connect: Shared subject population — the individual/consumer borrower or cardholder — so disclosure, APR/cost-of-borrowing and term-change rules in the finance rules clarification carry across to card products.

Obligation chain: card issuance and operation rules expressly reference the debt collection regime, so post-default conduct (contact limits, treatment of arrears, permitted collection practices) is imported into the card lifecycle rather than sitting separately.

Hierarchy is visible: base rules (credit cards, debt collection) sit under SAMA circulars that clarify specific articles and APR calculation, and the circular is the operative interpretation for compliance decisions.
Cross-regime link: the counter-fraud guide attaches fraud prevention, detection and customer-liability expectations to card operations, bridging consumer protection and operational-risk obligations.
Two members are duplicates of the debt collection and credit card rules — treat as the same instrument to avoid double-counting obligations.

Updated Debt Collection Regulations for Individual Customers

data.theme: Governance disclosure of board and board-committee remuneration — what must be reported, to whom and in what form.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster; no internal cross-references, so its obligations must be read against the wider corporate governance and disclosure regime rather than against peers here.
Relevance is mainly as a reporting duty feeding supervisory oversight of governance and remuneration practices.

data.theme: Prudential liquidity regulation for banks: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio, including the amended calibrations and the associated supervisory reporting returns.
how_members_connect: Direct cross-reference: the circular on amended prudential returns and NSFR operates off the revised LCR regulations, so the reporting obligation is derivative of the substantive ratio requirement.
Amendment hierarchy matters — the later circular revises earlier LCR text, so effective dates and superseded provisions determine which calibration binds.
Both sit in the same Basel-derived liquidity framework, sharing defined terms (high-quality liquid assets, net outflows, stable funding) that should be read consistently across the two.

SAMA Circular: Amended LCR Prudential Returns & NSFR

data.theme: Oversight of systemically important payment systems — the standards a designated system operator must meet for safety, efficiency and risk management.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster; the standards function as the apex of the payments oversight regime and should be read alongside the payments/PSP licensing and operational rules held elsewhere in the knowledge base.
Key scope question is designation: the obligations bite only on systems assessed as systemically important, so applicability analysis precedes compliance analysis.

data.theme: Commercial registration and trade-name requirements as a gateway condition for lawful business identity in KSA, relevant to onboarding/KYB and licensing checks by supervised entities.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: the application of the Commercial Register and Trade Names Law, acting as the source of legal-entity identity evidence relied on elsewhere (e.g. customer/merchant due diligence).
Links outward rather than inward — it supplies the registration status and trade-name concepts that licensing and KYB obligations presuppose.
start_here: Application of Commercial Register and Trade Names Law

data.theme: Macroprudential capital buffer setting — the countercyclical capital buffer rate applied to banks' capital adequacy requirements.
how_members_connect: Standalone circular instrument: sets or confirms the CCyB rate, operating as an add-on to the prudential capital adequacy regime rather than a self-contained rulebook.
Its consequence is read together with capital adequacy and risk management obligations found in the broader prudential cluster.

data.theme: SAMA's counter-fraud regime: the obligation on supervised entities to establish governed, risk-assessed fraud prevention, detection and response capability, measured against a maturity model.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy runs from the Counter-Fraud Framework and its Fundamental Requirements down to the four domains (Govern, Prevent, Detect, Respond), with the Maturity Model as the assessment yardstick.
Governance chain: board/Counter-Fraud Governance Committee, Head of Counter-Fraud and a dedicated Counter-Fraud Department own fraud risk appetite, the fraud risk assessment and KRIs.
Sector-specific overlay: the Anti-Fraud Rules for Finance Companies sit alongside the Framework, so finance companies face both general and sectoral requirements.

Cross-regime hooks: supervisory notification duties, the Sectorial Anti-Fraud Committee, the IT Governance Framework, authentication standards and the Whistle Blowing Policy — note the distinction between fraud reporting and AML/CTF suspicious transaction reporting.

data.theme: The core SAMA legal architecture — central bank mandate, real estate finance and leasing, refinance companies and the secondary market — intersecting with AML/CTF, consumer protection, responsible lending and advertising rules applicable to financial institutions.
how_members_connect: Law-to-regulation chains: the Saudi Central Bank Law grants supervisory authority; the Real Estate Finance Law and Finance Lease Law each have implementing regulations, with further rules governing real estate refinance companies and Capital Market Law interaction for secondary-market securitisation.

Shared defined terms — notably Financial Institution, Customer Due Diligence, Licensed Credit Bureau and Real Estate Finance Contract — bind the prudential, AML/CTF and consumer-facing instruments together.

Conduct layer: Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules, complaints handling, data and privacy protection, outsourcing and the advertising rules (including compliance-department pre-review) apply across product lines.

Credit-granting chain: Responsible Lending Principles require creditworthiness assessment and observance of the deductible ratio using credit bureau data; amendments (deletion of Article 4, amendment of Article 16) must be checked for the version in force.
Prudential obligations for refinance companies — capital adequacy and liquidity, corporate governance, risk management and compliance — cross-reference the counter-fraud and AML regimes.
start_here: Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules

data.theme: Requirements applying where a licensed entity markets or issues products under more than one trademark or brand, addressing brand transparency and the risk that consumers cannot identify the responsible licensed institution.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster; the obligation stands alone as a product-labelling/branding condition rather than part of a referenced chain.
Legally it sits downstream of consumer protection and licensing principles: the licensed entity remains accountable for products regardless of the trademark used.
Read alongside consumer disclosure and advertising obligations in other regimes when assessing a multi-brand product launch.

data.theme: Physical security obligations for supervised entities regarding installation, operation and retention standards for CCTV/surveillance systems at branches, ATMs and cash handling points.
how_members_connect: Isolated compliance requirement with no internal cross-references in this graph.
Operationally linked to cash handling, branch network and premises-security regimes; breaches are supervisory findings rather than consumer-protection matters.
Retention and access to footage interact with data protection and evidentiary/investigation duties.

data.theme: The core prudential and conduct architecture for banks, payment systems and payment service providers in KSA: licensing, capital, safeguarding of client funds, agents and outsourcing, systemic payment infrastructure oversight, and the consumer-facing conduct layer (framework contracts, unauthorised transactions, complaints, bancassurance, savings products, financial inclusion).
how_members_connect: Clear hierarchy: primary laws (Central Bank Law, Banking Control Law, Law of Payments and Payment Services, Currency Law, Credit Information Law, Cooperative Insurance Companies Control Law) feed implementing regulations (Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments, SAMA Payment Services Regulation, Implementation Rules for the Banking Control Law) and then licensing guidelines and circulars.

Obligation chains radiate from the Payment Services Regulation: capital, protected-funds safeguarding, agent appointment, e-money distribution, outsourcing, framework contracts, AIS/PIS, unauthorised-transaction liability and complaints all attach to the same defined 'payment service provider' and 'payment service user' terms.
Payment-system oversight branch runs law to supervisory framework to international benchmarks (PFMI) via self-assessment and supervisory assessment, keyed to systemic importance designation.

Banking-side members (large exposures, related parties, loans-to-deposits, Shariah governance and Shari'ah-compliant capital add-ons, IFSB standards, branch network policy) share the Banking Control Law/Central Bank Law root, while bancassurance links the banking and insurance regimes through bank and company obligations under a single agreement framework.
start_here: Law of Payments and Payment Services
Supervisory Framework for Payment Systems and Operators

data.theme: Administrative obligation on supervised entities to designate and maintain a main user for SAMA's eServices portal, governing authorised access to regulatory submissions and communications.
how_members_connect: Standalone circular; no internal references in this cluster.
Functions as the procedural gateway for filings and notifications required under substantive regimes, so failures here can cascade into reporting breaches.
Designation and delegation of the main user role carries accountability implications for governance and authorised-signatory arrangements.
start_here: eSAMA eServices Portal Main User Circular

data.theme: Operational readiness of currency supply and exchange services during peak demand periods (Ramadan and Hajj), when cash, foreign-currency and pilgrim-servicing volumes spike.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a standalone seasonal instruction directed at banks and money exchangers rather than a rule family.
Sits at circular/instruction level under SAMA's supervisory authority over currency issuance, cash handling and exchange activity.
Interacts with business-continuity and branch-service obligations; non-compliance is a supervisory conduct issue, not a licensing one.
start_here: Currency Exchange Readiness for Ramadan and Hajj Seasons

data.theme: Protection of specified beneficiary payments (martyrs' entitlements) from enforcement action, limiting banks' ability to apply judicial seizure or set-off to those amounts.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: an exemption instruction that carves out a defined category of funds from general attachment/seizure execution duties.
Legal linkage runs to enforcement-court cooperation obligations and account-freezing procedures; the exemption operates as a scope limit on them.
Consequence for decision-making: banks must identify and ring-fence the exempt amounts before executing a seizure order.
start_here: Exemption of Martyrs' Cheque Amounts from Judicial Seizure

data.theme: Physical safety and premises-compliance duties of supervised financial institutions, specifically appointing and empowering a fire safety officer in line with civil-defence requirements.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a compliance instruction transposing a national fire-safety regulation into SAMA-supervised entities' obligations.
Legally sits alongside operational-risk and business-continuity governance rather than prudential or conduct regimes.
Accountability point is an appointed responsible person, creating a named-role obligation verifiable on inspection.
start_here: Compliance with Fire Safety Officer Responsibilities Regulation

data.theme: Consumer credit affordability and conduct across BNPL and finance-lease activity: who may be licensed, how credit capacity must be assessed before granting, and what disclosure, advertising and consumer-protection duties attach.
how_members_connect: The BNPL rules act as the hub instrument and expressly pull in responsible lending principles, debt burden ratio caps, advertising controls and their own licensing, activity and consumer-protection chapters — a rulebook-to-annex hierarchy.

Shared affordability chain: responsible lending principles set the assessment duty, debt burden ratios set the quantitative ceiling, and BNPL activity provisions apply both to deferred-payment exposures.
Finance Lease Law anchors the leasing side; the total-economic-loss verification instruction is a downstream operational rule interpreting lessee/insurer outcomes under that law.
Definitional caution: the BNPL regime's 'Consumer' is narrower than the AML/CTF 'Customer', so CDD, merchant-as-customer and KYB duties are not satisfied by BNPL consumer-protection compliance alone.

data.theme: Prudential risk management for Shari'ah-compliant banking, taxonomising the risk categories a bank must identify, measure and control (credit, market, liquidity, equity investment, operational and Shari'ah non-compliance risk), together with the operational-risk sub-taxonomy and the insurance/internal-control mitigants available to management.
how_members_connect: The Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking sits at the top and enumerates each risk category as a distinct obligation area, with the Shari'ah Governance Framework and PSIAs Rules supplying the governance and profit-sharing-account context that makes those risks Shari'ah-specific.
Shari'ah non-compliance risk is treated as a sub-set of operational risk, which creates an obligation chain: operational risk controls and reporting must also capture SNCR events.

The Operational Risk Management Guide elaborates operational risk into criminal, professional and political sub-risks (fraud, forgery, electronic crime, professional/D&O liability) and links them to risk-transfer options — self insurance, regular insurance, bankers blanket bond, finite risk — plus the Risk Management Evaluation Questionnaire as the assessment instrument.
Cross-regime anchors: SAMA Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks and the Companies Law provide the board/management accountability baseline on which the Shari'ah risk framework is layered.
start_here: Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking

data.theme: SAMA notifications fixing official holidays and the corresponding RTGS (real-time gross settlement) operating hours, which determine settlement value dates and payment cut-offs.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: an operational notice rather than a rule-making instrument, but it conditions payment-system obligations and timing defences across the payments regime.
start_here: Official Holidays and RTGS Working Hours

data.theme: Mandatory trade repository reporting for OTC derivatives — who must report, to which SAMA-authorised trade repository, in what data fields and identifiers, and how lifecycle events and collateral updates must be maintained.
how_members_connect: The core circular splits obligations into Section A (trade reporting) and Section B (risk mitigation), and supersedes/builds on the earlier SAMA OTC circular, so scope and effective dates must be read against the prior instrument.
Reporting duties run to the SAMA Authorised Trade Repository Operator, making TR authorisation status a precondition for discharging the reporting obligation.

Data-level members (Common Data Reporting table, UTI, UPI, action type/lifecycle events, collateral evolutive fields) are the prescribed content of the reporting obligation; UTI and action type together govern how amendments, terminations and corrections are recorded.
A duplicate circular entry is semantically equivalent to the core instrument — confirm which version is the operative text before citing.
start_here: Trade Repository Reporting and Risk Mitigation Requirements for OTC Derivatives

data.theme: Bilateral risk-mitigation and documentation governance for non-centrally-cleared OTC derivatives: valuation, portfolio reconciliation and compression, and dispute handling between counterparties.
how_members_connect: Governance of Trading Documentation is the umbrella obligation, requiring documented, agreed procedures that in turn invoke valuation, reconciliation, compression and dispute resolution requirements.
These members are the substantive content of the risk-mitigation limb (Section B) of the OTC derivatives regime, so they should be read together with the trade repository reporting cluster.
Valuation outputs feed reconciliation and dispute processes, creating a sequential obligation chain rather than independent duties.

data.theme: Regulatory reporting of counterparty identity and transaction data, including the identifier standards and the rules determining who must report what and when.
how_members_connect: Appendix A Table 1 sets the counterparty data fields to be reported, and fixes entity identification by reference to the ISO 17442 LEI standard.
Appendix C carries the reporting obligation itself (scope, reporting party, timing) and cross-refers to the Table 1 data set as the content of that obligation.
Effectively a hierarchy: obligation rule -> prescribed data schedule -> incorporated external identifier standard; the LEI reference makes an external standard enforceable through the reporting rule.
Practical consequence: a data-field defect in Table 1 terms is a breach of the Appendix C obligation, not a mere technical issue.

data.theme: Prudential treatment of interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB), specifically the prescribed shock scenarios banks must apply when measuring and reporting rate sensitivity.
how_members_connect: The standardised shock scenarios are drawn from and cite the Basel Committee IRRBB framework, so the local requirement operates as adoption of an international standard.
Linkage is hierarchical in substance: international standard-setter guidance -> SAMA-applied prudential measurement requirement.
Interpretation of scenario calibration and scope should follow the Basel source unless SAMA has expressly varied it.

data.theme: The requirement to obtain and use the National Address for customers and correspondence, a KSA-specific identification and communication data point that intersects with CDD, consumer notification and records obligations.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster: the National Address / postal services requirement stands alone but functions as an input to identification and customer-communication duties elsewhere in the framework.
Relevant where other regimes require verified address data (CDD/KYC records, consumer disclosures, statement delivery).

data.theme: The core KSA AML/CTF statutory regime: the AML Law and the CTF Law, the preventive measures they impose on financial institutions and DNFBPs, the powers of supervisory authorities and the FIU, confiscation, and the official data sources used to verify beneficial ownership.
how_members_connect: Two parallel statutes (AML Law and Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism) share the same architecture and cross-refer: preventive measures for FIs/DNFBPs, supervisory authority powers, FIU reporting, and confiscation.

Preventive-measures provisions form an obligation chain: CDD and beneficial owner identification duties feed suspicious transaction reporting to the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence, enforced through supervisory authority powers and sanctions.

Watheq, the non-profit associations beneficial owner inquiry service and Awqaf services are operational verification channels that derive their legal basis from the AML Law's beneficial owner requirements - useful for evidencing verification, not substitutes for the statutory duty.

Data-sharing items (e.g. residential real estate finance data with SIMAH) sit at the intersection of AML record-keeping/verification and the credit information regime, so confidentiality and permitted-purpose limits in both regimes must be read together.
Note the defined-term boundary: 'Customer' under AML differs from client/consumer concepts in BNPL and consumer protection rules, which affects who must be subjected to CDD.
start_here: Preventive Measures for FIs and DNFBPs
Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism

data.theme: Debt instruments and recurring payment authorisations used by finance entities: how promissory notes may be taken, held and enforced against borrowers, and the controls governing standing payment orders on customer accounts.
how_members_connect: Both address instruments by which a finance entity secures or collects repayment from a Consumer/borrower, and both sit under SAMA's supervisory instructions for finance entities.
Shared obligation chain: disclosure and consent at contracting, limits on the amount and use of the instrument, and constraints on enforcement/deduction without fresh customer authorisation.
Cross-regime interaction with consumer protection principles (fair treatment, transparency) and with finance company conduct rules on collection practices.
start_here: Instructions on Dealing with Promissory Notes for Finance Entities
Standing Payment Order Controls for Finance Entities

data.theme: Accessibility obligations requiring financial institutions to make products, branches, channels and disclosures usable by persons with disabilities.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster; the duty is best read as an extension of consumer protection principles (fair treatment, clear disclosure, non-discrimination) applied to a defined beneficiary group.
Interacts with branch/channel operating rules and with account-opening and CDD requirements where assisted or alternative identification/consent arrangements are needed.
start_here: Services for Persons with Disabilities in Financial Institutions

data.theme: Minimum physical security and video surveillance standards for financial sector premises, covering what must be monitored and the technical baseline for cameras and recording infrastructure.
how_members_connect: A parent specification document with three dependent components: stated surveillance objectives, camera requirements and recording-server requirements, all cross-referencing the parent standard.
Hierarchy is standard-to-specification: the objectives define the control purpose, while the camera and NVR items set the compliance-testable parameters.
Camera and NVR items are operationally coupled (capture, retention and retrieval of footage), which matters for evidentiary and retention obligations in fraud, AML and incident investigations.
start_here: CCTV Specifications for the Financial Sector

data.theme: Cyber threat intelligence expectations for supervised financial entities: what intelligence capability must exist, at which levels (strategic, operational, technical/tactical), and how it feeds broader cyber resilience and threat-led testing.
how_members_connect: A central principles document anchors the cluster; the core and level-specific CTI items are subordinate elaborations that reference it.

Cross-framework linkage: the CTI principles and the ethical red teaming framework both reference the Cyber Security Framework, forming a framework-to-framework obligation chain (governance baseline, intelligence capability, threat-led testing).
Methodology references (kill chain, adversary technique taxonomies) are incorporated as analytical standards for operational CTI rather than as independent obligations.
Practical consequence: intelligence outputs are expected to be usable inputs to red teaming scope and to board-level risk reporting.
start_here: Financial Sector Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles
Financial Entities Ethical Red Teaming Framework (FEER)

data.theme: Prudential/supervisory notification duty triggered when a supervised entity raises capital or undertakes an investment round, so SAMA can assess ownership, control and funding changes before they take effect.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster: the obligation stands alone as a notification/no-objection step rather than a substantive licensing rule.
Legally it sits upstream of change-of-control and shareholding approval requirements — a notification failure is a supervisory breach independent of the merits of the round.
Read with governance and licensing regimes for the entity type (fintech, PSP, finance company) to identify who signs and when the clock starts.

data.theme: Currency-handling standards for banks and cash handlers: fitness sorting, authentication and recirculation of a specific Saudi banknote issue.
how_members_connect: Isolated instruction-level item; its force comes from SAMA's currency-issuance mandate rather than cross-references to other regimes.
Operationally binding on cash-handling institutions and their outsourced cash service providers, so obligations flow through outsourcing arrangements.
Distinguish from counterfeit-reporting and AML cash-transaction duties, which are separate regimes.
start_here: Fine Sorting Instructions for Sixth Issue of Saudi Banknotes

data.theme: Consumer-facing price transparency and contractual fairness in finance and savings products: how cost of credit must be calculated, disclosed pre-contract, and reflected in standard contract terms on early repayment, late payment and default.
how_members_connect: The disclosure rules supply the calculation and presentation standard (APR) that the standard consumer finance contract must embed, creating a disclosure-to-contract obligation chain.
Early repayment, late payment and default clauses are components of the same standard contract instrument, so their limits are read as mandatory contractual content, not optional terms.
