Practically, an agent's KYC output must be capable of satisfying the principal's CDD and EDD obligations, and residual accountability stays with the regulated institution; verify the primary text on reliance and responsibility.

Treat these as the two sides of one client-money outcome: the payments instrument obliges the payment institution to protect and safeguard protected funds, while the bank account rules govern how a bank may open and manage the collection account in which payment companies' client funds are held. The link is inferred from the common subject — segregation and safekeeping of client funds — with obligations falling on different parties (the PSP and the account-holding bank). For a decision, both must be satisfied: a safeguarding arrangement is not compliant merely because the PSP intends segregation if the account is not opened and operated on the prescribed terms, and the bank acts as a gatekeeper. Confirm the specific account conditions in the primary text before approving an arrangement.

When deciding whether a covered bond holding can be counted in the liquidity buffer, the definitional instrument and the HQLA classification rules must be read together: the former sets the structural characteristics of a covered bond (segregated cover pool serving bondholders on issuer failure), the latter determines whether such an instrument qualifies as Level 2A subject to rating and the aggregate Level 2 cap. The relationship is inferred from the shared defined term rather than an express cross-citation. Consequence: structural conformity alone does not confer HQLA status, and HQLA treatment cannot be claimed for an instrument that does not meet the covered bond definition plus the rating and cap conditions. Verify the eligibility criteria in the primary liquidity text before recognising the asset.

Treat these as two separate amendments feeding the same account-opening and customer due diligence rulebook, so neither can be applied in isolation when revising bank account procedures. One adjusts eligibility and account-opening treatment for non-resident real estate owners, the other addresses how a bank may rely on an external public-sector source (the General Authority for Awqaf) when verifying beneficial owners — both sit downstream of the Rules for Bank Accounts and the AML/CTF identification and verification duties. The link is inferred rather than textual, so the practical consequence is that a compliance team should reconcile both against the latest consolidated Rules for Bank Accounts before concluding what identification evidence is acceptable for a given customer category, and verify the primary text for scope and effective dates.

Before contracting a money transfer services provider, decide first whether the arrangement is also an outsourcing of a material function, because the contracting conditions for transfer providers (licensing, international recognition, supervisory oversight in the home jurisdiction) address counterparty acceptability, while the Outsourcing Rules address the institution's retained accountability, contract content, documentation and non-transferability of regulatory responsibility. The relationship is one of cumulative obligations rather than substitution, anchored in the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations for finance companies. Because the link is inferred, confirm the entity scope of each instrument in the primary text — the transfer-provider conditions may sit in a rulebook addressed to a different licence category, in which case the Outsourcing Rules bind only if the contracting party is a finance company.

When approving an outsourcing arrangement that touches customer-facing activity, satisfy the outsourcing regime and the consumer protection regime at the same time, as they test different things. The Outsourcing Rules govern the institutional process — materiality assessment, contracting, documentation and supervisory accountability — while the consumer protection outsourcing principle makes the institution answerable for the service provider's conduct toward consumers and requires the provider to observe the applicable consumer protection requirements. Practically, an outsourcing file that is compliant on process can still fail if the contract and oversight do not carry consumer protection duties through to the provider; verify the scope wording of the consumer protection instrument for the institution types it covers.

Read the two instruments as overlapping conditions on the same decision to outsource: the finance company Outsourcing Rules set the general governance, contracting and record-keeping requirements, while the cyber security outsourcing principle requires cyber security controls to be defined, embedded in the outsourcing policy and monitored through the outsourcing lifecycle. This is a layering of a specialised risk requirement onto a general regime, not a duplication, so a compliant outsourcing policy must carry both dimensions. The connection is inferred, so confirm in the primary text whether the entity falls within the definition of Member Organization used by the cyber security framework before treating that principle as directly binding rather than indicative good practice.

These bear on the same appointment decision from two angles: the institutional requirement to establish a compliance function with a written compliance policy defining its tasks and responsibilities, and the personal eligibility requirement that a finance company's compliance officer hold the mandated compliance certificate. Having an adequate compliance policy and structure does not cure an unqualified appointment, and vice versa. Practically, confirm certification status as a condition of appointment or continuation in role, and check the primary text for the exact scope, recognised certifications and any transitional period, since this link is inferred rather than expressly cross-referenced.

When assessing whether an aggregation-activity provider is properly authorised and what enforcement exposure it faces, treat the Finance Companies Control Law as the enabling statute behind the Aggregation Instructions, which SAMA issued under powers conferred by that Law and its Royal Decree. That hierarchy means the Instructions cannot be read in isolation: the Law's licensing, supervisory and sanction machinery supplies the legal force and remedies for breaches of the Instructions. Practically, a compliance conclusion on aggregation should cite both the specific Instruction and its statutory anchor, and should not assume that silence in the Instructions displaces a general obligation in the parent Law.

For a decision on how a finance company must classify credit exposures and set provisions, read the Rules as the detailed elaboration of provisioning duties that originate in the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation. The Law establishes the requirement to provision against losses in line with criteria set at regulation level, and the Rules supply those criteria within the broader credit risk management framework. Consequently, a provisioning judgment that satisfies the Rules is also discharging a statutory obligation, and any gap or ambiguity in the Rules should be resolved by reference to the parent Law rather than treated as unregulated.

When testing a finance company's liquidity governance — including whether an ALCO and related management arrangements are adequate — the Rules on Liquidity Risk Management operate as SAMA's prudential elaboration of duties applicable to entities licensed under the Finance Companies Control Law. The Law defines the regulated population and supervisory powers; the Rules set the substantive expectations for that population. Note that some elements in the Rules are framed as recommendations rather than strict requirements, so the reader should distinguish mandatory from advisory language in the primary text before characterising a shortfall as a breach.

For any question about a deposit-taking finance company, the compliance baseline is cumulative rather than substitutive: the DTFC Regulations add deposit-specific prudential requirements on top of, not instead of, the Finance Companies Control Law and SAMA's general finance company regulations. The DTFC framework itself directs compliance with the parent Law and other applicable finance company rules. So a DTFC assessment must cover both layers, and satisfying the DTFC-specific requirements alone does not evidence compliance with the generally applicable finance company regime.

When determining whether a supervised institution's anti-fraud arrangements are adequate, the Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements are SAMA-issued expectations addressed to Member Organizations, so they form part of the supervisory baseline SAMA will examine against — including periodic staff training, awareness of fraud risk and fraud culture. The link simply identifies SAMA as the issuing and supervising authority, which determines who enforces and to whom the duties run. Practically, scope turns on whether the entity falls within the defined Member Organization population, and the reader should confirm that scope and the mandatory versus recommended phrasing in the primary text.

When deciding whether a payment-related activity or monitoring expectation applies, first confirm whether the actor falls within the payment services perimeter that SAMA supervises under the Law of Payments and Payment Services. The link reflects that SAMA is the licensing and supervisory authority for the defined payment services, payment instruments, e-money and payment wallet activities set out in that Law, so its transaction-monitoring and red-flag expectations attach to entities inside that defined scope. Practically, classify the entity against the Law's definitions before applying SAMA payment-sector obligations, and note that AML/CTF duties run in parallel rather than being displaced by payments licensing.

Treat the repurchase agreement guidelines as SAMA-issued supervisory expectations rather than an independent legal source, since SAMA is the issuing authority. That authorship matters for weight: the guidance sits below statute and binding rules in the hierarchy but still frames how SAMA assesses supervised institutions' repo practices. For a decision, apply the guidelines as the supervisory benchmark while checking that any conflicting primary instrument or higher-ranking rule controls.

When applying the Targeted Financial Sanctions Rules, read their defined terms and obligations against the Anti-Money Laundering Law they cite, because the Rules import that Law's definitional framework. This creates an obligation chain: the statutory AML regime supplies the legal foundation and definitions, and the TFS Rules operationalise freezing, screening and reporting duties on top of it. In practice, a sanctions determination should be justified by reference to both instruments, and the statutory definitions govern where the Rules are silent or ambiguous.

Use the SAMA AML/CTF Guide as supervisory elaboration of the statutory duties in the Anti-Money Laundering Law, not as a substitute for them. The Guide references the Law because the Law and its Implementing Regulation are the binding source of CDD, record-keeping, reporting and internal-control obligations, while the Guide sets SAMA's expectations for how supervised institutions meet them. For a compliance decision, ground the legal obligation in the Law and treat the Guide as the supervisory standard against which adequacy is judged.

Before approving or renewing an agent banking arrangement, assess it against the Anti-Money Laundering Law as well as the agent banking requirements, since the Regulation cites that Law. The link signals that outsourcing customer-facing functions to an agent does not transfer AML/CTF responsibility: the bank remains the accountable institution for CDD, monitoring and reporting on customers onboarded or served through agents. Consequently, agent due diligence, contract terms and renewal assessments should evidence that statutory AML duties continue to be discharged by the bank.

When deciding how far an Agent's identification and verification steps must go, treat the KYC definition as an operational label rather than a self-standing standard: its substantive content is set by the AML Law regime it points to. The definition covers identifying Customers and beneficiaries and verifying identity, which maps onto the statutory customer due diligence duties under the Anti-Money Laundering Law and its Implementing Regulation. Practically, an Agent cannot satisfy KYC by meeting only the narrower wording of its own instrument; the AML Law's CDD, beneficial ownership and record-keeping requirements govern, and note the term mismatch between the instrument's "Customer" and any narrower product-level term.

If a financial institution wants to rely on a third party's CDD, the permission is conditional and its conditions sit in the AML Law framework, not only in the instrument granting the reliance. The reliance provision allows another financial institution or a DNFBP to perform due diligence measures, but the underlying AML Law regime retains ultimate responsibility with the relying institution and imposes conditions on immediate access to information and record availability. For a decision: reliance may reduce duplicated onboarding steps but does not transfer liability, so the institution must still be able to evidence AML Law-compliant CDD on demand.

A sandbox applicant should read the AML Law as a live admission criterion, not a post-authorisation concern. The guidance notes for the SAMA Regulatory Sandbox application direct applicants to address how the proposed activity will meet applicable legal requirements, and the AML Law applies to the activity regardless of the testing status of the firm. Consequence: AML/CTF controls, customer identification and reporting arrangements must be described and defensible at application stage, and sandbox participation does not create an exemption from statutory AML duties.

For a Deposit Taking Finance Company, prudential compliance under the DTFC Regulations does not discharge AML obligations, which arise separately under the AML Law. The DTFC Regulations expressly layer on top of the Finance Companies Control Law, SAMA finance company rules and other applicable laws, and the AML Law is one such law of general application to financial institutions. Practically, a DTFC must run both regimes in parallel: capital, liquidity and governance requirements from the DTFC framework, and CDD, suspicious transaction reporting and record-keeping from the AML regime, with deposit-taking raising the AML risk profile.

Where responsible lending assessments concern real estate finance to individuals, the affordability and conduct expectations of the Responsible Lending Principles operate alongside the specific statutory duties in the Real Estate Finance Law. That law imposes its own obligations on the real estate finance entity, including verifying the title deed and the absence of in rem rights before contracting, which is a security and validity check distinct from borrower creditworthiness. For a decision, a lender cannot treat a satisfactory affordability assessment as completing its pre-contract obligations; the title verification duty applies independently. Because the linkage is a cross-reference between a conduct instrument and a primary law, verify the precise articles applicable to the product in the primary text.

Decide first which licensing regime the real estate financier sits under: a bank carrying on real estate finance remains a bank supervised under the Banking Control Law, so the real estate finance obligations (such as title-deed and in rem rights verification before contracting) sit on top of, not instead of, its banking prudential and supervisory duties. The cross-reference reflects that both statutes are SAMA-administered and that the Banking Control Law is the general licensing and supervision instrument against which sector-specific finance laws are read. Practically, a compliance sign-off on a real estate finance product needs to clear both the product-level conditions and the bank's general banking-law obligations, and enforcement can be grounded in either. Because the cited excerpts do not themselves spell out the interaction, verify the specific referencing provision in the primary text before relying on it.

If a BNPL company plans to hand any activity to a third party — credit assessment support, collections, customer onboarding, technology operation — treat the Outsourcing Rules for Finance Companies as directly applicable, not merely analogous. Both instruments are issued by SAMA under the Finance Companies Control Law, and the BNPL Rules pull the outsourcing regime in by reference, so a BNPL licensee falls within the defined population of finance companies for outsourcing purposes. The consequence is that outsourcing does not transfer regulatory responsibility: the BNPL company remains accountable to SAMA for the outsourced function and must satisfy the outsourcing regime's approval, materiality and oversight conditions alongside its BNPL-specific consumer obligations.

When scoping an IT governance gap assessment, do not read the IT Governance Framework as the complete control set: it expressly defers cyber security (and business continuity) requirements to the separate Cyber Security Framework. The two are parallel SAMA supervisory frameworks for the same regulated entities, so the reference is a scope-boundary signal rather than a subordination. The practical consequence is cumulative compliance — cyber policy, standards and procedures are assessed against the Cyber Security Framework and its own maturity expectations, and a finding closed under one framework does not evidence compliance with the other.

Treat IT risk management as a required component of the IT governance structure rather than a separate optional discipline: the governance framework identifies IT risk management as one of its domains and relies on the IT risk instrument for the substantive risk identification, treatment and acceptance concepts. Because the defined terms (risk treatment options such as avoidance, mitigation, transfer and acceptance) sit in the risk instrument, they carry the same meaning when applied under the governance framework. For a decision, this means governance-level roles, board oversight and accountability must be evidenced over the IT risk process itself, and inconsistent internal definitions of risk treatment across the two areas would be a finding.

Expect compliance with the IT governance requirements to be judged on a graded maturity scale rather than as a binary yes/no, because the framework routes assessment of each control domain to its maturity model. The model is the measurement instrument attached to the framework, so the substantive obligations and the scoring method must be read together. Consequently, self-assessments and SAMA reviews should state the achieved maturity level per domain and the target level, and a control that exists but is undocumented or unmeasured may still score below the expected level.

When assessing whether a member organisation's technical cyber controls are adequate, read the operations and technology control domain as a sub-component of the overarching Cyber Security Framework rather than a standalone checklist. The operations and technology controls expressly tie back to the Framework's governance, policy and risk management articles, so the documented policy hierarchy (policies, standards, procedures) is the reference point against which operational controls are judged. In practice, a gap in the parent governance or policy layer undermines compliance with the operational controls even where the technical measure itself is present.

For a decision on whether change management practice is compliant, treat the system change management requirement as an application of the Cyber Security Framework's documentation hierarchy. The change management process must sit under an approved, periodically reviewed policy and procedure, which is precisely the policy–standard–procedure structure the Framework mandates, including refresh on significant IT or regulatory change. Consequently, an undocumented or stale change management policy is both a change management failing and a Framework documentation failing, and the periodic review trigger must be evidenced.

When testing board-level accountability for liquidity, read the board oversight expectations together with the Rules on Liquidity Risk Management, which supply the governance architecture (senior management committee such as an ALCO drawing on risk, treasury and financial control) through which oversight is exercised. The board oversight requirements on identification, measurement, monitoring and reporting are the internal control outcomes; the Rules describe who operationalises them. Note the scope difference: the Rules address finance companies, so confirm which entity type your subject falls under before applying the ALCO expectation, and verify the primary text.

If you are deciding what counts as an adequate liquidity buffer, the HQLA classification (Level 1, Level 2A/2B with the 40% cap and associated haircuts) supplies the asset-eligibility standard that the broader liquidity risk management regime relies on when measuring and monitoring liquidity. The link is one of obligation chain rather than identity: the Rules set the governance and measurement duty, HQLA defines the qualifying instruments. Because HQLA is a Basel-derived banking standard while the Rules on Liquidity Risk Management address finance companies, confirm in the primary text whether the HQLA taxonomy is formally imposed on your entity or is being used as a reference benchmark.

For any bank licensing decision, the Licensing Guidelines and minimum criteria are not free-standing: they operate as SAMA's articulation of the licensing power conferred by the Banking Control Law and its implementing rules. The Law is the parent statute and hierarchy therefore runs from it to the implementing rules to the Guidelines, so the Guidelines cannot be read to narrow or displace a statutory licensing condition. Practically, an applicant must satisfy both the statutory conditions and the minimum criteria, and any ambiguity in the Guidelines should be resolved by reference back to the Banking Control Law.

When assessing whether an authentication control set is adequate, do not treat the Authentication Standard as self-contained: it directs member organisations to apply it alongside SAMA's other frameworks and expressly points to the Cyber Security Framework for the underlying cyber security requirements. The two instruments therefore sit in one obligation chain under SAMA's supervisory mandate, with the Framework supplying the governance, policy and control architecture that authentication requirements presuppose. Practically, an authentication design that satisfies the Standard but is not anchored in the entity's Framework-based cyber security policies, standards and risk management will still be exposed on supervisory review.

In deciding whether identity/verification controls for onboarding (including the additional controls applied to lending activity) are sufficient, read the Minimum Verification Controls together with the Cyber Security Framework rather than in isolation. The verification controls set the functional minimum, while the Framework supplies the governing expectations — notably that cyber security risk is assessed at project inception and that requirements are met by existing or newly developed controls aligned to the entity's cyber security standards. The consequence is that a lending or finance entity must be able to show both the specific verification measures and the Framework-level risk assessment and control ownership behind them.

Treat the Red Team Evaluation Report not as a standalone deliverable but as an output required under the SAMA cyber security regime, since the RTER text is carried within the Framework family itself. The report records the red teaming provider's assessment of the member organisation's resilience against the executed attack scenarios, and its status derives from the Framework's testing and assurance expectations. For a compliance decision, this means the RTER's scope, content and follow-up remediation are supervisable items, and gaps identified in it feed back into the entity's Framework obligations rather than sitting with the third-party provider.

If the question is who is accountable for a cyber security control failure, the Framework routes the answer to its leadership and governance domain. The Framework establishes the documentation hierarchy of policies, standards and procedures, and the governance provisions cross-refer to cyber security governance, the cyber security policy and cyber security risk management as the controls that allocate ownership and oversight. The reader should therefore expect accountability to be evidenced at board/senior management level and through an approved policy set, not only at the level of individual technical controls.

When judging compliance with the Framework, the relevant test is not binary presence of controls but the maturity level achieved against SAMA's predefined maturity model. The Framework's documented policies, standards and procedures are the evidence base, and the maturity model is the measurement instrument SAMA applies to them. Practically, a member organisation should assess and report its position against the required maturity target, since falling short of the expected level is itself a supervisory finding even where controls nominally exist.

When assessing whether a member organisation's IT governance arrangements are adequate, the governance-level expectations cannot be evaluated in isolation from the operational layer they are meant to control. The IT Governance Framework sets the leadership, risk-identification and oversight structure, and points to IT operations management as the ongoing function that keeps applications and infrastructure delivering the agreed service levels to the business; both sit within the same SAMA technology governance regime and share defined terms such as Member Organisation. Practically, an assessment or gap analysis of governance controls should be evidenced through the operations-management controls it drives, and weaknesses in day-to-day IT operations are properly treated as governance findings, not purely technical ones.

If you are deciding whether a change-management control set is compliant, you must test it against cyber security requirements as well as IT governance requirements. The system change management domain requires an approved, monitored and periodically reviewed change policy and procedure, refreshed on significant IT-environment or legal/regulatory change, and it draws on the Cyber Security Framework's documentation hierarchy of policies, standards and procedures. Consequently, change-management documentation should be traceable to the cyber security policy/standard layer, and an uncontrolled or undocumented change is exposed as a finding under both regimes simultaneously.

For a bank licensing decision, cyber security readiness is part of the entry criteria rather than a post-authorisation matter. The Licensing Guidelines set out SAMA's process and minimum criteria for licensing banks and reference the Cyber Security Framework as the benchmark for the applicant's security policies, standards and procedures. An applicant should therefore be able to demonstrate a CSF-aligned control and documentation structure at application stage, and reviewers should treat CSF gaps as capable of affecting the licensing outcome, not merely supervisory follow-up.

When evaluating a proposed Digital-Only Bank, its technology and cybersecurity framework must be measured against the existing sector-wide framework rather than a bespoke standard. The Digital-Only Bank technology and cybersecurity expectations direct applicants to design and implement in line with the Cyber Security Framework (alongside national cybersecurity authority requirements), including performing a risk assessment at project inception so that cyber risks are either covered by existing CSF-based controls or newly built. The practical consequence is that a digital-only applicant carries the full CSF control expectations from project design onward, and evidence of early-stage risk assessment is a reviewable licensing input.

Where fraud has a technology vector, the counter-fraud and cyber security regimes must be applied together rather than assigned to separate owners. The Counter-Fraud Framework places responsibility on the Board, Executive and Senior Management for counter-fraud governance and direction, and references the Cyber Security Framework's policy, standard and procedure structure for the controls that underpin it. In practice, counter-fraud policies should be reconciled with the cyber security documentation set, and Board-level accountability under the counter-fraud regime extends to cyber-enabled fraud controls.

When deciding whether a bank's Shariah governance arrangements are merely best practice or an enforceable supervisory requirement, treat them as the latter: the Shariah Governance Framework is issued by SAMA under the authority of the Banking Control Law and its implementing rules, which is the parent statute for licensed banks. That anchoring means the framework's composition requirements — the Shariah committee, internal Shariah audit and related functions — carry the same supervisory and enforcement consequences as other prudential banking rules. For the reader, non-compliance is a supervisory breach against a licensed bank, not a reputational or self-regulatory matter, and the scope follows the Banking Control Law's definition of the institutions caught.

If the question is whether a bank can contract out responsibility for an outsourced material business activity, the answer is no: the Rules on Outsourcing are issued under the Banking Control Law, so the licensed bank remains the accountable regulated entity regardless of the service provider arrangement. The board-approved outsourcing policy and material-activity framework are therefore obligations of the licensee under its banking licence, not contractual terms negotiable with the vendor. Practically, board approval and the outsourcing governance framework must be evidenced to SAMA, and any supervisory action for outsourcing failures lands on the bank.

To determine whether an entity is in scope of the Banks Investment Rules, apply the Banking Control Law licensing test rather than any commercial notion of 'bank' — the Rules expressly limit themselves to banks licensed under that Law and to investments reported as net investments on the balance sheet. The parent statute therefore fixes both the perimeter and the enforcement basis. Consequently, non-bank financiers or SAMA-licensed entities under other regimes are not captured here, and the reader must confirm licensing status and balance-sheet classification before applying the investment limits.

When assessing which entities and which consolidation level the Basel capital requirements bite at, read the Guidance Note's scope provisions against the Banking Control Law, which supplies SAMA's authority to set minimum capital requirements for licensed banks. The CET1, Tier 1, buffer and Pillar 2 requirements described in the guidance are thus enforceable prudential obligations of the licensee, not optional Basel international standards. The reader should treat breaches of the capital ratios and buffers as supervisory breaches under the banking law, and use the licensing perimeter to decide group and solo application.

For a decision on what the AML/CTF function must report upward, read the board-reporting expectation together with the transaction monitoring section of the same Guide: monitoring is the operational source of the unusual and suspicious activity findings, and reporting is the governance channel through which obstacles in that monitoring must reach the board. Because both sit within the single SAMA AML/CTF Guide and support the risk-based approach, they form one obligation chain rather than two separable duties. The consequence is that purely statistical MI on alerts and STRs is insufficient — the institution must also escalate monitoring weaknesses and implementation challenges to the board.

When deciding how to discharge a suspicion trigger identified anywhere in the AML/CTF Guide, you must route the decision through the Guide's own Reporting of Suspicious Transactions section rather than treating detection and reporting as separate duties. The Guide's general compliance obligations expressly point to that section for the reporting procedure, including immediate notification to the SAFIU once suspicion arises and preparation of the supporting technical report. Practically, the internal cross-reference means the timing standard and report content in the reporting section govern, so any escalation or approval step that delays filing beyond the point of suspicion is non-compliant.

Before allowing a financial institution to rely on a third party's CDD, check that the reliance sits within the statutory CDD duty, not outside it. The Guide's third-party reliance provision operates against the AML Law obligation on financial institutions and DNFBPs to apply customer due diligence, with the Implementing Regulation specifying when and what measures apply. The consequence is that reliance shifts execution but not accountability: the relying institution remains answerable for the adequacy of the measures and for obtaining the underlying information, and the permitted class of third parties is limited to other FIs and DNFBP owners.

Treat this link with caution: the excerpts pair the definition of the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing with an agent banking contract-renewal article, and no obvious obligation chain connects the two on the face of the text. A defensible reading is that agent banking arrangements remain subject to the CTF regime, so banks renewing agent contracts must factor terrorism-financing risk into the comprehensive reassessment; but that is inferred, not stated in the quoted material. Do not rely on this link for a compliance position without verifying the primary text of both instruments to confirm an actual cross-reference.

If a bank appoints or renews a banking Agent, assess the arrangement under the Rules on Outsourcing as well as the Regulation of Agent Banking, since agency is a form of delegating activity to a third party. The Outsourcing Rules require board (or delegated authority) approval of an outsourcing policy covering Material business activities and a framework for managing all outsourcing arrangements, which supplies the governance layer the agent banking regime presupposes. Consequently, the periodic reassessment before contract renewal should be evidenced at the governance level required by the Outsourcing Rules, and an agent arrangement that is Material attracts the fuller approval and oversight obligations.

When a real estate refinance company delegates any part of its Real Estate Refinance Activity, the outsourcing section of these same Rules is the controlling internal standard, so the question is not whether a general outsourcing regime applies but what the Rules themselves permit. Because the link is internal to one instrument, the defined term Real Estate Refinance Activity carries through unchanged and fixes the scope of what may and may not be outsourced. The practical effect is that outsourcing approvals and restrictions must be read against the licensed activity definition, and core licensed functions cannot be contracted away merely because a third party performs them.

When applying the 25% large exposure limit, you cannot stop at the named legal counterparty: the LEX Rules direct you to the treatment of collective investment undertakings, securitisation vehicles and similar structures to decide whether exposure must be looked through to underlying assets or assigned to the structure itself (or to an unknown-client bucket). This is an internal cross-reference within the same instrument, so the look-through provisions are part of the same enforceable exposure-measurement chain, not optional guidance. Practically, exposures held through funds and SPVs must be identified and aggregated with direct exposures to the same counterparty before testing the limit.

Any calculation of minimum credit risk capital must be run together with the credit risk mitigation rules, because those rules set the only recognised ways an exposure amount or risk weight may be reduced for collateral, netting, guarantees or credit derivatives. The mitigation framework sits inside the same capital-adequacy instrument and operates as a conditional relief on the base requirement, with eligibility and operational conditions attached. For the reader, CRM benefit is not assumed: the base capital charge stands unless the mitigation conditions are demonstrably met.

Treat the collateralised-transactions provisions as one branch of the wider credit risk mitigation regime rather than a standalone rule: recognition of collateral depends on the general CRM preconditions (legal certainty, eligibility, no double-counting) as well as the branch-specific haircut and calculation method. The relationship is parent-to-component within the standardised approach, so the general conditions govern where the collateral rules are silent. Consequently, a transaction that meets the collateral mechanics but fails a general CRM condition yields no capital relief.

On-balance sheet netting is a recognised CRM technique only on the terms set by the credit risk mitigation framework, which lists it alongside collateral and guarantees and imposes the common legal-enforceability and monitoring conditions. The link is structural: the netting provisions are a sub-section of the CRM chapter and inherit its gating requirements. For a decision on whether assets and liabilities may be reported net for capital purposes, both the netting-specific criteria and the overarching CRM conditions must be satisfied.

Where reliance is placed on a guarantee or credit derivative, the CRM framework routes the assessment to the guarantee provisions, which govern eligibility of the protection provider, the operational conditions for recognition, and substitution of the protection provider's risk weight for the obligor's. This is an internal obligation chain within the same standardised-approach instrument, so the general CRM conditions and the guarantee-specific conditions apply cumulatively. The consequence is that unrecognised or non-conforming protection leaves the original obligor's risk weight in place, regardless of commercial expectations.

If you are deciding whether recognised credit protection can change a capital number, you cannot treat the guarantee/credit-derivative provisions as a standalone concession: they operate through the risk-parameter estimation rules, in this case PD. The guarantees and credit derivatives provisions permit recognition of protection only where the stated minimum operational conditions are met, and the effect is then expressed as a substitution or adjustment within the estimation of the obligor's default probability. Practically, a recognition decision must be evidenced against both limbs — eligibility/operational conditions and conformity with the PD estimation rules — and failing either means the exposure stands unmitigated for capital purposes.

When assessing counterparty credit risk capital, the CCR framework does not itself produce the number; it directs you to the exposure at default measure, which is the quantum the risk weight is applied to. The reference is an obligation chain within the same SAMA capital instrument: the CCR framework sets scope and approach eligibility, and EAD supplies the measurement input. For a decision, any CCR-related conclusion (netting recognition, collateral effect, approach choice) must be traced through to how it alters EAD, because that is where the capital consequence crystallises.

Where a bank is not using an internal models method for counterparty exposures, the CCR framework routes it to SA-CCR as the standardised measurement method, so the framework's requirements are only operable once SA-CCR is applied. The cross-reference also carries a floor that is expressed consistently across SA-CCR, the comprehensive approach within standardised credit risk, and the internal models method, indicating the framework intends a common minimum regardless of route. The practical consequence is that approach selection does not escape the floor, and a compliance review should confirm the floor has been applied under whichever method the bank has adopted.

A question about counterparty credit risk treatment resolves, in the standardised case, into the SA-CCR calculation rules, so the general CCR provisions should be read as scope and definition rather than as a self-contained method. The link is an internal cross-reference within the same SAMA capital instrument, and it carries the same minimum floor that applies across the standardised comprehensive approach and the internal models method. For the reader, this means a CCR determination is incomplete until SA-CCR application and the applicable floor have been checked.

Before applying foundation IRB parameters to any portfolio, the decision must first clear the IRB overview rules on asset classes and scope of adoption. The overview sets the expectation that once an IRB approach is taken up for part of an asset class it extends across all holdings in that class, which constrains selective or cherry-picked use of F-IRB. Consequently, a proposal to use F-IRB for a subset of exposures should be tested against the asset-class definitions and roll-out expectation in the overview, not merely against the F-IRB parameter rules.

If you are computing minimum credit risk capital on an exposure that is a securitisation position, you cannot stop at the general credit risk chapter — you must route the exposure into the securitisation chapter's hierarchy of approaches. Both sit inside the same SAMA capital adequacy instrument and share defined terms (notably the risk-class taxonomy distinguishing non-securitisation from securitisation credit spread exposures), so the securitisation chapter operates as the specific regime carving out of the general one. Practical consequence: classify the exposure first; a mis-classified securitisation position produces the wrong risk weight and an understated capital requirement, so confirm the treatment in the securitisation chapter's primary text before finalising the calculation.

When a bank applies the IRB treatment for purchased receivables, it needs to test whether the receivables pool is in substance a securitisation, because the two chapters lead to different RWA outcomes. The purchased receivables rules use the IRB asset-class list (including corporate purchased receivables), while the securitisation chapter supplies its own IRB route with KIRB, attachment/detachment points and the supervisory parameter — and KIRB itself is derived from the underlying IRB capital on the pool, creating a direct obligation chain between the two. Consequence for the reader: decide the characterisation before choosing the approach, and where a pool is tranched, expect the securitisation chapter to govern and to require the underlying IRB inputs as a precondition.

Before you can recognise collateral in a collateralised transaction, you must satisfy the eligibility, legal certainty and haircut conditions set out in the standardized approach credit risk mitigation chapter. The collateralised transactions provisions expressly point back to the simple and comprehensive approaches defined there, so the CRM chapter is the source of the operative conditions rather than a parallel option. Consequence: any capital relief claimed on collateral is conditional — if the CRM chapter's recognition criteria are not met, the exposure must be treated as uncollateralised.

For derivative and margined transactions where exposure fluctuates with market value, the collateralised transactions rules interact with SA-CCR: SA-CCR determines the counterparty credit risk exposure amount, and the collateral recognition rules determine how posted or received collateral is reflected. Both chapters sit in the same SAMA capital framework and share the defined transaction types (repo, reverse repo, securities lending and borrowing, margin lending, long settlement transactions), which fixes which measurement route applies. Consequence: identify the transaction type first, because the choice between the CRM collateral approaches and SA-CCR exposure measurement is driven by that classification, not by bank preference.

The decision here is how collateral flows into the loss estimate: under the foundation IRB approach, recognised collateral (eligible financial collateral plus the wider set of eligible IRB collateral) adjusts the supervisory LGD rather than being applied as a standalone exposure reduction. The comprehensive approach supplies the haircut mechanics and eligibility gate, while the LGD chapter governs how the resulting loss rate is derived and, for advanced IRB, how own estimates must reflect long-run default-weighted averages. Consequence: collateral relief is only as good as its LGD recognition — check both chapters together, since collateral that is ineligible or unsupported by loss data will not reduce the capital requirement.

When deciding which IRB risk-weight function and estimation requirements apply to a given book, start from the overview's categorisation of exposures and then apply the retail definition to test whether the exposure actually falls in that asset class. The overview establishes the exhaustive asset-class taxonomy for the IRB approach and expressly carries the retail definition as one of its components, so the retail criteria are not free-standing but operate as the scope gate within that taxonomy. Practically, a classification conclusion cannot be defended by reference to the retail criteria alone; the reader must confirm the exposure is not captured by the corporate, sovereign, bank or specialised lending definitions in the same overview.

If the bank has adopted IRB for an asset class, the overview's roll-out expectation means specialised lending within that class must also be brought under an IRB treatment, and the supervisory slotting criteria are the route where the bank cannot meet the own-estimate requirements. The link is an obligation chain: the overview sets scope and adoption expectations across asset classes, while the slotting provisions supply the prescribed risk weights and expected-loss treatment for project, object, commodities finance, income-producing real estate and HVCRE. For a decision, partial IRB adoption within an asset class is not the default position, and any specialised lending left outside own estimates should be evidenced as slotted rather than simply excluded.

Classifying a facility as HVCRE is not merely descriptive: it determines which capital treatment applies, because the supervisory slotting provisions set distinct risk weights and expected-loss outcomes for HVCRE separately from other specialised lending categories. The HVCRE definition, resting on higher loss-rate volatility in commercial real estate financing, is the defined term that triggers that separate column of the slotting framework. The reader should therefore resolve the HVCRE characterisation first, since a misclassification as ordinary income-producing real estate changes the applicable weights and understates capital.

Before applying the purchased-receivables RWA mechanics, confirm the pool qualifies as eligible purchased receivables under the definitional provisions, since that asset class is carved out of the general corporate category. The definition determines entry into the class; the IRB credit-risk instrument then supplies the consequences, including separate treatment of default risk and dilution risk, purchase price discounts and recognition of credit risk mitigants. The decision consequence is sequencing: an ineligible pool must be risk-weighted under the underlying obligor treatment instead, and dilution risk cannot be ignored once the receivables treatment is engaged.

The connection here appears to run through the shared disclosure and scope trigger applying to banks using either foundation or advanced IRB, so a bank on F-IRB does not escape the purchased-receivables RWA requirements or the associated reporting. In substance, F-IRB governs which parameters the bank may estimate itself versus take from supervisory values, and those parameter sources then feed the purchased-receivables calculations. Because the linkage is drawn from overlapping scope language rather than an explicit cross-reference in the operative text, the reader should verify the primary provisions to confirm precisely which F-IRB parameter constraints apply to receivables pools.

If you are deciding whether a collateral arrangement or guarantee can reduce capital for an IRB-treated exposure, you cannot answer from the CRM rules alone — recognition operates by adjusting the IRB risk components rather than by a standalone deduction. The CRM chapter cross-refers to the PD/LGD/EAD/M framework (substitution of the guarantor's PD, LGD adjustment for eligible collateral, and splitting covered from uncovered portions), and some recognitions, such as internally rated guarantors under the foundation IRB approach, are expressly subject to SAMA's discretion. Practically, a CRM benefit is only defensible if the bank holds the relevant IRB approval, meets the qualification standards for the exposure type, and can evidence the parameter treatment; otherwise the mitigation cannot be recognised as claimed.

When determining whether a given mitigant reduces risk-weighted assets, the applicable rule set depends on which credit risk approach the exposure sits in — the CRM chapter contains a distinct standardised-approach track covering collateralised transactions, on-balance-sheet netting, and guarantees and credit derivatives. That track is drafted by reference to the standardised approach's risk-weight and risk-class definitions, since recognition there generally works through substitution of the protection provider's risk weight or haircut-adjusted exposure values. The consequence is that a bank on the standardised approach must apply the standardised eligibility criteria and haircuts, and cannot import IRB-style recognition; mismatching the two tracks would misstate RWA.

Before applying any securitisation capital treatment, you must first settle the scope-of-application question — which entities and which consolidation perimeter the framework binds — because the guidance note on scope and minimum credit risk capital requirements sets that perimeter and defines the CET1/Tier 1 ratios, buffers and Pillar 2 add-ons that securitisation RWA ultimately feed. The securitisation chapter (including SEC-SA, resecuritisation treatment and the STC-based alternative treatment) is therefore a downstream computation within that same minimum capital obligation, not a separate regime. In practice, resolve the consolidation and approach-eligibility questions first; the securitisation hierarchy you may use follows from them, and an error there flows straight through to the reported capital ratios.

Treat the standardised approach as a component of, not an alternative to, the minimum credit risk capital obligation: the enforceable requirement is to hold minimum capital against credit risk, and the standardised approach supplies the default method and shared defined terms (including the risk-class taxonomy) for computing it. Exposures for which the bank lacks supervisory approval for an internal model fall back into this approach by operation of the minimum-capital rules. For a compliance decision this means standardised-approach outcomes must be read against the overarching minimum ratio requirement, and any approach change or scope carve-out needs to be justified under that parent obligation.

This link matters when the same obligor or issuer generates both banking-book credit exposure and trading-book positions: the IRB approach governs default risk capital in the banking book, while the DRC requirement captures jump-to-default risk for trading-book instruments not captured by credit spread shocks. The cross-reference reflects shared default-risk concepts — notably the use of IRB-derived loss-given-default and default-probability inputs and IRB approval status when characterising pools and exposures. The practical consequence is that the banking-book/trading-book boundary determines which capital charge applies, and parameter definitions should be applied consistently across the two so that default risk is neither double-counted nor omitted; verify the primary text on which inputs may be carried across.

When deciding whether a bank may use its own risk parameters for a given exposure, the A-IRB designation is what unlocks internal LGD estimation, so the two provisions must be read together rather than separately. The advanced IRB provisions expressly rely on the LGD definition and on the bank's ability to estimate default-weighted average loss rates given default reliably, meaning LGD is a dependent parameter whose permissible source is fixed by the approach the bank is approved to use. Practically, a reviewer confirming A-IRB status must also confirm that the LGD estimation and reliability conditions are satisfied; failure on the LGD side undermines the A-IRB treatment and the resulting RWA and disclosure template population.

If an exposure is risk-weighted under the supervisory slotting criteria rather than by internal parameters, the expected loss calculation and the provisions comparison must follow the slotting-specific route, so the two chapters cannot be applied in isolation. The expected loss chapter governs the general IRB method for computing EL and reconciling it with provisions, while the slotting approach sets separate EL outcomes for specialized lending categories, and the general chapter cross-refers to that treatment. For a decision, first classify the exposure (specialized lending under slotting versus other IRB exposures), because that classification determines which EL figure feeds the provisions shortfall or excess adjustment to capital.

Where a bank is on the foundation IRB approach it does not set LGD itself, so the operative question becomes which collateral is recognized and how it adjusts supervisory LGD — a determination made by the eligible collateral rules in the other instrument. The LGD provisions point to the collateral recognition framework, which extends the standardized approach list of eligible financial collateral with additional eligible IRB collateral. The consequence is that an F-IRB credit risk mitigation decision must be tested against the eligibility and operational conditions in the collateral instrument before any LGD reduction is claimed; collateral that fails those conditions yields no LGD benefit.

The linkage matters when quantifying exposure on off-balance-sheet and undrawn items: the credit conversion factor is the mechanism that converts a committed or contingent amount into the exposure at default used for RWA and for defaulted-exposure reporting. EAD is therefore not a freestanding input but the output of applying the prescribed or estimated CCF to the relevant facility amount. In practice, any challenge to the CCF applied (supervisory versus own estimates, and the facility classification behind it) flows directly through to reported EAD, capital requirements and the stock-of-defaulted-exposures disclosures. Note the excerpts here are imperfectly aligned, so the reader should verify the specific CCF and EAD paragraphs in the primary text before relying on them.

For derivative and counterparty credit risk positions, replacement cost is a core component of the exposure measure, so determining EAD requires first establishing RC on the netting set. The framework also prescribes a conservative fallback where replacement cost cannot be determined, substituting notional amounts and adjusting the multiplier, which directly inflates the resulting exposure. The decision consequence is that data gaps on RC are not neutral: they force the conservative proxy and a higher EAD, so a bank asserting a lower counterparty exposure must be able to evidence a properly calculated replacement cost.

When deciding how an exposure is capitalised, the boundary question comes first: credit risk minimum capital rules apply to banking book positions, while positions assigned to trading desks under the Trading Book Policy Statement fall into the market risk regime and attract credit spread risk charges instead of (or alongside) credit risk charges. The link reflects that both sit within SAMA's Basel-aligned capital framework and share the defined risk classes used to allocate instruments. Practically, the reader must confirm the desk structure and TPS designation before selecting the credit risk treatment, since misclassification changes the applicable capital calculation and the boundary-breach consequences.

For a decision on capital charges, this link signals that credit-related risk is capitalised in two distinct ways depending on book allocation: credit risk minimum capital requirements for banking book exposures, and credit spread risk within the market risk standardised approach for trading book instruments. Both instruments use the same defined risk classes, so the cross-reference is a definitional and scope bridge rather than an independent obligation. The reader should therefore determine book placement first, then apply only the corresponding methodology to avoid double-counting or a capital shortfall.

If a bank is using the market risk standardised approach, the sensitivities-based method is one of its mandatory components, alongside the default risk charge and residual risk add-on, so it cannot be selected or omitted in isolation. The relationship is hierarchical: the standardised approach is the parent methodology and the sensitivities-based method supplies the delta, vega and curvature calculations for instruments held in trading desks. Note also that the simplified standardised approach is a separate, permission-dependent route, so the reader must confirm which approach the bank is authorised to use before applying these calculations.

The residual risk add-on is a top-up, not an alternative: it applies to instruments with exotic or other residual risks that the sensitivities-based method does not adequately capture, so a bank cannot treat a position as fully capitalised once the sensitivities charge is computed. Both components share the defined risk classes of the market risk framework and sit under the same standardised approach. For the reader, this means screening in-scope trading book instruments for residual risk features in addition to running the sensitivities calculation, otherwise the market risk capital requirement will be understated.

The sensitivities-based method as issued by SAMA is a domestic implementation of the Basel market risk standards, so interpretive questions about scope, risk classes and trading desk allocation should be read against the Basel Framework text that SAMA has adopted. The citation establishes the source hierarchy: Basel supplies the methodology, but SAMA's issuance is the enforceable requirement in the Kingdom, including any national discretions or calibrations. The reader should apply the SAMA text as binding and use Basel only as interpretive support, verifying the SAMA primary text where the two appear to diverge.

When computing the standardised default risk capital charge, you cannot treat it as a free-standing calculation: the framework's liquidity horizon concept governs the holding-period assumption applied to positions, so the same defined term drives both the sensitivities-based and default risk components. The reference means the DRC provisions must be read together with the liquidity horizon definition rather than against a bank's own internal holding-period view. Practically, a capital submission that uses a bespoke horizon for jump-to-default exposures is not compliant unless it matches the horizon specified in the market risk text, which should be verified in the primary articles.

For exposures held through funds, indices or other pooled vehicles, the decision on how to measure jump-to-default risk is determined by the look-through approach, which the DRC provisions invoke. The link signals an obligation chain: the DRC charge is calculated on the underlying constituent obligors where look-through is required and available, not on the vehicle as a single name. The consequence is that failure to look through can understate the default risk capital requirement and would be treated as a misapplication of the standardised approach.

The framework lists default risk among the risks that must be captured for market risk capital purposes, which is the point at which the default risk charge and value-at-risk style measurement interact. The reference matters for the choice of methodology: VaR-based internal measurement does not displace the separate default risk capital requirement, because jump-to-default is expressly identified as a risk that credit spread modelling may not capture. For a decision, treat the default risk charge as additive and not substitutable by a VaR output unless the primary text expressly permits it; confirm the relevant provisions before relying on any offset.

The default risk capital requirement is a constituent component of the standardised approach, not an alternative to it, so any assessment of standardised capital adequacy is incomplete without it. This is a hierarchy relationship: the standardised approach provisions set the overall structure and the DRC section specifies one of its mandatory inputs. Consequently, a bank applying the standardised approach must calculate and report the default risk charge alongside the other components, and cannot scope it out on materiality grounds absent an express exemption.

The residual risk add-on is defined in the market risk terminology instrument and operates as one of the three summed components of the standardised approach capital requirement set out in the market risk rules. The link is a definitional and structural cross-reference across the two instruments: the defined risk classes and add-on concept in one document are given calculation effect in the other. For a compliance decision, the standardised capital figure must include the add-on for instruments carrying residual risks, and the definitions instrument should be used to determine which exposures fall within scope.

If you are validating a bank's counterparty credit risk capital numbers, you cannot assess the exposure-at-default figure in isolation: for derivative and long-settlement transactions the EAD is built from a replacement cost element plus a potential future exposure component, and the PFE add-on rules supply the aggregate add-on and multiplier that drive that second element. The two instruments therefore sit in one obligation chain — the EAD definition sets what must be measured, the PFE add-on provisions set how part of it is calculated. Practically, an error or unapproved simplification in the add-on aggregation or multiplier treatment flows straight through to reported EAD and risk-weighted assets, so both texts must be checked together.

When deciding which EAD measurement basis a bank may lawfully use for counterparty credit risk, the internal models method is the conditional alternative: it is expressly a method for estimating EAD and is available only where SAMA approval has been obtained. The link is a hierarchy and permission point within the same framework — the EAD requirement is the obligation, IMM is a permitted route to satisfy it subject to supervisory authorisation and the associated model conditions and floors. If approval is absent, lapsed, or limited to certain portfolios, the bank must fall back to the non-model approach for the affected exposures.

For a decision on how a bank must compute derivative EAD absent internal model approval, SA-CCR is the standardised default and is cross-referenced from the EAD provisions, including the shared floor that is mirrored across SA-CCR, the comprehensive approach under the standardised credit risk rules, and IMM. The relationship is a defined-term and cross-reference one: EAD is the quantity to be reported, SA-CCR prescribes one prescribed method for arriving at it. Consequence: confirm which method the exposure falls under before testing the calculation, and check that the common floor has been applied consistently whichever route is used.

If a bank holds purchased receivables under the IRB approach, the decision point is that capital must be held for two distinct risks, not one: default risk on the obligors and dilution risk arising from reductions in the receivable amount through credit notes, offsets, returns and similar events. The RWA rules for purchased receivables carry a separate dilution risk computation, so the defined term governs the scope of a standalone capital charge within that same framework. A bank that capitalises only default risk on a purchased receivables pool is under-capitalised unless the applicable exemption conditions in the primary text are met.

These are the parent rule and its sub-component: the purchased receivables RWA provisions set out the overall treatment (default risk, dilution risk, purchase price discounts, recognition of credit risk mitigants) and the dilution risk RWA provisions govern one of those limbs. Because the two appear in separate instruments here, confirm which document and version is the operative source for the reporting period before relying on either, since the framework text has been reissued. The practical consequence is that a dilution risk assessment must be read against the full purchased receivables treatment — in particular how purchase price discounts and mitigants interact with the charge — rather than applied standalone.

When a bank decides how to capitalise commodity exposures in the trading book, the sensitivities-based method is the calculation engine and commodity risk is one of the prescribed risk classes fed into it. The link is definitional and hierarchical: the market risk framework fixes a closed list of risk classes, and the sensitivities-based method applies delta, vega and curvature charges to instruments within each class. Practically, commodity positions cannot be capitalised under a bespoke bucket — they must be mapped to the commodity risk class and run through the sensitivities-based method's prescribed risk weights and correlations.

For equity trading book positions, the decision of which charge applies is resolved by reading the two together: equity risk is a defined risk class, and the sensitivities-based method is the mechanism that converts equity sensitivities into a capital number. The relationship rests on the shared defined term "risk class" in the market risk framework, which constrains how instruments are allocated. The consequence is that equity exposures must be bucketed and weighted under the sensitivities-based method rather than treated outside the standardised risk-class taxonomy.

FX risk is one of the market risks subject to capital requirements, and this link tells you it is captured through the sensitivities-based method's risk-class structure. Note the scope point that matters for the decision: FX risk (like commodity risk) is captured for banking book as well as trading book instruments, whereas most other listed risks are trading-book only. So a bank cannot exclude banking book FX positions from the market risk calculation simply because they sit outside trading desks; verify the precise scope wording in the primary text before drawing the perimeter.

This is a parent–component relationship: the sensitivities-based method is one of three additive elements of the standardised approach capital requirement, alongside the default risk capital requirement and the residual risk add-on. Deciding the standardised approach charge therefore cannot stop at the sensitivities-based method output — the three components are simply summed. The practical consequence is completeness: a calculation that omits DRC or RRAO understates the required capital, even if the sensitivities-based method has been applied correctly.

The default risk capital requirement sits inside the market risk standardised approach but reaches across to the credit risk framework, so the two regimes must be read together when capitalising jump-to-default exposure on trading book instruments. The citation matters because it drives consistency of inputs and treatment between the credit risk rules and the DRC component rather than allowing a standalone market risk methodology. For a compliance decision, check that trading book default exposures are neither omitted nor double-counted against banking book credit risk charges, and confirm the exact cross-referenced provisions in the primary text before relying on a specific alignment.

When deciding how a position is capitalised, first settle which risk regime it falls under: the credit risk minimum capital rules and the market risk IMA are separate calculation frameworks under the same SAMA capital hierarchy, and the market risk text cross-refers to credit-risk concepts (credit spread risk classes, counterparty credit risk under SA-CCR versus IMM). The link matters because RWA and capital reporting must be subdivided by approach, so a bank using internal models for market risk does not thereby model counterparty or banking-book credit exposures. Practically, confirm the boundary allocation of each exposure before applying IMA outputs, and check the credit risk text directly for the treatment of counterparty and securitisation spread exposures.

Treat the IMA provisions as a subordinate part of the market risk framework, not a free-standing permission: the parent instrument sets the minimum capital requirements for market risk and supersedes earlier SAMA market risk circulars, and the IMA is one of the measurement methodologies it authorises, with its own qualitative disclosure requirements. Any reliance on internal models therefore inherits the scope, supervisory approval and disclosure obligations of the parent framework. For a decision, read the IMA conditions only within the parent's scope and effective-date provisions.

The two approaches are alternatives at desk level but not mutually exclusive at bank level, so the decision is which portfolios sit where. The framework permits a choice between the standardised approach and the IMA, while requiring that portfolios in desks not eligible for or not using the IMA be capitalised under the standardised approach. Consequently a bank on internal models must still maintain standardised approach capability and calculation for the residual perimeter, and should verify the eligibility conditions in the primary text before assuming IMA coverage.

The trading desk is the unit of account for IMA permission, so desk definition drives the capital outcome. The IMA provisions require a bank using internal models to also compute the standardised approach capital requirement for each IMA-eligible desk as a standalone regulatory portfolio, with no offsetting across desks. That means desk boundaries cannot be drawn for convenience: how positions are assigned determines both eligibility and the parallel standardised calculation that must be produced.

Before applying IMA methodology, establish scope: the framework runs a sequential test that first identifies eligible trading desks, then determines which of those desks are in scope for the IMA, and then which risk factors within them may enter the expected shortfall model. The IMA disclosure and calculation obligations attach only to that in-scope perimeter, with non-modellable risk factors and out-of-scope desks handled separately. For a decision, confirm the scope determination is documented and current, since a change in desk or risk-factor eligibility shifts capital to the standardised approach.

If you are sizing capital for a credit exposure, you cannot settle it from the credit risk chapter alone where the position also sits in the trading book: the default risk charge for non-securitisation instruments is set out separately and is referenced from the credit risk requirements. Both sit within the same SAMA capital framework and share the defined risk-class taxonomy (including credit spread risk, non-securitisation), so the boundary between banking-book credit RWA and market-risk default risk capital is a definitional one, not a matter of choice. Practically, classify the exposure first, then apply the correct charge, and check the non-securitisation DRC text before concluding that the credit risk treatment is exhaustive.

For correlation trading portfolio positions, the credit risk capital requirements point outward to the default risk capital treatment for securitisations in the CTP, so a determination made only under the credit risk chapter is incomplete. The link is a cross-reference inside one capital framework, resting on the shared risk-class definitions that separate securitisation (CTP) from non-securitisation and non-CTP securitisation exposures; the CTP rules themselves further build on the non-CTP securitisation methodology. The consequence is that CTP classification drives which computation applies, and the CTP provisions must be read alongside both the credit risk chapter and the non-CTP securitisation default risk rules.

When deciding whether an exposure attracts credit risk capital or market risk capital, note that the market risk scope expressly captures credit spread and default risk for trading book instruments, and FX and commodities risk even outside the trading book. That scope provision is referenced from the credit risk requirements because both derive from the same SAMA capital framework and the same enumerated risk classes, so the classification of the instrument, not its label, determines the applicable charge. Read the market risk scope text before concluding that a position is captured only by credit risk requirements, since some positions attract charges under both regimes.

Where a bank calculates counterparty credit risk exposure using the Internal Models Method, the CCR requirements are not self-contained: they reference the IMM provisions, which govern how EAD is modelled and how the resulting RWA are reported and explained. This is an obligation chain within one capital framework, where the general CCR rules set the requirement and the IMM chapter sets the conditions and disclosure expectations for that particular measurement approach. For a decision on derivatives or SFT exposures, confirm whether IMM is being used and, if so, apply the IMM conditions and reporting requirements in addition to the general CCR rules.

Cross-product netting recognition for regulatory capital is available only within the Internal Models Method, so the netting analysis cannot be run independently of the bank's approved measurement approach. The cross-product netting rules are expressly framed as applying to netting across SFTs, or across SFTs and OTC derivatives, for capital computation under IMM, which requires prior supervisory approval to use IMM for EAD. The consequence is that if IMM approval is absent or the product set falls outside the stated scope, cross-product netting benefits should not be assumed; verify both the approval status and the scope wording in the primary text.

When computing capital for a derivatives or securities-financing book, a bank cannot settle the credit risk charge in isolation: the credit risk rules point across to the CVA framework, so the same counterparty exposures also attract a separate CVA risk charge under the basic or standardised approach. Both sit within SAMA's adoption of the Basel capital standard, and the credit-risk text uses risk-class definitions that are shared with the market/CVA risk taxonomy. Practically, a capital adequacy assessment or a supervisory submission that addresses credit risk RWA but omits the SA-CVA/BA-CVA computation for the same exposures is incomplete.

Deciding the capital treatment of undrawn commitments, guarantees, letters of credit and similar contingents requires reading the credit risk rules together with the off-balance sheet provisions, which convert those items into credit exposure equivalents via credit conversion factors before risk weighting. The OBS provisions are an operative step inside the same credit risk capital chain, not a separate regime. For the reader, this means an exposure measure built only on on-balance sheet assets understates RWA; the CCF step must be applied first, then the credit risk weights.

If you are determining which version of the credit risk rules applies, note that the Basel III post-crisis reforms document expressly identifies the credit risk minimum capital requirements as the governing calculation source within SAMA's Basel adoption, including its glossary references to earlier SAMA capital guidance. The reforms instrument is the umbrella framework; the credit risk document supplies the detailed calculation obligations it points to. Consequently, interpret the credit risk text as subject to the scope, transitional and output-floor settings established by the reforms framework, and cite both when justifying an RWA methodology.

Where a bank has SAMA permission to use internal ratings, the credit risk capital rules direct it to the IRB framework for the affected portfolios, covering default risk, dilution risk on purchased receivables and recognition of credit risk mitigants. The two documents are alternative but linked limbs of the same credit risk capital obligation, with the standardised approach still relevant for non-permissioned portfolios and for floor purposes. The reader should therefore confirm approach eligibility portfolio by portfolio rather than assuming a single method applies bank-wide.

For derivative and margined counterparty exposures, the exposure amount feeding the credit risk capital calculation is determined under SA-CCR (or the internal models method), and the credit risk text is expressly cross-referenced in setting the applicable floor alongside the comprehensive approach to collateral. The link is an explicit provision-level cross-reference within the same Basel-derived capital regime, so the two must be read as one continuous measurement chain. In practice, a counterparty credit risk capital number is only defensible if the SA-CCR exposure calculation and the credit risk floor provisions have both been applied consistently.

When deciding how to compute counterparty credit risk RWA, the credit risk minimum capital rules are the governing framework and IMM is one of the two permitted computation routes sitting under them, alongside SA-CCR.
