Because the credit risk framework expressly calls up IMM and requires RWA and capital to be subdivided between SA-CCR and IMM, the choice of method is not free-standing but a scope election within the parent capital rules — and IMM use is conditional on SAMA's supervisory acceptance of the model. Practically, a bank cannot read the IMM provisions in isolation: eligibility, permission and reporting subdivision all flow from the credit risk capital chapter.

If the bank uses IMM for counterparty exposures, it still has to answer separately how CVA risk capital is calculated, and the stand-alone CVA capital component is where that computation lands. The link reflects that IMM outputs feed the exposure measures used in the CVA charge, with SCVAc being the per-counterparty building block before eligible hedges and correlation effects are recognised. The consequence is that an IMM permission does not by itself dispose of the CVA capital question — the CVA calculation must be run and evidenced on its own terms.

For any decision about total capital against derivative and securities financing exposures, the CVA framework is an additional charge layered on top of the counterparty credit risk RWA computed under the credit risk minimum capital rules, not a substitute for it. The credit risk framework cross-refers to CVA because the two share the same counterparty exposure inputs while addressing different risks — default risk versus mark-to-market losses from counterparty credit spread and other risk-factor moves. Readers scoping a capital calculation should treat both charges as cumulative and confirm which counterparties fall within the CVA scope.

Whether a counterparty is a Qualifying Central Counterparty is a gating classification that changes the risk weighting and CVA treatment of cleared exposures under the credit risk minimum capital rules. The QCCP definition is referenced from the credit risk framework precisely because preferential treatment for trade and default fund exposures is conditional on that status being satisfied and maintained. In practice the bank must document the QCCP determination for each clearing relationship before applying any concessional weighting, and re-test it if the CCP's status changes.

The Q17 template is the supervisory reporting vehicle through which the credit risk capital calculations are submitted to SAMA, so the substantive rules and the reporting form must be reconciled line by line. The reference means the definitions and risk-class breakdowns used in the credit risk framework carry into how exposures are presented in Q17, including the required split between standardised and model-based approaches. For a compliance decision, any change in calculation methodology or counterparty classification has a corresponding reporting consequence that should be checked against the current template version.

When determining what a bank must publish, treat the Basel III post-crisis reforms package as the source of the capital measurement rules and the Pillar 3 framework as the disclosure obligation that reports them. The reforms document's glossary points to SAMA's capital adoption instruments (including the credit risk minimum capital requirements), which are the same defined measures the Pillar 3 templates require banks to present and signpost. Practically, a change in how a capital number is calculated under the reforms flows directly into the content and comparability of the Pillar 3 report, so the two must be read together rather than as separate compliance streams.

If you are deciding how to complete or review the RWA overview template, the governing formatting, frequency and retrospective-disclosure rules sit in the Pillar 3 framework, not in the template itself. OV1 (and related comparison templates such as CMS1/CMS2) is one of the prescribed disclosure requirements operating within that framework's general provisions on reporting periods, prior-period data and signposting. Consequently, a template-level judgement — for example whether a prior-period column may be omitted — must be resolved against the framework's general rules before it is defensible.

For scoping decisions, the Pillar 3 framework is the parent instrument that sets who discloses and at what level of consolidation, while Table OVA is a specific qualitative disclosure it mandates on risk strategy, governance and risk appetite. Because the framework directs that disclosures be made at the consolidated level unless SAMA specifies otherwise, the OVA narrative must describe board and senior management risk management for the consolidated group, not a single legal entity. This means a group-level, board-approved risk narrative is the compliant unit of disclosure unless a specific SAMA carve-out applies.

When converting off-balance-sheet commitments into exposure amounts, the credit conversion factor provisions cannot be applied standalone — they operate as a component of the standardised credit risk capital requirements. Both sit within the same SAMA capital instrument and share its defined terms (including the risk class taxonomy), so the CCF outcome feeds directly into the exposure base to which SCRE risk weights are applied. In practice, any classification or CCF judgement should be validated against the SCRE definitions and asset class rules rather than resolved in isolation.

Where regulatory exposure amounts differ from accounting carrying values, the credit risk capital rules supply the measurement basis and Template LI2 is the mechanism for explaining the resulting gaps to users. The link is a reconciliation chain: exposure amounts determined under the standardised credit risk requirements (net of scope-of-consolidation differences reported separately in LI1) are the figures LI2 must bridge back to the financial statements. For the reader, this means a decision to apply a particular regulatory exposure treatment carries a paired obligation to explain that treatment as a reconciling item.

When computing regulatory capital on any exposure that arises from a traditional or synthetic securitisation, the reader cannot rely on the general Basel III capital provisions alone but must route the exposure through the dedicated securitisation chapter. The Basel III guidance document expressly points to the securitisation scope and definitions as the operative test for which transactions fall in that framework, so the two sit in one obligation chain under the same SAMA capital regime rather than as alternatives. Practically, classify the transaction against the securitisation scope first; that classification then determines which capital treatment, deductions and provisioning interactions apply.

For market risk capital, the standardised approach is not an optional method to be weighed against internal models: the parent market risk framework directs all banks, D-SIBs and non D-SIBs alike, to compute the charge on that basis. The standardised approach chapter is therefore the implementing detail of the framework's headline requirement, and the framework also supersedes earlier SAMA market risk circulars. The consequence is that legacy methodologies or prior circular-based positions cannot be defended; the standardised calculation is the baseline compliance obligation.

Before populating the counterparty credit risk collateral template, read the FAQ, because it settles scope questions that the template itself leaves open, including that reported collateral is the total posted and received rather than only the portion recognised for risk mitigation, and it relaxes the requirement to show prior-period data points in defined circumstances. The FAQ is interpretive guidance issued under the same Pillar 3 disclosure instrument, so it governs how the template is completed rather than creating a separate obligation. A disclosure that is technically consistent with the template but inconsistent with the FAQ reading is still a reporting defect.

A finance company selling or transferring a residential mortgage portfolio to the SRC should treat the transaction as occurring inside the Finance Companies Control Law perimeter, not outside it, so licensing conditions, provisioning duties and SAMA supervisory powers continue to bite on the originator. The link is inferred from the Law and its Implementing Regulation being the parent authority for finance companies and for the provisioning treatment of their exposures, including how portfolio disposals affect required allocations. Treat this as a framing point rather than a cited cross-reference and verify the primary text of the SRC instrument for any express carve-out or specific transfer conditions before relying on it.

The connection is thematic rather than a direct cross-reference: sharing residential real estate finance data with the credit bureau sits in the credit information regime, while the AML Law governs customer due diligence, record keeping and suspicious transaction reporting, and the two only intersect where bureau data is used to verify or corroborate customer information. Do not read the data-sharing instrument as a lawful basis for AML purposes, nor as discharging any AML obligation, since each regime has its own defined terms, consent conditions and permitted-use limits. Because this link is ambiguous, confirm against the primary text of both instruments before relying on bureau data in an AML control or before treating an AML purpose as a permitted use of shared finance data.

Treat these as two expressions of the same licensing and prudential regime for finance companies rather than as independent rule sets, so a compliance position should be built on both and reconciled where wording differs. Both derive from the Finance Companies Control Law, with the Executive Regulation operationalising the statutory framework that the articles set out, meaning defined terms and scope limits carry across. Because the relationship is inferred rather than stated, the reader should confirm which instrument is the current, in-force version and whether one supersedes or amends the other before relying on a specific article number.

When a finance company performs its enterprise-wide risk work, the prudential risk-management duties under the Executive Regulation and the AML/CFT/CPF business risk assessment obligations must be satisfied on their own terms, not merged into a single exercise. The link is conceptual: both require documented, periodic assessment and board-level oversight of risk, but they sit in different regimes with different parent laws (finance companies control versus the AML Law and its implementing rules), so the risk taxonomy, triggers and reporting lines differ. Practically, a market/credit risk review will not discharge the money-laundering, terrorist-financing and proliferation-financing assessment duty; verify the primary text of each, as this association is inferred.

Read the circular prohibiting promissory notes for credit card financing as a specific constraint layered onto the general credit and consumer-protection duties applicable to entities regulated under the Executive Regulation. The general regulation sets the licensing and conduct framework; the circular narrows permitted security/collateral practice for a defined product, and the more specific instruction governs where the two touch. For a decision on taking promissory notes in card financing, the circular controls, and the reader should confirm the circular's addressees and effective date since the cross-reference here is inferred.

If the question concerns BNPL exposure limits, the operative ceiling comes from the circular raising the per-customer limit in the BNPL Rules, not from the general finance-companies framework. The Executive Regulation supplies the underlying licensing and supervisory regime, while the BNPL Rules and this amending circular are the specific, later instrument governing the quantitative cap; note also that BNPL uses its own defined term for the person financed, which does not automatically align with AML customer definitions. Apply the amended limit, and verify the circular's stated effective date and any conditions, as the linkage here is inferred.

Governance arrangements designed to meet the Executive Regulation should be tested against the governance principles circular, which imposes its own self-assessment, approved action plan and submission deadline to SAMA. The Executive Regulation establishes the baseline organisational and board requirements for finance companies; the circular adds a supervisory compliance step with a defined reporting channel and timeframe, so satisfying the regulation alone does not discharge the circular. Because the connection is inferred, confirm from the primary text whether the circular applies to the reader's licence category and whether the submission deadline has passed or been extended.

When deciding what a bank must publish for its securitisation activity, the overview of risk-weighted assets is not a standalone figure: it is the summary layer that the securitisation originator/sponsor template disaggregates. Both sit in the same SAMA Pillar 3 disclosure framework, so the RWA totals shown at overview level must reconcile with the banking-book securitisation exposures and capital charges reported where the bank acts as originator or sponsor. Practically, a reviewer checking disclosure completeness or internal consistency should read the two together and treat an unexplained mismatch as a disclosure defect rather than a presentational choice. Note the supplied excerpt text does not visibly track the overview template, so verify the primary disclosure section before relying on the exact scope.

For a decision on which figures drive the headline Pillar 3 metrics, the key metrics template draws its capital and RWA inputs from the overview of risk-weighted assets, so the two must be prepared as a single chain rather than independently. Both are disclosure requirements of the same SAMA Pillar 3 framework, which fixes the hierarchy: the overview template is the detailed RWA build-up and the key metrics template is its condensed, ratio-level expression. Consequently, any restatement or reclassification in the RWA overview flows through to the reported capital and leverage ratios and must be reflected in both templates for the same reporting period. The excerpt provided appears to relate to other comparison templates, so confirm against the primary text.

If a bank wants to use own estimates of loss given default, exposure at default and maturity, the advanced approach cannot be read alone: it operates inside the general internal ratings-based framework, which sets the shared rules on eligibility, supervisory approval, credit risk mitigation and the recognition of guarantees and credit derivatives. The advanced approach is one of the two recognition routes the general IRB provisions expressly contemplate, the other being the foundation route using supervisory loss given default values. The consequence is that permission to use own estimates does not displace the general IRB conditions, and any mitigation benefit claimed must still satisfy the framework-level requirements.

For a bank on the foundation route, the supervisory loss given default values and the wider list of eligible internal ratings-based collateral are conferred by, and bounded by, the general IRB framework rather than by a separate regime. The general provisions identify the foundation approach as the option for banks using supervisory loss given default values and set the corresponding treatment of guarantees and credit derivatives. Practically, collateral or protection recognised under the foundation approach must meet the framework-level eligibility and operational conditions, and any deviation requires reference back to the general IRB rules and SAMA approval.

When classifying retail exposures, the specific retail provisions apply only within the general internal ratings-based framework, which governs approval scope, parameter estimation and credit risk mitigation. This matters beyond retail lending itself: the framework treats a pool as an internal ratings-based pool only where the bank holds approval to apply the approach to the underlying exposure type, so retail approval status directly determines the capital methodology available for securitisations of retail assets. A reader deciding on a retail or retail-backed securitisation treatment must therefore first confirm the scope of the bank's IRB permission under the general provisions.

When assessing whether a financier may differentiate between customers in product terms or bundled insurance, treat the equality circular as a supervisory overlay on the consumer financing regime rather than a standalone rule. The circular's scope is bounded by the Regulations for Consumer Financing, which define Borrower and limit the regime to financing for purposes unconnected with commercial or professional activity, so the non-discrimination expectation attaches to those consumer products (personal, car, home improvement and similar SAMA-approved financing). Practically, apply the circular to in-scope consumer exposures and confirm separately how commercial or professional-purpose financing is treated; as the link is inferred, verify the circular's own stated scope in the primary text.

For any question about what a financier may charge a borrower, read the fees and administrative costs clarification together with the Regulations for Consumer Financing rather than in isolation. The clarification operates as SAMA guidance interpreting the cost and charge provisions of the consumer financing regime, whose defined terms (Borrower, Financing for non-commercial, non-professional purposes) set the population of contracts to which any fee cap or permitted-cost reading applies. The consequence is that a fee treatment permitted for commercial financing cannot be assumed for consumer financing, and vice versa; because the link is inferred, confirm the clarification's stated addressees and scope in the primary text.

If a bank is deciding whether it may share or obtain customer credit data, it must satisfy both the Credit Information Law and the banking secrecy and supervisory duties owed under the Banking Control Law. The Credit Information Law defines Member as an entity party to an exchange contract with a credit information company, which is the gateway that makes a bank's participation lawful, while the Banking Control Law and its implementation rules remain the source of SAMA's authority over the bank itself. Practically, membership and customer consent under the credit information regime do not displace banking confidentiality and supervisory obligations; treat this cross-reference as inferred and verify the specific provisions relied on.

When calculating government support amounts in responsible financing, treat the circular as a supervisory instruction whose binding force derives from SAMA's authority over banks under the Banking Control Law. That parent law and its implementation rules supply the enforcement and sanctioning basis, while the circular supplies the substantive calculation expectation. The consequence is that non-compliance with the circular is a supervisory breach in its own right, not merely a contractual or methodological preference; as the linkage is inferred, confirm the legal basis recited in the circular itself.

For questions about currency issuance, legal tender or dealings in banknotes by a licensed bank, the Currency Law and the Banking Control Law address different layers and should not be conflated. The Currency Law governs the monetary unit and SAMA's issuing function, whereas the Banking Control Law governs licensing, prudential control and supervisory powers over banks; both sit under SAMA's mandate, which is why they are conceptually paired. Practically, a currency-related restriction does not by itself create a banking licence condition, and a supervisory power under banking control does not extend to matters reserved to the currency regime; verify the operative article in the primary text before relying on either.

When structuring a lease-based product over a dwelling, decide which registration and title-verification duties apply cumulatively rather than choosing one regime. The Finance Lease implementing rules require the lease (and any ensuing sale contract and amendments) to be recorded in the Contracts Register, while the Real Estate Finance Law imposes a separate duty on the real estate finance entity to verify the title deed and confirm the absence of in rem rights before contracting; both sit within SAMA's finance-sector statutes governing asset-backed financing. The link is inferred, not an express cross-reference, so treat it as: a real estate finance lease can attract both sets of duties, and the reader should verify the primary texts and scope definitions before concluding either regime is displaced.

If you are scoping the internal audit charter and assurance plan for a bank with Islamic operations, treat Shariah audit as an assurance activity that must be reconciled with the general internal audit mandate rather than run as an unrelated silo. The Shariah governance requirements describe internal Shariah audit as an independent, objective assessment of compliance of the bank's Islamic activities, which mirrors and overlaps the internal audit department's third-line role in the governance framework. The practical consequence is that reporting lines, independence, competence and coverage must be settled so Islamic operations are audited without duplication or gaps; because the link is inferred, confirm in the primary texts whether Shariah audit is required to sit within, or separately from, the internal audit department.

For a debt buyout between finance companies, do not read the buyout instructions as a self-contained regime: the underlying exposure remains a Consumer Financing product and the Regulations for Consumer Financing continue to govern it. The buyout instructions operate as the specific rules for the transfer mechanics, while the general regulation supplies the defined terms and the creditor's standing duties on disclosure, pricing, code of conduct for sales and collections, and consumer treatment. Practically, the acquiring creditor inherits full consumer-protection obligations from the transfer date and must satisfy both instruments; where the buyout text is silent, default to the general regulation and verify the express cross-reference in the primary text.

When testing whether an APR disclosure to a borrower is compliant, the Regulations for Consumer Financing supply the definition and the obligation to disclose, while the APR Rules supply the binding calculation methodology. The two operate as one obligation chain: a disclosed rate is only correct if derived using the prescribed method and the prescribed treatment of charges and cash-flow timing. The consequence is that a technically disclosed APR computed on a different basis is still a breach of the consumer financing disclosure duty; check the APR Rules for the applicable formula and inclusions before signing off.

For contract execution controls in consumer finance, read the SAMA circular on signing all contract pages as a binding supervisory instruction that tightens the documentation and disclosure duties already imposed by the Regulations for Consumer Financing. The regulation sets the substantive content, currency and disclosure requirements for the consumer financing contract; the circular addresses how the consumer's assent to that content is evidenced across the whole document. The consequence is that a contract meeting the regulation's content requirements may still be non-compliant if execution formalities are not met; the connection is inferred from subject matter, so verify the circular's exact scope and addressees in the primary text.

If a finance company is executing the funds movement behind a purchase or transfer of consumer finance debt, treat the settlement leg as governed by the SARIE payment regime, not only by the finance-company instructions. The SARIE rules impose an exclusivity requirement on domestic remittances, so the debt-purchase instructions operate on top of that mandatory settlement channel rather than creating an alternative route. Practically, a compliance sign-off on a portfolio purchase should confirm both the finance-regime conditions for the assignment and that the domestic transfer of consideration is routed through the prescribed interbank system; verify the specific clause in the purchase instructions that invokes it.

When populating the CRM overview disclosure, the amounts reported should only reflect mitigation that is actually recognised under the credit risk mitigation rules (eligible collateral, on-balance-sheet netting, guarantees and credit derivatives), because the disclosure template is the Pillar 3 window onto the Pillar 1 treatment. The link is definitional rather than a citation: the template's line items inherit their meaning from the CRM chapter of the capital framework. Consequently a technique that fails the eligibility or legal-certainty conditions cannot be presented as covered exposure in the template. This relationship is inferred, so confirm the template's instructions and the CRM eligibility text directly.

Where a bank capitalises an equity investment in a fund using the mandate-based approach, derivative positions permitted by the fund's mandate must still be valued for exposure purposes under SA-CCR, so the counterparty credit risk rules feed directly into the fund look-through calculation. Both sit within the same capital adequacy framework, and the MBA provisions rely on the SA-CCR exposure-at-default definition rather than a separate measure. The practical consequence is that a bank cannot avoid SA-CCR mechanics by holding derivatives indirectly through a fund; the mandate ceiling is converted into exposure using the same methodology.

A bank managing profit sharing investment accounts should compute its liquidity ratios using SAMA's general LCR and NSFR requirements, with the PSIA-specific rules determining how those funds are classified and weighted rather than replacing the ratio methodology. The connection is one of hierarchy: the prudential liquidity circulars set the ratio framework that the Islamic-banking rules then direct institutions to apply to PSIA balances. For a decision, this means PSIA treatment is an input to, not an exemption from, the standard liquidity calculation. The link is inferred, so check the cross-referencing language in the PSIA rules before relying on it.

For a Shariah-compliant institution, two separate supervisory discretions interact: what qualifies as alternative high-quality liquid assets on the buffer side, and how investment account holder funds and their reserves are treated on the funding side. Neither rule set is self-contained, so a liquidity position assessed only under the HQLA eligibility provisions may misstate the institution's position if PSIA classification is not applied consistently. The practical consequence is that the composition of the buffer and the characterisation of PSIA funding should be reviewed together, with any haircuts or conditions imposed by SAMA identified. This relationship is inferred from subject matter rather than an explicit cross-reference, so verify the primary text of both instruments.

If you are deciding how much capital a bank must hold for derivative exposures, the CVA charge cannot be assessed on its own: it sits inside SAMA's minimum capital requirements for counterparty credit risk and CVA, which supplies the scope, approach-eligibility conditions and the basic approach (including the reduced BA-CVA variant) that the CVA provisions operate under. The link is a hierarchy/containment relationship rather than a mere cross-reference, so the defined terms and approach choices in the parent framework govern how the CVA text is read. Practically, a CVA capital determination should be validated against the parent CCR/CVA framework version in force (the December 2022 issue here) before it is relied on.

When classifying a trading-book position for market risk capital, the credit spread risk class is not a single bucket: the framework splits it by whether the exposure is non-securitisation, securitisation outside the correlation trading portfolio, or securitisation within the CTP. The link reflects that the CTP is a defined term used to partition CSR, so the CTP definition determines which CSR treatment and risk weights apply. For a decision, confirm the CTP scope test first, because misclassifying a securitisation position as inside or outside the CTP changes the capital outcome, not just the label.

SAMA's operational risk capital requirements are an adoption of the Basel III post-crisis reform package, so the Basel standard is the source instrument and SAMA's rules are the enforceable local implementation. That matters when the two diverge: the binding obligation on a KSA-licensed bank is the SAMA text and its glossary of adopted terms, with Basel serving as interpretive background rather than direct authority. Note that the supporting excerpts here are glossary material rather than an operative provision, so verify the specific citing article in the SAMA operational risk document before relying on it in an argument.

If you are testing whether a bank's operational risk capital has been correctly calibrated, the ILM cannot be verified without the Loss Component, since the ILM is defined as a function of the LC relative to the Business Indicator Component and equals one where the two are equal. The LC itself is fixed by a multiple of average annual operational risk losses over the preceding ten-year window, so the loss data set drives the multiplier. Consequently, challenges to the capital figure will usually turn on the completeness, quality and ten-year coverage of the internal loss data feeding the LC.

MPOR is a counterparty credit risk input that also conditions the regulatory CVA calculation, because exposure paths used for CVA must reflect the assumed close-out and re-margining horizon for margined netting sets. The link matters because regulatory CVA is not the accounting figure: it excludes the bank's own default and is subject to prescribed constraints, so MPOR assumptions must follow the regulatory specification rather than internal or accounting practice. In a review, check that the MPOR used for CVA is consistent with the CCR framework's prescribed floors and any extensions triggered by disputes or illiquid collateral, and confirm the point against the primary text.

Decide the asset-class classification first: whether an obligor exposure is ordinary corporate or falls into the specialized lending sub-class determines which IRB treatment you may apply. The corporate exposure definition in the SAMA minimum capital framework expressly carves out specialized lending (project, object, commodities finance, income-producing real estate and HVCRE) as a distinct sub-category within the corporate asset class, so the two provisions form a single classification chain. Practically, a facility captured as SL cannot be risk-weighted on generic corporate parameters where the framework directs the supervisory slotting criteria, and the classification must be documented and defensible to SAMA.

If a commercial real estate facility meets the HVCRE description, you are still inside the specialized lending regime but on a separate, more conservative risk-weight track. HVCRE is defined as the financing of commercial real estate exhibiting higher loss-rate volatility and is listed as one of the SL sub-categories, with its own slotting risk weights and expected-loss treatment distinct from PF, OF, CF and IPRE. The consequence is that mis-labelling HVCRE as ordinary IPRE understates capital; the HVCRE/IPRE boundary decision should be evidenced against the definitional criteria in the primary text.

This link suggests that the data quality, retention and traceability conditions governing model inputs also constrain what data may be relied on for parameter estimation, so a weakness in the data set is a defect in the estimate itself rather than a separate operational issue. The connection is inferred rather than stated: the extracted text concerns adjustments to risk-theoretical P&L input data and its alignment with hypothetical P&L, which sits in the market risk model-approval provisions, not obviously in the IRB PD estimation requirements. Treat the shared-data reading as tentative and verify in the primary text which data-maintenance article actually feeds the PD estimation obligations before relying on it for a model validation or capital decision.

When a bank holds equity in a fund and looks through to the underlying holdings, any securitisation exposures inside that fund must be capitalised under the securitisation framework rather than as plain equity. The fund provisions cross-refer to the securitisation approach hierarchy, under which SEC-ERBA is the external-ratings-based approach applied where the bank does not use (or is not permitted to use) SEC-IRBA or SEC-IAA. The practical consequence is that the look-through result is only as good as the securitisation approach selected for each underlying position, and the eligibility conditions for that approach must be met and evidenced.

For each banking book fund holding you must work down a prescribed hierarchy of approaches, and the mandate-based approach is the middle tier used where full look-through is not available but the fund's mandate or applicable regulation supports a conservative reconstruction of exposures. The equity-investments-in-funds provisions establish the three approaches and their ordering, with the fall-back approach applying where neither look-through nor mandate information suffices, and leverage adjustment and partial-use rules attaching to the choice. The consequence is that MBA is not freely elective: the bank must be able to show why look-through was unavailable, or the more punitive fall-back treatment applies.

When you are deciding the risk weight of a securitisation exposure from an external rating, you cannot read the ECAI provisions in isolation: they expressly borrow the eligibility concepts of the standardized approach to credit risk, including who counts as an eligible guarantor and how credit risk mitigation is recognised. The cross-reference makes the standardized approach chapters the controlling source for those defined terms, while the ECAI chapter governs how a rating that already embeds that protection is used. Practically, if the guarantor would not be eligible under the standardized approach, the rating-based treatment cannot be relied on for that protection, and the bank must avoid recognising the same mitigation twice.

Before populating the banking-book securitisation disclosure template, you must first settle classification under the securitisation framework, since the template reports positions whose scope and labels (securitisation versus resecuritisation, tranche versus non-securitisation asset) are defined there. This is an inferred rather than stated link: the disclosure serves the prudential framework, so a reclassification of an exposure upstream changes what is disclosed downstream. Treat the framework's classification rules as the determinant of the template's contents, and verify the primary text of both instruments before relying on this alignment.

The practical question is whether a specialised lending exposure can be risk-weighted off an external rating at all, or must fall into the supervisory slotting categories. The issue-specific and issuer rating rules set the threshold test for when an exposure is treated as rated (and when an issuer rating may or may not be extended to a particular claim), which feeds the specialised lending treatment for project, object, commodities finance, income-producing and high-volatility commercial real estate. Consequently, a bank cannot apply a favourable rating-based weight to a specialised lending exposure unless the rating attaches to that exposure under those rules; otherwise the slotting weights and the associated expected loss treatment apply.

When deciding how to recognise a guarantee or credit derivative, the governing chapter depends on how the underlying exposure is risk-weighted: the general credit risk mitigation provisions direct standardized-approach exposures to the simple or comprehensive collateral methods, while exposures under the internal ratings-based approach are recognised through the IRB guarantees and credit derivatives rules, which split further between foundation and advanced treatment. The cross-reference is an obligation-routing device rather than an alternative option. Applying the wrong chapter's mechanics to an exposure produces an unsupportable capital number, so confirm the exposure's approach first and then use the matching recognition rules and eligibility conditions.

This link tells you where mitigation is actually reflected in the calculation: under the standardized approach it adjusts the exposure amount or the applicable risk weight, whereas the general credit risk mitigation chapter routes IRB exposures to the risk-components rules, where protection is instead reflected in parameters such as loss given default and exposure at default. The two chapters therefore describe one obligation chain with two calculation routes, not two independent entitlements. The consequence is that a bank must recognise a given piece of collateral or protection once, through the route matching its approach, and should not combine a standardized-approach adjustment with a parameter-based benefit for the same exposure.

When deciding how to calibrate and apply the output floor, treat the SAMA instrument as the binding requirement in the Kingdom and the Basel Committee's 2017 post-crisis finalisation package as the parent standard it transposes. The SAMA text expressly traces the floor to that Basel reform and its stated purpose of constraining variability in risk-weighted assets between internal-model and standardised outcomes. Practically, Basel wording can inform interpretation of ambiguous terms or of the phase-in calibration, but any divergence or national discretion exercised by SAMA governs, so the local text must be checked before relying on Basel language.

If you are sizing exposure on commitments, guarantees or other off-balance-sheet positions, the credit conversion factor provision is the operative step that turns those positions into on-balance-sheet-equivalent credit exposure for RWA purposes. Both instruments carry the same provision and numbering, so they are two expressions of one rule within the credit risk framework rather than two independent obligations. The decision point is therefore which instrument and version is currently in force for your reporting date, since applying superseded conversion factors would misstate credit RWA.

A credit RWA calculation cannot be completed for derivative and other counterparty exposures without first determining exposure at default under the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk, which the credit risk rules cross-refer to directly. The reference also imports a floor that operates consistently across SA-CCR, the comprehensive approach to collateral within standardised credit risk, and the internal models method. For a compliance decision this means the two instruments form a single obligation chain: approach selection and any model permission on the counterparty credit side feed the credit risk capital number, and both sets of provisions must be evidenced together.

The backtesting disclosure template appears to bite only on banks that hold permission to use a foundation or advanced IRB approach, so the threshold question is approach eligibility under the IRB rules rather than the disclosure rules themselves. On that reading the substantive IRB requirements govern parameter estimation and the template governs how the resulting default-probability performance is reported, making the two an obligation-and-reporting pair. This link is inferred, and the template's stated scope also touches counterparty credit risk exposures, so the reader should verify the primary text to confirm exactly which portfolios and approach permissions trigger the filing.

Whether the slotting template must be completed turns on whether the bank operates under an IRB permission and holds exposures assigned to supervisory slotting categories rather than to own-estimated parameters, which is settled by the IRB rules, not the disclosure text. The template is therefore best read as the reporting face of an underlying IRB treatment, so a change in approach permission or in the classification of specialised lending exposures changes the disclosure obligation as well. The connection is inferred from scope language that also references counterparty credit risk, so confirm against the primary instruments before concluding that the template does or does not apply.

When classifying a corporate obligor, the first decision is whether the facility falls inside the specialized lending carve-out rather than being treated as a general corporate exposure. The corporate asset class definition itself points to specialized lending as a distinct sub-set, so the two provisions form one classification chain within the same SAMA credit-risk capital framework rather than alternative regimes. Practically, if the exposure meets the specialized lending characteristics (repayment primarily from the financed asset or project), the bank must apply the specialized lending treatment and risk weights, not the generic corporate risk-weight function; verify the definitional tests in the primary text before booking the classification.

The decision here is whether a corporate borrower qualifies as a corporate MSME, because that determines which capital treatment and any size-based adjustment applies. Corporate MSME is defined as a sub-category inside the same corporate exposure definition, so it is a refinement of the general corporate class, not a separate asset class, and the boundary with retail treatment also has to be checked. Consequence: misclassifying an MSME as a general corporate (or vice versa) changes the risk weight outcome, so the size/turnover criteria in the definitional provisions should be evidenced per obligor and verified against the primary text.

Before applying a risk weight to a property-secured exposure, the bank must first confirm the exposure qualifies as regulatory real estate and then test whether the currency mismatch multiplier is triggered. The multiplier provision relies on the real estate definitions (including the residential/commercial split) to fix its scope, so the two provisions operate as a single sequenced calculation within the same capital rules. The practical effect is that an otherwise favourably weighted real estate exposure can attract an uplift where the borrower's income currency differs from the lending currency and is unhedged; confirm the exact trigger conditions and any cap in the primary text.

Whether a piece of collateral can be recognized for credit risk mitigation often turns on a rating, and that rating only counts if it comes from a credit rating agency recognized as an ECAI under the framework's recognition process. The collateral eligibility provisions therefore depend on the ECAI recognition rules as a precondition, linking the mitigation chapter to the ratings chapter of the same SAMA instrument. Consequence: if an instrument is rated only by a non-recognized agency, the bank cannot rely on that rating to treat the collateral as eligible, and the exposure must be capitalised unmitigated or under another recognized route.

For a bank on the IRB approach, the decision is whether a corporate exposure belongs to one of the specialized lending sub-classes, because that determines the permitted methodology. The IRB corporate asset class expressly subdivides into specialized lending sub-classes, so the sub-class definitions govern which risk-weight route is available within the same approval perimeter. The consequence is that a bank unable to meet the estimation standards for the relevant parameters must fall back to the supervisory slotting treatment for those exposures, and the slotting categories and associated weights (including any distinct treatment for high-volatility exposures) apply instead of the bank's own modelled outputs.

When assigning a trading-book position to a capital charge, both terms draw on the same enumerated list of risk classes used as the basis for market risk capital requirements, so they must be read as complementary slots in one taxonomy rather than as free-standing labels. General interest rate risk captures the rate-curve component, while the specific/issuer-related component sits in the credit spread risk classes of the same list. Practically, the reader should allocate each exposure across both components consistently, avoiding either a gap or a double count in the market risk capital calculation.

Treat the leadership and governance controls as a domain sitting inside the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements structure, not as a separate obligation set: the Fundamental Requirements define the domain architecture and the governance domain populates it with control requirements. That domain is also expressly mapped to the corresponding governance, policy and risk management sections of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework, creating a layered obligation chain. For a compliance decision this means governance evidence must satisfy the cyber resilience requirement and remain consistent with the mapped Cyber Security Framework controls; assess both, and apply the stricter where they differ in detail.

The operations and technology controls are one of the cyber security and resilience domains defined by the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements structure, so scoping an operational cyber control gap starts from that parent architecture. The domain is likewise cross-mapped to Cyber Security Framework provisions, so the same operational control may be tested under both instruments. The reader should therefore scope assessments and remediation against the Fundamental Requirements domain while checking alignment with the mapped Cyber Security Framework references.

This link matters when checking whether what a bank says publicly about risk management matches what it does internally: the stress testing rules require a holistic process covering all material internal and external risks, while Table OVA requires a qualitative description of the bank's risk strategy, governance and risk appetite. The two are connected through the same underlying risk-management framework rather than by an express cross-reference, so the relationship is inferred. Practically, inconsistency between stress testing scope and the OVA narrative is a disclosure and governance exposure; verify the primary text of both instruments before relying on the connection.

The likely practical question is who validates and registers a retail finance lease and on what authority: the decision on the powers of the head of the contract registry appears to allocate registry authority, while the individual financial lease contract instrument sets the contractual form used in that regime. The connection is inferred from the shared finance leasing framework rather than from an explicit cross-reference in the provided material. Treat the registry-powers decision as procedural authority bearing on the lifecycle of the individual lease contract, but confirm the scope and any registration obligation directly in the primary texts before relying on it.

Treat these as parts of a single operational calendar rather than independent instructions: the general Ramadan working hours and Eid holiday circular sets the baseline schedule for supervised entities, while the SARIE notice fixes the corresponding operating window for the national payment settlement system. Because settlement cut-offs are what actually bind payment obligations and value dating, branch-hour planning must be reconciled against the SARIE timings for the same Hijri period. In practice, confirm both before committing to customer-facing service or payment execution commitments during Ramadan and Eid, as this pairing is inferred from subject-matter alignment and the reader should verify the operative dates in each primary text.

Read the ATM cash feeding and cash-in-transit hours notice as a carve-out or supplement to the general Ramadan working hours circular, not as a conflicting rule. Both govern the same 1447H seasonal period and the same supervised population, but the ATM notice addresses service-continuity and cash-availability expectations that persist outside normal branch hours. The consequence is that shortened branch hours do not relieve the entity of ATM replenishment and transport obligations; the link is inferred, so confirm the precise permitted windows in the primary text.

Before building a debt-collection compliance position, determine which of these two records is the operative instrument, because they appear to carry substantially the same updated rules on collection from individual customers. Where a duplicate or re-issued record exists, the governing text is the one with the controlling issuance date and version, and only that version's conduct requirements (contact limits, disclosure, treatment of debtors) are enforceable as such. Cite the authoritative record in any policy or customer-facing procedure; since the duplication is inferred, verify version metadata against the primary source before relying on either.

Treat these as the same credit card issuance and operation rulebook appearing twice in the knowledge base, and resolve which record is current before citing obligations on issuance, fees, disclosure and cardholder rights. Duplicate holdings create a real risk of quoting a superseded version, and card rules have been amended over time, so the version reference matters for supervisory defensibility. Anchor policies and customer terms to the controlling version; as this equivalence is inferred, confirm the issuance and amendment history in the primary text.

The practical question is whether complaints arising from electronic distribution of investment fund units by a SAMA-supervised entity fall within the complaint management framework, or whether they sit with the capital markets regime and its own complaint channels. The complaint management circular imposes handling, logging and escalation duties on SAMA-supervised entities generally, while the fund-unit distribution instrument concerns a specific permitted activity that intersects with CMA-regulated products. This link is ambiguous: do not assume automatic coverage, and verify in the primary texts whether the distribution activity is expressly brought within the complaint system's scope or whether complaints must be routed to the securities regulator.

Treat these as two versions of the same OTC derivatives reporting and risk-mitigation requirement rather than two independent obligations, so a counterparty should not assume duplicate or conflicting reporting duties. The near-identical scoping of reportable transactions (interest rate, FX, equity, credit and commodity derivatives routed to the SAMA-authorised Trade Repository) indicates a re-issued or duplicated circular within the same instrument family. For a compliance decision, apply the later/controlling version and confirm which circular reference and effective date SAMA regards as operative; because this link is inferred, verify the version history in the primary texts before relying on one over the other.

When determining what must be submitted for a given trade, the collateral fields and the common data table operate as one reporting record, not separable filings. The collateral evolutive fields (e.g. currency and value of excess collateral posted or received) sit alongside the common data elements that drive lifecycle handling, such as the action type used for modification reports on notional changes. Practically, a change reported through common data must be reflected consistently in the associated collateral values; inconsistency across the two tables is a reporting-quality failure under the same instrument, so confirm field-level linkage in the appendix itself.

A finance company setting or charging administrative fees to consumers must satisfy both the product-level consumer finance controls and the broader conduct and prudential framework for licensed finance entities. Both sit under the Finance Companies Control Law regime, with the Implementing Regulation providing the licensing, governance and supervisory base and the consumer finance controls operating as the more specific conduct rule on fee treatment. For a decision, the specific fee control governs the permissible charge while the Implementing Regulation governs the entity's capacity to levy it and SAMA's supervisory response; this relationship is inferred, so check the primary texts for any express cross-reference or scope limit.

Before deciding whether a debt collection counterparty must be separately licensed, read the outsourcing circular in light of the later cancellation of the licensing requirement for debt collection activity. The earlier instrument conditions outsourcing on engaging licensed entities; the subsequent instrument removes that licensing gate, altering the practical test for acceptable service providers. The consequence is that due diligence on collection agents shifts from licence verification to the firm's own outsourcing governance and conduct controls; because the link is inferred, confirm the effective date and whether the cancellation fully supersedes the outsourcing condition.

An applicant deciding whether its proposed activity requires a payment services licence should read the application guidelines as subordinate to, and interpreted by, the Law of Payments and Payment Services and its Implementing Regulation. The guidelines expressly rest on the Implementing Regulation's licensing articles, while the Law supplies the defined scope of Payment Services (execution and processing of payment transactions, payment instruments, transfers, e-money and payment wallets). Consequently, the statutory definition governs whether a licence is needed at all, and the guidelines only govern how to apply; where guidance appears narrower or broader, the Law and its Regulation control.

If you are testing a credit card product's cost disclosure, treat these two as a single disclosure obligation chain rather than alternatives: the consumer finance clarification addresses how the annual percentage rate is computed and how initial disclosure and the consumer's termination/withdrawal right operate, while the credit card rules impose how the rate and term cost must be presented to the cardholder. Both sit in the consumer-protection/finance disclosure regime, so the calculation basis taken from the finance rules feeds the figure the card issuer must display prominently. The practical consequence is that a compliant display format does not cure a rate computed on the wrong basis, and vice versa; because this link is inferred, confirm the scope of the consumer finance rules as applied to revolving card credit in the primary texts before relying on it.

Both instruments are directives channelling a category of activity through a single designated national counterparty — charitable donation collection through the authorised relief entity, and document verification through the designated e-government provider — so the decision framing is the same: where SAMA names an exclusive channel, an institution's own alternative arrangement is non-compliant regardless of its adequacy. The connection is thematic rather than textual; neither instrument defines or cross-references the other. Read each for its own addressees and activity scope, and verify the primary circulars before treating a conclusion drawn from one as authority for the other.

Both sit in the payments/acceptance regime and govern how a supervised institution may route and price card-based acceptance, but they address different channels: one concerns e-commerce payment support arrangements, the other point-of-sale acceptance routed through the Gulf payments network with its own tariff arrangements. For a decision, this means channel-specific rules and fee treatments must be identified per transaction type rather than generalised across acceptance. The link is inferred, so do not assume an e-commerce requirement extends to cross-border POS routing (or the reverse) without checking the scope clause of each circular.

The practical question is whether a firm providing e-commerce payment support is merely facilitating a transaction or is receiving and holding customer/merchant money, because the latter engages the safeguarding regime for Protected Funds — segregation, permitted holding arrangements and restrictions on use. The link runs through the defined term: if the funds flowing through the e-commerce arrangement fall within Protected Funds, the safeguarding obligations attach independently of the service description used commercially. The consequence is that the classification of the payment flow, not the label of the service, drives the safeguarding outcome; since the connection is inferred, verify the definition and scope provisions in the primary rules before concluding either way.

These are seasonal operational instructions that should be read together when planning service continuity for the same period: one addresses readiness of exchange centres for Ramadan and the Hajj season, the other sets working hours and holiday arrangements. The overlap is calendar-driven rather than based on a shared defined term or cross-reference, so readiness expectations must be reconciled with the permitted or required operating hours. Confirm the addressees and the Hijri year each instrument applies to in the primary text, since scope may differ between exchange centres and other supervised entities and these instructions are typically reissued annually.

When deciding how to verify beneficial ownership during CDD/KYB, the relevant question is which official source applies to the customer's legal form. Both provisions address reliance on authoritative registry-based beneficial owner verification, which supports the AML/CTF obligation to identify and take reasonable measures to verify the beneficial owner of a legal person; one addresses the general technical linkage to the Watheq verification channel, the other a dedicated inquiry route for non-profit associations. Practically, the reader should not assume a single verification path covers all customer types, and should confirm which channel is mandated or permitted for the entity category at hand. As this connection is inferred rather than stated, verify the primary texts before relying on one source as sufficient verification.

If a real estate finance entity is contemplating taking or increasing an equity stake in the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company, both instruments must be read together before the transaction is approved. The rules regulating real estate refinance companies set the licensing and prudential framework for the activity, while the linked provision imposes transaction-level conditions: satisfaction of legal and supervisory requirements, prior SAMA approval, fair market value pricing, and an aggregate shareholding ceiling of 30 percent. The consequence is that compliance sign-off depends on both entity-level authorisation and the specific shareholding conditions, and the ceiling is measured on an aggregate basis rather than per shareholder.

A finance entity conducting digital brokerage that delegates any function to a third party cannot treat the digital brokerage instructions as a self-contained rulebook. The activity-specific instructions operate alongside the outsourcing regime for finance companies, so the usual outsourcing conditions — notification or approval where required, written arrangements, due diligence and continuing accountability of the licensed entity — attach to the outsourced digital brokerage function. For the reader this means outsourcing governance is a separate approval and control gate, and responsibility for the outsourced activity remains with the licensee. The cross-reference is inferred, so confirm the exact triggering language in the primary text.

In assessing whether an audit committee is discharging its mandate, substantive responsibilities and procedural minimums must be tested together. One provision defines what the committee is accountable for in relation to compliance oversight; the other sets operating requirements for the same body, including a minimum of six meetings per year and the ability to invite the risk manager or others to attend without voting rights. The practical consequence is that meeting the meeting-frequency and composition requirements does not by itself evidence discharge of the committee's compliance oversight duties, and vice versa — a supervisory review is likely to look at both.

Where a finance entity secures or collects instalments from a consumer, the choice between relying on a promissory note and operating a standing payment order engages two parallel sets of SAMA controls that are best assessed together. Both instruments regulate how finance entities may take and enforce repayment mechanisms against obligors, and both sit within the consumer-protection constraints applicable to finance activity, including limits on stacking security or collection devices beyond the outstanding obligation. The reader should therefore confirm that the combination used is permitted, proportionate to the amount due, and properly disclosed. Because the link is inferred, verify the primary texts for any express restriction on using both mechanisms simultaneously.

When deciding who owns an AML/CTF obligation inside a supervised entity, read the AML/CTF rules together with the compliance function requirements: the former set the substantive duties (CDD, monitoring, reporting, record-keeping) while the latter establish the independent unit, its reporting line and its mandate to test and report on adherence. The link is a governance-to-substance chain rather than a cross-reference, so the compliance unit's independence, resourcing and board reporting are the mechanism through which AML/CTF compliance is evidenced to SAMA. Practically, an AML/CTF gap will usually also surface as a compliance-function adequacy finding, and remediation should address both. This connection is inferred, so confirm the exact allocation of AML/CTF responsibilities (including any MLRO-specific role) in the primary texts before assigning accountability.

For any assessment of compliance with the branch/facility surveillance requirements, the camera specifications and the recording server specifications must be satisfied together, not alternatively: they are two halves of one minimum standard set out in the same instrument. Camera capability determines what is captured, while the recording server requirements govern retention and availability of that footage for supervisory or investigative purposes. Consequently, meeting one table while falling short on the other leaves the overall physical security obligation unmet. The dependency is inferred from their shared scope; verify the specific retention and quality parameters in the primary tables.

These two maturity models use a parallel assessment logic and reporting rhythm but apply to different subject matter, so a decision about self-assessment scope should treat them as separate compliance exercises rather than one. The cyber security model measures control maturity against the cyber security framework; the IT governance model measures maturity against the IT governance framework. The practical consequence is that a satisfactory rating under one framework does not evidence compliance under the other, and SAMA's expected maturity level must be met separately for each. The similarity is inferred from structure; confirm the required target levels and submission obligations in each framework's own text.

Both provisions sit in the same board-level risk governance chain — the board approves the risk strategy, policies and measurement methodology — but they address distinct risk types, so a decision on committee mandates and approval evidence should cover each separately. Liquidity stress testing and contingency funding planning fall under liquidity risk governance; the three-stage classification is a credit risk measurement and provisioning matter. The overlap is that the same governing body must demonstrate periodic review and approval for both, and stressed conditions can be a common scenario input. The relationship is inferred rather than expressed as a cross-reference; check each instrument's primary text before treating a single board approval as covering both.

If you are assessing a finance company's buyout of an existing consumer debt, the buyout instructions must be read alongside the circular setting timeframes for issuing clearance letters and transferring the account or debt, because the latter fixes the deadlines that make the buyout operable. The buyout instructions govern eligibility and terms between financiers, while the timeframe instructions bind the transferring creditor to act within a set period, and delay is itself a breach. The practical consequence is that a compliant buyout requires evidence of both substantive eligibility and timely clearance/transfer, and consumer complaints about delay are assessed against the timeframe circular. The cross-reference is inferred from the cited circulars; verify the current effective deadlines, as these instructions have been amended.

If you are deciding whether an executive deed extract can validly be issued for a finance lease, you first have to confirm the contract's registry status under the entry-procedure controls. Both instruments sit within the same finance lease registration regime, where the enforceable extract derives its legal effect from a contract properly entered in the register, so the entry controls operate as an upstream condition on the extract controls. Treat registration defects as capable of undermining enforceability of the extract; because this linkage is inferred rather than expressly cross-referenced, confirm the sequencing in the primary text before relying on it.

When calculating or disclosing APR to a consumer, you need to decide which fees and administrative costs form part of the total cost of credit, and the circular functions as SAMA's clarification of that treatment alongside the APR rules. Both operate in the consumer finance disclosure regime, where the APR methodology sets the calculation framework and the circular narrows or explains permissible charges feeding into it. Read the circular as constraining the inputs to the APR figure rather than as a separate pricing permission; verify the circular's exact scope and effective date, since the relationship here is inferred.

For any customer or transaction raising financial crime concern, you generally have to apply both regimes in parallel rather than choosing one: the AML Implementing Regulation and the terrorist financing Implementing Regulations impose overlapping customer due diligence, record-keeping and reporting duties on the same financial institutions. They share definitional architecture and scope concepts drawn from their respective parent laws, and the CTF regulation's specification of covered financial activities largely tracks the institutions already captured by AML obligations. Practically, a CDD or suspicious transaction decision should be tested against both instruments, including the distinct terrorist financing and targeted financial sanctions triggers; check the primary texts for any divergence in thresholds or reporting channels.

When a PSP wants a third party to carry out customer-facing activity, the threshold decision is whether that party is an appointed agent or an e-money distributor, because the two provisions attach different authorisation, notification and control conditions. Both sit within the same payment services regulation and share the underlying principle that the licensed PSP remains accountable for the outsourced conduct, including AML/CTF and consumer protection outcomes. Characterise the arrangement carefully before onboarding, since mislabelling can leave activity conducted outside the permitted channel; as this pairing is inferred, confirm the precise definitions and conditions in the regulation itself.

Where a payment is initiated through a payment initiation or account information provider and the customer disputes it, you need to read the service-specific provisions together with the unauthorised transaction liability rules to decide who bears the loss and who must refund. Both provisions come from the same payment services instrument, and the liability allocation presupposes the authentication and consent standards that govern initiation and account access services. The consequence is that disputes should be triaged by reference to whether valid consent and authentication existed at initiation, not merely by which entity held the funds; verify the primary text, as this connection is inferred rather than expressly stated.

Treat these two circulars as parallel conduct obligations on the same supervised population — finance companies (including real estate financiers) acting through or alongside third parties — rather than as one governing the other. Both sit under SAMA's supervisory authority over finance activity, and both constrain how a financier deals with obligations that move outside its own direct handling: one where collection is outsourced to an external service provider, the other where the financier's duties continue in secondary-market dealings in the financing portfolio. Practically, when a real estate financing exposure is transferred or serviced externally, check compliance against both sets of duties, because responsibility for borrower treatment is not extinguished by the involvement of another party. The link is inferred rather than expressly cross-referenced, so confirm against the primary text before relying on it.

Read these together when assessing a real estate financier's lifecycle duties: one circular drives the front-end credit granting policy, the other governs obligations that persist once the financing is placed into the secondary market. Both are SAMA instructions to finance companies under the same finance-supervision framework, so the credit policy updates are the natural upstream control for exposures that may later be sold or securitised. For a decision, do not treat a policy as compliant at origination alone — verify it also accommodates continuing obligations after transfer. This association is inferred, so the reader should verify whether either circular expressly cross-refers.

The connection here is weak and should be used only as context: one circular addresses how finance companies set and update credit granting policies, the other directs finance entities to deliver financial awareness programmes to SMEs and report quarterly to SAMA. The common thread is the SME borrower — credit assessment standards on one side, borrower education and periodic reporting on the other — but they are distinct obligations with different deliverables and deadlines. For a compliance decision, do not assume satisfying one discharges the other; the awareness circular carries its own reporting duty. The link is ambiguous, so verify the primary text before treating them as a single workstream.

When justifying an institution's ML/TF risk assessment methodology and risk appetite, FATF standards are the interpretive source from which the assessment obligation derives, not a free-standing requirement in themselves. The AML/CTF rules define FATF as the standard-setter for legal, regulatory and operational AML/CTF measures, and the risk assessment duty — including setting risk appetite against regulatory, reputational, legal and financial consequences before designing mitigating controls — operationalises the FATF risk-based approach in KSA. The consequence is that the enforceable obligation on a financial institution is the SAMA/Saudi rule; FATF material supports interpretation and supervisory expectation but should be cited as context, not as the legal basis. This is an inferred relationship, so confirm the exact wording in the primary text.

For onboarding and ongoing due diligence, these two are sequential steps in the same CDD chain rather than alternatives: you must first identify and verify the beneficial owner from authenticated, independent sources, and that outcome then feeds the PEP determination, which is itself described as a CDD measure applying the risk-based approach. The practical consequence is that a PEP screening performed only on the named account holder is incomplete — if a beneficial owner (or their close associate/family member, per the applicable definition) is a PEP, enhanced due diligence and senior management approval obligations are triggered at the relationship level. Treat a failure to resolve beneficial ownership as blocking a defensible PEP conclusion. The linkage is inferred from the structure of the CDD provisions, so verify the specific article wording before relying on it in a file decision.

Treat these as two renderings of the same advertising rulebook rather than two independent obligations, so the practical question is which version is currently in force for the institution you are advising. Both set the same consumer-protection duty on financial institutions to exercise due diligence over advertising content and approach and to avoid tempting, misleading, inaccurate or exaggerated claims, which is why the texts track each other almost word for word. Because the similarity is inferred rather than an explicit supersession statement, cite the version applicable to your entity type and effective date, and verify against the primary text before relying on either as the controlling source.

When a bank onboards or renews an agent, the AML/CFT obligation and the agent qualifying-criteria obligation must be satisfied together, not sequentially or in isolation. Both sit in the same agent banking instrument: the bank remains accountable to SAMA for AML/CFT and KYC compliance (including document production and periodic reporting) across activity conducted through agents, while the qualifying criteria and per-agent non-objection process govern who may act in that channel. The consequence is that integrity and AML control weaknesses in an agent are a barrier to the SAMA non-objection and an ongoing supervisory exposure for the bank, so agent assessment and AML risk assessment should be evidenced as one chain; confirm the exact article allocation in the primary text.

A bank cannot treat agent due diligence and fit and proper screening as alternative gates; the due diligence article expressly routes back to the fit and proper requirements set out in Article 13. That cross-reference means the qualifying criteria applied under the due diligence article (outreach, efficiency, integrity, IT infrastructure and related factors) are assessed alongside, and constrained by, the Article 13 standard, and the same linkage carries down to sub-agents engaged under exclusive or multiple agent arrangements. Practically, the bank retains overall responsibility for the agency relationship and must be able to show both assessments were completed before seeking SAMA's non-objection for each agent.

Read "Secondary Market" consistently across both real estate finance instruments, because each defines it as trading of the rights of real estate finance entities arising from primary market contracts. The shared definition signals a common parent framework for real estate finance, so an activity characterised as secondary market trading under one instrument should not be re-characterised under the other to escape a licensing or conduct requirement. Before relying on that consistency, confirm the scope clause of each instrument, since identical wording does not guarantee identical application to the entity or transaction in question.

These address two halves of one governance chain: the constitution of the Shariah committee (board formation and member appointment on the nomination and remuneration committee's recommendation, subject to the required prior approval) and the downstream Shariah compliance and audit function that tests adherence to that committee's rulings. A decision about the adequacy of Shariah oversight therefore cannot rest on the existence of a committee alone; the independent compliance and audit arm must also be in place and reporting properly. Note the second node's text is not reproduced here, so the reader should verify the precise oversight obligations and reporting lines in the primary instrument before concluding on compliance.

Treat these as two separate supervisory instructions rather than one obligation chain: a link here does not let you read requirements about real property in-kind registration into fintech membership arrangements, or vice versa. The only evident basis is that both are SAMA circulars issued under its supervisory authority over licensed entities, with no shared defined term or cross-reference visible in the material provided. Practically, scope each circular to its own addressees and subject matter, and verify the primary text of both before relying on any combined reading.

If you are papering or reviewing a consumer finance or lease arrangement, check both: the standard contract fixes the mandatory terms and disclosures owed to the consumer, while the lessor data instruction bears on how customer information arising from that relationship is handled and reported. The connection appears to be the shared finance/leasing regime and the same customer relationship rather than an express cross-reference, so the interaction is inferred. Compliance with the standard contract form does not by itself discharge the data-related duty, but confirm the scope and addressees in the primary text of each instrument.

When deciding whether to restrict an account because identification documents have lapsed, read the freezing provision as the enforcement consequence of the ongoing KYC/CDD duty in the same Rules, not as a standalone penalty. Both sit within the account rules, which require the banking relationship to begin and continue on valid identification, so an expired ID is a CDD-maintenance failure that triggers the prescribed freeze. Keep this distinct from a sanctions or TFS freeze: the legal basis, notification path and unfreezing conditions differ, and misclassifying the action can produce the wrong reporting outcome.

Before opening or maintaining an account for a non-Saudi party, classify the applicant precisely, because these two parts of the same account rules set different eligibility tracks — licensed foreign investment projects (including permitted sub-accounts) versus non-resident persons who generally require prior written approval. The link is internal to one instrument, so the provisions are meant to be read together as a complete gateway rather than as alternatives.
